This isolates whether pooling several profiles helps. 3. Why it is the best next run: profile setting is a structural choice that affects about two-thirds of the remaining search space, so its answer guides most later decisions. Moving the PCA RNA model from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool gave a large gain (0.485 to 0.591 accuracy; F1 0.464 to 0.573). Multiprofile is therefore the most promising direction. That isolates the effect of aggregation and shows whether a learned, attention-based summary across profiles adds value beyond simple averaging. 3. It builds directly on the strongest result with a single-variable change, so it tests a likely improvement while also answering a design question. The answer shapes many later choices, because aggregation appears in most of the remaining multiprofile and multimodal configurations. Testing multimodal fusion or other RNA encoders before settling this would leave a key, widely shared factor unresolved.

The experiment therefore exploits the best-known configuration while answering an open question cleanly. The other untested axis, the scVI encoder, can follow, ideally within whichever fusion setting performs better here.

This tells us whether the image-modality gain still holds on top of the stronger scVI representation, or whether scVI already captures most of the useful signal. 3. Why now: It exploits the best-supported settings for representation, profile setting, aggregation and fusion while changing only one factor relative to two existing runs. Either outcome is informative and directly guides the remaining budget, and it is the most likely candidate for a new best.

1) Evidence: scVI is the strongest RNA encoder so far (about 0.650 to 0.653 accuracy), well ahead of PCA (0.591) and scGPT (0.530). Multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile for PCA (0.591 vs 0.485). 1) Evidence: Only two single-profile baselines exist. RNA (pca_n2000) reaches 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. Image (resnet50) reaches only 0.208 accuracy and 0.172 F1. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only is far stronger than image-only (accuracy 0.485 vs 0.208). Moving RNA (pca_n2000) from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool gave a large gain, raising accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591 and F1 from 0.464 to 0.573. So multiprofile RNA is the most promising direction so far. However, only one aggregation method has been tried, so we do not know whether the gain comes from multiprofile information itself or depends on simple averaging. 2. What this tests: config_003 keeps the current best setup (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000) and changes only avgpool to transformer. This directly measures the effect of the aggregation method. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: it builds on the strongest result while changing a single design choice, so any difference can be attributed to aggregation. Aggregation is used by every multiprofile configuration, including all multimodal ones. Settling this question now therefore guides many later choices before we spend budget on encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT) or multimodal fusion.

It sets a baseline accuracy and F1 for the RNA modality with a standard, low-complexity representation. 3. Why it is the best use of this experiment: Every later comparison can change one factor from this anchor. Examples are swapping the encoder (scVI, scGPT), adding multiple profiles (avgpool, transformer), switching to image-only, or adding image fusion. Each effect can then be measured cleanly against a known reference. Starting with a simple model also avoids assuming that more complex multimodal or multiprofile setups will win, and it uses only one of the 10 experiments.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. The RNA-only, single-profile, PCA baseline (config_001) reached 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1, which says nothing about the other modality. The biggest open question is whether imaging carries more predictive signal than RNA. 2) This experiment runs an image-only single-profile ResNet50 baseline. It keeps the profile setting the same (single-profile, no aggregation) and changes only the modality, giving a direct comparison of RNA versus image. 3) This is the most important unknown to resolve early with 8 experiments left. The result will show whether later budget should go to image encoders, RNA encoders, or multimodal fusion, and it provides a reference for judging whether fusion adds value. Encoder and aggregation variants can then be tested within the stronger modality.

1) RNA-only with pca_n2000 single-profile (0.485 acc, 0.464 F1) clearly beats image-only resnet50 single-profile (0.208 acc). So RNA is the strongest signal so far, but we have only one data point per modality. 2) This experiment keeps the RNA-only pca_n2000 setting fixed and switches from single-profile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). That isolates whether pooling multiple profiles improves accuracy. 3) Profile setting affects every remaining branch (RNA-only, image-only and multimodal), so answering this early tells us where to spend the other 7 runs. Building on the best baseline is efficient exploitation, and testing the most broadly relevant open design choice reduces uncertainty. Comparing RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) and the transformer aggregation are logical next steps after this.

1. Evidence: RNA is clearly the stronger modality (0.485 accuracy for RNA single-profile vs 0.208 for ResNet50 image-only). Moving RNA PCA from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool gave a large gain, from 0.485 to 0.591 accuracy, with F1 rising alongside. Multiprofile RNA with pca_n2000 is the current best direction, but only one aggregation method has been tried. 2. This experiment keeps everything in the best configuration (config_002) fixed and swaps avgpool for transformer aggregation. That isolates whether learned, attention-based pooling across profiles adds more than simple averaging. 3. Aggregation applies to every multiprofile configuration, including future encoder comparisons and multimodal ones, so settling it early narrows the search efficiently. Encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT) can follow with the better aggregator fixed.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile with avgpool (config_002, acc 0.591, F1 0.573). It clearly beats single-profile (0.485) and transformer aggregation (0.519). Image-only resnet50 is weak (0.208), so adding images is unlikely to be the biggest lever yet. All RNA results so far use pca_n2000, so the RNA encoder is the main untested design choice. 2) Test: Keep the winning setup (rna_only, multiprofile, avgpool) and swap only the encoder to scvi_n200. This isolates the encoder effect and shows whether a learned latent space beats PCA in the strongest setting. 3) Why now: It exploits the best direction while resolving a major uncertainty with a one-variable change. The answer will guide which RNA encoder to carry into the remaining scGPT and multimodal-fusion experiments.

1) Evidence: multiprofile avgpool clearly beats single-profile (0.591 vs 0.485 for PCA) and beats transformer aggregation (0.519). Switching the RNA encoder from PCA to scVI under the same avgpool setup gave the largest gain so far (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). So the RNA encoder is a high-impact choice, but the third encoder, scGPT, is still untested. The single image-only run was weak (0.208), so image fusion is a riskier direction. 2) This run keeps the best setup fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder to scGPT. It shows whether scGPT embeddings beat scVI. 3) It cleanly settles the most influential open choice before spending the remaining 3 runs on multimodal fusion, which can then be built on whichever RNA encoder wins.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is scVI with multiprofile avgpool (config_005, accuracy 0.650, F1 0.628). Across RNA-only runs, multiprofile beat singleprofile and avgpool beat transformer. Image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.208 accuracy), so it is uncertain whether adding images to the best RNA setup helps or adds noise. 2. Test: This run keeps the best RNA setup fixed (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds ResNet50 image features through weighted fusion. That isolates the effect of the image modality on top of the strongest configuration. Weighted fusion should let the model down-weight the weak image signal, so it is the safer of the two fusion choices. 3. Value: It exploits the strongest direction while answering an important open question, whether multimodality helps here. The other options look less useful: config_006 tests the transformer, which already underperformed with PCA. The result also tells us whether to spend the last two experiments on fusion or image-encoder variants, such as ViT-L or concat fusion, or to return to RNA-only refinements.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_031 (scVI + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. It beats the scVI RNA-only model (0.650), so adding images helps a little. Within RNA, scVI beat PCA and scGPT, and avgpool beat transformer aggregation. The biggest untested choice is the image encoder: ResNet50 alone was weak (0.208), and ImageNet ViT-L has not been tried at all. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration fixed and swaps only ResNet50 for ViT-L. That isolates whether a stronger image representation adds more to the scVI RNA signal. 3) With 2 experiments left after this one, the image encoder seems the change most likely to raise the best score, more so than switching fusion from weighted to concat. Whichever encoder wins, the remaining runs can test fusion type (concat vs weighted) on top of it.

1) Evidence: multiprofile avgpool clearly beats single-profile (0.59 vs 0.48) and beats transformer aggregation (0.52 with PCA). scVI is the strongest RNA encoder (0.65). Adding images with weighted fusion helps further: 0.678 with ResNet50 and a best of 0.706 with ViT-L (config_037). Fusion type is the one major design choice not yet tested, since every multimodal run used weighted fusion. 2) config_036 keeps the best setup fixed (scVI, ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only weighted to concat. This isolates the effect of fusion. 3) With two experiments left, this is a low-risk extension of the leading configuration that could beat 0.706. It also tells the final experiment which fusion to pair with any remaining test, such as transformer aggregation. Transformer aggregation underperformed earlier, so changing aggregation now looks less promising than testing fusion.

Evidence: the best result so far is scVI + ViT-L + avgpool + concat at 0.715 (F1 0.687). ViT-L beat ResNet50 under weighted fusion (0.706 vs 0.678), and concat edged weighted with ViT-L. PCA and scGPT RNA encoders were clearly weaker, so swapping the RNA encoder or downgrading the image encoder is unlikely to beat 0.715. For example, scVI + ResNet50 + concat (config_030) would probably land near 0.69. The main untested choice in the top branch is aggregation. Transformer aggregation was tested only once, with weak PCA features in an RNA-only model, where it underperformed avgpool. That single result says little about richer scVI + ViT-L multimodal inputs. This run tests whether transformer aggregation beats avgpool when everything else matches the best configuration. Since this is the last experiment and only the best accuracy counts, it is the remaining option with a realistic chance of exceeding 0.715.

1) There is no history yet, so every design choice is uncertain: modality, encoders, single vs. multiprofile, aggregation and fusion. 2) This config is a middle-of-the-road anchor: multimodal, multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation, simple concat fusion, a compact scvi_n200 RNA encoder and a standard resnet50 image encoder. It tests whether a reasonably capable but not overly complex model performs well. It also does not assume the most complex options (transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, foundation-model encoders) are better. 3) Every major design choice has a one-change neighbor in the pool, so the next experiments can isolate each effect: RNA-only (config_005), image-only (config_011), single profile (config_028), transformer aggregation (config_032), weighted fusion (config_031), and encoder swaps (config_036, config_042). Starting here gives the most informative reference point for a 10-experiment budget.

1. Evidence: the only result so far is config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.632 validation accuracy and 0.607 F1. One run cannot tell us which parts drive that score, and the biggest open question is whether the image branch adds value. 2. Test: config_005 is the exact RNA-only counterpart. It keeps scVI, multiprofile and avgpool fixed and changes only one thing, removing the image modality. This directly measures what ResNet50 images contribute. 3. Why now: whether modality matters decides how the remaining 8 runs should be spent. If RNA-only matches or beats multimodal, effort should go to RNA encoders and aggregation. If it clearly drops, image encoder and fusion choices are worth exploring. This simple, isolated comparison cuts more uncertainty than changing several factors at once.

1. Evidence: The RNA-only scVI multiprofile avgpool model (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1) beat its multimodal counterpart with ResNet50 concat fusion (0.632, 0.607). This suggests the RNA representation is the main driver, and adding images by simple concat did not help. However, we have tested only one RNA encoder, so its effect is still unknown. 2. Test: config_008 keeps everything fixed (rna_only, multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps scVI for scGPT. This isolates the effect of the RNA encoder. 3. Why now: The encoder is likely a high-impact choice. Settling it early will guide both the RNA-only and the multimodal searches in the remaining 6 experiments. Aggregation (transformer) and fusion (weighted) are better tested once the strongest RNA encoder is known.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only scVI with multiprofile avgpool (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). Swapping in scGPT under the same setup dropped accuracy sharply to 0.530. Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion to scVI did not help (0.632). This suggests the RNA encoder is a major driver of performance. However, pca_n2000, the third encoder option, is still untested. 2. Test: config_002 keeps the setup fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and only changes the encoder to pca_n2000. This completes a clean three-way encoder comparison. 3. Why now: The encoder choice shows the largest effect seen so far. Knowing whether PCA matches or beats scVI decides which encoder to carry into later experiments on aggregation (transformer), fusion (weighted) and image encoders. It also has a real chance of beating the current best. Settling it first makes the remaining 6 experiments more efficient.

1. Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder so far (0.650 acc versus 0.591 for PCA and 0.530 for scGPT, all rna_only, multiprofile, avgpool). Adding resnet50 with concat fusion did not help (0.632). Every run so far has used avgpool, so the effect of aggregation is completely unknown. 2. Test: switching only avgpool to transformer on the best configuration (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200) isolates the aggregation effect. 3. Why now: this exploits the strongest encoder while resolving a major open design choice. The result will show whether later experiments, including multimodal ones, should use transformer aggregation, which makes it a high-value use of the remaining budget.

1. Evidence: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (about 0.65, versus 0.59 for PCA and 0.53 for scGPT). Transformer and avgpool aggregation are nearly tied (0.653 vs 0.650), so aggregation looks like a minor factor. Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion (config_030) gave 0.632, below RNA-only (0.650), possibly because concat cannot down-weight a noisier image signal. 2. Test: config_031 keeps everything in config_030 the same except swapping concat for weighted fusion. This isolates whether the fusion method, rather than the image modality itself, explains the multimodal shortfall. 3. Why now: weighted fusion is the most plausible way for a multimodal model to beat the RNA-only best, and changing only fusion gives a clean answer. If it helps, the remaining 3 runs can try ViT-L or transformer aggregation under weighted fusion. If it does not, the budget can move to profile setting (e.g., singleprofile scVI) or refining RNA-only.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_031 (scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. Weighted fusion clearly beat concat (0.632), and scVI is the strongest RNA encoder tested. Transformer aggregation gave only a negligible gain in the RNA-only setting (0.653 vs 0.650). The image encoder is the largest remaining uncertainty, because every multimodal run so far has used ResNet50. 2. Test: config_037 keeps everything from config_031 and swaps only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates whether a stronger image representation adds value to the best fusion setup. 3. Why now: the image encoder could have a large effect, while the aggregation choice looks small. Settling the encoder first lets the remaining 3 experiments build on the better one, for example by adding transformer aggregation afterward.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Two choices look strong. Weighted fusion beat concat by about 4.6 points with ResNet50, and ViT-L beat ResNet50 by about 2.9 points under weighted fusion. Aggregation is the main open question. Transformer was only marginally better than avgpool in the RNA-only comparison (0.653 vs 0.650), which is too small to trust, and it has never been tested with multimodal fusion. 2. Test: config_039 keeps everything from config_037 and changes only the aggregation to transformer. This isolates whether learned aggregation across profiles adds value when combined with the stronger image encoder. 3. Why now: With two experiments left, a one-variable change to the best configuration is the most direct way to raise the best accuracy. It is also the remaining unresolved choice most likely to help. Its result will guide the final experiment, for example testing single-profile against multi-profile.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_039 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, acc 0.725, F1 0.685). Across the history, scVI beats PCA and scGPT, ViT-L beats ResNet50, and transformer aggregation beats avgpool. Weighted fusion beat concat once, with ResNet50 and avgpool (0.678 vs 0.632). That fusion result is a single comparison and has not been checked in the strongest backbone setting. 2) Test: config_038 changes only the fusion method relative to the current best. This shows whether weighted fusion's advantage holds with ViT-L features and transformer aggregation, or whether concat catches up or does better there. 3) Why now: it is a controlled comparison next to the best configuration, so it can either confirm config_039 or find a better one. The other options look weaker. PCA, scGPT and ResNet50 variants have consistently underperformed. Single-profile models lose the multiprofile aggregation that has helped so far. This keeps the final experiment free for whatever this result suggests.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_039 at 0.725 accuracy (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion). Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L raised multimodal accuracy by about 3 points. That suggests the image representation drives much of the gain. Transformer aggregation and weighted fusion each helped slightly. No image-only model has been tested, so it is unknown how much the RNA branch actually adds. 2) This tests image-only ViT-L with transformer aggregation on multiple profiles, which isolates the image modality under the best aggregation setting found so far. 3) This is the last experiment, so I want the run with the best chance of beating 0.725. The other options look less promising: PCA, scGPT and ResNet50 all underperformed scVI or ViT-L, and avgpool or concat variants of config_039 were slightly worse. Removing a possibly noisy RNA branch is the main untested change that could plausibly beat the current best. If it does not, the run still shows how much the RNA branch contributes.

1. Evidence: no experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about which modality, RNA or image encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion works best. 2. Test: config_036 is a central anchor. It is multimodal, multiprofile with avgpool aggregation and concat fusion, using scvi_n200 (a mid-range RNA encoder) and imagenet_vit_l. Every major design axis is active, so each later experiment can change one factor against this anchor. Planned one-factor comparisons: rna_only via config_005, image_only via config_014, singleprofile via config_034, transformer aggregation via config_038, weighted fusion via config_037, and the PCA or scGPT encoder swaps. 3. Why now: with only 10 experiments, an anchor that is plausibly strong and supports clean ablations reduces uncertainty fastest on the most important choices. It also keeps a realistic chance of a high-accuracy result early. A minimal baseline such as config_001 would offer fewer single-factor comparisons that lead toward the best configuration.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: We have only one result. The multimodal, multiprofile config_036 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) reached 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. We do not yet know whether the image branch adds anything beyond RNA. 2. What this tests: config_005 is the matching RNA-only model, with the same scvi_n200 encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation. Only the image modality and its fusion step are removed, so the comparison isolates the image branch's contribution. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: Most of the remaining search space is multimodal. Knowing early whether adding the image branch improves on RNA alone tells us whether to spend the remaining 8 experiments refining fusion, aggregation and encoders within multimodal configurations, or to focus on cheaper unimodal ones.

1. Evidence: with scvi_n200, multiprofile and avgpool held fixed, adding imagenet_vit_l features through concat fusion raised validation accuracy from 0.650 (RNA only) to 0.715, and F1 rose in step. We still don't know whether that gain comes from combining the two modalities or simply from the image features being stronger on their own. 2. Test: config_014 runs the image-only model with imagenet_vit_l under the same multiprofile avgpool setting. Comparing it with config_036 isolates what fusion adds over images alone, and comparing it with config_005 shows how strong each modality is by itself. 3. Why now: this single, controlled change decides where the remaining 7 experiments should go. If image-only matches or beats the multimodal model, the search should shift toward image encoders and image aggregation. If it falls clearly short, fusion is adding value and later runs can exploit fusion type, aggregation and RNA encoder choices with more confidence.

1) Evidence: multimodal scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l with avgpool and concat fusion scored best (0.715 acc, 0.687 F1). That beats RNA-only (0.650), and image-only is weak (0.332). So fusion adds signal on top of RNA, and multimodal is the direction to exploit. Aggregation is still untested and could matter a lot in the multiprofile setting. 2) This experiment changes one factor from the best config, aggregation from avgpool to transformer, keeping encoders, profile setting and fusion fixed. It tests whether learned attention over profiles improves on mean pooling. 3) Aggregation is the main untested axis on the current best backbone. A single-variable change gives a clean comparison and has a realistic chance of a new best. Fusion type (weighted) and RNA encoder (scgpt, pca) can be tested in later experiments.

1. Evidence: Multimodal multiprofile models (about 0.715–0.721) clearly beat RNA-only (0.650) and image-only (0.332). This suggests RNA carries most of the signal, with images adding a complementary gain. Transformer and avgpool aggregation differ by only about 0.006, and F1 points the other way, so aggregation looks like a minor factor. The main uncertainty is that only one RNA encoder (scvi_n200) has been tested, even though RNA is the dominant modality. 2. Test: Swap scvi_n200 for scgpt in the current best setup (config_038: multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat), changing nothing else. This isolates whether a foundation-model RNA representation improves the fused model. 3. Rationale: The RNA encoder probably has more potential impact than fusion type or the choice between the two aggregation methods. Resolving it early tells the remaining 5 experiments which RNA backbone to build on, for example when testing weighted fusion later.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA carries most of the signal. RNA-only scVI scored 0.650, image-only ViT-L scored 0.332, and multimodal scVI+ViT-L scored about 0.715-0.721. The RNA encoder matters a lot, since scGPT dropped accuracy to 0.507. Aggregation made only a small difference (transformer 0.721 vs avgpool 0.715, with avgpool slightly higher on F1). Fusion strategy has never been tested; every multimodal run so far used concat. 2. What this tests: config_039 keeps the current best setup (config_038: scVI, ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer) and changes only the fusion from concat to weighted. This isolates the fusion effect. Weighted fusion may also suit this setting, because it could learn to down-weight the much weaker image modality. 3. Why it is the best next step: it is a one-variable extension of the best configuration, so it has a good chance of beating it. It also answers a question the search has not touched. Comparisons of the PCA RNA encoder and the ResNet50 image encoder can follow in the remaining 3 experiments.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: the RNA encoder is the most influential choice tested so far. Replacing scvi_n200 with scgpt dropped accuracy from about 0.72 to 0.51. RNA-only scvi reached 0.65, while ViT-L image-only reached only 0.33, so RNA carries most of the signal. Aggregation and fusion changes gave only small gains (0.715 to 0.721 to 0.725), which may be noise. The current best is config_039 (scvi_n200, ViT-L, transformer, weighted), but pca_n2000 has never been tested. 2. What this tests: config_027 keeps everything from config_039 and swaps only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. This isolates whether a higher-dimensional PCA representation beats scvi_n200 in the best-performing setup. 3. Why it is the best next use of the budget: RNA representation is the factor most likely to produce a large accuracy gain. Testing it now leaves two experiments to exploit whichever encoder wins, for example by trying the resnet50 image encoder next.

1) Evidence: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder. It beat PCA (0.586) and scGPT (0.507) in otherwise similar setups. Within scVI multimodal runs, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion gave small, mutually consistent gains, and config_039 is best at 0.725. All multimodal runs so far used imagenet_vit_l, which was weak on its own (0.332 image-only), so the image encoder is the largest untested design choice. 2) This run keeps the best configuration fixed (scVI, multiprofile, transformer, weighted) and swaps only the image encoder to resnet50. That isolates whether a different image representation adds more complementary signal to RNA. 3) The remaining aggregation and fusion options are likely to change accuracy only slightly. Changing the image encoder has the best chance of a meaningful improvement and resolves the main open uncertainty. That leaves two runs to exploit the result, for example testing avgpool or concat variants with the winning encoder.

1) Evidence: scVI is clearly the best RNA encoder (about 0.71-0.72, versus 0.59 for PCA and 0.51 for scGPT). The best result so far is config_039 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer, weighted) at 0.725. Changing aggregation, fusion or image encoder has shifted accuracy by only about 0.005-0.01, so those choices look nearly saturated. Every run so far has used the multiprofile setting, so profile setting is the one major design choice with no evidence at all. 2) This run keeps the best components (scVI, ViT-L, weighted fusion) and switches to singleprofile, where aggregation is None. It isolates whether multiprofile aggregation actually helps, or whether a simpler single-profile model matches or beats it. 3) Another small aggregation or fusion tweak would most likely move accuracy by less than 0.01. Resolving the profile-setting question is the most informative use of the budget. If singleprofile does well, the last run can exploit it (for example with config_034). If not, the last run can go back to refining the multiprofile setting (for example with config_037).

1) Evidence: The strongest setup is multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 RNA encoder with imagenet_vit_l images. Within it, transformer+weighted (config_039, 0.725) edges out transformer+concat (0.721) and avgpool+concat (0.715). The RNA encoder matters most, with scvi far ahead of pca and scgpt. Image encoder, aggregation and fusion give only small differences that may be noise. 2) Test: config_037 (avgpool + weighted) is the one untested cell in the aggregation-by-fusion grid for the best backbone. It shows whether the small weighted-fusion gain carries over to avgpool, or whether avgpool's simpler pooling can match or beat the transformer. 3) Why this: As the final run, the goal is the best chance of exceeding 0.725 by staying close to the top region. It changes only one design choice from config_039 and finishes the grid. The main alternative, config_032 (resnet50 + concat), is less promising because resnet50 trailed vit_l under weighted fusion and concat trailed weighted with vit_l.

1) There is no prior evidence yet. Nothing is known about how modality, RNA or image encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion affect validation accuracy. 2) This experiment sets a simple, low-variance reference point: RNA-only, single profile, PCA with 2000 components, and no aggregation or fusion. It measures how much signal the basic RNA representation carries on its own. 3) With 9 experiments left, a clean anchor is the most useful first step. Each later experiment can change one factor against it: encoder (scVI or scGPT), profile setting (multiprofile with avgpool or transformer), modality (image-only or multimodal) and fusion. Starting with a complex multimodal configuration would confound several design choices at once, and it would not be clear whether added complexity helps.

1) Evidence: we have one result, a single-profile RNA-only PCA baseline at 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. We know nothing yet about the image modality, which is the largest open design choice and sets the ceiling for any multimodal model. 2) This experiment runs the matched single-profile image-only ResNet50 baseline (config_010). It varies only the modality while profile setting, aggregation and fusion stay fixed, so it shows whether images carry more, less or similar signal than RNA. 3) With 8 experiments left, establishing both unimodal baselines early tells us which modality to invest in and whether multimodal fusion is worth exploring. This is more useful than refining RNA encoders or aggregation around a single data point.

1. Evidence: RNA-only (pca_n2000, singleprofile) reached 0.485 accuracy, far above image-only resnet50 (0.208), so RNA is the stronger modality. Whether multiprofile input helps is still completely unknown. 2. Test: this run keeps the RNA encoder fixed and switches from singleprofile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation, so any change is attributable to the profile setting alone. 3. Why now: profile setting is a high-impact choice that applies to every later RNA and multimodal configuration. Settling it on the strongest single-modality baseline, with the simplest aggregation, tells us where to spend the remaining 7 experiments (aggregation type, RNA encoder, fusion) before adding image features.

1) Evidence: RNA is far stronger than image (0.485 vs 0.208 for single-profile), and moving RNA PCA from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool gave a large gain (0.485 to 0.591 accuracy, with F1 rising alongside). Aggregation is now the most promising lever, but only the simplest method, avgpool, has been tried. 2) This experiment keeps the current best setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, pca_n2000) and changes only avgpool to transformer. That isolates whether learned attention over profiles improves on mean pooling. 3) Multiprofile aggregation gave the largest gain so far, so finding the better aggregator is a high-value, low-confound step. The result will set the aggregation choice for later encoder comparisons (scVI, scGPT) and any multimodal tests in the remaining budget.

1. Evidence: RNA carries most of the signal. RNA-only PCA reached 0.485 in the single-profile setting, while ResNet50 image-only reached only 0.208. Multiprofile with avgpool is the best result so far (0.591 accuracy, 0.573 F1). That beats both single-profile (0.485) and transformer aggregation (0.519), and F1 agrees. The RNA encoder has only been tested with PCA, so it is the largest untested factor on the strongest axis. 2. Test: keep the winning multiprofile avgpool setup and swap PCA for scGPT embeddings. Only the encoder changes, so the result isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model representation beats PCA. 3. Why now: this is a one-factor extension of the current best, so it has a real chance of setting a new best while resolving a key design choice. If scGPT does not help, scVI (config_005) can be tested next under the same setup. Multimodal fusion is better tested after the best RNA encoder is known, given how weak the image signal has been so far.

1) Evidence: Multiprofile avgpool with PCA RNA is the clear leader (0.591 accuracy, 0.573 F1). It beats single-profile PCA (0.485), transformer aggregation (0.519) and the scGPT encoder (0.530). Image-only ResNet50 is weak (0.208), but it was tested only single-profile, so it is unknown whether image adds complementary signal on top of RNA. 2) This experiment keeps the best RNA setup fixed (PCA, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds ResNet50 image features with weighted fusion. That isolates one question: does adding the image modality help? Weighted fusion is chosen over concat because it can down-weight a weak modality, so image noise is less likely to swamp the strong RNA signal. 3) Multimodal fusion is the largest untested design dimension and could raise the best score. The remaining scVI encoder question (config_005) is still available for a later slot. If weighted fusion helps, later experiments can test concat fusion or ViT-L image features. If it hurts, we can return to tuning the RNA encoder.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA, ResNet50 image, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.639 accuracy and 0.620 F1. That beats the best RNA-only model (config_002, 0.591), so adding images helps even though ResNet50 alone was weak (0.208). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation, and PCA beat scGPT, in the RNA-only multiprofile setting. The image encoder is the least explored choice, since ImageNet ViT-L has not been tested at all. 2. Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (about 0.71-0.725, versus 0.60 for pca_n2000 and 0.51 for scgpt). Transformer aggregation is slightly better than avgpool. 1) Evidence: The scVI-200 RNA encoder clearly beats PCA and scGPT. 1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (about 0.72 versus 0.60 for pca_n2000 and 0.51 for scgpt). Multiprofile with transformer aggregation beats both avgpool and singleprofile. 1) Evidence: scVI RNA with multiprofile multimodal input is clearly the strongest family. config_017 (ViT-L, transformer, weighted) is best at 0.725. 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet, so every design choice is uncertain. 1. Evidence: we have only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile setup with scVI, ResNet50, avgpool and weighted fusion (config_016) reached 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1 at 5.9 GPU hours. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Within multiprofile multimodal models, scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder. 1) Evidence: scVI RNA with the ViT-L image encoder is clearly the strongest combination so far. config_033 (transformer, weighted) leads at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1, and config_027 (transformer, concat) is close behind at 0.721. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Only one result exists. 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so I am relying on priors. In multimodal cellular profiling, combining RNA and image features and aggregating across multiple profiles usually beats single-modality or single-profile setups. 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_003 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + resnet50, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) reached 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1 for 6.22 GPU hours. 1. Evidence: Only two experiments are done, and both used scVI RNA, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion. Test: Keep the current best setup (ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer, weighted fusion) and swap scVI for scGPT. 1) Evidence: the RNA encoder is the factor with the largest observed effect so far. With the same vit_l, transformer and weighted backbone, scvi_n200 reached 0.725 accuracy while scgpt reached only 0.520. The image encoder mattered much less: vit_l was slightly better than resnet50 on accuracy (0.725 vs 0.713) and was cheaper (3.6 vs 6.2 GPU h). pca_n2000 is the only RNA encoder not yet tested. 2) Test: config_002 keeps the best configuration (config_018) fixed and swaps scvi_n200 for pca_n2000. 1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder so far (0.713–0.725 accuracy, versus 0.586 for pca_n2000 and 0.520 for scgpt). 1) Evidence: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, at 0.713–0.725 versus 0.586 for PCA and 0.520 for scGPT. 1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder (0.71-0.725 vs 0.52 for scgpt and 0.59 for pca). 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_018 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted fusion, 0.725 accuracy, 3.6 GPU h). 1. Evidence: The strongest region is clear. scVI beats pca_n2000 by about 0.14 and scGPT by about 0.20. Transformer aggregation beats avgpool by about 0.019. Multiprofile beats singleprofile by about 0.19, and multimodal beats RNA-only by about 0.07. Within this region, the best result is config_018 (ViT-L, weighted, 0.725). Why it is the best use of the slot: every other remaining option drops at least one component that clearly helped. 1) Evidence: the strongest region is clear. It is multimodal, multiprofile, with an scVI-n200 RNA encoder and an ImageNet ViT-L image encoder. The best run is config_018 (transformer, weighted) at 0.725, followed by config_042 (concat) at 0.721 and config_016 (avgpool) at 0.706. Swapping in scGPT or PCA for RNA dropped accuracy sharply (0.52–0.59). 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so every design choice is uncertain. These choices are modality, single vs. multiple profiles, RNA and image encoder, aggregation and fusion. Prior expectation is that combining both modalities and aggregating multiple profiles should give the strongest signal, but this is unconfirmed here. 2. What it tests: config_001 is a multimodal, multiprofile setup built from the cheaper components: scVI-200 RNA embeddings, a ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation and simple concat fusion. Its accuracy will show whether the multimodal + multiprofile direction is promising before paying for more expensive parts. 3. Why now: It is a mid-cost anchor that later experiments can compare against by changing one factor at a time. 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile config_001 (scVI-200 RNA, ResNet50 images, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1 at 7.27 GPU hours. That gives a reasonable baseline in what is probably the strongest region of the space, but every design axis is still untested. 2) Test: config_049 changes exactly one factor, swapping avgpool for transformer aggregation. Any difference can therefore be attributed to how the multiple profiles are combined. A learned, attention-based aggregator could plausibly beat mean pooling, while the RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion choices stay fixed. 3) Why now: aggregation is likely a high-impact choice that affects many of the remaining multiprofile configurations, so settling it early guides much of the remaining 8-experiment budget. Swapping in the ViT-L image encoder instead would likely cost more. Evidence: with everything else held fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, concat), transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool on both accuracy (0.688 vs 0.632) and F1 (0.659 vs 0.607). It was also cheaper (5.16 vs 7.27 GPU h), so transformer aggregation is the current anchor. The image encoder is still untested and is a high-impact choice, since ViT-L representations are much richer than ResNet50. This experiment keeps the best configuration (config_049) and changes only the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l. That cleanly measures the encoder's effect and exploits the strongest known direction. It is the best use of a limited budget because the encoder choice likely moves accuracy more than fusion type, and the answer shapes most of the remaining search. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_049, roughly 1.3-1.8x, because ViT-L features are larger, though transformer aggregation should keep it under about 8 GPU h. If the gain is small, later experiments can return to cheaper ResNet50 variants such as weighted fusion or scGPT.

1) Evidence: with the scVI RNA encoder and concat fusion fixed, transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632 with ResNet50). Swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L under transformer aggregation raised accuracy to 0.721 (F1 0.681), the current best (config_018). Fusion has never been varied: every run used concat. The RNA encoder alternatives (PCA, scGPT) are also untested. 2) Test: config_007 matches the best configuration except for weighted fusion instead of concat. This one-factor change isolates the effect of fusion on top of the strongest setup, and F1 can confirm whether any gain is real. 3) Why now: it directly exploits the best configuration found so far while resolving an unexplored design choice that affects every future multimodal candidate. Weighted fusion only adds learned modality weights to the same encoders, so I expect it to cost about the same as config_018 (roughly 4.5-5.5 GPU hours). That is cheaper than the avgpool baseline run and no more expensive than switching to a heavier encoder such as scGPT, which can be tested next on whichever fusion wins.

1. Evidence: Every run so far uses the scvi_n200 RNA encoder. Three image/aggregation/fusion choices have clear evidence. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 5.6 points (0.688 vs 0.632). ViT-L beat ResNet50 by about 3.3 points (0.721 vs 0.688). Weighted fusion edged out concat (0.725 vs 0.721, with F1 also slightly higher), though that gap is small. The biggest untested axis is the RNA encoder. 2. Test: config_024 keeps the best-known setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, weighted fusion) and swaps in scGPT. Why now: this extends the strongest direction while reducing uncertainty on the main open design choice. If scGPT helps, the remaining budget can refine around it. 1) Evidence: transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632 with resnet50). imagenet_vit_l beats resnet50 (0.721 vs 0.688). Weighted fusion is slightly ahead of concat (0.725 vs 0.721), a small difference. Swapping the RNA encoder to scgpt in the best setup collapsed accuracy to 0.520, so the RNA encoder is a high-impact choice. pca_n2000 is the only RNA encoder not yet tested. 2) config_005 keeps the best setup (multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) and changes only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. This shows whether scvi_n200 is truly the best RNA representation or whether a higher-dimensional PCA input does better. 3) It is the factor with the largest remaining uncertainty and a plausible chance of a new best result, while staying in the strongest region of the search space. 1) Evidence: every run so far has used multiprofile. The best result is config_007 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, acc 0.725, F1 0.685). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 0.06, ViT-L beat ResNet50, and weighted fusion was slightly ahead of concat. scVI is clearly the best RNA encoder, well ahead of PCA (0.586) and scGPT (0.520). 2) Untested choice: whether to aggregate across multiple profiles at all. This run keeps the strongest components (scVI, ViT-L, weighted fusion) and switches to singleprofile, which directly tests that axis. avgpool variants such as config_012 are unlikely to win given the earlier aggregation gap. 3) Why now: single-profile models skip the costly aggregation step, so this should be the cheapest multimodal run yet, likely below the roughly 3.6 to 4.7 GPU hours of earlier ViT-L runs. If it matches or beats config_007, the last runs can focus on cheaper single-profile variants. If it falls short, it confirms multiprofile with transformer as the backbone, and I would use the final runs to test image-only and RNA-only references (configs 029 and 040).

Evidence: the best result so far is config_007 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725 accuracy, 0.685 F1). Within this neighbourhood, scVI clearly beats scGPT and PCA, ViT-L beats ResNet50, and weighted fusion edges concat by a small margin. The weakest-tested choice in the top region is aggregation. Transformer beat avgpool only once, with ResNet50 and concat fusion (0.688 vs 0.632), and avgpool was never tried with ViT-L features. This experiment keeps the best configuration and swaps transformer for avgpool. It checks whether that earlier gap holds with the stronger image encoder, since richer ViT-L embeddings could make simple pooling competitive or better. It is the most direct exploit-plus-uncertainty test left, and the other neighbours (ResNet50, PCA, scGPT, single-profile) already have strong negative evidence. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_007 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1). That shows the RNA branch strongly shapes results, but we still do not know whether a ViT-L image-only model is competitive. 2) This experiment tests image-only ViT-L with multiprofile transformer aggregation, the strongest image-side setup. 1) Evidence: the best result is config_007 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. 1. Evidence: no experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence and uncertainty covers every design axis. Priors from multimodal cell profiling suggest that combining RNA and image signals, and aggregating several profiles per sample, usually gives the highest accuracy. 2. What this tests: it sets a strong anchor for the likely best region of the search space, a multimodal multiprofile model. It uses a compact, well-regularized RNA embedding (scVI, 200 dimensions), a strong image encoder (ImageNet ViT-L), weighted fusion and simple average pooling. Later runs can change one factor at a time against this anchor: transformer versus avgpool aggregation, scGPT or PCA versus scVI, ResNet50 versus ViT-L, single versus multiple profiles, and unimodal ablations. 3. Why it is the best use of this run: starting with a likely high performer protects the final best-accuracy objective while still setting up informative comparisons. 1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_050 at 0.725 accuracy (scVI-n200 RNA, ViT-L images, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion). Concat fusion on the same backbone was nearly as good at 0.721. scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, ahead of PCA (0.586) and scGPT (0.520). Multiprofile beats singleprofile, and multimodal beats RNA-only. Every scVI multimodal multiprofile transformer variant has already been tested. The only remaining scVI multimodal multiprofile options use avgpool aggregation. 2. This experiment tests whether concat fusion does better than weighted fusion under avgpool with the stronger ViT-L encoder. Weighted avgpool with ViT-L (config_001) scored 0.706. Concat and weighted were close under the transformer, so concat may differ under avgpool, which would show a fusion-by-aggregation interaction. 3. On the last experiment, the goal is the best chance of matching or beating 0.725. This configuration keeps the best-supported components: scVI, ViT-L, multimodal and multiprofile. The alternatives look weaker: ResNet50 avgpool variants, PCA or scGPT combinations, and unimodal models. Expected cost is moderate, roughly 4.5-5 GPU hours, similar to config_001 and config_037. A gain over 0.725 is uncertain, since avgpool has so far trailed the transformer.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet. The main open question is whether combining both modalities and aggregating over multiple profiles beats simpler setups. Priors for multimodal cellular profiling suggest that both help, but nothing has been measured here. 2. What this tests: config_038 is a multimodal, multiprofile anchor that uses the simplest and cheapest component at each choice. It pairs a compact scVI-200 RNA embedding with a ResNet50 image encoder, using avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. Its result gives a reference point for the likely high-performing region. Later runs can then change one factor at a time: transformer vs avgpool, weighted vs concat, ViT-L vs ResNet50, scGPT vs scVI, or dropping a modality or multiprofile to measure how much each contributes. 3. Why it is the best use of experiment 1: It starts directly in the region most likely to contain the best configuration, rather than spending budget on probably weaker unimodal or single-profile baselines. It does so at moderate cost. Expected relative cost is medium: multiprofile aggregation and two modalities add time, but the small representations, avgpool and concat keep it much cheaper than ViT-L, scGPT or transformer-based variants.

1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_038 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 RNA, ResNet50 image, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1 at 7.27 GPU hours. That gives a reasonable baseline but says nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2. Test: config_024 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to a learned transformer, and keeps everything else fixed. Any change in accuracy can therefore be attributed to aggregation. A transformer can learn which profiles are informative instead of weighting them all equally, so this choice could plausibly have a large effect in a multiprofile setup. 3. Why now: this is one of the most important unresolved choices, and the answer guides the rest of the search. If the transformer helps, later runs can build on it, for example with ViT-L or weighted fusion. If it doesn't, we can stay with cheaper avgpool. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_038, perhaps about 1.2–1.5x (roughly 9–11 GPU hours), because of the extra attention layers. It should still be cheaper than switching to the ViT-L image encoder, so it is a well-controlled, informative step at reasonable cost.

Evidence: the only two runs share scvi_n200, resnet50 and concat fusion, and differ only in aggregation. Transformer aggregation reached 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1, against 0.632 and 0.607 for avgpool. That is a clear gain from one comparison, and transformer was also cheaper here (5.16 vs 7.27 GPU hours), so it is the anchor to build on. Still untested are the image encoder, the RNA encoder and the fusion method. What this tests: config_025 keeps the best setup and swaps only resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l. This isolates whether a stronger pretrained image backbone improves accuracy. Image representation quality is likely one of the larger levers in multimodal cell profiling, probably larger than concat vs weighted fusion. Why now: changing one factor keeps the result interpretable. If ViT-L helps, it sets the image encoder for the remaining runs, and fusion and RNA encoder can then be checked cheaply on top. If it does not help, we stay with resnet50 and save compute later. Expected cost: moderately higher than config_024, perhaps about 6-9 GPU hours, because ViT-L features are larger. This is justified because the image encoder could plausibly give the largest accuracy gain.

Evidence: across three multimodal multiprofile runs, transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 5.6 points (0.688 vs 0.632 with resnet50). Swapping resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l added about 3.3 more points, giving the current best, config_025 at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Fusion is the one design choice not yet tested at all, since every run so far used concat. This experiment keeps the best setup fixed (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer) and changes only fusion to weighted. That isolates whether learned modality weighting improves on concatenation. It is a direct one-factor extension of the strongest configuration, so it both exploits the best region and settles a design choice that affects every later multimodal candidate. Once fusion is settled, the RNA encoder (scgpt or pca) can be tested next with the better fusion. Expected cost is similar to config_025, roughly 4.5–5.5 GPU hours, because weighted fusion adds little over concat. That is cheaper than the avgpool runs measured so far.

Evidence: across four multiprofile multimodal runs, transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 5.6 points (config_024 vs config_038, both scVI+ResNet50+concat). ViT-L beat ResNet50 by about 3.3 points (config_025 vs config_024). Weighted fusion edged out concat by about 0.4 points (config_035 vs config_025), with a matching F1 gain, though that gap is small. The RNA encoder is the main design choice still untested: every run so far used scvi_n200. This experiment keeps the best-known setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, weighted fusion) and swaps scVI for the scGPT foundation-model embeddings. It isolates the RNA encoder effect, which is the most plausible remaining source of a sizeable gain. It is the best use of the next slot because it exploits the established best direction while closing the largest gap in our knowledge. Whatever the result, it tells us which RNA encoder to carry through the remaining four experiments; PCA can be checked later if scGPT does not help. Expected cost is moderate, similar to the other transformer ViT-L runs (about 4–5 GPU hours), possibly slightly more because scGPT embeddings are larger.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_035 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted fusion), with 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632 with resnet50). ViT-L beat resnet50 (0.721 vs 0.688). Weighted fusion was slightly better than concat, but the gap is too small to rely on. Swapping in scGPT as the RNA encoder caused a large drop (0.520). The main open question is the RNA encoder: pca_n2000 has never been tested. 2) This experiment keeps the strongest image encoder, aggregation and fusion settings and swaps in pca_n2000. It directly tests whether a higher-dimensional PCA RNA representation can beat scVI within the best architecture. 3) This is the most informative remaining design choice that could still raise the best accuracy, and it builds on strong existing evidence. Expected cost is moderate, about 4 to 5 GPU hours. That is similar to config_025 and config_035, perhaps slightly more because of the 2000-dimensional RNA input, and well below the avgpool/resnet50 run (7.27 h).

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_035 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted fusion, 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1), with config_025 (concat fusion) close behind. Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632 with ResNet50). ViT-L beats ResNet50. Weighted and concat fusion are roughly equal. The RNA encoder matters a great deal: swapping scVI for scGPT (0.520) or PCA (0.586) causes large drops. The most important open question is whether the RNA branch adds value at all, or whether the image pathway (ViT-L + transformer) is doing most of the work. Weak RNA encoders appear to actively harm the model. 2) This experiment: image-only multiprofile ViT-L with transformer aggregation isolates the strongest image pathway. If it matches or exceeds about 0.72, multimodal fusion is not essential, and the remaining budget should shift to image-centric variants. If it falls clearly below, scVI-based fusion is confirmed as the main driver, and the last runs can refine around config_035. 3) Why now: the remaining near-best multimodal variants mostly swap in components already shown to be inferior (avgpool in config_029, ResNet50 in config_042), so they are unlikely to beat 0.725. This run resolves the largest remaining design uncertainty (modality contribution) and has a plausible chance of being competitive. Expected cost is low to moderate, likely below the roughly 3.6–4.7 GPU hours of the multimodal ViT-L transformer runs, because there is no RNA encoder or fusion.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_035 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted fusion, 0.725 accuracy). Each single-factor change from it has been worse. Swapping the RNA encoder to scGPT gave 0.520 and to PCA gave 0.586. Switching the image encoder to ResNet50 (in the concat setting) cost about 0.03. Using avgpool instead of transformer aggregation cost about 0.056. Image-only performance is very poor (0.260), and weighted fusion edging out concat hints that the model may be down-weighting the image branch. 2) What this tests: the remaining single-swap neighbours of the best config look unlikely to beat it. ResNet50 + weighted (config_042) would be expected near 0.69, and ViT-L + avgpool (config_029) near 0.67. The largest open question is therefore how much the image modality actually contributes. config_032 keeps the winning scVI encoder and transformer aggregation but drops the image branch. If it matches or beats 0.725, the last run should focus on RNA-centric variants. If it falls clearly below, image fusion is confirmed as useful and the final run can refine the multimodal configuration. 3) Why now and cost: it resolves a key design question that no other experiment addresses and has some chance of matching the best result. Without an image encoder it should be among the cheapest runs, likely about 1–2 GPU hours, similar to the 1.44 h image-only run and well below the 3.6–7.3 h multimodal runs.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_035 (multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Within this space the evidence is fairly consistent: scVI beats PCA and scGPT, ViT-L beats ResNet50, transformer aggregation beats avgpool (+0.056 with ResNet50), and weighted fusion is slightly better than concat. The remaining untested multiprofile neighbours of the best config each change one of these choices in the direction that has lost so far. config_042 swaps in ResNet50 (expected about 0.69), and config_029 or config_007 swap in avgpool (expected about 0.66–0.67). So they are unlikely to beat 0.725. The one major design choice never tested is single-profile versus multiprofile input. 2. Test: config_014 keeps the best components (scVI, ViT-L, weighted fusion) but uses single-profile input with no aggregation. This shows whether multiprofile aggregation is actually needed or whether a simpler setup does as well or better. 3. Why now: Among the options, this is the one with real uncertainty and a plausible chance of exceeding 0.725, rather than a near-certain loss. If it does well, it also points the final experiment toward single-profile variants. Expected cost is low: with no multiprofile aggregation it should be cheaper than the roughly 3.6–4.7 GPU-hour multiprofile ViT-L runs, likely around 2 GPU hours or less.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_035 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted fusion, 0.725 accuracy, 0.685 F1). Three choices are consistently strong: the scVI RNA encoder (clearly ahead of scGPT and PCA), transformer aggregation (about 0.056 better than avgpool on ResNet50), and multimodal fusion (ahead of RNA-only at 0.653 and image-only at 0.260). Weighted fusion beat concat only slightly (0.725 vs 0.721). The one untested combination within this scVI + transformer family is ResNet50 with weighted fusion. This experiment tests whether the weighted-fusion gain carries over to ResNet50, which scored 0.688 with concat. That would show whether the image encoder and the fusion choice interact. With no budget left, a nearby variant of the strongest family is a better final bet than avgpool variants such as config_029, which history suggests will underperform. It is also better than PCA or scGPT variants, which have done poorly. Winning outright is unlikely, since ResNet50 has trailed ViT-L, so config_035 will probably stay the best. Expected cost is moderate, about 4–5 GPU hours, similar to config_024.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we have no data on any design choice. Domain priors suggest that multimodal fusion and multiprofile aggregation with a learned (transformer) aggregator are the most likely to give high accuracy. Which RNA encoder and image encoder work best is still the largest open question. 2) What this tests: config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 RNA, ResNet50 image, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) is a strong-prior, near-full-capacity baseline. Its result anchors the search. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time: ViT-L vs ResNet50, scGPT/PCA vs scVI, avgpool vs transformer, concat vs weighted, and unimodal ablations. 3) Why now: starting from a likely-good configuration gives a competitive incumbent early, which protects the best-found accuracy, while keeping compute moderate. Expected relative cost is medium. Multiprofile aggregation plus a transformer and two modalities add cost. The compact 200-dimensional scVI embedding and the ResNet50 backbone keep it well below the ViT-L or scGPT multiprofile variants.

1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ResNet50, transformer, weighted fusion) reached 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1 at 6.22 GPU hours. That is a reasonable anchor, but one run tells us nothing about which design choices matter. 2. Test: config_046 changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, and keeps everything else fixed. This isolates the effect of the image representation, which may be one of the highest-impact factors for multimodal accuracy. 3. Why now: a one-factor change from a known anchor gives a clean, interpretable result. If ViT-L clearly helps, later experiments can tune the RNA encoder, aggregation and fusion on top of it. If it does not, we can stay with the cheaper ResNet50 backbone. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_019, perhaps about 1.3 to 1.8 times, because the ViT-L features are larger. This is justified because the image encoder could be the deciding factor for the best accuracy.

1. Evidence: Two multiprofile, transformer, weighted-fusion runs differ only in the image encoder. ImageNet ViT-L reached higher accuracy than ResNet50 (0.725 vs 0.713) and used much less compute (3.6 vs 6.2 GPU h), though its F1 was slightly lower. That gives a tentative lead to ViT-L, but the RNA encoder, fusion and aggregation choices are still completely untested. 2. Test: This run keeps the current best setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) and swaps scVI-200 for scGPT. It isolates the RNA encoder, which is a major design axis likely to shift accuracy more than fusion or aggregation details. 3. Why now: Testing the RNA encoder exploits the promising ViT-L direction while reducing a key uncertainty early, so the remaining budget can be focused on the better RNA backbone before tuning fusion (concat) and aggregation (avgpool). Expected cost is moderate, similar to or slightly above config_046 (about 3.5-5 GPU h), and well below the ResNet50 run.

1. Evidence: The RNA encoder has had the largest effect so far. Swapping scvi_n200 for scgpt, with everything else held fixed, dropped validation accuracy from 0.725 to 0.520. The image encoder mattered much less. imagenet_vit_l scored 0.725 against 0.713 for resnet50, a small gap, and was cheaper (3.6 vs 6.2 GPU hours), though resnet50 had slightly higher F1. The third RNA encoder, pca_n2000, is still untested. It could plausibly match or beat scvi. 2. Test: config_035 keeps the current best setup (vit_l, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) and swaps only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. This is a clean one-factor comparison with config_046 and config_002. 3. Why now: Because the RNA encoder has shown the highest impact, settling it should come before tuning smaller factors like fusion (concat vs weighted) or aggregation (avgpool vs transformer). Those can be tuned on the winning encoder in the remaining 6 experiments. Expected cost is moderate, roughly 3-4 GPU hours, similar to config_046. PCA features are cheap, and vit_l runs have so far been cheaper than resnet50 runs.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder so far (about 0.71-0.72 accuracy, versus 0.59 for pca_n2000 and 0.52 for scgpt). With scvi, imagenet_vit_l gave slightly higher accuracy than resnet50 (0.725 vs 0.713) and was cheaper to train (3.6 vs 6.2 GPU h). That makes config_046 the current best and the cheaper base to build on. 2) Uncertainty: every run so far used weighted fusion with transformer aggregation, so the fusion choice is completely untested. config_039 keeps the best setup (multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer) and changes only fusion to concat. This isolates the effect of fusion and could beat 0.725. 3) Why now: it is a one-factor change around the best configuration, so it directly exploits the strong evidence while clarifying an untested design choice. The aggregation question (avgpool, config_001) can follow in the remaining budget. Expected cost is similar to config_046, about 3.5-4 GPU hours, since concat fusion adds little overhead.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder. It reached 0.713 to 0.725, while scgpt reached 0.52 and pca_n2000 reached 0.59. With scvi, imagenet_vit_l slightly beat resnet50 (0.725 vs 0.713) and cost less. Weighted and concat fusion were nearly tied (0.725 vs 0.721, F1 0.685 vs 0.681). Every run so far used transformer aggregation, so the aggregation choice is still completely unknown. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, weighted) and swaps transformer aggregation for avgpool. That isolates whether a simpler aggregator matches or beats the transformer. 3) It is the most informative remaining test around the current best region, and it could improve the top accuracy. Expected cost is at or below config_046's 3.6 GPU hours, since avgpool is cheaper than transformer aggregation. That makes it a low-cost test of a high-value design choice.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_046 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer, weighted) at 0.725. Changing the RNA encoder moved accuracy a lot: scVI reached about 0.71-0.72, PCA 0.586 and scGPT 0.520. Changing the image encoder (ResNet50 0.713 vs ViT-L 0.725), the fusion method (concat 0.721) or the aggregation (avgpool 0.706) moved it much less. So the RNA branch seems to drive performance, and it is unclear how much the image branch adds. The remaining multimodal scVI variants (ResNet50 or avgpool with concat) look unlikely to beat 0.725, given their components each tested lower. 2. Test: config_022 is the RNA-only scVI model with the transformer aggregator. It shows whether the image branch genuinely helps or mostly adds noise and compute. If RNA-only matches or beats 0.725, it becomes the new best and points the last experiments toward RNA-centric variants. If it falls clearly short, that confirms multimodal fusion matters and the remaining budget should refine around config_046. 3. Why now: it resolves the biggest open design question (modality) using the strongest RNA encoder and the best aggregator. It is also likely cheaper than the multimodal runs (estimated about 2-3 GPU hours versus 3.6-6.2) because there is no image encoder or fusion step.

Evidence: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder. It scored 0.70-0.725, compared with 0.52 for scGPT and 0.59 for PCA. Within scVI multimodal runs, the transformer beat avgpool, ViT-L beat ResNet50, and weighted fusion edged out concat (0.725 vs 0.721, also with slightly higher F1). The best so far is config_046 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted). The remaining scVI multiprofile variants (e.g. ResNet50+concat, avgpool+concat) combine choices that each scored lower, so they are unlikely to beat 0.725. The main unexplored design axis is the profile setting: every run so far used multiprofile. Test: config_040 is config_046 with singleprofile instead of multiprofile (scVI, ViT-L, weighted fusion, no aggregation). It isolates whether multiprofile aggregation actually helps. Why now: with 2 experiments left, this resolves the largest remaining uncertainty and has some chance of a surprise improvement. If singleprofile proves competitive, the last run can exploit it, for example with concat fusion. Expected cost is low, likely below config_046's 3.6 GPU hours, because no multiprofile aggregation is involved.

1. Evidence: the scVI RNA encoder with multiprofile transformer aggregation is clearly the strongest family. config_046 (ViT-L, weighted) is best at 0.725, config_039 (ViT-L, concat) reached 0.721 and config_019 (ResNet50, weighted) reached 0.713. Switching to scGPT or PCA RNA encoders, avgpool aggregation, single-profile input or RNA-only all lowered accuracy substantially. 2. Test: config_031 (scVI, ResNet50, transformer, concat) is the only untested combination in this top family. It checks whether concat fusion helps the ResNet50 image encoder, since the fusion choices differed by only about 0.004 accuracy with ViT-L. 3. Why now: every remaining alternative relies on a choice that has already hurt performance, such as avgpool, a weaker RNA encoder or dropping a modality. config_031 is therefore the most plausible remaining chance to match or slightly beat 0.725, although I expect it to land around 0.71 to 0.72, so a gain is uncertain. Expected cost is relatively high, about 5–6 GPU hours, similar to config_019 (6.22 GPU hours) because of ResNet50 multiprofile multimodal processing. I accept this cost because no cheaper configuration has a realistic chance of beating the current best.

1. Evidence: The scVI-n200 RNA encoder with the ViT-L image encoder under multiprofile aggregation is clearly the strongest region. Results so far are config_046 (transformer, weighted) at 0.725, config_039 (transformer, concat) at 0.721 and config_001 (avgpool, weighted) at 0.706. ResNet50 trails ViT-L by about 0.01–0.03. scGPT and PCA RNA encoders, single-profile and RNA-only models all perform much worse. Every scVI + ViT-L + multiprofile configuration except avgpool with concat has already been tested. 2. This run tests that last cell (avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) and checks whether concat interacts better with avgpool than weighted fusion did. 3. Why it is the best final pick: it is the only untested configuration in the top-performing region, so it has the highest remaining chance of matching or beating 0.725. The alternatives are weaker. ResNet50 avgpool variants (config_011, config_032) start from a weaker image encoder. Image-only models dropped the RNA signal that multimodal runs relied on. Any scGPT or PCA run is likely to score well below the best. Expected cost is moderate, about 4.5–5 GPU hours, similar to config_001 and config_039 and cheaper than the ResNet50 transformer runs.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: no experiments have been run yet, so every design choice is open: modality, profile setting, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation and fusion. Prior expectation is that multimodal multiprofile models perform best in cellular profiling, but neither that nor the relative cost of each choice has been measured. 2) What this tests: config_020 sets a mid-complexity multimodal multiprofile anchor using scVI (200-dim), ResNet50, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. These are moderate, commonly strong defaults. Later runs can change one factor at a time against this baseline (transformer aggregation, ViT-L image encoder, weighted fusion, single-modality ablations) to attribute gains to specific components. 3) Why now: it likely sits in the high-accuracy region (multimodal plus multiprofile), which helps the best-found objective. It also avoids starting with the most expensive options (ViT-L with transformer aggregation) before knowing whether that cost pays off. Expected relative cost: moderate. Multiprofile and multimodal add cost, but the compact scVI latent, ResNet50 and avgpool keep it well below ViT-L/transformer configurations.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: We have one result. The multimodal, multiprofile config_020 (scVI RNA, ResNet50 image, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1. No design choice has been compared yet. 2. What this tests: config_003 changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, and keeps everything else the same. Any difference can therefore be credited cleanly to the image encoder, which is likely one of the most influential choices. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: larger pretrained ViT image features often improve morphology representations, so this has a good chance of raising the best accuracy. 1. Evidence: swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L, with everything else held fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200, avgpool, concat), raised validation accuracy from 0.632 to 0.715. Aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) is the main open design choice still untested. 2. This experiment keeps the current best setup and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation, so any change in accuracy can be attributed to aggregation alone. 3. Attention-based multiprofile aggregation is a likely source of further gains, so this extends the strongest direction while answering an important open question. Its result will guide later tests of RNA encoders (PCA, scGPT) and fusion type. 1) Evidence so far: the image encoder is the dominant factor. With the same scVI RNA encoder, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion, ViT-L scored 0.715 accuracy versus 0.632 for ResNet50, and it was also cheaper (4.49 vs 7.27 GPU hours). Evidence: ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50 (0.715-0.721 vs 0.632). Transformer and avgpool aggregation are about tied (0.721 vs 0.715, with F1 slightly favoring avgpool). The RNA encoder has a large effect: swapping scVI for scGPT dropped accuracy to 0.507. The pca_n2000 RNA encoder, an important design choice, is still completely untested. Test: this keeps the best configuration (config_002: ViT-L, transformer, concat) fixed and swaps scVI for PCA-2000. It isolates whether a simpler, higher-dimensional RNA representation beats scVI. Why now: since the RNA encoder has shown the largest swing so far, resolving this choice is worth more than testing the smaller fusion question (weighted vs concat) first. That can follow on whichever encoder wins. Expected cost: moderate, roughly 4-5 GPU hours, similar to config_002. 1. Evidence: Five experiments show scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder (0.72 vs 0.60 for pca_n2000 and 0.51 for scgpt). imagenet_vit_l beats resnet50 (0.715 vs 0.632) and was also cheaper. Test: config_026 keeps the best setup (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer) and changes only concat to weighted. This isolates the effect of fusion on top of the current best of 0.7207. 3. Why now: This is the most direct test that could beat the current best, and it settles the last major design choice in one controlled run. 1) Evidence: the scvi_n200 RNA encoder with the imagenet_vit_l image encoder is clearly the strongest pairing (0.715 to 0.725). Swapping either encoder hurts a lot: scgpt gave 0.507, pca_n2000 gave 0.599 and resnet50 gave 0.632. Within this pairing, aggregation and fusion change accuracy only slightly. These gaps are too small to read much into, and F1 is mixed (avgpool+concat has the highest F1 at 0.687). 2) Test: config_044 (scvi_n200, vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is the one untested cell in the aggregation × fusion grid for the best encoders. It shows whether weighted fusion helps independently of aggregation and whether avgpool+weighted can beat the current best of 0.725. 3) Why now: it exploits the best-supported region at low expected cost, about 3.5 to 4.5 GPU hours, similar to or cheaper than the transformer variants since avgpool is lighter. Riskier moves such as image-only or singleprofile runs can wait for the remaining 3 experiments.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_026 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy. Transformer aggregation and weighted fusion give only small, uncertain gains over avgpool and concat. The RNA encoder matters much more: replacing scVI with PCA dropped accuracy to 0.60, and scGPT dropped it to 0.51. ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50. 2) Open question: We have not tested whether the RNA branch adds anything beyond the image signal. Weak RNA encoders hurting the model this much suggests it might be dragging performance down. Image-only ViT-L with transformer aggregation (config_013) isolates the image contribution. It tests whether dropping RNA could match or beat 0.725, and it shows how much scVI really contributes. 3) Why this is the best use of the budget: All close neighbours of the current best are either already tested or use the clearly worse ResNet50 or RNA encoders. Test: config_029 is RNA-only scVI with multiprofile transformer aggregation. It keeps the strongest RNA encoder and aggregator and drops the image modality. It shows whether the RNA signal alone matches or beats the multimodal best, or whether fusion gives a real gain worth refining. 3. Why now: The remaining small multimodal variants (concat with ResNet50, avgpool with ViT-L) are unlikely to exceed 0.725 based on the observed trends. This ablation is informative either way: it could find a better and simpler model, or confirm that multimodal is needed and focus the last two experiments there. Expected cost is low, likely about 1.5 to 3 GPU hours, cheaper than any multimodal run so far because there is no image encoder.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_025 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy. scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (scGPT reached 0.52 and PCA 0.59). Transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.713 vs 0.678 with ResNet50). Weighted and concat fusion perform about the same (0.725 vs 0.721). Multimodal clearly beats RNA-only (0.653). Why now: With 2 experiments left, this clears up the largest remaining uncertainty near the current best configuration.
