1. Evidence: the scVI RNA encoder and transformer aggregation are clearly the key choices. Replacing scVI with PCA dropped accuracy to 0.586 and with scGPT to 0.520. Replacing transformer with avgpool dropped it from 0.713 to 0.678. Single-profile input reached only 0.537. Within the scVI + transformer + multiprofile family, ViT-L/weighted is best (0.725), ViT-L/concat is close (0.721) and ResNet50/weighted is a bit lower (0.713). 2. Test: config_039 (scVI, ResNet50, transformer, concat) is the only untested setup in this family. Why now: every other untested option changes a factor already shown to hurt accuracy (avgpool, PCA or scGPT, single-profile), or drops RNA entirely. 1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder (pca and scgpt scored 0.52–0.59). imagenet_vit_l slightly beats resnet50 and costs less. Multiprofile beats singleprofile by a wide margin. 1) Evidence/uncertainty: no experiments have been run yet, so every design axis is uncertain: modality, single vs. multiprofile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation and fusion. Prior knowledge from cellular profiling suggests that multimodal fusion and multiprofile aggregation usually beat unimodal, single-profile models, but this has not been checked on this task. 2) What it tests: config_033 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + resnet50, avgpool, concat) is a strong but simple anchor. It combines both modalities and multiple profiles while using the most basic aggregation (avgpool) and fusion (concat) and compact encoders. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result so far. config_033 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + resnet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1, so we have a reasonable baseline but no comparisons yet. The image encoder is a key untested choice, and a large pretrained ViT-L could plausibly give stronger morphological features than ResNet50. 2. Evidence: with the RNA encoder (scvi_n200), multiprofile setting, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion held fixed, swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L raised validation accuracy from 0.632 to 0.715 (F1 0.607 to 0.687). Aggregation is likely the most influential of these in the multiprofile setting, because a transformer can learn attention over profiles while avgpool simply averages them. What this tests: config_024 keeps the best configuration (config_012) and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. That gives a clean one-factor comparison on a design choice that could add substantial accuracy. Why now: it exploits the strong ViT-L signal while resolving a major open choice early, so later experiments (weighted fusion, scGPT or PCA RNA encoders) can build on the better aggregator. Expected cost: moderately higher than config_012 because of the transformer aggregator, roughly 5-7 GPU hours. That is likely still at or below the ResNet50 run's cost and justified by the potential gain.

1) Evidence: three experiments show the image encoder matters most. ImageNet ViT-L (0.715 to 0.721 accuracy) clearly beats ResNet50 (0.632), and it was also cheaper to train (about 4.5 vs 7.3 GPU hours). Changing only the RNA encoder isolates its effect, which is likely larger than the effect of fusion type. 3) This is the best use of the next experiment because it reduces uncertainty on a potentially high-impact design choice while staying in the region that already performs best, so it can directly yield a new best result. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_024 (scvi_n200, ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.721 accuracy. config_012 differs only in avgpool aggregation and reached 0.715. 1. Evidence: The image encoder and RNA encoder have the largest effects so far. imagenet_vit_l clearly beats resnet50 (0.715 vs 0.632 with avgpool/concat). scvi_n200 clearly beats scgpt (0.721 vs 0.507 with the same ViT/transformer/concat setup). Why now: Trying the remaining minor aggregation/fusion variants offers little expected gain, while an RNA encoder that beats scVI is the most plausible route to a clearly higher accuracy. 1) Evidence: scvi_n200 plus imagenet_vit_l is clearly the strongest combination so far (0.715 to 0.725). 1. Evidence: the strongest region is clearly scVI RNA + ImageNet ViT-L + multiprofile. Within it, avgpool/concat scored 0.715, transformer/concat 0.721 and transformer/weighted 0.725 (best so far). 1) Evidence: no experiments have been run, so we have no data on any design choice. 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_001 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 RNA, ResNet50 image, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) reached 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1 for 6.22 GPU hours. Evidence: the RNA encoder matters most so far. scvi_n200 clearly beats pca_n2000 (0.599) and scgpt (0.507) when paired with ViT-L. ViT-L beats ResNet50 when paired with scVI (0.721 vs 0.688). 1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_013 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. 1. Evidence: No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which modality, profile setting, encoder, aggregation or fusion works best. What this tests: config_009 combines RNA and images over multiple profiles, so it directly checks whether that design is as strong as expected. 1. Evidence/uncertainty: Only one result exists. The multimodal, multiprofile setup (scVI-200 + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) reached 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_043 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725. Concat fusion (0.721) is essentially tied. 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet, so every design axis is open. These axes are modality, single- vs multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation and fusion. My prior is that multimodal, multiprofile models are most likely to reach the highest accuracy, but that is still untested. 2. What this tests: config_037 is a mid-complexity anchor in that region: multimodal, multiprofile, the compact scVI-200 RNA encoder, a ResNet50 image encoder, average-pool aggregation and concat fusion. It gives a strong baseline. Later runs can then change one axis at a time: ViT-L instead of ResNet50, a transformer instead of average pooling, scGPT or PCA instead of scVI, weighted instead of concat fusion, and single-modality or single-profile ablations. 3. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: We have one data point. The multimodal, multiprofile setup with scVI RNA, ResNet50 images, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1, at 7.27 GPU hours. We do not yet know which design axis matters most. 2. What this tests: config_004 changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, and keeps everything else fixed. That gives a clean one-factor comparison of image representation quality, which I expect to be one of the largest drivers of accuracy for morphology-based profiling. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: if the ViT-L result is clearly better, later experiments can build on it by testing transformer aggregation, weighted fusion and other RNA encoders. If it is not better, we can stay with the cheaper ResNet50 and explore aggregation or RNA encoders instead. Either outcome sharpens the search early. That makes the scVI + ViT-L + multiprofile + concat setup the strongest base so far. Uncertainty: the effects of aggregation, RNA encoder and fusion are still unknown. The result will cleanly show whether attention-based aggregation improves on averaging. ViT-L is clearly better than ResNet50 (0.715 vs 0.632 under avgpool and concat). Any accuracy or F1 difference can therefore be attributed to the image backbone. Why now: settling the backbone question early guides the remaining 8 experiments. I can then vary aggregation, RNA encoder and fusion on top of the stronger backbone, rather than spreading the budget across all factors at once. Expected cost: higher than config_022, roughly 1.5-2x (about 11-15 GPU hours), because ViT-L is a larger image encoder. 1) Evidence: with everything else held fixed (scvi_n200, multiprofile avgpool, concat), switching the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l raised validation accuracy from 0.632 to 0.715. Learned attention over multiple profiles could capture cross-profile structure that mean pooling discards. 3) Why now: aggregation may have a larger effect than fusion type or RNA encoder, and it is a one-variable change, so the result will be clear. If it helps, later runs can vary fusion and RNA encoder on top of the transformer. If it doesn't, we return to avgpool with little lost. Expected cost: moderately higher than config_007, perhaps about 5–7 GPU hours, because of the added transformer aggregator. That is still at or below the resnet50 run.

1) Evidence: The image encoder is the dominant factor so far. ViT-L beat ResNet50 by about 8 accuracy points (0.715 vs 0.632) and was also cheaper (about 4.5 vs 7.3 GPU hours). The RNA encoder (only scvi_n200 tested) and fusion (only concat tested) are completely unexplored. 2) This experiment keeps the best-known setup (multimodal, multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, concat) and swaps scvi_n200 for scGPT. 1) Evidence so far: the imagenet_vit_l image encoder clearly beats resnet50 (0.715 vs 0.632 with the rest held fixed). scvi_n200 clearly beats scgpt (0.721 vs 0.507). 1. Evidence: The ViT-L image encoder clearly beats ResNet50 (0.715 vs 0.632 under the same setup). Among RNA encoders, scVI far outperforms scGPT (0.721 vs 0.507). Remaining refinements to the scVI branch look marginal, while the RNA encoder has shown large swings, so the chance of a new best is highest here. 1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder. It beats pca_n2000 (about 0.59) and scgpt (about 0.51) by large margins, and imagenet_vit_l beats resnet50 (0.715 vs 0.632 under avgpool+concat). Within scvi+vit_l, the aggregation and fusion effects are small: avgpool+concat scored 0.715, transformer+concat 0.721 and transformer+weighted 0.725 (the current best). 2) This experiment fills the one untested cell of the aggregation × fusion 2×2 for the best encoder pair: avgpool+weighted. 1) Evidence: all four multimodal multiprofile scVI + ViT-L variants have been tested. They sit in a tight 0.706–0.725 band, with the transformer + weighted variant (config_030) best at 0.725. Evidence: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (0.70-0.725, versus about 0.51 for scGPT and 0.59 for PCA). ViT-L beats ResNet50 (0.715 vs 0.632). 1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence about which modality, profile setting, encoder, aggregation or fusion works best. Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_004 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ResNet50, transformer, weighted fusion) reached 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. 1) Evidence: scVI-200 is clearly the best RNA encoder, at 0.715–0.725 versus 0.63 for PCA and 0.51 for scGPT. ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50 (0.715 vs 0.632). Every remaining multimodal option would swap in a component already shown to be worse (PCA, scGPT or ResNet50), so none is likely to beat 0.725. The main open question is whether the image branch helps at all. scVI drives most of the performance, and the ViT-L image features may add noise. 2) This experiment tests RNA-only with scVI-200, multiprofile and transformer aggregation, which keeps the winning RNA and aggregation choices and removes the image modality. 3) It is the only remaining option with a realistic chance of exceeding the current best, and it settles an important design question on the final run. Expected cost is low, likely below the roughly 3.6–4.6 GPU hours of the multimodal transformer runs, because there is no ViT-L image processing.

1. Evidence: no experiments have been run, so there is no data yet. Priors suggest that multimodal fusion and multiprofile aggregation are the most likely sources of the highest accuracy. 2. What it tests: config_008 combines multimodal input, multiprofile transformer aggregation, the compact scVI-200 RNA embedding, the cheaper ResNet50 image encoder and weighted fusion. It gives a strong reference point for the likely best architecture family. 3. Why now: a high-ceiling anchor is worth more than a weak baseline. Later runs can then change one factor at a time: ViT-L vs ResNet50, transformer vs avgpool, RNA encoder, fusion type, and single-modality ablations. Expected cost is medium: multiprofile transformer and multimodal processing add time, but ResNet50 and the 200-dimensional scVI input keep it well below the ViT-L multiprofile options.

1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_008 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, ResNet50, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) reached 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1 at 6.22 GPU hours. That is a reasonable baseline, but no design choice has been compared yet. 2. What this tests: config_050 changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, and keeps everything else fixed. Any gain or loss can therefore be attributed cleanly to the image encoder. The image backbone is likely one of the highest-impact choices, and larger pretrained ViT features often give richer morphology representations. 3. Why now: this is a one-factor test with high upside. If ViT-L helps, it sets a stronger base for later RNA-encoder (scGPT vs. PCA) and fusion or aggregation comparisons. If it does not, we learn that the cheaper ResNet50 is enough. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_008, roughly 1.3–1.6x (about 8–10 GPU hours), because ViT-L features are larger. That is justified because this configuration has a realistic chance of being the best performer.

Evidence: the two runs share the same setup (scvi_n200, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) and differ only in image encoder. Swapping resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l raised accuracy from 0.713 to 0.725 and cut cost from 6.22 to 3.60 GPU hours. F1 dropped slightly (0.695 to 0.685), so the gain is modest but it favors the ViT-L backbone. The RNA encoder is still untested and could matter a lot in this setting. This experiment keeps the best known setup (imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) and swaps scvi_n200 for scGPT. That isolates whether a foundation-model RNA embedding beats scVI, and the result directly shapes the next several choices (PCA, concat fusion, avgpool). It is the best use of the next run because it exploits the current best configuration while resolving a major untested design axis with a single change. Expected cost is moderate, roughly similar to or somewhat above config_050 (about 3.5–5 GPU hours), and below config_008.

1) Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. With everything else fixed (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, weighted), scVI reached 0.725 accuracy and scGPT only 0.520. The image encoder mattered much less: ViT-L scored 0.725 and ResNet50 0.713 with scVI. ViT-L was also cheaper here (3.6 vs 6.2 GPU hours). The third RNA option, PCA-2000, is still untested and could beat scVI. 2) This experiment keeps the best known setup (ViT-L, transformer, weighted) and swaps only the RNA encoder to PCA-2000. That isolates the factor with the largest observed effect. 3) It is the best use of the next run because it settles the highest-impact open question before spending the remaining five runs on smaller choices such as fusion and aggregation. Expected cost is moderate, about 3.5-4.5 GPU hours, similar to config_050. The 2000-dimensional PCA input may add slightly more cost than scVI's 200 dimensions.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder so far (0.713 to 0.725, versus 0.586 for pca_n2000 and 0.520 for scgpt). The best result is scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted at 0.725. That run was also cheaper than the resnet50 version (3.60 vs 6.22 GPU hours), though its F1 was slightly lower. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_050 (scVI_n200 + ViT-L + transformer + weighted fusion, 0.725 accuracy). The RNA encoder matters a lot: scVI clearly beats PCA (0.586) and scGPT (0.520). The image encoder and aggregation effects are smaller. ViT-L beat ResNet50 (0.725 vs 0.713), and transformer beat avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706). Test: config_023 keeps the best backbone (scVI + ViT-L + transformer, multiprofile) and changes only fusion to concat. Why now: It exploits the strongest direction while closing the main remaining uncertainty, and it could directly beat the current best. 1) Evidence: The RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. With ViT-L, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion, scVI scored 0.725, PCA 0.586 and scGPT 0.520. The image encoder (ViT-L 0.725 vs ResNet50 0.713), fusion (weighted 0.725 vs concat 0.721) and aggregation (transformer 0.725 vs avgpool 0.706) changed accuracy only slightly. If it matches or beats 0.725, the remaining budget should go to cheap RNA-only or lightly fused variants. If it falls clearly short, the gain from fusion is confirmed and I can return to refining multimodal scVI settings. 3) Why now: further multimodal tweaks have mostly shown small differences, so measuring the modality contribution reduces uncertainty about the most important unexplored design axis while still having a real chance of a new best. Expected cost: low, likely about 2–3 GPU hours, below the multimodal runs, since there is no image encoder or fusion.

1. Evidence: Every multimodal multiprofile run so far points to scvi_n200 as the clearly best RNA encoder. Behind it are pca_n2000 (0.586) and scgpt (0.520). ImageNet ViT-L is slightly ahead of ResNet50 (0.725 vs 0.713). Transformer aggregation is slightly ahead of avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706). Weighted and concat fusion are nearly tied (0.725 vs 0.721). The remaining multiprofile variants with scvi_n200 only swap in options that have already scored the same or slightly worse, so they are unlikely to beat 0.725. The one major design choice we have never tested is the profile setting, since all seven runs were multiprofile. 2. Test: config_043 keeps the best known components (scvi_n200, ViT-L, weighted fusion) and switches to singleprofile. Why now: it resolves the largest open uncertainty with one of our two remaining experiments. It still has a real chance of a new best, and the final experiment can exploit whichever answer it gives. Expected cost is relatively low, likely below the ~3.6–4.8 GPU hours of the multiprofile ViT runs, because there is no multiprofile aggregation step.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder (about 0.71-0.72 vs 0.52 for scgpt and 0.59 for pca). Multiprofile with transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706) and single-profile (0.537). 1. Evidence: scVI-200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, at 0.65 to 0.72 accuracy, versus 0.52 to 0.59 for scGPT and PCA. ViT-L beats ResNet50 at fixed settings (0.725 vs 0.713 with weighted fusion, 0.721 vs 0.688 with concat). Transformer aggregation beats avgpool, but only modestly (0.725 vs 0.706). Every scVI + ViT-L + transformer combination has now been tested, and the only untested scVI + ViT-L multiprofile option is config_024 (avgpool + concat). 2. Test: whether concat fusion helps the avgpool aggregator more than weighted fusion did. This is the one remaining combination of the two strongest components whose result is genuinely uncertain. 3. Why this is the best last pick: config_024 is a long shot, since the avgpool penalty makes beating 0.725 unlikely. Still, its expected accuracy is higher than any other remaining option. 1) Evidence/uncertainty: no experiments have been run yet, so the main open questions are whether multimodal fusion and multiprofile aggregation help, and which encoders work best. 2) What this tests: config_012 is a strong, mid-cost anchor. It is multimodal and multiprofile, using scGPT (a pretrained RNA foundation model), ResNet50 (a cheaper image encoder than ViT-L), and the simplest options for aggregation (avgpool) and fusion (concat). Evidence: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile config_012 (scGPT + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.512 accuracy and 0.477 F1 at 4.33 GPU hours. With a single data point, no design choice is resolved yet. Test: config_015 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, and keeps everything else the same. This gives a clean read on whether learned attention over multiple profiles beats simple averaging. Why now: aggregation is a high-impact axis because it is shared by most remaining multiprofile candidates, so the answer prunes about half the search space. The image-encoder and RNA-encoder comparisons can follow as separate single-variable tests. Expected cost: moderately higher than config_012, roughly 1.2-1.5x (about 5-6.5 GPU hours), because transformer aggregation is heavier than avgpool. That is still cheaper than adding ViT-L as well.

1) Evidence: with scGPT + ResNet50 + concat held fixed, avgpool aggregation (config_012, acc 0.512, F1 0.477) beat transformer aggregation (config_015, acc 0.471, F1 0.442) at about half the cost (4.33 vs 9.06 GPU hours). Accuracy and F1 agree, so avgpool is the better anchor for now, though this is still a single comparison. Neither encoder choice has been tested yet. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, scGPT, avgpool, concat) and swaps only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. Because just one factor changes, the result directly shows whether the larger image backbone improves accuracy. 3) The image encoder is a major untested design choice, and the answer narrows the image side for many remaining configurations. Avgpool keeps the cost moderate. I expect it to cost somewhat more than config_012 because of the larger ViT-L features, roughly 5–6 GPU hours, which is still well below the transformer run. The RNA-encoder and fusion swaps (config_037/004, config_009) remain cheap follow-ups for later in the budget.

1) Evidence so far: avgpool aggregation clearly beat transformer (0.512 vs 0.471), and the transformer cost about twice as much. ViT-L gave only a small gain over ResNet50 (0.518 vs 0.512) at about 1.7x the cost. The RNA encoder is still completely untested, since every run so far used scGPT, and it may matter more than the image backbone. 2) This experiment swaps scGPT for scVI (n200) and keeps the cheaper ResNet50 + avgpool + concat setup. That makes it a clean comparison against config_012 that isolates the effect of the RNA encoder. 3) It addresses the largest remaining uncertainty at low cost. If scVI helps, the next step is to pair it with ViT-L and test weighted fusion. If it does not, the search can focus on fusion choices around scGPT + ViT-L.

1) Evidence: The RNA encoder is by far the strongest lever so far. Swapping scgpt for scvi_n200 (config_012 to config_004) raised accuracy from 0.512 to 0.632, with F1 rising alongside it. Image encoder choice mattered little (ViT-L gave about +0.005 with scgpt but cost 66% more). Transformer aggregation hurt accuracy and doubled cost versus avgpool. The third RNA encoder, pca_n2000, is still completely untested, which is the largest open uncertainty on the most important design axis. 2) This experiment: config_037 keeps the best-known setup (multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. This gives a clean comparison against config_004 and config_012 and shows whether a simpler expression representation can match or beat scvi_n200. 3) Why now: If PCA wins, the remaining budget should pivot to it. 1) Evidence: The RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. scvi_n200 reached 0.632 acc / 0.607 F1, and pca_n2000 reached 0.619, both far above scgpt at about 0.51. pca_n2000 also cost about 5x more than scvi (36.4 vs 7.3 GPU h). Swapping resnet50 for ViT-L changed accuracy only slightly (+0.005 with scgpt). The transformer aggregator hurt and roughly doubled the cost. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_033 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted fusion, 0.678 accuracy / 0.646 F1). scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder. Weighted fusion gave a large gain over concat with the same backbone (+0.046). Avgpool beat the transformer aggregator with scGPT (0.512 vs 0.471), and the transformer roughly doubled training cost. The image-encoder choice is still uncertain: ViT-L was only marginally better than ResNet50 (0.518 vs 0.512), and that comparison was made only with the weak scGPT encoder. 2) Test: This run keeps the best recipe (scVI + avgpool + weighted) and swaps ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. It isolates whether a stronger image representation adds accuracy once paired with the best RNA encoder and fusion. 3) Why now: It is the most direct exploitation of the leading configuration and resolves the one important open axis. It avoids the transformer aggregator, which so far has been costly and harmful. Expected cost is moderate, about 7–9 GPU hours: somewhat more than config_033's 5.9 hours because of the larger ViT-L features, but far below the PCA-based runs (~36 hours). That leaves room in the remaining budget to test the transformer or concat variants afterward if useful.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_035 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Each component upgrade has helped: scVI over scGPT, weighted over concat fusion, and ViT-L over ResNet50. Aggregation is the main design choice left untested in this strong setting. The only transformer result (config_015, 0.471 vs 0.512 for avgpool) used the weak scGPT and ResNet50 pairing, so that single data point is weak evidence. 2. Test: config_051 changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation, keeping scVI, ViT-L and weighted fusion. This isolates whether learned aggregation helps once the encoders and fusion are strong. 3. Why now: it is the most direct remaining extension of the best configuration, and the result will guide the last two experiments. If it improves, I can refine around transformer aggregation; if not, I can fall back to avgpool variants. The PCA alternatives look poor value: PCA gave no accuracy gain over scVI and cost about 36 GPU hours. Expected cost is moderate, about 1.5 to 2 times config_035, so roughly 8 to 10 GPU hours, judging from config_015's 9.06 hours. This is well below the PCA options.

1. Evidence: Every comparison so far favors weighted fusion over concat (+4.6 points with resnet50, +18.9 with ViT-L) and ViT-L over resnet50. Transformer aggregation gave a further gain in the best configuration, config_051 (scvi_n200 + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725 accuracy). The main open question is the RNA encoder. scGPT is clearly worse. pca_n2000 came close to scVI under concat (0.619 vs 0.632 accuracy) and had higher F1 (0.610 vs 0.607), so it could match or beat scVI inside the best architecture. 2. Test: config_034 keeps the winning setup (ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) and swaps scVI for PCA-2000. This directly tests whether the richer PCA representation helps once fusion and aggregation are strong. The other options look less promising: concat variants (config_026) and resnet50 variants (config_043) are expected to underperform, and singleprofile options would drop aggregation, which helped. 3. Why now: with only one more experiment left after this, this is the most plausible candidate to beat 0.725. Cost: expected to be relatively high, since the only PCA run took 36.4 GPU hours, many times the cost of the scVI runs. I accept that cost because this configuration has the best chance of improving the top accuracy.

Evidence: scVI-200 RNA embeddings with weighted fusion clearly lead this search. The best result is config_051 (scVI, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Weighted fusion beat concat by about 0.046 with scVI and ResNet50. The transformer beat avgpool by about 0.019 with scVI and ViT-L, though it hurt with scGPT and ResNet50, so its benefit may depend on the encoders. One combination in this top family is still untested: scVI with ResNet50, transformer and weighted fusion. What it tests: whether transformer aggregation also helps the scVI, ResNet50, weighted setup (config_033, 0.678 with avgpool). That shows whether the aggregation gain carries across image encoders and gives the last realistic chance of matching or passing config_051. Why this is the best final pick: the other options are much weaker bets. Concat fusion and the PCA or scGPT encoders have consistently underperformed. Single-profile and unimodal setups have been ignored rather than tested, but they drop components that look important. Expected cost is moderate, roughly 4-9 GPU hours, similar to past scVI multiprofile runs and well below the 36-hour PCA run.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet, so all design choices are untested. Priors from multimodal cellular profiling suggest three things. Combining RNA and image usually beats either modality alone. Aggregating multiple profiles usually beats a single profile. Learned transformer aggregation may capture more than average pooling. 2. What this tests: config_044 is a strong anchor that combines these favoured choices: multimodal, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, scVI-200 RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder and weighted fusion. It shows whether the full-capacity design direction reaches high accuracy. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time from this anchor: encoder (scGPT/PCA, ViT-L), fusion (concat), aggregation (avgpool) and modality ablations. 3. Why now: Starting with a likely high performer improves the chance of a good best-found result early. It also gives a reference point for one-factor comparisons. The compact scVI-200 embedding and the ResNet50 backbone keep cost moderate, well below ViT-L or scGPT variants. Expected relative cost is medium: higher than single-profile or unimodal runs because of multiprofile transformer aggregation and two modalities, but lower than the ViT-L multimodal configurations.

The one result gives no information yet about which component limits performance. 2. Why it is the best next experiment: With 8 experiments remaining, settling the image-encoder choice early will guide most of the later search, since roughly half the space depends on it. 1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder (about 0.71-0.72, versus 0.59 for pca_n2000 and 0.52 for scgpt). Multiprofile beats singleprofile by a wide margin (0.725 vs 0.537), and multimodal beats rna_only (0.725 vs 0.653). Transformer aggregation is slightly ahead of avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706). Weighted and concat fusion are essentially tied with ViT-L (0.725 vs 0.721), and resnet50 is close behind ViT-L under weighted fusion (0.713). The current best is config_049 at 0.725.
2) This run tests scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer + concat. It is the only untested cell in the image-encoder by fusion grid for the strongest backbone (scvi, multiprofile, transformer). It will show whether resnet50 pairs better with concat than with weighted fusion.
3) Why this one: all other untested options are expected to score lower, because they use avgpool, a weaker RNA encoder, a single modality or a single profile. This is the remaining configuration closest to the top region and so has the best chance of matching or beating 0.725, though gains over config_049 are likely small. Expected cost is relatively high, about 5-6 GPU hours, similar to config_044's 6.22 h, because resnet50 multiprofile transformer runs were the slowest so far. That cost is justified here because no cheaper option has comparable expected accuracy.

1. Evidence: The strongest results all use multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 with the imagenet_vit_l encoder. The best is config_049 (transformer, weighted) at 0.725, and config_035 (transformer, concat) is close at 0.721, so fusion type matters little. Changing the RNA encoder to scGPT or PCA, or using a single profile, lowered accuracy sharply. Switching the image encoder to resnet50 cost about 0.01 to 0.03. Avgpool aggregation cost about 0.02 relative to the transformer, based on one paired comparison (config_030 vs config_049). Within the strong region, the untested gap is avgpool combined with concat fusion. 2. Test: config_019 checks whether concat fusion pairs better with avgpool aggregation than weighted fusion does (config_030, 0.706). It also completes the 2x2 grid of fusion by aggregation for the best encoder pair. 3. Why this one: With one experiment left, configurations outside the scvi_n200 + ViT-L region are unlikely to beat 0.725. The other choices are resnet50 avgpool variants, which combine two weaker settings, or image-only models, which are probably weaker given the large multimodal gain over RNA-only. I expect config_019 to land around 0.70 to 0.72, so it is unlikely to beat config_049. However, it is the most plausible remaining candidate in the best region and it settles the remaining aggregation and fusion question. Expected cost is moderate, about 4.5 to 5 GPU hours, similar to config_030 and config_035.

1) No experiments have been run yet, so every design choice is uncertain. Priors from multimodal cellular profiling suggest that combining RNA and image signals, and aggregating over multiple profiles, usually improves accuracy. PCA on 2000 genes is a strong, cheap RNA baseline, ImageNet ViT-L tends to give richer image features than ResNet50, and avgpool with concat fusion is the simplest aggregation and fusion. 2) This run tests the likely strong region (multimodal + multiprofile + strong image encoder) using the simplest components. It sets a high anchor score, and later runs can vary aggregation (transformer), fusion (weighted), RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT) or modality (unimodal ablations) one at a time against it. 3) It is the best first use of the budget because it is likely near the top performers while avoiding the extra cost of transformer aggregation and the uncertain scGPT encoder. Expected relative cost is medium to high: multiprofile multimodal processing with ViT-L features costs more than single-profile or unimodal runs, but less than transformer-aggregation variants.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_043 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 RNA, ViT-L images, avgpool, concat) reached 0.629 accuracy and 0.599 F1 at 4.54 GPU hours. That is a reasonable baseline, but it tells us nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2) Test: config_039 changes one factor, swapping avgpool for transformer aggregation while keeping everything else the same. This shows directly whether learned, attention-based pooling across profiles beats simple averaging. That is one of the most likely sources of a large accuracy gain in a multiprofile setup. 3) Why now: because only one factor changes, the result can be attributed cleanly. If it helps, later experiments can build on transformer aggregation while varying RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT) and fusion type. If it does not, the cheaper avgpool stays as the default. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_043, roughly 1.2–1.5x (about 5.5–7 GPU hours), because of the transformer aggregator. The cost is justified because aggregation is a high-impact choice.

Evidence: with multimodal multiprofile PCA-2000 + ViT-L + concat, avgpool aggregation (0.629 acc, 0.599 F1) beat transformer aggregation (0.599 acc, 0.578 F1). Both accuracy and F1 agree, which suggests the simpler avgpool is at least as good here, though this is only a single comparison. The RNA encoder is still completely untested, and it is likely one of the highest-impact design choices. Test: config_047 keeps the best setup so far (multimodal, multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) and swaps only PCA-2000 for the pretrained scGPT encoder. Changing one factor gives a clean read on whether a foundation-model RNA embedding beats the PCA baseline. Why now: this builds on the current best while resolving a major uncertainty. The answer will guide the remaining 7 experiments (for example, fusion type, or scVI vs. ResNet50 for cheaper variants). Expected cost is similar to config_043, about 4.5–5 GPU hours, possibly slightly more if scGPT embeddings are larger. That is justified because this branch is the most likely to contain the best configuration.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_043 (pca_n2000 + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.629 accuracy. Swapping in the scGPT RNA encoder cut accuracy by about 0.11, which was the largest effect seen. Transformer aggregation was about 0.03 worse than avgpool. So the RNA encoder looks like the most influential design choice, yet the third option, scvi_n200, is still untested. 2) This run keeps the best setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder to scvi_n200. That gives a clean test of whether a compact learned embedding beats PCA. 3) The RNA encoder has shown much larger effects than aggregation, and fusion is still untested, so closing this gap is the most likely route to a new best. Expected cost is about the same as config_043 (~4.5 GPU hours) or slightly less, given the 200-dimensional input versus 2000, and far below the 7.2 hours of the scGPT run. If scvi_n200 underperforms, PCA is confirmed as the encoder. The remaining budget can then go to weighted fusion (config_004) and to ResNet50 or unimodal baselines.

1) Evidence: The RNA encoder has the largest effect so far. scvi_n200 (0.715 acc, 0.687 F1) clearly beats pca_n2000 (0.629) and scgpt (0.518) with ViT-L, avgpool and concat. Avgpool also beat transformer aggregation (0.629 vs 0.599, F1 agreeing). Fusion is the one major design choice not yet tested: every run so far used concat. 2) Test: config_050 changes only fusion, from concat to weighted, on the best configuration (scvi_n200, ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool). This isolates whether fusion is a lever for further gains. 3) Why now: It is a one-factor change from the current best, so it exploits the strongest evidence while removing uncertainty about an untested dimension. That is more informative than another aggregation test, where avgpool already looks better. Cost: about the same as config_049 (~4.5 GPU hours), because weighted fusion adds negligible overhead over concat. Cheaper checks, such as swapping in ResNet50 or dropping the image modality, can follow with the remaining budget.

Evidence: the RNA encoder is the strongest factor so far. scVI (0.715) clearly beats PCA (0.629) and scGPT (0.518). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation with PCA (0.629 vs 0.599). Weighted fusion gave no gain over concat with scVI (0.706 vs 0.715, with lower F1). The image encoder is the one major design choice not yet tested, since all five runs used ViT-L. This experiment keeps the best setup (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) and swaps in ResNet50 to see whether the image backbone matters. It is the cleanest test of the largest remaining uncertainty. ResNet50 produces smaller image features than ViT-L, so I expect it to cost somewhat less than the roughly 4.5 GPU hours of the ViT-L runs. If it matches or beats 0.715, it is a cheaper path to the best accuracy. If not, it confirms ViT-L, and the last 3 experiments can go to the scVI + ViT-L variants (for example transformer aggregation).

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_049 (scVI-200 + ViT-L, multiprofile avgpool, concat) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Changing the RNA encoder had the largest effect (scVI > PCA > scGPT). Other changes were neutral or harmful: ViT-L beat ResNet50, avgpool beat transformer, and concat edged out weighted fusion. The profile setting is still a major unknown, because every run so far has been multiprofile. 2. Test: config_032 keeps the best RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion, and switches only to singleprofile. This isolates whether multiprofile aggregation actually adds accuracy or whether single-profile inputs match or beat it. 3. Why now: Singleprofile models skip the aggregation step, so this run should be cheaper than the roughly 4.5 GPU-hour multiprofile ViT-L runs. It tests the largest unexplored design axis while staying anchored to the best-known components, and the result tells the last two experiments which profile setting to refine.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_049 (scVI-200 + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. The RNA encoder matters a lot (scVI > PCA > scGPT), and so does the image encoder (ViT-L well above ResNet50). Multiprofile beats singleprofile by a wide margin, and weighted fusion did not beat concat (0.706). Both modalities clearly carry signal, so a multimodal model is the likely winner. The one key design choice not yet tested on the strong scVI+ViT-L backbone is the aggregator. Transformer aggregation was about 3 points worse than avgpool only with the weaker PCA encoder, which is a single comparison and could depend on the encoder. 2) This experiment swaps avgpool for transformer aggregation in the best configuration and keeps everything else fixed. It tests whether learned set aggregation can exploit the richer scVI embeddings to beat 0.715. 3) It is the only remaining one-change neighbor of the best configuration with real upside. It also settles the aggregation question for the final experiment. Expected cost is moderate, about 4.8 GPU hours, similar to the other ViT-L multiprofile runs and much cheaper than the ResNet50 and scGPT runs, which took over 7 GPU hours.

1) Evidence: scVI-n200 RNA and ImageNet ViT-L images are clearly the strongest choices. scVI beats PCA and scGPT by about 0.09 to 0.20 accuracy, and ViT-L beats ResNet50 by about 0.08. Multiprofile input far outperforms singleprofile. Within this best region, transformer and avgpool aggregation are close (0.721 vs 0.715). Weighted fusion was slightly worse than concat under avgpool (0.706 vs 0.715), though its F1 was similar enough that the gap may be noise. 2) This run tests the one untested neighbor of the current best (config_027): scVI + ViT-L + transformer with weighted fusion. It checks whether weighted fusion pairs better with transformer aggregation than with avgpool. 3) With only 2 experiments left, exploiting the top region gives the best chance of exceeding 0.72. Unimodal or ResNet and PCA variants are unlikely to beat it given the strong image-encoder and RNA-encoder effects. Expected cost is moderate, about 4.7 to 4.9 GPU hours, similar to the other scVI/ViT-L multiprofile runs and cheaper than ResNet50 or scGPT runs.

1. Evidence: the scVI RNA encoder with a multiprofile setup is clearly the strongest choice so far. The best result is config_029 (scvi_n200, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) at 0.725, with config_027 at 0.721. Every scVI + ViT-L multiprofile variant has now been tested. Swapping ViT-L for ResNet50 cost about 0.08 accuracy (0.631 vs 0.715), and single-profile cost about 0.18 (0.532). The remaining multimodal options (ResNet50, PCA or scGPT encoders, single-profile) are therefore unlikely to beat 0.725. 2. What this tests: config_017 (RNA-only, scVI, transformer aggregation) checks an untested design choice, namely how much the image branch actually contributes, using the best RNA encoder and best aggregation. The ResNet50 drop shows image features affect results, but it does not show whether the RNA signal alone is close to or even better than the fused models. 3. Why it is the best final pick: none of the remaining configurations is likely to beat config_029. This one has the most uncertainty around a plausible score near the top, whereas the ResNet50 and single-profile variants have clear evidence against them. It should also be cheaper than any multimodal multiprofile run, since there is no image encoding or fusion, probably around 2–3 GPU hours versus 3.6–7.3.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so every design choice is open. The most important unknowns are whether multimodal fusion beats single modalities and whether multiprofile aggregation helps. In multimodal cellular profiling, the usual prior is that combining RNA and image data and aggregating across profiles improves accuracy, but that has not been tested here. 2) What this tests: config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 RNA, resnet50 image, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) is a strong but not maximal-cost anchor. It probes the likely high-performing region while using the compact scVI RNA representation and the cheaper ResNet50 image encoder instead of ViT-L. Later runs can vary one factor at a time from this baseline: avgpool vs. transformer, ViT-L vs. ResNet50, scGPT/PCA vs. scVI, weighted vs. concat, and single-modality or single-profile ablations. 3) Why now: A strong anchor early gives a good incumbent and a clean reference for one-factor comparisons over the remaining 9 runs. Expected relative cost is medium-high: multiprofile transformer aggregation and dual-modality processing add cost, but the ResNet50 and 200-dim scVI choices keep it well below the ViT-L multimodal options.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile setup with scVI, ResNet50, transformer aggregation and concat fusion (config_030) reached 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. With one data point, which design choices matter is still unknown. The image encoder is likely one of the highest-impact choices, because ImageNet ViT-L usually gives much richer image features than ResNet50. 2) Test: config_002 changes only the image encoder to ViT-L and keeps everything else the same. This gives a clean one-factor comparison that shows whether a stronger image backbone improves accuracy within this strong multimodal, multiprofile setup. 3) Why now: if ViT-L helps, it sets the backbone for the remaining 8 experiments, which can then cover RNA encoder, fusion and aggregation. If it does not help, later runs can use the cheaper ResNet50. Expected cost is higher than config_030's 5.16 GPU hours, perhaps 1.5 to 2 times as much, because ViT-L features are larger. This is justified because it may well become the best configuration and it resolves a key design question early.

Evidence: with scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer aggregation and concat fusion held fixed, imagenet_vit_l beat resnet50 (0.721 vs 0.688 accuracy, with higher F1 as well). That is one comparison, but it is consistent, so the vit_l setup is the current anchor. The RNA encoder is the next largest untested design choice. This experiment keeps everything else from the best configuration (config_002) and swaps scvi_n200 for scgpt. That isolates the RNA encoder's effect, and scgpt is the most plausible candidate for a further accuracy gain. Whichever RNA encoder wins, later experiments can test fusion (weighted) and aggregation (avgpool as a cheaper option) on top of it. Expected cost is similar to config_002, roughly 4.5-5.5 GPU hours, possibly slightly more if the scgpt embeddings are larger. It is a medium-to-high-cost run, but it targets the most likely path to the best accuracy.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_002 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer, concat) at 0.721 accuracy. ViT-L beat ResNet50 under the same setup (0.688). The RNA encoder had by far the largest effect: switching to scGPT dropped accuracy to 0.507. The third RNA option, PCA-2000, is untested. Since the RNA encoder is the highest-impact design choice seen so far, this is the biggest remaining uncertainty. 2) Test: config_011 keeps the best known setup (ViT-L, multiprofile transformer, concat) and swaps only scVI for PCA-2000. This isolates whether a simpler, higher-dimensional RNA representation matches or beats scVI. 3) Why now: fixing the best RNA encoder before tuning smaller choices (fusion type, avgpool vs transformer) puts the remaining 5 experiments on the strongest base. Expected cost is similar to config_002, about 4.5–5 GPU hours. That is moderate, but no cheaper configuration answers this question cleanly.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_002 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Among RNA encoders, scVI clearly beats PCA (0.599) and scGPT (0.507), with ViT-L as the image encoder held fixed. Among image encoders, ViT-L beats ResNet50 (0.688), with scVI held fixed. The two untested design choices are fusion (weighted vs concat) and aggregation (avgpool vs transformer). 2) Test: This experiment keeps the best backbone (scVI + ViT-L + transformer) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. That isolates the effect of fusion on the strongest configuration. 3) Why now: It directly exploits the best region while resolving an open design choice that could raise peak accuracy. Aggregation can be tested next, for example avgpool via config_021 or config_012. Expected cost is similar to config_002, about 4.5–5 GPU hours, since weighted fusion adds little overhead.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder (0.72 vs 0.60 for PCA and 0.51 for scGPT). ViT-L beats ResNet50 (0.721 vs 0.688). Weighted fusion is slightly better than concat (0.725 vs 0.721) and was cheaper (3.60 vs 4.65 GPU h), though that gap is within noise. Aggregation is the main design choice not yet tested: every run so far used the transformer. 2) This run changes only the aggregation of the current best (config_027) from transformer to avgpool. It shows whether the transformer aggregator is needed or whether a simpler pooling does as well or better. 3) It isolates an important untested factor around the best-known setup. It is also likely the cheapest multiprofile multimodal option, since avgpool has no attention layers. Expected cost is somewhat below config_027's 3.6 GPU hours, roughly 3 GPU hours. The result will decide whether the remaining budget goes to transformer or avgpool variants, or to single-profile and unimodal checks.

1. Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. With the other settings fixed, scVI gave 0.72 accuracy, PCA 0.60 and scGPT 0.51. The image encoder mattered much less (ViT-L 0.72 vs ResNet50 0.69). Fusion and aggregation changes were also small: weighted fusion scored 0.725 vs 0.721 for concat, and the transformer scored 0.725 vs 0.706 for avgpool. The best result is config_027 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer, weighted, 0.725 accuracy, 0.685 F1). Further fusion or aggregation tweaks are likely to give only marginal gains. The major untested question is whether the image modality actually helps or adds noise, since all six runs were multimodal. 2. Test: config_009 is RNA-only scVI with the multiprofile transformer. It is the closest RNA-only counterpart to the best configuration, so it isolates the contribution of the image branch. If it matches or beats 0.725, later runs should focus on RNA-centric variants. If it drops clearly, multimodal fusion is confirmed and the last two runs can refine around config_027. 3. Why now: it resolves a high-impact design uncertainty while the budget still allows follow-up. Without the large image encoder, it should be cheaper than the multimodal runs, likely about 2–3 GPU hours versus 3.6–5.2.

1) Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_027 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy. Its close neighbours have mostly been tested. Concat fusion (0.721) and avgpool aggregation (0.706) were slightly worse. ResNet50 (0.688) and other RNA encoders (scGPT 0.507, PCA 0.599) were clearly worse, so switching encoders is unlikely to beat it. 2) Uncertainty: Profile setting is the one major design choice not yet tested; every multimodal run so far was multiprofile. This experiment keeps the best encoders and fusion (scVI + ViT-L, weighted) and switches to single-profile. It tests whether multiprofile aggregation is actually needed or whether a simpler model matches or beats it. 3) Why now: The remaining multiprofile variants all change a component the data already disfavours. This run is the most informative remaining experiment that still has a plausible chance of a new best. It is also expected to be cheaper than the 3.6–5.2 GPU-hour multiprofile runs, since there is no aggregation over multiple profiles; I estimate roughly 1–3 GPU hours.

Evidence: the best result is config_027 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725 acc, F1 0.685). Its neighbours point the same way. scVI clearly beats PCA and scGPT. ViT-L beats ResNet50 by about 0.033 under concat. Transformer beats avgpool by about 0.019 under weighted fusion. Weighted fusion is only marginally better than concat (about 0.004, within noise). Multiprofile beats singleprofile by a wide margin. Uncertainty: the one untested cell in the scVI + ViT-L multiprofile block is avgpool + concat. Because the fusion effect is small, it is unclear whether fusion and aggregation interact, for example whether concat pairs better with simple pooling. What this tests: config_021 completes the 2x2 aggregation-by-fusion grid for the strongest encoder pair. That tells us whether the transformer + weighted combination is truly the best or whether an interaction gives an upside. Why this experiment: the other near-neighbour, config_028, swaps in ResNet50, whose roughly 0.033 deficit is unlikely to be closed by a weighted-fusion gain of about 0.004. PCA, scGPT, singleprofile and unimodal options have shown or implied clearly lower accuracy. This is the remaining configuration most likely to match or exceed 0.725. Expected cost: moderate, about 4-5 GPU hours, similar to the other multiprofile ViT-L runs. This leaves the final experiment for a last refinement.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 RNA is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (scgpt 0.507, pca 0.599). Multiprofile transformer aggregation with weighted fusion is the best design (config_027, 0.725 acc, 0.685 F1). Every scvi_n200 + ViT-L multiprofile combination has now been tested. The only untested axis near the best region is the image encoder under weighted fusion: ResNet50 has been tried only with concat (config_030, 0.688). 2) This run tests whether weighted fusion closes the ResNet50 gap, completing the scvi/transformer/weighted cell of the design grid. 3) The alternatives look weaker. The large drops when scgpt or pca replace scvi suggest image features alone are not strong enough to beat 0.725, which argues against image-only runs. Configurations using pca or scgpt are dominated. config_028 is therefore the closest untested neighbor of the incumbent and the most plausible remaining chance of matching or exceeding it, though the expected gain is modest. Expected cost is about 3.6-5 GPU hours, similar to the other multimodal multiprofile transformer runs.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so only priors are available. For cellular profiling, the usual expectation is that combining RNA and image modalities and aggregating over multiple profiles beats single-modality, single-profile setups. A learned transformer aggregator is expected to beat average pooling. Among encoders, scVI latents (n200) are a compact, strong RNA representation and ImageNet ViT-L gives rich image features. 2. What this tests: It sets a high-performing anchor from the most promising region (multimodal, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, scVI plus ViT-L, concat fusion). Later experiments can then vary one factor at a time from this point: fusion type, image encoder, RNA encoder, aggregation, or removing a modality. 3. Why now: Securing a strong baseline early guards the best-found accuracy within the 10-experiment budget and gives a clear reference for ablations. Concat fusion is the simpler, lower-risk fusion choice. Expected relative cost is high, since it combines multiprofile transformer aggregation, multimodal processing and large ViT-L representations. That cost is justified because this region is the most likely to contain the best configuration. Cheaper variants, such as ResNet50 in place of ViT-L or avgpool in place of the transformer, can then be checked against it.

1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) reached 0.7207 accuracy and 0.6815 F1 at 4.65 GPU hours. This is a reasonable baseline, but nothing yet shows which of its components drive performance. 2. What this tests: config_004 changes only the aggregation, from transformer to avgpool, and keeps everything else fixed. This isolates whether the learned transformer aggregator is worth its extra cost over simple mean pooling across profiles. 3. Why now: aggregation is a central design choice for every multiprofile configuration, so the answer shapes how the remaining 8 experiments are spent. If avgpool matches or beats the transformer, later tests of RNA encoders (e.g., scGPT), image encoders and fusion can use the cheaper aggregator. If it clearly underperforms, the transformer is confirmed for exploitation. Expected cost: somewhat lower than config_019's 4.65 GPU hours, since avgpool skips the attention-based aggregation step, so roughly 3.5-4 GPU hours.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Two multimodal multiprofile runs with scVI and ViT-L and concat fusion differ only in aggregation. Transformer reached 0.7207 accuracy and avgpool reached 0.7150, while avgpool had slightly better F1. So aggregation looks like a minor factor. The RNA encoder, fusion method and image encoder are all untested. 2. What this tests: Swapping only the RNA encoder from scVI to scGPT, keeping the current best setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, concat), isolates the effect of the RNA representation. Foundation-model RNA embeddings could plausibly shift accuracy by more than aggregation choices do. 3. Why now: With 7 runs left, settling the most influential untested design axis early guides later exploitation, such as fusion and image encoder choices. Expected cost is similar to or slightly above config_019 (about 4.7–5.5 GPU hours), because scGPT embeddings may be larger.

1) Evidence: The RNA encoder is the only choice that has made a large difference so far. With the ViT-L image encoder and concat fusion, scVI reached 0.721 accuracy and scGPT reached 0.507. Transformer versus avgpool aggregation changed accuracy by only about 0.006 (0.721 vs 0.715), and F1 slightly favored avgpool, so aggregation looks minor. The third RNA option, PCA (2000 components), is untested, and so are fusion type and the ResNet50 image encoder. 2) Test: config_034 keeps the best setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, concat) and swaps scVI for PCA. This isolates the high-impact RNA encoder choice. If PCA beats scVI, we gain a better base to tune fusion and image encoder on. If it does not, scVI is confirmed and the remaining budget can go to fusion and image-encoder tests. 3) Why now: the choice that has already shown large effects is more likely to move accuracy than the low-impact aggregation choice. Expected cost is similar to the earlier multiprofile ViT-L runs, about 4-5 GPU hours. PCA input is larger than scVI's, but the ViT-L image features probably dominate training time.

1) Evidence: The RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. scvi_n200 (0.721 and 0.715) clearly beats pca_n2000 (0.599) and scgpt (0.507). Transformer and avgpool aggregation are within noise of each other: transformer has slightly higher accuracy, avgpool slightly higher F1. Two design choices are still untested: fusion (only concat tried) and image encoder (only ViT-L tried). 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration (config_019: scvi_n200 + ViT-L + transformer) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. That isolates whether learned modality weighting improves on the current best. 3) Fusion is the most direct untested lever around the leading configuration, so it is the best way to improve the top accuracy while keeping inference clean. Expected cost is similar to config_019, about 4.5–4.8 GPU hours, so the extra spend is modest. A cheaper ResNet50 variant (config_017) remains a good follow-up.

1. Evidence: The scVI RNA encoder clearly beats PCA (0.599) and scGPT (0.507). Aggregation (transformer 0.721 vs avgpool 0.715) and fusion (weighted 0.725 vs concat 0.721) both make small differences. The best so far is config_002 (scVI, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) at 0.725, which was also the cheapest run (3.60 GPU h). Every run so far used the ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, so the image encoder is the largest untested design choice. 2. Test: config_003 keeps the best known settings (scVI, multiprofile, transformer, weighted) and swaps ViT-L for ResNet50. This isolates the image-encoder effect and shows whether a different visual representation could beat the current best. 3. Why now: Further aggregation or fusion tweaks are unlikely to give large gains, given the small differences seen. Resolving the image-encoder question directs the remaining 3 experiments. Expected cost is moderate and likely below the ViT-L runs (about 3 GPU h or less), since ResNet50 produces smaller features, so the information gained per GPU hour is high.

1. Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder. It reached about 0.72 accuracy, compared with 0.60 for pca_n2000 and 0.51 for scgpt. The best result so far is config_002 (scvi_n200, ViT-L, transformer, weighted fusion) at 0.725. Weighted fusion edged out concat (0.725 vs 0.721) and was cheaper (3.60 vs 4.65 GPU h). ResNet50 gave slightly lower accuracy than ViT-L (0.713) at a higher cost (6.22 GPU h). The one remaining open choice within the best family is aggregation under weighted fusion. Avgpool trailed transformer only slightly under concat (0.715 vs 0.721) and had a marginally higher F1, so the gap is within noise. 2. Test: config_035 is the avgpool + weighted version of the best configuration. It shows whether weighted fusion's small gain adds to avgpool and could beat 0.725, or whether transformer aggregation is reliably better. 3. Why now: this is the most direct exploitation step in the clearly best region. Alternatives such as RNA-only, single-profile or other encoders are unlikely to beat the current best. 1) Evidence: only one result exists so far. config_014 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1 at 7.27 GPU hours. This gives a clean comparison on how profiles are aggregated, a key choice in the multiprofile setting, since learned attention over profiles could capture structure that mean pooling discards. 3) Why now: the ResNet50 and scVI backbone stays cheap, so the expected cost is only moderately higher than config_014, roughly 1.1 to 1.3 times its cost (about 8 to 9 GPU hours). That is cheaper than switching to the ViT-L image encoder first. The result tells us whether to carry transformer aggregation into later tests of the image encoder (ViT-L), fusion type and RNA encoder.

1) Evidence: with the RNA encoder (scvi_n200), image encoder (resnet50) and fusion (concat) held fixed, transformer aggregation (config_045) beat avgpool (config_014). Accuracy rose from 0.632 to 0.688, F1 rose from 0.607 to 0.659, and the transformer run was also cheaper (5.16 vs 7.27 GPU hours). That is only one comparison, but it is a clear gain, so I will keep transformer aggregation. The image encoder, RNA encoder and fusion method are all still untested. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration (config_045) and changes only the image encoder, from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l. It tests whether a stronger pretrained image representation adds accuracy on top of transformer aggregation. 3) The image backbone is likely one of the most influential remaining choices, and a one-factor change keeps the result easy to interpret. Its outcome will also decide which image encoder to use when testing the RNA encoder (scgpt or pca) and weighted fusion in later runs. Expected cost: moderately higher than config_045, roughly 6-9 GPU hours, because ViT-L features are larger. That cost is justified if it turns out to be the strongest direction.

1) Evidence: Transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool, scoring 0.688 vs 0.632 with ResNet50. Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L gave a further gain, reaching 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1 in config_013. The RNA encoder has only been tested as scvi_n200, and fusion only as concat, so both remain the biggest open questions. 2) This experiment changes one factor from the current best: it replaces scvi_n200 with the scGPT foundation-model RNA encoder and keeps ViT-L, transformer aggregation and concat fixed. It tests whether richer pretrained RNA embeddings add accuracy on top of the strongest image and aggregation choices. 3) The RNA encoder is plausibly a larger lever than fusion type, which can be checked next with config_037. Expected cost is similar to or somewhat above config_013's 4.65 GPU hours, roughly 5–6 GPU hours, because scGPT embeddings may be larger; this is moderate and justified by the potential gain.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_013 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + concat, acc 0.721, F1 0.681). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632 with resnet50). ViT-L beat ResNet50 (0.721 vs 0.688). The RNA encoder had by far the largest effect: switching scvi_n200 to scGPT dropped accuracy to 0.507. The third RNA option, pca_n2000, has never been tested, and fusion type is also still untested. 2) Test: config_044 keeps the best pipeline and swaps only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. 1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_013 (scVI-n200 + ViT-L + transformer + concat, acc 0.721, F1 0.681). The comparisons each changed one setting from a near-identical baseline and point the same way. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632 with ResNet50). ViT-L beat ResNet50 (0.721 vs 0.688). scVI was clearly the best RNA encoder, ahead of PCA (0.599) and scGPT (0.507). Fusion is the one major design choice not yet tested: every run so far used concat. 2. Question: config_037 keeps the best configuration and swaps concat for weighted fusion. Why now: this exploits the strongest direction while closing the last open uncertainty about the design space. The result also tells us whether later runs should use weighted fusion. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy. It is only slightly ahead of its concat twin, config_013 (0.721), so fusion type matters little. The other design choices have clear effects. Transformer beat avgpool by about 5.6 points (0.688 vs 0.632 with ResNet50). ViT-L beat ResNet50 (0.721 vs 0.688). The RNA encoder matters most: swapping scVI for PCA cost about 12 points, and swapping in scGPT cost about 21 points. So weak RNA features actively drag down the fused model, and we do not yet know how much even the scVI branch adds over images alone. 2) This experiment: The image-only counterpart of the best setup (ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer) isolates the RNA contribution. If it comes close to or exceeds 0.725, that points the remaining budget toward image-centric variants. If it falls clearly below, multimodal scVI fusion is confirmed as essential, and the last runs can refine around config_037. 3) Why now: Most single-step changes around the best configuration have already been tested, and the untested ones (avgpool, single-profile) are expected to do worse. The modality question is the largest remaining uncertainty and has a plausible chance of matching the best. Expected cost is low: below the roughly 3.6–4.7 GPU hours of the ViT-L multimodal runs, since there is no RNA branch or fusion step.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Weighted and concat fusion score almost the same (0.725 vs 0.721). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 5.6 points with ResNet50. scVI is clearly the best RNA encoder, and ViT-L beats ResNet50. Image-only scored very low (0.26), so RNA appears to carry most of the signal. The main open question is how much the image branch actually adds. This experiment tests RNA-only scVI with transformer aggregation, the RNA half of the best setup. If it gets close to or above 0.725, image fusion adds little or adds noise, and the last experiment should move toward RNA-centric variants. If it falls well below, the image branch matters and the last experiment should refine the multimodal setup (for example, the avgpool variant or single-profile versions). The other untested options are less promising: avgpool, ResNet50, and the pca/scGPT encoders were all worse earlier, and fusion type barely matters. Expected cost is low, likely about 1.5-3 GPU hours since it drops the image encoder and fusion, compared with about 3.6-5 hours for multimodal ViT-L runs. That makes it an informative, cheap experiment with a real chance of matching the current best.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_037 (scVI_n200 + ViT-L, multiprofile transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Weighted fusion edged out concat (0.721). ViT-L beat ResNet50 (0.721 vs 0.688). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632). scVI beat PCA and scGPT by a wide margin. If it wins, the gain matters; if not, the last experiment can go back to refining multiprofile. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_037 at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. It uses scVI RNA, ViT-L image, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion, all multiprofile. One-factor comparisons point the same way. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 0.056 (resnet50 concat). ViT-L beat ResNet50 by about 0.033. scVI clearly beat PCA and scGPT. Weighted fusion edged out concat by about 0.004, which is within noise. Multimodal multiprofile beat both single-modality and singleprofile settings. 2) What this tests: none of the untested options changes only a winning component, so every remaining choice gives up one good factor. config_036 keeps scVI, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion and swaps only the image encoder to ResNet50. Expected cost is moderate, about 4–5 GPU hours, similar to config_045 (5.16 h) and a bit above config_037 (3.6 h). 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet. Without measurements, the best prior is that combining RNA and image data (multimodal) and pooling multiple profiles per sample (multiprofile) will give the highest accuracy, but this is untested. 2. What this tests: config_039 is a mid-cost member of that family. It uses scVI-200 RNA embeddings, a ResNet50 image encoder, average pooling and concat fusion. Why it is the best next experiment: if it performs well, later runs can upgrade one component at a time (image encoder to ViT-L, aggregation to transformer, fusion to weighted) and attribute any gain to that change. 1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile setup (scVI-200 + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1 for 7.27 GPU hours. Why now: aggregation is a central design choice for every multiprofile configuration, so the answer will guide much of the remaining search. 1) Evidence: with scvi_n200, resnet50 and concat held fixed, transformer aggregation (0.688 acc, 0.659 F1) clearly beat avgpool (0.632 acc, 0.607 F1). 1) Evidence: the transformer aggregator clearly beat avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632 with resnet50). Switching the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l gave a further gain to 0.721, with F1 rising the same way (0.682). All three runs used scvi_n200 RNA and concat fusion, so neither the RNA encoder nor the fusion choice has been tested. 2) This experiment keeps the current best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, vit_l, transformer, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to scgpt. 1. Evidence: Within the scvi_n200 multiprofile setup, the transformer beat avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632) and ViT-L beat ResNet50 (0.721 vs 0.688). Weighted fusion is slightly ahead of concat (0.725 vs 0.721, with F1 also slightly higher), but that gap is small and should not be overread. Test: config_009 keeps the current best setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, weighted fusion) and swaps scvi_n200 for pca_n2000. Why now: The RNA encoder has shown the largest effect on accuracy, so resolving the remaining encoder option is the most valuable question. If PCA wins, 4 runs remain to refine around it. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_024 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted fusion, 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1). Concat fusion scored almost the same (0.721), so fusion type is a minor factor. The RNA encoder matters a lot: scVI clearly beats PCA and scGPT. A transformer beat avgpool with ResNet50, and ViT-L beat ResNet50. All six runs used multiprofile, so the profile setting has never been tested. 2) This run keeps the best encoders and fusion (scVI + ViT-L + weighted) but switches to the singleprofile setting. It tests whether multiprofile aggregation is actually needed or whether a simpler per-profile model matches or beats it. 3) Profile setting is the largest unexplored design choice, so this is the most informative remaining experiment. It could also find a new best. If it underperforms, that confirms multiprofile with transformer as the right setting, and the last two runs can go to refinements such as an image-only ViT-L transformer baseline. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_024 at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. It uses multimodal, multiprofile data with scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, a transformer aggregator and weighted fusion. Within this family the choices are fairly settled. ViT-L beat ResNet50 (0.721 vs 0.688), transformer beat avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632) and multiprofile beat singleprofile (0.725 vs 0.537). Weighted and concat fusion were nearly tied (0.725 vs 0.721). The RNA encoder matters a lot: swapping in scGPT dropped accuracy to 0.507 and PCA to 0.586. So a weak RNA branch clearly hurts, but we have not tested whether even scVI RNA adds anything over images alone. 2) This experiment tests the image-only version of the best setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer aggregation). It shows whether the image branch carries most of the signal and could match or beat the multimodal best. It also tells us how much the RNA modality actually contributes. 3) The remaining nearby multimodal variants look unlikely to beat 0.725. ResNet50 with weighted fusion and avgpool with ViT-L both swap in components that already lost in direct comparisons. Removing a modality is the largest untested design choice, and it is plausible it could win. Expected cost is low to moderate: probably below the roughly 3.6–4.7 GPU hours of the multimodal ViT-L transformer runs, since there is no RNA branch or fusion step. If it underperforms, the last two experiments can go back to refining the multimodal setup.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_024 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Single runs suggest that scVI clearly beats PCA and scGPT, that transformer aggregation beats avgpool by about 0.056, that ViT-L beats ResNet50 by about 0.033, and that weighted fusion edges out concat by a small margin. The remaining untested variants of the leading setup each change one of these choices. 2. Test: config_031 keeps scVI, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion, and swaps the image encoder to ResNet50. This checks whether the ViT-L advantage holds under weighted fusion, since the ResNet50 comparison was only measured once, with concat fusion. 3. Why now: Among the one-step variants, this one changes the design choice with the smaller observed penalty. An avgpool swap (config_019) is expected to land lower, around 0.67. RNA-only and singleprofile options have trailed badly. That gives config_031 the best remaining chance of matching or beating 0.725. Expected cost is moderate to high, roughly 5 GPU hours, based on the earlier ResNet50 multiprofile runs. That is somewhat more than the ViT-L runs, but justified by its higher expected accuracy.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_024 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion; acc 0.725, F1 0.685). Its weighted-fusion counterpart with ResNet50 (config_031) is close behind (acc 0.713, F1 0.695). Within the scVI family, the transformer clearly beat avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632 under ResNet50 concat). The remaining untested scVI multiprofile options all use avgpool, so they are likely below the current best. scGPT and PCA encoders performed poorly. Image-only reached just 0.26, so most of the signal appears to come from the scVI RNA representation. 2) Test: config_036 is RNA-only scVI with multiprofile transformer aggregation. It measures how much the image branch actually adds on top of the strongest RNA encoder with the best aggregator. Image features look weak, so RNA-only has some chance of matching or edging past the multimodal models by avoiding noise from the image branch. 3) Why this is the best final experiment: every remaining option is unlikely to beat 0.725. This one has a non-trivial chance of competing while also answering an open ablation question.
