1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so every design axis is uncertain. These axes are modality, single vs. multiprofile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation and fusion. My prior is that multimodal, multiprofile models are the most likely to reach the highest accuracy, but this has not been tested. 2. What this tests: config_020 is a mid-range anchor inside that likely-best region. It uses multimodal input, multiprofile training, the compact scVI (200-dim) RNA encoder, ResNet50 images, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. Its result will show whether the multimodal-multiprofile family performs well. Later runs can then vary one axis at a time against it, such as a transformer aggregator, ViT-L images, other RNA encoders, weighted fusion, or unimodal and single-profile ablations. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: it starts in the region most likely to contain the winner while avoiding the most expensive options (transformer aggregation plus ViT-L). That keeps the first run's cost moderate. Expected relative cost is medium: multiprofile and multimodal processing add cost, but the low-dimensional scVI input, ResNet50 and avgpool keep it well below transformer or ViT-L variants.

1. Evidence: we have one result. The multimodal multiprofile model (scVI-200 + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1 for 7.27 GPU hours. That gives a baseline but says nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2. Test: config_039 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to a transformer, with everything else held fixed. This shows whether learned attention across profiles beats simple mean pooling, which is a key design choice for multiprofile models. 3. Why now: a single-variable change gives a clean answer, and the result decides which aggregation to carry into later tests of image encoder (ViT-L), RNA encoder and fusion. Keeping ResNet50 avoids the larger cost of ViT-L. Expected cost is moderately higher than the baseline, roughly 1.2–1.5x (about 9–11 GPU hours), because of the transformer aggregator.

Evidence: in two otherwise identical scvi_n200 + resnet50 + concat multiprofile runs, transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 5.6 points in accuracy (0.688 vs 0.632). F1 improved too (0.659 vs 0.607). The transformer run was also cheaper (5.16 vs 7.27 GPU h). That is only one comparison, but it is a reasonable signal, so I will keep transformer aggregation as the working base. The largest untested design choice is now the image encoder. This experiment changes only that, swapping resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l while keeping scvi_n200, transformer and concat fixed. It will show whether a stronger, larger image representation adds accuracy on top of the current best setup. A single-variable change gives a clean answer and could produce a new best directly. Fusion (weighted) and RNA encoder (scGPT, PCA) can be tested in later runs from whichever base wins. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_039, likely around 6–9 GPU h, because ViT-L features are larger. 1) Evidence: three multimodal multiprofile runs suggest two trends. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632 with ResNet50). ViT-L beat ResNet50 under transformer aggregation (0.721 vs 0.688, with F1 also higher). The best so far is config_009 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + concat). Each trend rests on only one comparison, and fusion has never been varied: all runs used concat. 2) Test: config_046 keeps config_009 fixed and switches only the fusion to weighted. Evidence: so far the transformer aggregator beat avgpool by about 5.6 points (0.688 vs 0.632, ResNet50/concat), and ViT-L beat ResNet50 by about 3.3 points (0.721 vs 0.688). Weighted fusion beat concat by only about 0.4 points (0.725 vs 0.721), with F1 moving the same way. That gap is small, so I treat weighted and concat as roughly tied. Experiment: config_023 keeps the current best backbone (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) and swaps scVI for scGPT. Changing only one factor isolates whether a foundation-model RNA embedding beats scVI. Why now: the RNA encoder could plausibly give a gain similar to the image-encoder change. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_046 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted fusion), at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. ViT-L clearly beat ResNet50, transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool, and weighted fusion was slightly better than concat (0.725 vs 0.721), as well as cheaper. 1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (0.71-0.725, versus 0.52 for scgpt and 0.59 for pca_n2000). Swapping to resnet50, avgpool or concat fusion each lowered accuracy slightly, so those multiprofile variants look close to exhausted. 2) Open question: every multimodal run so far used multiprofile, so the profile setting has never been tested. config_042 keeps the best encoders and weighted fusion but uses singleprofile input. This directly tests whether multiprofile aggregation is actually needed. 3) Why now: the remaining multiprofile scvi variants (resnet50 or avgpool combinations) are each predicted to fall below 0.725 from the observed one-factor changes. Testing the unexplored profile dimension has more chance of an upside surprise and is informative for the final experiment either way. Expected cost: relatively low, likely below the roughly 3.6-4.8 GPU hours of the multiprofile vit_l runs, since there is no aggregation over multiple profiles.

1) Evidence: The scVI-n200 RNA encoder with multiprofile transformer aggregation is clearly the strongest family. config_037 (ViT-L, weighted) is best at 0.725 accuracy, and config_035 (ViT-L, concat) reached 0.721. The ResNet50 weighted variant (config_008) scored 0.713 accuracy but had the highest F1 so far (0.695), so ResNet50 is competitive and may give better-balanced predictions. Swapping out scVI (scGPT 0.52, PCA 0.59), dropping a modality (RNA-only 0.65) or going single-profile (0.54) all hurt badly. Avgpool was also weaker than transformer (0.706). 2) Test: The one untested combination of the strong components is scVI + ResNet50 + transformer + concat fusion. It asks whether concat fusion pairs better with ResNet50 features than weighted fusion did. Weighted versus concat differed by only about 0.004 with ViT-L, so an interaction with the image encoder could plausibly push past 0.725. 3) Budget: With only two experiments left, exploiting the proven scVI/transformer/multimodal backbone has the best chance of improving the best accuracy. Weaker-family or image-only runs are unlikely to win. Expected cost is relatively high, about 5–6 GPU hours, similar to config_008 (6.22), because ResNet50 multimodal runs have been the slowest so far. That cost is justified because this is among the most likely untested configurations to match or beat the current best.

1. Evidence: the scVI-n200 RNA encoder is clearly the strongest choice. Every top result uses it, while pairing ViT-L with scGPT or PCA dropped accuracy to 0.52–0.59. ImageNet ViT-L beat ResNet50 under both fusion types. Transformer aggregation (0.725) edged out avgpool (0.706), and weighted fusion (0.725) and concat (0.721) are nearly tied. Image-only models are untested, but the large RNA-encoder effect suggests RNA carries most of the signal, so an image-only model is unlikely to beat 0.725. 2. Test: the only untested scVI + ViT-L multiprofile combination is avgpool with concat fusion. It tells us whether concat fusion makes up for avgpool's weaker aggregation. 3. Why this one: with one experiment left, only the best accuracy counts. This configuration stays inside the best-performing region (scVI + ViT-L + multiprofile) and has a small chance of matching or beating 0.725. The ResNet50 or non-scVI alternatives have lower expected accuracy. Expected cost is moderate, about 4.5–5 GPU hours, similar to config_013 and config_035.

1) There are no completed experiments, so there is no evidence yet on any design axis: modality, single vs multi-profile, encoders, aggregation or fusion. 2) config_044 is a strong anchor point. It is multimodal and multiprofile with transformer aggregation, which usually gives the highest accuracy when aggregating cell profiles. It pairs this with the cheaper encoders (PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50 image) and simple concat fusion. Later experiments can then vary one factor at a time from this baseline: avgpool vs transformer, weighted vs concat, scGPT/scVI vs PCA, ViT-L vs ResNet50, and single-profile or unimodal ablations. 3) Starting from a likely high-performing but moderately priced setup gives a competitive early best score while keeping GPU hours down. It also anchors the comparisons for the remaining 9 experiments. Expected relative cost is medium: multiprofile transformer aggregation with multimodal inputs costs more than single-profile or unimodal runs, but less than variants using ViT-L or scGPT.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. Config_044 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50 images, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) reached 0.579 accuracy and 0.563 F1 for 6.76 GPU hours. A single point says nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2) Test: config_002 is a one-factor change that swaps the PCA RNA encoder for the pretrained scGPT foundation-model embedding and keeps everything else fixed. Any accuracy or F1 difference can therefore be attributed to the RNA representation. This is likely one of the most influential choices, and it determines which encoder to carry forward in later combinations with ViT-L images, avgpool aggregation or weighted fusion. 3) Why now: the result points directly at the more promising RNA encoder while keeping the strong multiprofile-transformer backbone. With 8 experiments left, establishing the RNA encoder first lets later runs build on the stronger choice. Expected cost is similar to or slightly above config_044 (about 7 to 8 GPU hours), because scGPT embeddings are larger than PCA features but the rest of the architecture is unchanged.

1) Evidence: with resnet50, transformer aggregation and concat fusion held fixed, pca_n2000 RNA beat scgpt by about 11 points in accuracy (0.579 vs 0.471), and F1 showed the same gap. That makes pca_n2000 the current anchor. The image encoder is the other major untested axis and could have a similarly large effect. 2) This experiment changes one factor from the best configuration, config_044, swapping resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l. It tests whether stronger ViT-L image features improve accuracy while RNA encoder, aggregation and fusion stay the same, so any difference can be attributed to the image encoder. 3) A large-effect design choice is the best use of an early slot. Whichever image encoder wins can then serve as the base for cheaper refinements such as weighted fusion or avgpool aggregation. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_044 (about 7-9 GPU hours versus 6.76) because ViT-L produces larger image representations. That cost is justified because this configuration is a plausible candidate for the best result.

1. Evidence: The RNA encoder is the strongest factor seen so far. With the same resnet50, transformer and concat setup, pca_n2000 reached 0.579 accuracy versus 0.471 for scGPT, a gap of about 0.11. Swapping the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l gave a smaller gain, to 0.599 accuracy and 0.578 F1 (config_042, the current best). The third RNA encoder, scvi_n200, has never been tested. 2. Test: config_007 keeps config_042's best setup (vit_l, multiprofile, transformer, concat) and swaps only the RNA encoder to scvi_n200. This is a clean one-variable comparison of RNA encoders on the strongest backbone. 3. Why now: the RNA encoder has shown the largest effect, so leaving scVI untested is the biggest remaining uncertainty that could change the overall best. Fusion type (weighted) and aggregation (avgpool) are likely smaller refinements that can be tested in later experiments on whichever RNA encoder wins. Expected cost is low to moderate, similar to or slightly below config_042's 4.76 GPU hours, because the 200-dimensional scVI input is compact. That makes it cheaper than the resnet50 and scGPT runs (6.76 and 9.06 GPU hours).

1) Evidence: The strongest signal so far is the RNA encoder. scVI (config_007, 0.721 acc / 0.681 F1) clearly beats PCA (0.599) and scGPT (0.471) when combined with ViT-L, transformer aggregation and concat fusion. ViT-L also slightly beats ResNet50 and is cheaper (about 4.7 vs 6.8 GPU h). All four experiments used transformer aggregation and concat fusion, so neither choice has been tested. 2) This run keeps the best scVI + ViT-L + concat backbone and swaps transformer aggregation for avgpool. It tests whether the more complex aggregator is actually needed for multiprofile inputs. 3) Aggregation is a major untested design choice, and the experiment exploits the best region found so far. Avgpool should be somewhat cheaper than transformer aggregation, roughly 3.5 to 4.5 GPU h versus 4.65 for config_007, so it also checks whether a cheaper setup matches or beats it. The result will tell us whether to explore fusion (config_014 or config_019) on top of transformer or avgpool in the remaining runs.

Evidence: scvi_n200 RNA paired with the imagenet_vit_l image encoder is clearly the strongest combination so far. Transformer and avgpool aggregation scored about the same (0.721 vs 0.715 accuracy), and avgpool had slightly higher F1 (0.687 vs 0.681) at lower cost (4.49 vs 4.65 GPU hours). Fusion is the main design choice still untested: every run so far used concat. Test: config_019 keeps the best scvi_n200 + ViT-L multiprofile setup with the cheaper avgpool aggregation and switches fusion to weighted. This isolates whether weighted fusion can push past about 0.72. Why now: it exploits the best-performing region while settling an open design question, which leaves 3 runs to follow up (e.g., weighted fusion with transformer aggregation if it helps). Expected cost is low, similar to config_034 at roughly 4.5 GPU hours, and among the cheapest multimodal multiprofile options.

1) Evidence: The RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. scvi_n200 reaches 0.706-0.721, while pca_n2000 is about 0.58-0.60 and scgpt is 0.47. imagenet_vit_l beat resnet50 under pca (0.599 vs 0.579) and was cheaper. With scvi plus ViT-L, transformer and avgpool aggregation give nearly the same result (0.721 vs 0.715). Weighted fusion was slightly below concat with avgpool (0.706 vs 0.715), but that is a single, small difference. 2) This experiment: It tests weighted fusion with transformer aggregation on the current best backbone (scvi_n200 + ViT-L). It is the last untested one-factor variant of the top configuration that keeps both of the strongest encoders. It shows whether learned modality weighting interacts with transformer aggregation to beat 0.721, or confirms that concat is the better fusion choice. 3) Why now: Weaker encoders, single-profile and unimodal options look unlikely to beat 0.72. Exploiting the best region is therefore the most promising use of the remaining budget. Expected cost is moderate and similar to config_007, about 4.7-5 GPU hours.

Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor. With ViT-L, moving from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 raised accuracy from about 0.60 to about 0.72. All four aggregation and fusion combinations of scvi_n200 + ViT-L multiprofile are now tested and fall within a narrow 0.706–0.725 band (F1 0.667–0.687), so that local neighborhood is largely exhausted. ViT-L beat ResNet50 for PCA (0.599 vs 0.579), so swapping in ResNet50 with scVI is unlikely to raise the best result. The main untested question is how much the image modality actually contributes, given how strongly RNA drives performance. This experiment runs scvi_n200 RNA-only with transformer aggregation, matching the best setup without the image branch. If it matches or beats 0.725, that is a direct gain. If it is clearly worse, it confirms that the multimodal design matters, and I can use the last experiment on a refinement near the current best. Expected cost is lower than the multimodal runs (roughly 2–3 GPU hours versus 3.6–4.8), since there is no image encoder or fusion.

Evidence: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder. scVI runs scored 0.706-0.725, versus about 0.58-0.60 for PCA and 0.47 for scGPT. The scVI + ViT-L multiprofile grid is now complete (aggregation x fusion), and its four results fall within about 0.02 of each other. The best is config_014 (transformer + weighted, 0.725 acc), so more aggregation or fusion tweaks with ViT-L offer little upside. The image encoder is the main design choice not yet tested with scVI. With PCA, ResNet50 trailed ViT-L by only about 0.02, a gap small enough that it may not carry over to the stronger RNA encoder. This experiment pairs scVI with ResNet50 using the best-performing transformer + weighted setup. It tests whether a different image representation complements scVI better. It is the only remaining multiprofile multimodal direction with a realistic chance of beating 0.725; single-profile and scGPT options look clearly weaker from current evidence. Expected cost is moderate to high. Past ResNet50 multiprofile runs took about 6.8-9 GPU hours, above the 3.6-4.8 hours of the ViT-L runs. This is acceptable because it addresses the last important open axis, and the final experiment can then exploit whichever image encoder wins.

1. Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder. Its multimodal multiprofile runs scored 0.706-0.725, compared with 0.47-0.60 for pca and scgpt and 0.653 for RNA-only. The current best is config_014 (scvi + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725). Aggregation and fusion choices differ by only about 1-2 points, so they are within noise. The scvi + ResNet50 + transformer + weighted run (config_032) reached 0.713 accuracy with the highest F1 seen so far (0.695), which suggests ResNet50 pairs well with scvi. 2. Test: config_016 completes the scvi/ResNet50/transformer pairing with concat fusion. Concat matched weighted fusion on the ViT-L transformer runs (0.721 vs 0.725) and slightly beat it under avgpool (0.715 vs 0.706). This gives another realistic shot at a new best within the strongest region of the search space. 3. Why it is the best final use: with no budget left, exploiting the proven scvi multimodal multiprofile region is the most likely route to beating 0.725. Untested single-profile variants are cheaper but unlikely to beat multiprofile aggregation. Expected cost is moderately high, about 6-6.5 GPU hours, similar to config_032 because of the ResNet50 multiprofile transformer pipeline.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet, so I am relying on priors. The design choices most likely to drive accuracy are multimodal versus unimodal input and multiprofile versus single-profile input. Combining RNA and imaging data across several profiles, with learned transformer aggregation, is the most plausible high-accuracy region. 2. What this tests: config_001 combines multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 RNA embeddings, a ResNet50 image encoder, transformer aggregation and concat fusion. It is a strong mid-cost anchor in that region. Later runs can each change one factor from it: avgpool versus transformer, weighted versus concat fusion, ViT-L versus ResNet50, or unimodal and single-profile ablations. 3. Why now: it targets the likely best region without starting with the most expensive ViT-L combinations. That gives an early high baseline while leaving budget for one-factor comparisons. Expected relative cost is medium-high: multiprofile transformer aggregation over two modalities costs more than unimodal or single-profile runs. The compact scVI and ResNet50 encoders keep it cheaper than the ViT-L or scGPT variants.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: we have only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile baseline (scVI-200 + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) reached 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1 at 5.16 GPU hours. With a single data point, every design choice is still uncertain. The image encoder is probably among the highest-impact choices, since ImageNet ViT-L gives much richer representations than ResNet50. 2. What this tests: config_049 changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ViT-L and keeps everything else identical. Any change in accuracy can therefore be attributed to the image encoder. The result will tell us which backbone to carry into later multimodal experiments. 3. Why now: this is the clearest single-factor test of an important choice, and it also has the most likely upside for raising the best accuracy. Cheaper ablations such as avgpool, RNA-only or a different RNA encoder can follow once we know which image backbone to use. Expected cost is about 1.5–2x config_001, roughly 8–10 GPU hours, because ViT-L features are larger and multiprofile transformer aggregation adds cost. That is justified because this configuration is a strong candidate for the best performer.

Evidence: the two runs differ only in image encoder. ImageNet ViT-L beat ResNet50 (val acc 0.721 vs 0.688, F1 0.681 vs 0.659) and was also slightly cheaper (4.65 vs 5.16 GPU hours). This is a single comparison, but it is enough to keep ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer aggregation and concat fusion as the working base. The RNA encoder is the largest untested design choice so far, since only scVI has been tried. This experiment swaps scVI for the scGPT foundation-model embedding and keeps everything else fixed, so any change can be attributed to the RNA encoder. That is the best use of the next run because it tests a high-impact axis with clear upside while building on the best configuration found so far. Fusion type (weighted vs concat, config_017) and aggregation (avgpool) can be tuned afterward on whichever RNA encoder wins. Expected cost is similar to config_049, roughly 4.5–5.5 GPU hours, possibly slightly more if scGPT embeddings are larger.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_049 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. ViT-L beat ResNet50 by about 3 points. The RNA encoder had by far the largest effect: swapping scVI for scGPT dropped accuracy to 0.507. The third RNA option, PCA (2,000 components), is completely untested, so the RNA encoder is the largest remaining uncertainty. 2) Test: config_010 keeps config_049's setup and changes only the RNA encoder to PCA. This isolates whether PCA matches or beats scVI. 3) Why now: because the RNA encoder shifts accuracy so much, settling it first gives the most information and the best chance of a new top score. Fusion (weighted vs concat) and aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) can be refined afterwards on the winning encoder. Expected cost is similar to config_049, roughly 4.5–5 GPU hours (multiprofile, multimodal, transformer). PCA features may make it slightly cheaper than scVI, which is attractive at similar or better accuracy.

1) Evidence: the RNA encoder matters a lot. With ViT-L, transformer aggregation and concat fusion held fixed, scVI reached 0.721 accuracy, PCA 0.599 and scGPT 0.507. Swapping to ResNet50 with scVI gave 0.688, so ViT-L looks better, and its run was no more expensive. Fusion and aggregation have not been varied at all: every run so far used transformer aggregation with concat fusion. 2) This run keeps the best setup (scVI + ViT-L + transformer) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. It isolates whether learned modality weighting improves on plain concatenation. That is plausible here because the two modalities differ clearly in quality, as the large encoder-dependent swings suggest. 3) Fusion is the most important untested design choice around the current best, so this is the right balance between exploiting the best setup and resolving a key uncertainty. The result will guide whether the avgpool aggregation test (config_012 or config_043) should use concat or weighted fusion. Expected cost is about the same as config_049, roughly 4.5–5 GPU hours. Weighted fusion adds negligible overhead.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder. It reached 0.72 with ViT-L, versus 0.60 for pca_n2000 and 0.51 for scgpt. ViT-L beats resnet50 (0.721 vs 0.688 with concat). Weighted fusion is marginally better than concat (0.725 vs 0.721, F1 0.685 vs 0.681) and was cheaper (3.60 vs 4.65 GPU hours). Aggregation is the main untested design choice: every run so far used the transformer. 2) Test: config_012 keeps the best setup (scvi_n200 + ViT-L + weighted fusion) and swaps the transformer for avgpool. This shows whether the transformer adds accuracy or whether simple pooling matches or beats it. 3) Why now: it exploits the best-known components while resolving a key uncertainty, and the result will guide the last 4 experiments (e.g., whether to test singleprofile next). Expected cost is similar to or lower than the transformer runs, roughly 3–3.5 GPU hours, because avgpool is a lighter aggregator than the transformer.

1) Evidence: every experiment so far has been multiprofile. Within that setting the best configuration is clear: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted (config_017, 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1). The RNA encoder matters a lot: scvi is far ahead of pca and scgpt. ViT-L beats ResNet50, transformer slightly beats avgpool, and weighted fusion is marginally better than concat. The profile setting is the one major design axis that has never been tested. 2) This experiment keeps the best encoder and fusion choices fixed and switches to single-profile (no aggregation). That isolates how much multiprofile aggregation actually contributes. 3) Remaining gains from the encoder, aggregation and fusion axes look small and are largely settled. Testing the untested profile axis reduces the most uncertainty about whether a better region exists. It is also likely the cheapest run so far, because no multiprofile aggregation is needed (well below the ~3.6–5 GPU hours of the multiprofile runs). If it underperforms, it confirms multiprofile, and the last two experiments can go to refinements such as unimodal ablations.

1) Evidence: The best result is config_017 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Each tested axis favours the choices it already uses. The RNA encoder matters most: scVI scored 0.72, PCA 0.60 and scGPT 0.51. Image encoder (ViT-L over ResNet50), aggregation (transformer over avgpool) and fusion (weighted over concat) give smaller gains of 0.004 to 0.033. Multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile. So the remaining multimodal scVI variants (config_026, 043, 013, 045) each swap in a choice that was weaker, and are predicted to land below 0.725. 2) Uncertainty: The large RNA-encoder sensitivity suggests performance is driven mainly by the RNA representation, but no unimodal baseline has been tested. This experiment tests whether scVI RNA-only with transformer aggregation is competitive with, or better than, the multimodal model. That would show whether the image branch adds signal or noise, and would inform the final experiment, either a unimodal refinement or a final multimodal check. 3) Why now: It is the highest-uncertainty experiment that could still produce a new best, unlike the predictable multimodal variants. With 2 runs left, it also leaves one run for exploitation. Expected cost is lower than the multimodal multiprofile runs (about 2 to 3.5 GPU hours versus 3.6 to 5.2) because there is no ViT-L image branch.

1) Evidence: the best result is config_017 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. The nearby variants all scored lower. Concat fusion gave 0.721, avgpool gave 0.706 and ResNet50 gave 0.688. The scGPT (0.507) and PCA (0.599) RNA encoders were much worse, and single-profile was much worse (0.537). So the remaining untested neighbours of config_017 (config_043 avgpool+concat, config_026 ResNet50+weighted, config_027 PCA) are each expected to fall below it. 2) Open question: the main untested design choice is whether the ViT-L image modality alone, with transformer aggregation, matches or beats fusion. RNA-only reached 0.653, and a weak RNA encoder clearly dragged multimodal models down, so RNA may add noise as well as signal. This experiment measures how much image-only contributes. 3) Why now: of the remaining options, it has the highest outcome variance and a plausible chance of exceeding 0.725. It also tells the final experiment whether to keep RNA. Expected cost is moderate, about 2-3 GPU hours, cheaper than multimodal multiprofile runs (3.6-5.2 h) because no RNA branch or fusion is trained.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_017 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy. scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (scGPT 0.507, PCA 0.599). ViT-L beats ResNet50 by about 0.033 under concat fusion. Transformer beats avgpool by about 0.019 under weighted fusion. Weighted and concat fusion are nearly tied (0.725 vs 0.721). Multiprofile and multimodal settings are essential. Every high-value direction near the top has been tested except a few scVI multimodal variants.

2. What this tests: config_043 (scVI + ViT-L + avgpool + concat) is the remaining untested combination closest to the best configuration. It changes only the cheaper avgpool aggregation and keeps the stronger ViT-L image encoder. Because fusion choice made little difference, its expected accuracy (~0.70) is above the ResNet50 alternative config_026 (~0.69). It also checks whether avgpool's penalty depends on fusion type.

3. Why it is the best final pick: Beating 0.725 is unlikely with any remaining option, but config_043 has the highest expected accuracy among them and so the best chance of a new maximum through run-to-run variance. Expected cost is moderate, about 4.5–5 GPU hours, similar to config_012.

1. Evidence: no experiments have been run yet, so we have no data on any design factor (modality, single vs. multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation, fusion). 2. What this tests: config_036 is a central anchor. It is multimodal and multiprofile, which I expect to be competitive, and uses a mid-sized RNA encoder (scVI with 200 dimensions) and a strong image encoder (ImageNet ViT-L). It also uses the simplest aggregation (average pooling) and the simplest fusion (concatenation). This gives a reasonably strong first result without committing to the more complex transformer aggregation or weighted fusion. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: later experiments can change one factor at a time from this anchor. That includes switching to RNA-only or image-only, to single-profile, to transformer aggregation, to weighted fusion, or to a different encoder. Each of these comparisons then isolates the effect of one design choice, which is more informative under a limited budget than starting from a minimal baseline far from the likely optimum.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: There is only one result so far. config_036 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) reached 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. We do not yet know how much of this comes from the image branch versus the RNA branch. 2) What this tests: config_005 keeps everything the same except that it removes the image modality (RNA-only, scVI, multiprofile, avgpool). This one-factor change shows directly whether adding images improves on RNA alone. 3) Why now: Whether to use multimodal input is the decision with the widest consequences in this search space. Answering it first tells us whether to spend the remaining budget on fusion, image-encoder and aggregation variants, or on RNA-encoder choices. That makes it a better use of one experiment than fine-tuning secondary settings such as aggregation or fusion type.

Evidence: with the scvi_n200 RNA encoder and avgpool aggregation fixed, multimodal concat with imagenet_vit_l scored 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. RNA-only scored 0.650 accuracy and 0.628 F1, about 6.5 points lower. Uncertainty: we cannot yet tell whether this gain comes from combining the two modalities or simply from the image features alone. Test: image-only imagenet_vit_l with avgpool uses the same image encoder, profile setting and aggregation, so it completes the RNA-only, image-only and multimodal comparison. If image-only is close to 0.715, RNA adds little, and future runs should focus on image encoders and aggregation rather than RNA encoders or fusion. If it is clearly lower, the two modalities are complementary, and tuning fusion, aggregation and RNA encoder within multimodal configurations is justified. Why now: this question decides which design dimensions deserve the remaining budget, so it is a better use of one experiment than a single-dimension tweak of the current best.

1) Evidence: the multimodal model (config_036, scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) scored best at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. RNA-only reached 0.650 and image-only only 0.332, so the RNA signal carries most of the performance and the image adds a meaningful amount on top. Every run so far used avgpool, so we do not know whether aggregation matters. That is a major untested design axis for multiprofile inputs. 2) Test: config_038 changes only avgpool to transformer and keeps the rest of the best configuration fixed. This isolates whether learned, attention-based aggregation across profiles beats simple mean pooling. 3) Why now: it is a one-factor exploitation of the current best direction, so the result is directly interpretable as an aggregation effect. If the transformer helps, it becomes the new base for later tests of the RNA encoder (scGPT, PCA) and the fusion method (weighted). If it does not, we can confidently use the cheaper avgpool for the rest of the budget.

1. Evidence: multimodal models (about 0.715 to 0.721 accuracy) clearly beat RNA-only (0.650) and image-only (0.332). RNA is therefore the dominant signal and images add a useful complement. Aggregation looks like a minor factor: transformer beat avgpool by about 0.006 in accuracy, but avgpool had slightly higher F1, so the result is inconclusive. The RNA encoder has never been varied (only scvi_n200 tested), and RNA carries most of the predictive signal, so this is the largest untested source of uncertainty. 2. This experiment keeps the best multimodal setup (multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) and swaps scvi_n200 for scGPT. Any change can then be attributed to the RNA encoder alone. 3. Under a limited budget, this tests the design choice most likely to move performance substantially and stays within the promising multimodal region. Fusion type and image encoder are worth testing later, but they likely have smaller effects given that the image modality is weak.

1. Evidence: multimodal scVI plus ViT-L is the clear best direction, at about 0.715–0.721 accuracy. It beats RNA-only (0.650) by a wide margin, while image-only is weak (0.332). Avgpool and transformer aggregation are nearly tied: transformer is slightly higher on accuracy, avgpool slightly higher on F1, so aggregation looks minor. scGPT clearly underperforms scVI. Fusion strategy has never been tested; every multimodal run so far used concat. 2. This experiment keeps the best-performing setup (scVI, ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer) and swaps concat for weighted fusion. That isolates the effect of fusion directly. Weighted fusion is a plausible improvement here because the image modality is much weaker than RNA, and learned modality weighting could down-weight noisy image features. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: it builds on the strongest region of the search space and resolves an entirely unexplored design axis with a single controlled comparison. The result will tell us whether fusion should be fixed or explored further before spending runs on secondary axes such as the image encoder or PCA features.

1) Evidence: RNA is the dominant modality. RNA-only scvi reached 0.650, while image-only ViT-L reached only 0.332. The main open question is the image encoder: every image-containing run so far used ResNet50, and ImageNet ViT-L has never been tried. 2) This experiment keeps the current best setup fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swaps only ResNet50 for ViT-L. That isolates the image-encoder effect. 3) Best use of budget: it resolves the largest untested design choice with a single-variable change. It also has a realistic chance of beating the current best. Testing transformer aggregation (config_033) instead would probe a factor the evidence already suggests matters little.

Evidence: weighted fusion clearly beat concat with ResNet50 (0.678 vs 0.632). Swapping in ViT-L gave a further gain to 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1, the current best. Aggregation is still the open question: transformer was only marginally better than avgpool in the RNA-only setting (0.653 vs 0.650, essentially a tie), and it has never been tested in a multimodal model, where attention over multiple profiles of two modalities could matter more. Test: config_039 keeps the best setup (scVI, ViT-L, multiprofile, weighted fusion) and changes only avgpool to transformer. This isolates the effect of aggregation in the most promising region. Why now: it is a direct, controlled extension of the strongest evidence, so it could plausibly improve the best result. Either outcome also settles whether aggregation matters, so later budget can go elsewhere, such as testing PCA as the RNA encoder or running image-only baselines.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Weighted fusion beat concat (0.678 vs 0.632 with resnet50). ViT-L beat resnet50 (0.706 vs 0.678). Transformer aggregation added a further gain (0.725, the current best, config_039). The RNA encoder is the least explored important axis. scVI clearly beat scGPT in RNA-only runs (0.650 vs 0.530), but pca_n2000 has never been tested in any setting. 2. What this tests: config_027 keeps every component of the best configuration (ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) and swaps scVI for PCA-2000. This isolates whether a simpler, higher-dimensional RNA representation matches or beats scVI in the strongest multimodal setup. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: It is a one-factor change in the best-performing context. It resolves an unexplored design choice, and it could also yield a new best model. Tests of profile setting or image-only baselines are informative but less likely to change which configuration we pursue.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_039 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer, weighted, 0.725 accuracy / 0.685 F1). The best RNA-only run reaches about 0.653. Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L and concat for weighted fusion both helped. Swapping scVI for PCA in the same multimodal setup dropped accuracy to 0.586, so a weak RNA encoder can pull the fused model down. No image-only model has been tested, so we do not know how much of the multimodal gain comes from the image branch alone. 2) Test: config_015 is the image-only counterpart of the best model (ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer). It shows whether fusion beats the image modality alone. If image-only nears 0.72, RNA adds little and the search should focus on image and aggregation choices. If it is well below, fusion is confirmed as useful and RNA encoder quality matters. 3) Why now: Modality contribution is the largest untested design question, and this one run anchors the interpretation of every multimodal result. It is more informative than small fusion or aggregation tweaks around the current best.

1. Evidence: All nine experiments so far used multiprofile inputs. The best result is config_039 (scVI, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1. Across encoders and fusion types, scVI beats PCA and scGPT, ViT-L beats ResNet50, and weighted fusion beats concat. Transformer aggregation gives only small gains over avgpool (0.706 to 0.725 multimodal, 0.650 to 0.653 RNA-only). So the profile setting has never been tested, and we cannot tell whether multiprofile aggregation itself drives performance. 2. What it tests: config_035 keeps the strongest known components (scVI, ViT-L, weighted fusion) and switches to singleprofile. This isolates the value of the multiprofile design against the best avgpool and transformer results. 3. Why now: Tuning aggregation or fusion further is likely to yield small increments. This experiment instead resolves the largest untested design axis, which tells us whether the remaining budget should go to refining multiprofile variants or to exploring singleprofile alternatives.

1) No experiments have been run yet, so nothing is known about which design choices matter: modality (RNA, image, or both), single vs. multi-profile, encoder choice, aggregation, or fusion. 2) config_018 is a central baseline that sits in the middle of most axes. It is multimodal, uses multiple profiles with simple avgpool aggregation, the simplest encoders (pca_n2000 for RNA, resnet50 for images) and simple concat fusion. Its result can be compared later against single-modality runs (config_002, config_011), a single-profile run (config_016), and runs that change one component at a time: encoder (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L), aggregation (transformer) or fusion (weighted). 3) With a limited budget, a simple, interpretable baseline in the region likely to perform well is the most efficient first step. Each later experiment can then change one factor against it. Starting with a complex configuration would mix several factors together and make the results harder to interpret.

1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile config_018 (PCA + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. A single point says nothing about which modality drives this performance, so we cannot yet tell whether to prioritize RNA encoder choices (PCA, scVI, scGPT) or image encoder choices (ResNet50, ViT-L). 2. Test: config_002 is the matched RNA-only ablation. It uses the same PCA encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation, and drops only the image branch. Comparing it with config_018 measures how much the ResNet50 image features add on top of RNA. A large drop would mean images matter, so image encoder and fusion variants deserve priority. Little or no drop would mean RNA carries the signal, so RNA encoder upgrades are the better lever. 3. Why now: this controlled one-factor comparison resolves the most fundamental design question, whether multimodality helps. Its answer then guides how the remaining limited budget is split across the large encoder, aggregation and fusion space. Running it early avoids spending many runs on a dimension that may not matter.

1) Evidence: with all other settings fixed (multiprofile, PCA RNA, avgpool), adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion raised accuracy from 0.591 to 0.619 and F1 from 0.573 to 0.610. That suggests image features add useful signal, but it is a single comparison. Image encoder, RNA encoder, aggregation and fusion are all still untested. 2) This experiment changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, and keeps everything else the same as the current best (config_018). It tests whether a stronger image backbone extracts more of the image signal behind the gain. 3) Changing one factor from the best configuration gives a clean comparison and could also improve the best result. The image encoder is a major axis that appears across half of the remaining multimodal space, so the answer will help prune or prioritise many configurations. Aggregation and fusion are likely to be smaller effects and are better tested later.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multimodal fusion beats RNA-only by about 3-4 points in accuracy (0.619 and 0.629 vs 0.591), so multimodal multiprofile is the promising region. The two image encoders give similar results with mixed signals: ViT-L has higher accuracy (0.629 vs 0.619) but lower F1 (0.599 vs 0.610). That encoder difference is too small to over-interpret. Every run so far has used avgpool aggregation, concat fusion and the PCA RNA encoder, so these choices are completely unexplored. 2. What this tests: This run keeps the current best configuration (config_024: PCA + ViT-L, multiprofile, concat) and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. Any difference can therefore be attributed to aggregation, a choice that affects every multiprofile configuration. 3. Why this is the best next run: It exploits the strongest region found so far while answering a broad, previously untouched design question. A clear aggregation result will guide many later choices, including RNA encoder and fusion comparisons. A transformer that learns to weigh profiles could also produce a new best.

1. Evidence so far: multimodal models beat RNA-only (0.619 and 0.629 vs 0.591). With ViT-L, avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.629 vs 0.599), though this is a single comparison. ViT-L and ResNet50 gave similar results: ViT-L had slightly higher accuracy, ResNet50 slightly higher F1. The RNA encoder is the largest untested design choice, since every run so far used PCA. Weighted fusion and single-profile settings are also untested, but each is a single binary change. 2. This run keeps the best setup fixed (multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) and swaps only the RNA encoder from PCA to scGPT embeddings. It is a direct comparison with config_024, so it shows whether a pretrained RNA foundation model improves on PCA. 3. RNA is a core modality, and the choice of RNA representation could plausibly shift performance more than fusion type. Testing it inside the current best setup gives a clean comparison and keeps a real chance of beating the current best. If scGPT helps, later runs can extend it; if it does not, PCA can be kept and the budget moved to fusion and scVI.

1) Evidence so far: multimodal beats RNA-only (0.619-0.629 vs 0.591). PCA clearly beats scGPT (0.629 vs 0.518). Avgpool beats transformer aggregation on ViT-L (0.629 vs 0.599). ViT-L and ResNet50 are close: ViT-L is slightly higher on accuracy and ResNet50 slightly higher on F1, so encoder choice is unresolved and not worth another run yet. Fusion method has never been varied; every multimodal run used concat. 2) config_025 keeps the current best setup (multiprofile, PCA, ViT-L, avgpool) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. This gives a clean one-factor test of whether weighted fusion improves accuracy or the weaker F1 of the ViT-L configuration. 3) It is the best use of the budget because it explores a completely untested design dimension while staying in the most promising region. It has a real chance of becoming the new best, and either outcome tells us which fusion method to use for later tests of scVI and single-profile settings.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_025 (PCA-2000, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion; accuracy 0.635, F1 0.618). Within that setup, avgpool beat transformer aggregation by about 0.03. Weighted fusion beat concat by a small margin (+0.007 accuracy, +0.019 F1). ViT-L and ResNet50 are close. RNA encoder choice is the biggest effect observed: swapping PCA for scGPT cut accuracy by about 0.11. The scVI-200 encoder, however, has never been tested, so a high-impact axis remains open. 2) Test: config_037 keeps the best context fixed (ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) and changes only the RNA encoder to scVI-200. This isolates whether a learned low-dimensional latent space beats PCA, or whether pretrained and learned encoders generally underperform here. 3) Why now: RNA encoding is the axis with the largest demonstrated effect and an untested option. This single-factor change could raise the best score, or it could confirm PCA and let the remaining budget shift to secondary axes such as single- vs multiprofile.

Evidence: swapping the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 (config_025, 0.635) to scvi_n200 (config_037, 0.706) gave the largest gain so far, under ViT-L, avgpool and weighted fusion. That rests on a single run. Weighted fusion beat concat only slightly with PCA (0.635 vs 0.629), so it is unclear whether the scVI gain depends on weighted fusion. Test: config_036 is the same as config_037 but uses concat fusion. If it stays near 0.70, the scVI benefit is confirmed under a second fusion method and fusion matters little. If it drops, weighted fusion interacts with scVI and should be kept. Why now: this one controlled change replicates the most promising design choice and settles the fusion question in the best region of the search space, before spending budget on other image encoders or the transformer aggregator, which has so far hurt (0.599 vs 0.629).

1. Evidence and uncertainty: switching the RNA encoder to scVI gave the largest gain so far, with config_036 reaching 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Concat and weighted fusion perform similarly. Transformer aggregation scored below avgpool in the one pca/ViT-L comparison, and scGPT underperformed. Every experiment so far has used multiprofile, so whether multiprofile helps at all is completely untested. 2. What this tests: config_034 keeps the best setup (scVI + ImageNet ViT-L + concat) and changes only the profile setting to singleprofile. This cleanly measures the value of multiprofile aggregation in the strongest region of the search space. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: profile setting is a major design axis with no evidence yet. The other axes already have at least preliminary comparisons. A single-factor ablation at the current best configuration reduces the largest remaining uncertainty, and it could reveal a simpler, equally strong model.

1. Evidence: Switching the RNA encoder from PCA to scVI gave by far the largest gain (about 0.63 to 0.71). By comparison, image encoder choice (ResNet50 vs ViT-L, about 0.01), fusion type (concat vs weighted, under 0.01) and adding images to PCA RNA (0.59 to 0.62) produced small effects. Avgpool beat transformer aggregation, and multiprofile beat singleprofile. 2. Question: This RNA-only scVI multiprofile avgpool run isolates how much the image modality adds on top of strong scVI embeddings, compared directly with config_036 (0.715 acc, 0.687 F1). If RNA-only scVI comes close to 0.71, the image branch adds little, and the remaining budget should go to RNA-side and aggregation choices. If it drops clearly, multimodal fusion is confirmed as important, and image-side refinements such as testing ResNet50 with scVI become worthwhile. 3. Why now: The modality contribution is the most important unresolved design question once the RNA encoder changes. Answering it with one experiment guides all later allocation better than another small fusion or encoder tweak around the current best.

1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet on any design axis: modality, single vs. multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation or fusion. 2) This run sets a central reference point that is likely to perform well. It is multimodal and multiprofile, which should give the strongest signal if extra information helps. It pairs a standard compact RNA encoder (scVI) with a strong pretrained image encoder (ViT-L), and uses the simplest aggregation (avgpool) and fusion (concat). It tests whether a reasonable full-information setup works before adding complexity. 3) Under a limited budget, starting at this central configuration is efficient. Later runs can each change one factor (drop to RNA-only or image-only, switch to single-profile, use transformer aggregation or weighted fusion, swap encoders), so every follow-up gives a clean one-factor comparison. Starting from a minimal baseline would mean many steps before reaching the likely high-performing region.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_036 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) reached 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. With no comparison point, we cannot tell which parts of that setup drive performance. 2) What this tests: config_005 keeps the same profile setting, RNA encoder (scvi_n200) and aggregation (avgpool), but removes the image branch. Because only one factor changes, the accuracy and F1 difference directly measures how much the ViT-L image modality adds on top of RNA. 3) Why now: whether multimodal fusion beats RNA alone is the most basic design question in the search space. It determines whether later budget should go to image encoder and fusion choices or to RNA encoders and aggregation. A clean one-factor ablation reduces the most uncertainty per experiment before tuning secondary choices such as transformer aggregation or weighted fusion.

Evidence: with scvi_n200, multiprofile and avgpool held fixed, the multimodal model (config_036, acc 0.715, F1 0.687) beats RNA-only (config_005, acc 0.650, F1 0.628). That is about +6.5 points. But we cannot yet tell whether the gain comes from fusing the two modalities or simply from the ViT-L image features being strong on their own. Test: config_014 is image-only with imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile and avgpool. It completes a matched three-way modality comparison, changing only which inputs the model sees. Why now: the result decides how to spend the rest of the budget. If image-only is close to 0.715, RNA adds little, and later experiments should focus on image encoders and aggregation rather than RNA encoders or fusion. If image-only is clearly below 0.715, the modalities are complementary. That would justify exploring fusion (weighted vs concat), aggregation (transformer) and RNA encoders (scgpt, pca) within the multimodal space. Settling this foundational question first is a better use of one experiment than tuning a secondary setting.

1. Evidence: The multimodal model (0.715 acc, 0.687 F1) clearly beats RNA-only (0.650) and image-only (0.332), all using scVI-n200, ViT-L, avgpool and concat. RNA carries most of the predictive signal, and the image branch adds a meaningful but smaller gain. Every run so far used scVI, so the choice of RNA encoder, likely the biggest lever, is completely untested. 2. What it tests: config_048 changes only one thing from the best run, swapping scVI-n200 for scGPT, with the multimodal, multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool and concat settings kept the same. Any change in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed to the RNA encoder. 3. Why now: Because RNA dominates performance, the RNA encoder is the dimension most likely to move accuracy substantially. It also tells us whether a foundation-model representation helps, which shapes where later experiments should focus. Aggregation and fusion are secondary refinements and are better tested once the strongest RNA encoder is identified.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is multimodal scVI + ViT-L with avgpool and concat (0.715 accuracy, 0.687 F1). It beats RNA-only scVI (0.650) and image-only ViT-L (0.332), so the two modalities appear complementary. The RNA encoder matters a lot: scGPT dropped to 0.518. Every run so far has used avgpool aggregation, so the effect of aggregation is completely unknown. 2) Test: this experiment keeps the best configuration and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. Any difference can then be attributed to aggregation alone. A learned, attention-based aggregation over multiple profiles may capture relationships between profiles that mean pooling discards. 3) Why now: aggregation is a major design axis with no data yet, and it applies to all multiprofile configurations. Testing it on the strongest backbone could improve on the current best (exploitation) while settling an important open question (exploration). Fusion type and the PCA encoder are reasonable follow-ups once aggregation is resolved.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multimodal scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l is clearly the strongest direction so far (0.715–0.721 accuracy), well ahead of RNA-only scVI (0.650) and image-only (0.332). scGPT appears much weaker (0.518). Avgpool and transformer aggregation are nearly tied: transformer has slightly higher accuracy and avgpool has slightly higher F1. Fusion is the most important design choice not yet tested, since every multimodal run so far used concat. 2. What this tests: Keeping the best backbone and aggregation fixed (scvi_n200 + ViT-L + transformer) and switching only to weighted fusion isolates the effect of fusion on the most promising configuration. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: It exploits the leading configuration while resolving an untested design dimension. Either outcome will guide later choices among the remaining scVI/ViT variants. It is also more informative than re-probing aggregation, where the current difference is too small to interpret.

1. Evidence: The RNA encoder is the dominant design choice so far. RNA-only scVI reached 0.650, while image-only ViT-L reached only 0.332. Swapping scVI for scGPT in the multimodal concat/avgpool setup dropped accuracy by about 0.20 (0.715 to 0.518). By contrast, aggregation and fusion changes moved accuracy by only about 0.01, too small to read much into, and the F1 scores do not clearly favor one variant. The PCA_n2000 RNA encoder has never been tested, which is the largest remaining uncertainty on the most influential axis. 2. Test: config_027 swaps only the RNA encoder to PCA_n2000 within the current best setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, weighted). This isolates whether a simple PCA representation matches or beats scVI. 3. Why now: Because RNA encoder choice has produced the largest swings, this experiment has high information value. It could reveal a better RNA representation, or confirm scVI as the right choice so later experiments can focus on secondary choices such as image encoder or single- vs multi-profile.

1. Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder tested so far. In the multimodal setting it reached about 0.72 accuracy, versus 0.59 for pca_n2000 and 0.52 for scGPT. Multimodal models beat RNA-only (0.65), so the image signal adds value. Aggregation and fusion changes moved accuracy by only about 1 point (0.715–0.725), and F1 shifted inconsistently, so those choices look minor. The image encoder is still completely untested: every run used imagenet_vit_l, which scored only 0.33 when used alone. 2. This experiment keeps the best configuration (config_039: scvi_n200, transformer, weighted) and swaps imagenet_vit_l for resnet50. The single change isolates whether the image encoder is a major lever. 3. This is the largest remaining uncertainty among the design choices. Testing it in the strongest context gives a direct, interpretable comparison and could also produce a new best model. Further tuning of aggregation or fusion is unlikely to give meaningful gains.

1. Evidence: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, beating scGPT (0.52) and PCA (0.59). Multimodal fusion clearly beats RNA-only (0.72 vs 0.65), and image-only is weak (0.33). Swapping aggregation (avgpool vs transformer), fusion (concat vs weighted) or image encoder (ViT-L vs ResNet50) changes accuracy by only about 1 point, within likely noise. The main gap is that every run so far used multiprofile, so the single-profile versus multi-profile choice has never been tested. 2. Test: config_035 keeps the strongest components (scVI, ViT-L, weighted fusion) and switches to single-profile input. That makes it a close comparison to the current best, config_039 (0.725). It shows whether multi-profile aggregation is actually contributing, or whether a simpler single-profile model performs as well. 3. Why now: the remaining small aggregation and fusion variants would likely move accuracy by less than noise. Resolving an untested, potentially large design factor is a better use of the limited budget, and it stays near the high-performing region in case single-profile turns out competitive.

1. Evidence: Several choices are already settled. scVI clearly beats scGPT (0.518) and PCA (0.586). Multiprofile beats singleprofile (0.537). Multimodal beats RNA-only (0.650) and image-only (0.332). Among the scVI + ViT-L multiprofile runs, the remaining differences are small: avgpool+concat 0.715, transformer+concat 0.721, transformer+weighted 0.725 (best). The F1 values (0.681–0.687) do not consistently favor any one of these. It is therefore unclear whether transformer aggregation or weighted fusion gives a real gain, or whether the two interact. 2. What this tests: config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted) is the only missing cell in the 2x2 grid of aggregation × fusion for the strongest encoder pair. Running it lets us estimate the main effect of each factor and check for an interaction, rather than reading a ranking into differences of about 0.01. 3. Why now: It exploits the best-performing region while resolving the main open uncertainty. If avgpool+weighted matches or exceeds 0.725, the cheaper aggregation is sufficient and the remaining budget can go to other factors, such as the choice of image encoder. If it falls short, transformer aggregation is confirmed as the source of the gain.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about whether multimodal fusion beats single modalities, whether multiprofile aggregation helps, or which encoders work best. 2) What this tests: config_018 is a central, moderately complex multimodal model: PCA RNA features, a ResNet50 image encoder, multiprofile avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. Each choice is the simplest or most standard option on its axis, while still using both modalities and multiple profiles. The result sets a baseline that later runs can be compared against one factor at a time: config_002 or config_011 for the modality contribution, config_016 for multiprofile vs single-profile, config_020 for transformer vs avgpool, config_019 for weighted vs concat fusion, and configs 030, 042 and 024 for encoder choices. 3) Why it is the best use of the first experiment: Starting from a central configuration lets each later experiment change one factor and attribute performance differences to it. This uses the limited budget better than starting at an extreme, such as the simplest single-modality model or the most complex foundation-model/transformer combination. It also has a reasonable chance of performing competitively.

Evidence: only one experiment has been run (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA + ResNet50, avgpool, concat), reaching 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. With a single data point, every design choice is still uncertain. Test: config_020 keeps everything the same and changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer. Any difference in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed to the aggregation method alone. Why now: aggregation is shared by every multiprofile configuration, which is most of the search space, so this answer will guide many later choices. This makes it a cheap, informative one-factor test that also has a reasonable chance of improving on the current best.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Only two experiments exist. Both use multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA and ResNet50 image features with concat fusion. Avgpool (0.619 acc / 0.610 F1) beat transformer aggregation (0.579 / 0.563), so avgpool is a tentative best choice. No other design axis has been tested yet. 2. What this tests: config_024 keeps the best setup and changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates whether a larger pretrained image representation improves accuracy and F1. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: The image encoder is likely a high-impact choice that will shape every later multimodal comparison. A one-factor change from the current best gives a clean comparison and still has a reasonable chance of beating it. Fusion type, RNA encoder and unimodal ablations can follow once the image backbone is resolved.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: All three runs so far use the pca_n2000 RNA encoder with concat fusion. Within that setting, avgpool beat transformer aggregation by about 4 points in both accuracy and F1, a fairly consistent signal. ViT-L and ResNet50 are nearly tied: ViT-L is about 1 point higher in accuracy but about 1 point lower in F1. The RNA encoder, with three options, is the largest untested design axis and could plausibly matter more than the image backbone. 2. What this tests: config_042 swaps only the RNA encoder, from PCA to the scGPT foundation-model embedding. Everything else matches config_018 (multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, concat), the run with the best F1. This gives a clean one-variable comparison of RNA representation. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: Refining the near-tied image encoder or the fusion choice now would add little information. A clean test of the RNA encoder on the strongest observed base resolves a high-uncertainty choice and still has a real chance of improving performance. scGPT is the alternative most different from PCA, so it should be the most informative first probe.

1) Evidence so far: PCA RNA with avgpool and concat fusion is the strongest setup. ViT-L (0.629 acc) and ResNet50 (0.619 acc) are close on accuracy, and ResNet50 has the better F1, so the image-encoder choice is still unsettled. Transformer aggregation (0.579) and scGPT RNA (0.512) clearly underperformed. Fusion strategy is completely untested, since every run used concat. 2) This experiment changes only the fusion method (weighted instead of concat) on the current best configuration (config_024). That gives a clean one-factor comparison of fusion type. 3) Fusion is a major design axis with zero evidence, so this run reduces the most important remaining uncertainty. It is also anchored to the best-performing setup, so it may give an immediate improvement. The scVI encoder and single- vs multi-profile remain open and can be tested next.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Within multiprofile multimodal runs, pca_n2000 is clearly better than scgpt (0.619 vs 0.512 with resnet50/avgpool/concat). The third RNA encoder, scvi_n200, has never been tested. Among the other choices, avgpool beat transformer (0.619 vs 0.579), and imagenet_vit_l was slightly better than resnet50. The current best run is pca_n2000 + vit_l + avgpool + weighted (0.635 acc, 0.618 F1), but weighted fusion's edge over concat is small. 2. What this tests: config_037 keeps the best image encoder, aggregation and fusion fixed and swaps in scvi_n200. That makes it a direct one-variable comparison with the best run and shows whether a compact learned RNA latent beats or matches PCA features. 3. Why it is the best next run: The RNA encoder has had the largest observed effect so far, and its main open option is still unexplored. Fine-tuning fusion or aggregation choices offers smaller expected gains. This run therefore reduces uncertainty on the most important design choice while still having a realistic chance of becoming the new best configuration.

1. Evidence: The largest gain so far came from switching the RNA encoder. scVI scored 0.706 accuracy (config_037), compared with 0.635 for PCA under the same settings (config_025), and scGPT trailed. Image encoder and fusion changes moved accuracy by only about 0.01. This suggests the RNA side may drive most of the performance, but every run so far has been multimodal, so the image modality's actual contribution is unknown. 2. Test: config_005 runs RNA-only scVI with multiprofile avgpool, matching config_037 except for the image branch. Comparing the two directly measures what adding ViT-L images contributes. 3. Why now: Whether to use both modalities is the most basic design choice, and it has never been tested. A near-tie with config_037 would mean later runs should focus on RNA-side choices rather than image encoders or fusion. A clear drop would confirm multimodality and justify exploiting the scVI+ViT-L direction next, for example single vs multiprofile or transformer aggregation.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion): 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. It clearly beats every PCA-based multimodal run and the scVI RNA-only baseline (0.650), so scVI with ViT-L is the strong direction. Fusion type (0.635 vs 0.629) and image encoder (0.629 vs 0.619) show only small differences. Aggregation has a larger gap: the transformer underperformed avgpool by about 4 points (0.579 vs 0.619). However, that comes from a single comparison on the weakest backbone (PCA + ResNet50, concat), so it may not hold for stronger encoders. 2. Test: config_039 keeps the best configuration fixed and switches only aggregation to transformer. This isolates whether learned set aggregation helps once the per-profile features are richer, or whether avgpool is reliably better. 3.
