If RNA-only plus transformer approaches 0.72, later budget should go to aggregation and RNA choices. If it stays near 0.65-0.68, the image contribution is confirmed and further multimodal refinement is justified. That makes it more informative than a small fusion or image-encoder tweak around the current best.

Evidence: every completed run used multiprofile, so whether multiprofile modeling helps at all is still untested. Other factors are better supported. scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, since scGPT (0.52) and PCA (0.59) fell well behind scVI (0.72) with the same ViT-L, transformer and weighted-fusion setup. Weighted fusion beat concat (0.678 vs 0.632, one comparison), the transformer beat avgpool (0.713 vs 0.678), and ViT-L slightly edged ResNet50 (0.725 vs 0.713). Test: config_035 keeps the best encoder pair (scVI + ViT-L) and weighted fusion but switches to singleprofile, so it directly measures the value of multiprofile modeling against the current best, config_039. Why now: this is the largest unexplored design axis, and one run either confirms multiprofile with transformer aggregation as essential or shows a simpler single-profile model is competitive. Further tuning of fusion or image encoders within the multiprofile region would add less information per experiment.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_039 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy. RNA-only models with scVI score about 0.65 under both aggregators. scGPT and PCA RNA encoders hurt badly, and single-profile input is clearly worse. Weighted fusion and transformer aggregation each beat their alternatives in the ResNet comparisons. What remains untested is how much the image modality achieves by itself. We cannot tell whether the multimodal gain comes from true complementarity or whether images alone already carry most of the signal. This matters because weak RNA encoders (scGPT, PCA) drag performance far below RNA-only, which suggests RNA quality strongly shapes results. 2) This experiment runs an image-only model with ViT-L and transformer aggregation over multiple profiles, the exact image-side counterpart of the current best. It shows whether fusion with scVI adds real value over images alone and how strong ViT-L features are without RNA. 3) Under a limited budget, this single run answers a top-level question (which modalities to use) that no experiment so far has touched. That is more informative than fine-tuning fusion or aggregation details around config_039, where the evidence already points in a consistent direction.

1. Evidence: no experiments have been completed, so every design choice is uncertain. These choices are modality, single- vs multi-profile input, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation and fusion. 2. What this tests: config_036 is a central anchor (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI RNA encoder, ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion). It uses a plausibly strong but not extreme option on each axis. Avgpool and concat are the simplest multiprofile aggregation and fusion choices, which keeps the result easy to interpret. scVI and ViT-L are reasonable middle-to-strong encoders. The result gives a realistic estimate of the attainable accuracy and F1. Each later experiment can then change one factor at a time from this point: drop to a single modality, switch to single-profile, try transformer aggregation or weighted fusion, or swap an encoder. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: starting from a central, likely-competitive configuration supports both goals. It may already perform well (exploitation), and it is the most useful reference point for later one-factor contrasts (exploration). A minimal baseline would tell us less about where the high-performing region lies.

1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile config_036 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) reached 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. That gives a baseline, but no evidence yet about which design choices matter. 2. What this tests: config_038 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, and keeps everything else fixed. Aggregation is likely one of the most influential choices in the multiprofile setting, because a learned attention-based pooling may capture relationships between profiles that mean pooling discards. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: this clean comparison should reveal whether learned aggregation is worth pursuing across the many untested multiprofile configs. It also has a reasonable chance of improving on the current best, so it supports both learning and exploitation. Later experiments can isolate fusion, encoder and modality effects against the better of the two aggregation methods.

1. Evidence: only two runs exist, both multimodal multiprofile with scVI, ViT-L and concat fusion. They differ only in aggregation. Transformer was slightly higher on accuracy (0.721 vs 0.715), while avgpool was higher on F1 (0.687 vs 0.681). That is too small and mixed to call, so aggregation looks like a minor factor for now. The RNA encoder, image encoder, fusion method and profile setting are all still untested. 2. This run changes one factor from the current best (config_038): the RNA encoder goes from scVI to scGPT. Everything else stays fixed, so any difference can be attributed to the RNA representation. Swapping a foundation-model embedding for a VAE embedding could plausibly shift performance more than the aggregation choice did. 3. Under a tight budget, this one-factor comparison next to the current best both answers an important design question and has a realistic chance of improving accuracy. That makes it a better next step than refining aggregation or fusion first.

1. Evidence so far: scvi_n200 clearly beats scGPT (about 0.72 vs 0.51 accuracy with otherwise identical settings), so the scvi_n200 + ViT-L multiprofile branch is the promising region. Within it, avgpool and transformer aggregation are nearly tied (0.715 vs 0.721 accuracy, with F1 slightly favoring avgpool), so aggregation looks like a minor factor. Fusion is still a complete unknown, because every run so far used concat. 2. This run changes only the fusion method (weighted instead of concat) on the best configuration so far (config_038). That isolates whether fusion matters while staying in the high-performing region. 3. It is the best use of the budget because it answers an untested question about an important design choice and also has a reasonable chance of improving on the current best. A clean one-factor comparison is more informative than another small aggregation comparison or an exploratory jump to a weaker region.

1) Evidence: three scVI + ViT-L multiprofile runs all land in a narrow 0.715–0.725 accuracy band. That means aggregation (avgpool vs. transformer) and fusion (concat vs. weighted) appear to be minor, second-order choices. Swapping the RNA encoder to scGPT, by contrast, cut accuracy by about 0.21. The RNA encoder is therefore the most influential choice seen so far, yet only two of its three options have been tested. 2) This run keeps everything else identical to the current best (config_039: ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) and swaps scVI for PCA (n=2000). This isolates whether a simpler, higher-dimensional RNA representation matches or beats scVI. 3) It is the best next use of budget because it explores the highest-impact unresolved factor while staying in the best-known context, so it could also directly yield a new best. Further aggregation or fusion tweaks would likely give only small, noise-level differences.

1. Evidence: The RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. scvi_n200 (0.715-0.725) clearly beats pca_n2000 (0.586) and scgpt (0.507). Within scvi_n200 + ViT-L, the aggregation and fusion choices differ by under 1 point, and F1 does not consistently favor any of them. They look like minor knobs. The image encoder, however, has never been varied: every run used imagenet_vit_l, so its contribution is a major open uncertainty. 2. Test: config_033 keeps the best setup (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer, weighted) and swaps only ViT-L for resnet50. Compared directly with config_039, it isolates the effect of the image encoder backbone. 3. Why now: Further aggregation or fusion tweaks are unlikely to be informative, and switching to a different RNA encoder looks unpromising. This experiment resolves a whole untested design dimension in one controlled run. It could also find a better configuration if resnet50 features suit cell images better than ImageNet ViT-L features.

Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. scvi_n200 reaches about 0.71-0.72 accuracy, while pca_n2000 gets 0.59 and scgpt 0.51. Swapping the image encoder (vit_l to resnet50), the aggregation method or the fusion type changes accuracy by only about 0.01, which is within noise, and F1 shows no consistent pattern. This raises the question of whether the image modality adds anything at all. Test: config_006 is the RNA-only counterpart of the best multimodal setup (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer aggregation). Comparing it with config_039 and config_033 directly measures how much the image modality contributes. Why now: the result determines where the remaining budget should go. If RNA-only matches the multimodal runs, further tuning of image encoder and fusion settings is low value, and effort should shift to the RNA and profile-setting dimensions. If it falls clearly below them, multimodal fusion is confirmed and fusion and image refinements become worth exploring.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder so far, well ahead of pca_n2000 (0.586) and scgpt (0.507). Multimodal also beats rna_only (0.725 vs 0.653). The other choices have only been compared with single experiments and show small gaps. Aggregation (transformer vs avgpool), fusion (weighted vs concat) and image encoder (vit_l vs resnet50) each differ by about 0.01 accuracy, with F1 sometimes pointing the other way. Profile setting is the largest untested choice: every multimodal run so far used multiprofile. 2) Test: config_035 matches the current best, config_039 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion), except that it uses singleprofile instead of multiprofile. This isolates whether combining multiple profiles is actually needed. 3) Value: small tweaks to aggregation or fusion are unlikely to change our conclusions. Resolving the profile-setting question settles a major design choice and tells us whether singleprofile options deserve more of the remaining budget.

1. Evidence: Three choices look settled. scVI clearly beats PCA and scGPT as the RNA encoder. Multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile. Multimodal beats RNA-only (0.725 vs 0.653). Within the strongest region (scVI + ViT-L + multiprofile), the remaining choices show only small differences. Transformer+weighted is best at 0.725. Transformer+concat reached 0.721. Avgpool+concat reached 0.715 accuracy but had the best F1 among the ViT-L runs (0.687). Avgpool+weighted is the one missing cell of this 2x2 aggregation-by-fusion grid. 2. Question: config_037 completes that grid. It tests whether the small gain from weighted fusion also holds with avgpool aggregation, or whether aggregation and fusion interact. It also checks whether avgpool's F1 advantage combined with weighted fusion could match or beat the current best. 3. Why now: this is a high-expected-value experiment in the best-performing region, so it serves exploitation. It also clarifies two design choices that the current data cannot separate from noise. That makes it a better use of the limited budget than revisiting the clearly inferior PCA, scGPT or singleprofile settings.

Evidence: the best configs pair the scvi_n200 RNA encoder with multiprofile transformer aggregation (config_039 at 0.725, config_038 at 0.721). Fusion type and image backbone change accuracy by only about 0.01, and resnet50 (config_033) even gives higher F1. RNA encoder choice matters far more: scgpt reached 0.51 and pca 0.59. The scvi RNA-only model scores 0.653. Uncertainty: no image-only model has been tested, so we cannot tell how much the image branch contributes on its own, or whether weak RNA encoders are actively hurting the fusion. Test: config_015 (image-only, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, transformer) uses the same image and aggregation setup as the best model, making it a matched ablation. It will show whether images alone come near 0.72 or whether the multimodal gain is truly complementary. It also shows whether bad RNA features pull the model below an image-only baseline. Why now: further fusion or backbone tweaks are likely to give only small, noisy differences. This baseline instead settles a key design question, the role of each modality, and guides whether the remaining budget should go to RNA encoder improvements or to the image and fusion side.

1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which design choices matter: modality, single- vs multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation or fusion. 2) This run sets an anchor using the simplest components in the richest setting: multimodal and multiprofile, with PCA RNA features, ResNet50 image features, average pooling and concatenation fusion. Every other design factor is one change away from it. Later runs can each change a single factor and be compared directly against this reference: dropping a modality (config_002, config_011), using a single profile (config_016), swapping in scVI/scGPT or ViT-L encoders, or trying transformer aggregation or weighted fusion. 3) Under a limited budget, a central, low-complexity anchor gives the most information per later experiment. It should also be reasonably competitive, because it uses both modalities and multiple profiles. That makes it a better first run than a narrow unimodal baseline or the most complex configuration, which would be hard to attribute.

1) Evidence: there is only one completed run, the multimodal multiprofile setup with PCA RNA, ResNet50 images, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion (acc 0.619, F1 0.610). So no design choice has been tested yet. 2) This run changes one factor, the image encoder (ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L), and keeps everything else fixed. That makes any difference in accuracy or F1 attributable to the image backbone. 3) The image encoder splits the multimodal and image-only search space in half, and a stronger backbone is plausibly one of the largest performance levers. A clean one-factor comparison on this axis reduces uncertainty over many remaining configurations and is also a reasonable bet for improving the best result. Aggregation, fusion and RNA encoder can then be tested with the better image backbone.

Evidence: swapping the image encoder from resnet50 (config_018) to imagenet_vit_l (config_024) changed accuracy by only +0.010, while F1 fell by 0.011. That is mixed, weak evidence that the image encoder matters much. Every completed run also fixes the RNA encoder at pca_n2000, so a factor with three levels is still unexplored. Test: config_048 changes only the RNA encoder to scgpt, keeping the slightly higher-accuracy config_024 setup (imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool, concat). This isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA embedding beats PCA features. Budget rationale: the RNA representation is likely a major driver of cell-profiling performance and has the most unexplored levels. A clean one-factor comparison against the current best gives a large reduction in uncertainty and a plausible chance of improvement. Aggregation (transformer vs avgpool) and fusion (weighted vs concat) can follow once the RNA encoder choice is clearer.

1) Evidence: The RNA encoder matters a lot. pca_n2000 beat scgpt by about 0.11 accuracy with the same image encoder. The image encoder choice is less clear: imagenet_vit_l scored slightly higher in accuracy (0.629 vs 0.619) but lower in F1 than resnet50, so that difference is small and ambiguous. Every completed run used avgpool aggregation and concat fusion, so we have no evidence yet on aggregation. 2) Test: config_026 keeps the best-performing setup (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, concat) and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. This is a clean one-variable test of whether learned set aggregation over multiple profiles beats mean pooling. 3) Why now: Aggregation is a major untested architectural choice that applies across all multiprofile configurations. Testing it on the strongest backbone combines exploitation, since it could beat 0.629, with exploration, since it resolves a key open design question. That makes it a better use of budget than revisiting the noisy image-encoder comparison or the clearly weaker scgpt branch.

1) Evidence: The best configuration so far is pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + concat (acc 0.629). ResNet50 with the same setup is close in accuracy (0.619) and slightly higher in F1, so the image encoder effect is small. scGPT clearly hurts (0.518), so the RNA encoder is a high-impact choice. Transformer aggregation underperformed avgpool (0.599). Fusion is the one design axis with no data at all, since every run used concat. 2) Test: config_025 changes only the fusion method (concat to weighted) on the current best setup. This gives a clean one-factor estimate of whether weighted fusion helps, which concat-only runs cannot reveal. 3) Why now: It resolves the largest remaining uncertainty while staying in the most promising region, so it has both high information value and a real chance of beating the current best. The result will also guide whether later runs (e.g., testing scvi_n200) should use concat or weighted fusion.

1) Evidence: The RNA encoder is the most influential factor tested so far. Swapping pca_n2000 for scgpt dropped accuracy by about 11 points (0.629 to 0.518). By comparison, the image encoder (ViT-L slightly ahead of ResNet50), aggregation (avgpool ahead of transformer) and fusion (weighted at 0.635 vs concat at 0.629, with better F1) show only small differences. scvi_n200 is the one RNA encoder never tested, so uncertainty is greatest there. 2) This run keeps the current best setup (ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) and changes only the RNA encoder to scvi_n200. That isolates whether scVI latents can match or beat PCA. 3) Because the RNA encoder showed the largest effect, resolving it is likely to shape the rest of the search more than tuning the small-margin factors. Using the best known setup also gives a fair chance of finding a new top configuration, so the run is both exploratory and exploitative.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: All six completed runs are multimodal. The clearest signal is the RNA encoder. Swapping pca_n2000 for scvi_n200 raised accuracy from 0.635 to 0.706 under the same image encoder, aggregation and fusion (config_025 vs config_037). scGPT was clearly worse (0.518). Image-encoder, fusion and aggregation differences were small (about 0.01 to 0.03) and could be noise. No unimodal baseline has been run, so we do not know how much the image branch actually contributes. 2) What this tests: config_005 is RNA-only with scvi_n200 and avgpool multiprofile aggregation, matching the best run's RNA side. It isolates the multimodal gain. If it scores near 0.70, the image branch adds little and the remaining budget should go to RNA-side choices. If it scores well below, image fusion is confirmed as valuable, and tuning image encoder, fusion and aggregation around config_037 is justified. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: Further small variations around config_037 would yield deltas we cannot interpret without this anchor. This run answers the most fundamental open design question, whether multimodality matters, at the cost of a single experiment.

1) Evidence: Every experiment so far used multiprofile, so the profile setting is a major design choice with no data at all. The other choices have some support. scVI clearly beats PCA and scGPT as the RNA encoder (0.706 vs 0.635 vs 0.518 with ViT-L and weighted fusion). Multimodal beats RNA-only for scVI (0.706 vs 0.650). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation in the one PCA comparison (0.629 vs 0.599). Weighted fusion beat concat only slightly (0.635 vs 0.629), with a larger F1 gap. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup (scVI, ViT-L, weighted fusion) and switches to singleprofile, which has no aggregation step. The result shows whether multiprofile aggregation drives the gains or whether singleprofile is competitive or better. 3) Fusion and aggregation already have some evidence, but nothing is known about profile setting. A controlled test against the current best (config_037) resolves the largest remaining uncertainty and could also open a better region of the search space.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion), with accuracy 0.706 and F1 0.667. It is clearly better than the PCA-based multimodal runs and the scVI RNA-only run (0.650), so the scVI encoder and adding images both appear to help. Multiprofile with avgpool also beats singleprofile and transformer aggregation in the runs so far. The image encoder choice is still unresolved. With PCA and concat fusion, ResNet50 and ViT-L were close: ResNet50 had slightly lower accuracy (0.619 vs 0.629) but higher F1 (0.610 vs 0.599). 2. Test: config_031 keeps every setting of the best configuration and swaps only the image encoder to ResNet50. This isolates whether the image backbone matters once the stronger scVI encoder is in place. 3. Why now: this is a one-variable exploit of the leading configuration, so the result is easy to interpret. It could find a better model, or it could confirm ViT-L as the image encoder before spending budget on lower-value fusion or aggregation variants.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion), at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Two choices look fairly settled. scVI beats PCA and scGPT, and multiprofile beats singleprofile by a wide margin. Aggregation is much less certain. Transformer aggregation was tried only once, with a weaker setup (PCA + ViT-L + concat), where it scored about 0.03 below avgpool. That single test may not carry over to the stronger scVI embeddings or to weighted fusion. 2. What this tests: config_039 keeps everything from the best configuration and changes only avgpool to transformer. This is a controlled test of whether learned aggregation across profiles helps once the RNA representation is strong. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: It resolves the main remaining design question in the most promising part of the search space. If the transformer wins, it could become the new best configuration. If it loses again, two consistent results justify fixing avgpool and spending the remaining budget elsewhere, such as checking weighted versus concat fusion with scVI.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about which design choices matter: modality, single vs multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation or fusion. 2) What this tests: config_030 is a central, moderately simple multimodal configuration. It uses multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation, the scVI RNA encoder, a ResNet50 image encoder and concat fusion. It sits in the middle of the design space and gives a reasonable performance anchor. Later runs can each change one factor from it, for example rna_only (config_005), image_only (config_011), singleprofile (config_028), transformer aggregation (config_032), weighted fusion (config_031), or swapping encoders. That makes clean one-factor-at-a-time comparisons possible. 3) Why it is the best first use of budget: It combines a plausible chance of strong immediate performance from multimodal, multiprofile input with the most useful reference point for later ablations. Each follow-up experiment can then be interpreted relative to a known baseline.

1. Evidence: Only one experiment has run so far. config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI RNA, ResNet50 image, avgpool, concat) reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1. With one result there is no comparison yet, so we cannot tell whether the image branch helps at all. 2. What this tests: config_005 changes only one factor from config_030 by removing the image modality (RNA-only, scVI, multiprofile, avgpool). The difference between the two isolates how much imaging adds on top of RNA. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: Whether to go multimodal is the top-level design choice. It decides whether later effort on image encoders (ResNet50 vs ViT-L) and fusion methods (concat vs weighted) is worth spending. If RNA-only matches config_030, we should focus on RNA encoders and aggregation. If it falls clearly short, multimodal is confirmed and we can tune the image and fusion choices with confidence.

1) Evidence: Adding ResNet50 images to scVI RNA with concat fusion (config_030, acc 0.632, F1 0.607) scored slightly below RNA-only scVI (config_005, acc 0.650, F1 0.628), with everything else equal. This is a small, single-run gap. It may mean the images add noise under naive concatenation, not that they lack useful signal. 2) Question: config_031 changes only the fusion from concat to weighted. This tests whether learned modality weighting can down-weight the weaker image features and match or beat RNA-only performance. 3) Why now: Whether multimodality helps at all is the central design choice and decides how much budget the remaining multimodal configurations deserve. A one-factor change gives a clean answer. If weighted fusion recovers or exceeds RNA-only, the next steps should be image encoder and aggregation variants. If not, RNA-only directions such as scGPT or transformer aggregation become the priority.

1. Evidence: In the scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool setting, weighted fusion (0.678 accuracy, 0.646 F1) beat concat fusion (0.632) and RNA-only (0.650). Both accuracy and F1 agree, so weighted fusion looks like the better way to use the image signal. Every experiment so far used avgpool aggregation, so we have no evidence on the aggregation choice. 2. Test: config_033 keeps the current best setup (scvi_n200, resnet50, weighted fusion, multiprofile) and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. This isolates whether learned attention over multiple profiles beats simple averaging. 3. Why now: Aggregation is a major untested design axis that affects every multiprofile configuration. A one-variable change from the current best gives a clean answer. It also exploits a promising direction, since it may improve on 0.678. Other open axes (scGPT or ViT-L encoders, single-profile) can be tested later once the aggregation choice is settled.

Evidence: Among scvi_n200 + resnet50 multiprofile models, weighted fusion beat concat (0.678 vs 0.632). Transformer aggregation then improved further to 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1, the best so far. The weighted multimodal models also beat RNA-only (0.650), which suggests the image modality helps when it is fused well. Uncertainty: the image encoder has never been varied. Every multimodal run used resnet50, so we do not know whether imagenet_vit_l gives better image features. Test: config_039 keeps the best setup (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer, weighted) and swaps only resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l. This gives a clean single-variable comparison. Why now: the image encoder is a major untested design choice and the next likely source of gains. Testing it on the strongest backbone exploits current evidence while answering a key open question. Other remaining questions, such as RNA encoder choice or a concat check under the transformer, can follow based on this result.

1. Evidence: All five completed runs used the scvi_n200 RNA encoder. Within that setting, weighted fusion beat concat (0.678 vs 0.632 accuracy, avgpool/resnet50). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.713 vs 0.678, weighted/resnet50). Both are moderately clear gains. ViT-L beat ResNet50 only slightly on accuracy (0.725 vs 0.713) and was a little lower on F1, so the image-encoder choice is still uncertain. The RNA encoder has never been varied, so its effect is the largest open question. 2. This run swaps scvi_n200 for scGPT inside the current best setup (ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion). It differs from config_039 in one factor only, so any change can be attributed to the RNA encoder. 3. Testing the untried RNA-encoder axis in the strongest known context both explores a key design choice and has a reasonable chance of improving on the best result. Revisiting the small image-encoder difference would be less informative per experiment.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Weighted fusion beat concat (0.678 vs 0.632 with avgpool). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.713 vs 0.678). ViT-L slightly edged ResNet50 (0.725 vs 0.713), with somewhat lower F1. The RNA encoder shows the largest observed effect: swapping scVI for scGPT dropped accuracy to 0.520. However, pca_n2000, the third RNA encoder, is completely untested. 2. What this tests: config_027 keeps the current best setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) and swaps only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. This cleanly isolates whether PCA is better or worse than scVI under the strongest known architecture. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: The RNA encoder is the design choice with the highest observed variance and the least coverage. This one experiment either finds a new best configuration or confirms scVI as the RNA backbone. It is more informative than a small refinement such as testing concat fusion or changing the image encoder, where the evidence already points in a clear direction.

Evidence: the RNA encoder choice dominates. scVI reached 0.725, while scGPT (0.520) and PCA (0.586) were far lower under the same multimodal setup. Transformer aggregation gave a clear gain over avgpool (0.678 to 0.713 with resnet50), and weighted fusion beat concat under avgpool (0.678 vs 0.632). The image encoder swap had only a small effect (0.713 to 0.725, with lower F1). The open question is how much of the best result comes from adding images versus from transformer aggregation over scVI RNA profiles. The only RNA-only comparison uses avgpool (0.650). This experiment tests an RNA-only model with scVI and transformer aggregation. Its result will separate the aggregation gain from the multimodal gain. If it approaches about 0.71, image features add little and the remaining budget should go to RNA-side choices. If it stays near 0.65, multimodal fusion is confirmed as important, which justifies further fusion and image-encoder exploitation. This ablation resolves a central design question that more variants of the top configuration cannot answer.

1) Evidence: Within multiprofile models, scVI is clearly the best RNA encoder (scGPT and PCA performed much worse with ViT-L). Weighted fusion beat concat by about 4.6 points with avgpool. Transformer aggregation helped multimodal models (0.678 to 0.713). ViT-L and ResNet50 are close: ViT-L had higher accuracy, ResNet50 had higher F1. The profile setting is the largest gap: every experiment so far used multiprofile, so the singleprofile option is entirely untested. 2) Test: config_035 keeps the best-performing components (scVI, ViT-L, weighted fusion) but switches to singleprofile. Compared with config_039, it isolates how much multiprofile input plus aggregation contributes. 3) Why now: This resolves the biggest open uncertainty, a whole design dimension, rather than chasing a small encoder or fusion difference. It also tells us whether further effort on aggregation choices is justified.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_039 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy. RNA-only scVI reaches about 0.65 with either aggregation (0.650 and 0.653), so it is not sensitive to aggregation. Multimodal gains appear only with weighted fusion and transformer aggregation. Swapping in a weaker RNA encoder (scGPT at 0.52, PCA at 0.59) with the same ViT-L image branch drops performance sharply, so RNA quality clearly matters. However, no image-only baseline has been run, so we cannot tell how much the image modality contributes alone, or whether fusion beats the stronger single modality. Test: config_015 (image-only, ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer) gives the image-side counterpart to config_006 under the same aggregation used by the best model. This shows whether the roughly 7-point multimodal gain over RNA-only reflects real complementarity or mostly a strong image signal. Why now: fusion and aggregation have already been partly probed. The missing image baseline is the largest structural gap in the evidence. It will guide whether the remaining budget should go to fusion and RNA-encoder refinements or to the image and aggregation side.

1. Evidence: No experiments have been run yet, so we know nothing about which modality, representation, profile setting, aggregation or fusion matters. 2. What this tests: config_020 is the simplest configuration available, an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA-2000 encoder and no aggregation or fusion. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 that later results can be measured against. 3. Why it is the best next run: PCA-2000 is the RNA encoder with the most direct one-factor partners in the list. These include the scVI and scGPT single-profile RNA models (encoder effect), the multiprofile avgpool and transformer RNA models (profile and aggregation effects), and the PCA-based single-profile multimodal models (effect of adding images, and concat versus weighted fusion). Starting from this baseline means each later experiment can change one factor at a time and still be interpreted cleanly. It also avoids assuming early on that more complex multimodal or multiprofile models will do better.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: We have one result so far. The RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_020) reached 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. We know nothing yet about the image modality, and most remaining configurations are multimodal or image-based. 2. What this tests: The image-only, single-profile ResNet50 model is the simplest image counterpart to the RNA baseline. Comparing the two in the same single-profile setting shows how much signal the images carry on their own. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: This one result guides a large share of the remaining search. If images are weak, the search should focus on RNA encoders and profile or aggregation choices. If images are competitive, fusion and multiprofile combinations become worth testing. It is a cleaner first step than jumping to a multimodal model, where a gain or loss could not be attributed to either modality.

1) Evidence so far: there are only two single-profile results. RNA-only with PCA reached 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. Image-only with ResNet50 reached only 0.208 accuracy and 0.172 F1. So RNA is clearly the stronger modality so far. 2) What this tests: config_030 keeps RNA-only and the PCA encoder fixed and changes only the profile setting to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates whether combining multiple profiles helps on its own, without fusion or a transformer aggregator confounding the result. 3) Why it is the best next step: most of the remaining search space is multiprofile, so the answer narrows that whole branch. A gain would justify exploring multiprofile aggregation and fusion next. No gain would point the search back toward single-profile setups and RNA encoder comparisons. Adding the weak image modality now would be less informative.

1) Evidence: RNA is far stronger than image. RNA PCA single-profile reached 0.485 accuracy, while ResNet50 image-only reached 0.208. Switching RNA PCA from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised accuracy to 0.591 (F1 0.573), so multiprofile avgpool with PCA is the best setting so far. We still do not know whether adding image features helps, does nothing, or hurts in this best setting. 2) config_019 keeps config_030 fixed (PCA, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds only ResNet50 image features through simple concat fusion. Comparing it with config_030 isolates the marginal value of the image modality, using the same image encoder already tested alone. 3) Whether to go multimodal is the decision that shapes most of the remaining search space, since most untested configs are multimodal. A single-change test of it from the current best gives the most information per experiment. If image adds nothing, we can focus the budget on RNA encoders and aggregation (e.g. config_010, config_003, config_045). If it helps, fusion type and image encoder become worth exploring.

1. Evidence: Multiprofile avgpool clearly helped RNA, raising accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591. Adding ResNet50 image features with concat fusion gave a further small gain, to 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. ResNet50 image-only performance was very weak (0.208), so the image representation is a key open question: the image branch may be adding little because the encoder is poor. 2. Test: config_037 keeps everything from the current best (config_019: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool, concat) and swaps only the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l. This isolates the effect of image representation in the strongest setup. 3. Why now: It is a one-variable change from the best configuration, so it works as both exploitation and a clean ablation. A gain would show that a better image encoder raises the value of multimodal fusion and point later experiments toward ViT-based variants. No gain would suggest the image modality adds little regardless of encoder, shifting the budget toward RNA encoder, aggregation and fusion choices.

1) Evidence: Multiprofile with avgpool is the largest gain so far. For RNA-only PCA it improved validation accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591. Adding image features gave a smaller gain: 0.619 with ResNet50 and 0.629 with ViT-L, though ViT-L had slightly lower F1 (0.599 vs 0.610). Profile aggregation is therefore the strongest lever found, but only avgpool has been tested. Transformer aggregation, weighted fusion and the non-PCA RNA encoders are all untested. 2) Test: config_047 differs from the current best (config_037) only in aggregation, transformer instead of avgpool. This isolates whether learned aggregation over profiles adds value beyond mean pooling. 3) Why now: This is a one-variable change on the best configuration, so the result can be attributed to aggregation. It also builds directly on the strongest signal so far. If the transformer helps, it becomes the new base for later fusion and RNA-encoder tests. If it does not, we can fix avgpool and spend the remaining budget on RNA encoders and fusion.

1. Evidence: Multiprofile clearly helps RNA (0.485 to 0.591). Adding images gives a modest further gain (0.619 with ResNet50, 0.629 with ViT-L). Transformer aggregation underperformed avgpool (0.599 vs 0.629). Fusion is the one design axis never tested: every multimodal run so far used concat. 2. Test: config_018 is identical to the current best, config_037 (pca_n2000, ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool), except it uses weighted fusion instead of concat. Changing only this one choice isolates the fusion effect. Weighted fusion may also let the model lean on the stronger RNA signal and down-weight the weak image modality. 3. Value: This answers an open design question with a clean single-variable comparison. It is also a reasonable exploitation step, since it extends the best configuration found so far. RNA encoder alternatives (scVI, scGPT) remain an important next axis to test afterward.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile with avgpool clearly beats singleprofile for RNA (0.591 vs 0.485). Adding images gives a smaller gain (up to 0.635), and imagenet_vit_l slightly beats resnet50. The transformer aggregator underperformed avgpool, and weighted fusion edged out concat (0.635 vs 0.629, also higher F1). The best result so far is config_018 (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted). RNA appears to be the dominant modality, yet every experiment so far has used pca_n2000. The RNA encoder is therefore the largest untested design choice. 2) What this tests: config_009 keeps the best setup fixed and changes only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scgpt. Comparing it with config_018 isolates the effect of the RNA representation. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: The encoder of the dominant modality probably has the largest remaining effect on accuracy. Testing it inside the current best configuration both explores an uncharted dimension and could directly improve the top result.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_018 (PCA-2000, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion; accuracy 0.635, F1 0.618). Swapping only the RNA encoder to scGPT (config_009) dropped accuracy sharply to 0.542, so the RNA encoder looks like the most influential choice. The other changes (fusion type, image encoder, aggregation) moved accuracy by only about 0.01–0.03. scVI-200 is the one RNA encoder that has never been tested. 2. This experiment keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only the RNA encoder to scVI-200. It cleanly tests whether a compact learned representation can match or beat PCA, or whether PCA's advantage holds across learned encoders. 3. It closes the largest remaining gap on a high-impact design choice with a single-variable comparison. It is also a plausible candidate for a new best, so it serves both exploration and exploitation.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_034 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. That is well above the matched PCA run, config_018 (0.635). Images alone look weak: single-profile ResNet scored 0.21. Fusion and image-encoder changes have shifted results by only about 0.01–0.03. So the big gain appears to come from the RNA representation, but it is unclear how much of config_034's score depends on the image modality at all. 2) This test: config_045 runs scVI RNA-only with multiprofile avgpool. Comparing it with config_030 (PCA RNA-only, multiprofile avgpool, 0.591) isolates the scVI effect without images. Comparing it with config_034 isolates the image contribution once RNA is strong. 3) Why now: if scVI RNA-only nearly matches config_034, the multimodal complexity adds little and the remaining budget should go to RNA-side choices. If it falls well short, fusion with images is confirmed as valuable, and later tests of concat versus weighted fusion and transformer aggregation with scVI are justified. One run answers a core design question that fine-tuning near config_034 would not.

1. No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which design choices matter. 2. config_051 (multimodal, multiprofile, scGPT, ImageNet ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) is a hub configuration. It gives a starting reference point and has untested neighbours that each differ by exactly one design choice: aggregation (config_049, avgpool), fusion (config_037, concat), RNA encoder (config_028 scVI, config_043 PCA), image encoder (config_001, ResNet50), modality (config_022 RNA-only, config_005 image-only) and profile setting (config_014, single-profile). 3. Under a limited budget, anchoring on this hub lets each later experiment isolate the effect of one choice. That is more informative than starting from an isolated configuration. 1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile model (scGPT + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion; config_051) reached 0.520 accuracy and 0.479 F1. We do not yet know how much each modality contributes. 2. What this tests: config_022 keeps the same RNA encoder (scGPT), multiprofile setting and transformer aggregation, but drops the image branch. Only the modality setting changes, so the comparison isolates what the ViT-L image features add on top of scGPT. 3. Why now: whether multimodality helps at all is the highest-level design choice. Its answer shapes how the rest of the budget is spent: refining fusion and image encoders if the image branch helps, or focusing on RNA encoders, profile setting and aggregation if it does not. Settling it first is more informative than tuning secondary choices around a single anchor result.

1) Evidence: Multimodal scGPT+ViT-L (transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) reached 0.520 accuracy and 0.479 F1. RNA-only scGPT with the same multiprofile and transformer setup reached 0.514 accuracy and a higher 0.498 F1. This small, mixed difference leaves open whether the image modality carries useful signal or adds little beyond RNA. 2) This experiment: Image-only ViT-L with the same multiprofile setting and transformer aggregation completes the modality comparison while holding profile setting and aggregation fixed. It shows directly how much predictive signal the image representation provides on its own. 3) Why now: If image-only performs poorly, the remaining budget should go to RNA encoders and aggregation or profile choices rather than fusion variants. If it performs well, fusion design (weighted vs concat) and image encoder choice deserve further exploration. Settling this modality question first is the most efficient way to guide the many remaining multimodal options.

1) Evidence: RNA carries most of the signal so far. RNA-only scGPT with transformer reached 0.514 accuracy and the best F1 (0.498). Image-only ViT-L scored only 0.260. Adding the image to scGPT gave a negligible accuracy gain (0.520) and a lower F1 (0.479), so how much the image helps is still unclear. The largest untested factor is the RNA encoder: only scGPT has been tried. 2) This experiment keeps everything the same as config_022 (RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer aggregation) and swaps scGPT for PCA (n=2000). That isolates the effect of the RNA representation and checks whether a pretrained foundation model actually beats a simple linear baseline. 3) Under a limited budget this is the best next step. RNA dominates performance, so the RNA encoder choice will shape every later multimodal and aggregation comparison. A clean single-factor test on the cheap RNA-only branch resolves this before spending experiments on fusion or image-encoder variants. If PCA matches or beats scGPT, the search should be redirected.

1. Evidence so far: all four completed runs use the multiprofile setting with transformer aggregation. RNA carries most of the signal. RNA-only models with scGPT (0.514 acc / 0.498 F1) and PCA (0.519 acc / 0.480 F1) are nearly tied. Adding ViT-L image features to scGPT gives only a marginal accuracy gain (0.520) and lowers F1. Image-only is weak (0.26). The main untested design choice is the profile setting: we do not yet know whether multiprofile aggregation helps at all compared with single-profile modeling. 2. What this tests: config_012 is the single-profile counterpart of config_022 (RNA-only, scGPT). It changes only the profile setting, giving a clean estimate of what multiprofile modeling contributes. 3. Why this is the best next run: the comparison costs little and isolates one variable, and its answer sets the direction for the rest of the budget. If single-profile matches or beats multiprofile, the search should shift toward simpler single-profile configurations. If it clearly underperforms, multiprofile is confirmed and later runs can focus on aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) and RNA encoder choice.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile clearly beat singleprofile for scGPT RNA-only (0.514 vs 0.411 accuracy). The two RNA encoders performed about the same (scGPT 0.514, PCA 0.519). Adding ViT-L images with weighted fusion gave no clear gain (0.520), consistent with image-only being weak (0.260). Every multiprofile run so far used transformer aggregation, so we do not know whether the transformer actually drives the multiprofile gain. 2. What this tests: config_006 keeps the strong scGPT RNA-only multiprofile setup (config_022) fixed and changes only aggregation, from transformer to avgpool. This is a clean single-variable test of aggregation. 3. Why it is the best next step: aggregation affects every multiprofile configuration, including all multimodal ones. Settling it in the simplest strong baseline will tell us how to prune or prioritize much of the remaining search space. It is more informative than another multimodal variant, where image gains so far look marginal.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, scGPT with avgpool (0.530 acc, 0.515 F1). With transformer aggregation, that same RNA-only setup reached 0.514. Adding ViT-L images with weighted fusion under transformer aggregation gave 0.520, only slightly higher. Image-only models are weak (0.26), so it is still unclear whether the image modality adds anything. 2. This experiment tests multimodal scGPT + ViT-L with avgpool and weighted fusion. It differs from the current best (config_006) only by adding the image modality. It also differs from config_051 only in aggregation. So it gives a clean check of whether images help on top of the strongest RNA setup, and whether the avgpool advantage holds in the multimodal setting. 3. It exploits the most promising direction (multiprofile, scGPT, avgpool) while settling the main open design question, whether multimodality is worth it, with a single-variable comparison. That makes it the most informative use of the next run.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_049 (multimodal scGPT + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; acc 0.542). Avgpool has beaten transformer aggregation in both the RNA-only pair (0.530 vs 0.514) and the multimodal pair (0.542 vs 0.520). Multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile (scGPT RNA-only: 0.411 vs 0.514–0.530). Fusion is the one design axis never tested, since every multimodal run used weighted fusion. 2) Test: config_038 changes only weighted to concat fusion on the best configuration. This isolates the fusion effect directly. It also shows whether a different fusion scheme makes better use of the weak image signal (image-only 0.26). That matters because multimodal's gain over RNA-only is small, and its F1 (0.483) is lower than RNA-only avgpool (0.515). 3) Value: This is a one-variable comparison anchored on the current best. 1. Evidence: Avgpool has beaten transformer aggregation twice: RNA-only scGPT (0.530 vs 0.514) and multimodal weighted (0.542 vs 0.520). The current best is config_049 (scGPT + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion). Under transformer aggregation, PCA_n2000 roughly matched scGPT in RNA-only (0.519 vs 0.514). So the RNA encoder choice is still unresolved, and scGPT may not be needed. 2. Test: config_045 keeps everything from config_049 and swaps only the RNA encoder to PCA_n2000. This isolates whether the foundation-model RNA representation helps in the best-performing setting, or whether a simpler PCA representation does as well or better. 3. Why now: It is a single-variable change to the current best configuration, so it exploits the strongest direction while also answering a key representation question. Image-only results are weak (0.26), so changing the image encoder is likely less informative than the RNA encoder, which drives most of the performance.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_045 (PCA RNA + ViT-L image, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.635 accuracy and 0.618 F1. That is well above every other run. With scGPT, multimodal gave only a modest gain over RNA-only (0.542 vs 0.530 under avgpool). Under transformer aggregation, PCA and scGPT performed about the same in RNA-only (0.519 vs 0.514). The missing control is RNA-only PCA with avgpool. Without it, we cannot tell whether config_045's jump comes from PCA plus avgpool alone or from PCA features combining well with image features in fusion. 2. What this tests: config_036 changes only one thing from config_045, removing the image modality. It also completes the RNA-only encoder × aggregation grid (PCA vs scGPT, avgpool vs transformer). If config_036 scores near 0.63, the RNA representation and aggregation drive performance. If it stays near 0.52–0.53, the gain comes from PCA-specific multimodal complementarity. 3. Why this is the best next run: The result decides where to spend the remaining budget. Either we exploit the multimodal PCA direction further (image encoder, fusion, transformer variants) or we focus on cheaper RNA-only refinements. It also checks how far config_045's single result can be trusted, before we build on it with less diagnostic exploitation runs.

1. Evidence: no experiments have been run yet, so we have no reference point for how well any representation, profile setting, aggregation or fusion choice performs. 2. What this tests: config_031 is the simplest configuration in the space. It uses RNA only, a single profile, a PCA (2000-component) encoder, and no aggregation or fusion. Its validation accuracy and F1 set a baseline floor. Later experiments can then each change one factor from this anchor: scVI or scGPT encoders for representation, multiprofile with avgpool or transformer for profile setting and aggregation, image-only for modality, and adding images with concat or weighted fusion. Each change can be attributed to that factor rather than confounded with others. 3. Why this is the best first use of the budget: starting from a complex multimodal, multiprofile model would leave us unable to tell whether any gain comes from images, multiple profiles, the aggregation method or the fusion method. A simple baseline also guards against assuming that complexity helps, and it maximises what every later comparison can tell us.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. The RNA-only, single-profile PCA (n2000) baseline reached 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. We know nothing yet about how profile setting, modality, encoder, aggregation or fusion affect performance. 2) Question: config_013 keeps the model setting (RNA-only) and RNA encoder (PCA n2000) fixed. It switches only to multiprofile with avgpool, the simplest aggregation. This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles improves on the single-profile baseline. 3) Why now: profile setting runs through most of the search space, since most multimodal configurations are multiprofile. Settling it early with a clean one-factor comparison against the existing baseline tells us whether to focus later experiments on multiprofile designs, before we spend budget on more complex aggregation, image or fusion choices.

1) Evidence: with RNA only and PCA features, moving from a single profile (config_031, acc 0.485) to multiple profiles with avgpool (config_013, acc 0.591, F1 0.573) gave a large gain on both metrics, about 0.10. That makes multiprofile avgpool a strong working baseline. The image modality is completely untested, and it is the largest open design question. 2) Test: config_045 keeps everything from config_013 the same (multiprofile, PCA RNA encoder, avgpool) and adds ResNet50 image features with concat fusion. Any change in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed to adding images. 3) Why now: whether images help or hurt decides whether the remaining budget goes to the many multimodal configurations or to refining RNA-only encoders and aggregation. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool gave a large gain for PCA RNA-only (0.485 to 0.591). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion gave a smaller gain (0.591 to 0.619, with F1 0.573 to 0.610). We do not know how much signal the image branch carries alone. The modest multimodal gain could mean images are weak, or that images are strong and concat fusion is not using them well. 2. What this tests: config_008 runs image-only with ResNet50, multiprofile and avgpool, matching config_045 except that the RNA branch is removed. It completes a clean modality ablation (RNA-only vs image-only vs multimodal) under the same profile and aggregation setting. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: The result decides where to spend the remaining budget. If image-only nears or beats multimodal, image encoder and fusion choices deserve priority. If it is weak, RNA encoder choice (scVI or scGPT) and aggregation become the main levers. One run answers this, which is a better use of budget than tuning secondary choices before the basic modality contributions are known.

1. Evidence: Moving RNA (PCA) from single-profile to multi-profile with avgpool gave the largest gain so far (0.485 to 0.591 accuracy). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion added only a modest further gain (0.619 accuracy, 0.610 F1). ResNet50 image-only is weak (0.328). So profile aggregation looks like the most influential design choice, but only the simple avgpool aggregator has been tried. 2. Test: config_005 keeps the current best configuration (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA, ResNet50, concat) and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. This isolates whether learned, attention-based aggregation across profiles improves on mean pooling. 3. Value: It builds directly on the best configuration while changing a single factor, so the result is interpretable. Whichever way it turns out, it tells us whether later experiments should use transformer or avgpool. Image-encoder (config_002) and fusion (config_030) swaps are the natural next one-factor comparisons, but aggregation is the design axis with the strongest evidence of large effects.

1) Evidence: RNA carries most of the signal. RNA-only multiprofile reached 0.591, while image-only ResNet50 reached only 0.328. Adding images to the PCA multiprofile model gave a modest gain (0.619 accuracy, 0.610 F1). Multiprofile clearly beat single-profile (0.591 vs 0.485), and avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.619 vs 0.579). The RNA encoder is the main untested choice: every run so far used pca_n2000, so we do not know whether scVI or scGPT embeddings would do better. 2) Test: config_025 keeps the current best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder to scvi_n200. This isolates the effect of the RNA representation on the dominant modality. 3) Why now: because RNA dominates performance, its representation is likely the most consequential remaining choice. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile with avgpool beats singleprofile (0.591 vs 0.485 RNA-only with PCA). Avgpool beats transformer aggregation (0.619 vs 0.579). Adding images helps modestly (0.591 to 0.619 with PCA). Swapping PCA for scVI gives the current best, config_025 at 0.632 accuracy, though its F1 is similar to PCA's. ResNet50 image features are weak on their own (0.328 image-only), and the alternative image encoder, imagenet_vit_l, has never been tested. So the image representation is a large untested design choice that may be limiting how much the image modality contributes. 2. What this tests: config_004 changes only the image encoder relative to the best configuration (ResNet50 to ViT-L, keeping scVI, multiprofile, avgpool and concat). Any difference can therefore be attributed to the image representation. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: it resolves the most consequential unexplored dimension with a single-variable comparison. It is also a logical extension of the strongest configuration, so it has good odds of improving the best result. Weighted fusion and scGPT can be tested afterwards on whichever image backbone wins.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_004 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Switching the image encoder from resnet50 to ViT-L gave about +8 points. Changing the RNA encoder from pca to scvi gave only a small, mixed gain (+1.3 accuracy, slightly lower F1). Multiprofile with avgpool beats singleprofile and transformer aggregation. scGPT has never been tested, so it is the largest open question among the RNA encoders. What this tests: config_034 changes only the RNA encoder (scvi_n200 to scGPT) within the best setup, isolating whether a foundation-model RNA representation adds value once the strong ViT image features are present. Why now: it explores a completely untested design level in the context most likely to perform well. Either outcome is informative: a gain would set a new best, and no gain would let us fix the RNA encoder and focus remaining budget on fusion (weighted) and ablations such as image-only ViT.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_004 (scVI + ImageNet ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Several design choices already have some evidence. Multiprofile beat singleprofile for PCA RNA (0.591 vs 0.485). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.619 vs 0.579). Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L improved results substantially with scVI (0.632 to 0.715). scGPT performed poorly (0.518). Why now: Fusion is the one major design axis with no evidence at all, so this experiment reduces the most uncertainty. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_004 (scVI + ImageNet ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 accuracy. Test: config_012 (image-only ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool) differs from config_008 only in the image encoder, giving a clean unimodal measure of ViT-L. Why now: This resolves a key uncertainty, whether the gain reflects true multimodal complementarity or simply a much better image representation. That guides whether remaining budget should go to RNA and fusion refinements or to image-side choices, at the cost of one experiment.

Test: config_041 keeps the modality (RNA-only) and encoder (PCA-2000) fixed and changes only the profile setting to multiprofile. 1) Evidence: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, at about 0.65 accuracy versus about 0.51-0.52 for scGPT and PCA. Multiprofile beats singleprofile by a wide margin (0.650 vs 0.520). Avgpool and transformer aggregation perform almost identically (0.650 vs 0.653). The one multimodal run, scVI + ResNet50 with avgpool and concat fusion, scored 0.632. Weighted fusion could let the model down-weight a weaker or noisier image signal rather than diluting the strong scVI representation. 3) Why now: the main open question is whether multimodality adds value over the strong RNA-only baseline. A single-variable fusion comparison on the best-known backbone answers it directly. It also has a realistic chance of becoming the new best configuration. If weighted fusion also fails to beat RNA-only, that points next to testing image quality, such as image-only or ViT-L runs, rather than spending budget on further fusion variants.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_024 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion; acc 0.678, F1 0.646). 1) Evidence: the best result so far is multimodal multiprofile scVI + ViT-L with avgpool aggregation and weighted fusion (config_045: 0.706 accuracy, 0.667 F1). Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L (config_024 to config_045) and concat for weighted fusion (config_022 to config_024) each improved results. scVI clearly beats scGPT and PCA, and multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile. The main gap is that no image-only model has been tested, so we cannot tell how much of the multimodal gain comes from the image features versus genuine fusion with RNA. 2) Test: config_046 is image-only, multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool. If image-only comes close to 0.706, effort should shift to image-side choices. If it falls well short, refining fusion and aggregation in the multimodal setup (for example config_034) is justified. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_045 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion), at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, and multiprofile beats singleprofile. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: the best result so far is config_040 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat; 0.715 accuracy). 1. The best result so far is config_040 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat fusion) at 0.715 accuracy. It clearly beats RNA-only scVI (about 0.65) and the ResNet50 multimodal variant (0.63). 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_040 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. 1. Evidence: there is only one result so far, an RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline at 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. Test: config_049 keeps the RNA encoder and profile setting the same and adds image features (ImageNet ViT-L) through simple concat fusion. Evidence: in the single-profile setting with PCA RNA features, adding ImageNet ViT-L image features via concat fusion raised validation accuracy from 0.485 to 0.535, and F1 rose in parallel. That gain has two possible explanations. Image features may complement RNA, or images alone may be the stronger signal, with RNA adding little or even diluting it. This experiment tests the image-only single-profile ViT-L model, which completes the modality comparison under identical profile and encoder settings. It will show whether the multimodal gain reflects true fusion benefit or mostly image signal. That answer shapes the rest of the search: either keep investing in fusion and RNA encoder choices, or prioritize image-centric and multiprofile image settings. Under a limited budget, one cheap baseline that removes the main ambiguity in the existing result is worth more than jumping to more complex multiprofile configurations, which would change several factors at once.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is multimodal single-profile PCA plus ViT-L with concat fusion (acc 0.535, F1 0.519). It beats RNA-only (0.485), and image-only is weak (0.227). This suggests RNA carries most of the signal and imaging adds some, but each setting has only one run. Profile setting has not been tested at all, and it is a major design axis. 2) Test: config_027 keeps the best configuration's RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion. It switches only to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool), which multiprofile requires. This gives a near-clean test of whether multiprofile inputs help over single-profile. 3) Why now: it builds directly on the strongest result while answering a large open question. If it helps, transformer aggregation (config_022) is the natural follow-up. If it does not, the budget can move to RNA encoder or fusion comparisons within the single-profile setting.

1. Evidence: Moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised validation accuracy from 0.535 (config_049) to 0.629 (config_027), with F1 rising similarly. Multimodal concat also beat RNA-only (0.485), and image-only was weak (0.227). The strongest signal so far is that multiprofile aggregation matters, but only one aggregation method (avgpool) has been tried. 2. Test: config_022 keeps everything from the current best fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, ViT-L, concat) and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. Why now: This extends the most promising direction while varying a single factor, so any change can be attributed to aggregation alone. 1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is clearly the dominant modality, with RNA-only at 0.485 versus image-only at 0.227. Adding images helps modestly (0.535 vs 0.485 single-profile). Evidence: the best result so far is config_007 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. scVI clearly beat PCA (0.629) and scGPT (0.518) under the same setup. 1. Evidence: Within RNA-only PCA models, multiprofile avgpool (0.591 acc, 0.573 F1) clearly beat singleprofile (0.485 acc, 0.464 F1). 1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_004 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) reached 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. 1. Evidence: Moving from single profile to multiprofile was the largest effect seen so far. With PCA RNA-only, accuracy rose from 0.485 to 0.591. Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion gave a smaller gain, to 0.619 with PCA and 0.632 with scVI. The scVI vs PCA gap is small, and F1 is slightly higher for PCA (0.610 vs 0.607), so the encoder choice is still uncertain. Every multiprofile run so far has used avgpool, so we do not yet know whether the aggregation method matters. 2. Test: config_012 keeps the current best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ResNet50, concat) and changes only avgpool to transformer. This directly isolates the effect of aggregation. 3. Why now: Multiprofile is the most influential factor found so far, so how the profiles are aggregated is likely an important lever. This one-variable change from the best configuration either exploits a promising direction or rules out transformer aggregation. In both cases it guides later choices of encoder and fusion more efficiently than changing several factors at once.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_012 (multimodal scVI + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. Switching from avgpool to transformer aggregation added about 0.056 accuracy, and multiprofile beat singleprofile clearly for PCA RNA-only. However, the image contribution looks modest: with PCA and avgpool, adding images raised accuracy only from 0.591 to 0.619, and image-only reached just 0.328. It is unclear whether the transformer gain comes from better use of multiple RNA profiles or from better cross-profile use of image features. 2. What this tests: config_004 is scVI RNA-only, multiprofile, with transformer aggregation. It differs from the best config only by removing the image modality. This isolates whether images add real value under the strongest aggregation, and it also gives a second data point on transformer versus avgpool for RNA alone. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: If RNA-only matches config_012, future experiments should focus on RNA encoders and aggregation rather than on image encoders or fusion. If it falls clearly short, that justifies spending later experiments on image-side choices (ViT-L) and weighted fusion. Either outcome changes how the remaining budget should be spent.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_012 (multimodal, scVI, ResNet50, transformer, concat) at 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. Transformer aggregation gave a clear gain over avgpool (0.632 to 0.688), and multiprofile beat singleprofile. Adding ResNet50 images improved accuracy over the matched RNA-only transformer model (0.653 to 0.688). This isolates the effect of the image representation within the strongest pipeline. 3. Why now: Image representation is a high-uncertainty choice with potentially large upside, given how weak the current image features appear. This single-factor exploitation step both tries to improve on the best model and answers an important open design question. Fusion type (config_007) and the scGPT encoder are natural follow-ups.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_019 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer, concat) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Prior runs show that transformer aggregation (0.688 vs 0.632) and the ViT-L image encoder (0.721 vs 0.688) both helped. Among RNA encoders, scVI only slightly beat PCA (0.632 vs 0.619). scGPT has never been tested, so it is the largest remaining gap on the representation axis. 2. Test: config_030 changes only the RNA encoder, from scVI to scGPT, and keeps everything else identical to the best setup. This isolates whether a foundation-model RNA representation beats scVI in the strongest pipeline. 3. Why now: RNA is the dominant modality, so the RNA encoder is likely the most important open design choice. This single-factor comparison could find a new best model while settling an uncertainty that applies to many remaining configurations. Weighted fusion (config_034) is also untested, but it is a natural follow-up once the best encoder is known.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_019 (scVI + ImageNet ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Earlier comparisons suggest transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632 with ResNet50) and ViT-L beats ResNet50 (0.721 vs 0.688), with each step changing one factor. 1. Evidence: no experiments have been run, so there is no information yet about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion matters. 2. What this tests: a simple single-profile, RNA-only model with the scVI encoder sets a reference level of performance. 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far, the RNA-only single-profile scVI baseline (config_004, acc 0.520, F1 0.498). No gain, or a loss, would steer the budget toward unimodal refinements such as other RNA encoders or multiprofile aggregation. Either outcome is informative under the limited budget.

1. Evidence: Only single-profile models have been tested. Adding ResNet50 image features to scVI with concat fusion gave a small gain over RNA-only (accuracy 0.536 vs 0.520, F1 0.516 vs 0.498). Test: config_019 keeps everything from the current best (config_005: scVI, ResNet50, concat) and switches only to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation, avgpool. The only change from config_005 is single vs multiprofile, with aggregation set to the simplest option that multiprofile requires. Whichever way it comes out, it tells us whether later experiments should invest in multiprofile variants, such as transformer aggregation or other encoders, or stay with single-profile.

1) Evidence: Going from single-profile (config_005, 0.536 acc) to multiprofile with avgpool (config_019, 0.632 acc, F1 0.607) gave a large gain. Adding images in the single-profile setting gave only a small gain over RNA-only (0.536 vs 0.520). If RNA-only multiprofile matches config_019, later experiments can focus on aggregation and RNA encoders. 1. Evidence: Using multiple profiles is the clearest effect so far. It raised accuracy by about 0.10 to 0.13 for both the RNA-only model (0.520 to 0.650) and the multimodal model (0.536 to 0.632). Adding ResNet50 images to multiprofile scVI did not beat RNA-only (0.632 vs 0.650, with F1 following the same pattern). Test: config_010 keeps the current best setup (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200) and changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to a transformer. This isolates whether learned attention over profiles adds value beyond simple averaging. 3. Why now: Aggregation is only relevant in the multiprofile setting, which has given the largest gains. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile input is the clearest effect so far, adding about 0.11 to 0.13 accuracy over singleprofile. Within RNA-only multiprofile, transformer (0.653) and avgpool (0.650) aggregation are essentially tied. Adding ResNet50 images under avgpool/concat (0.632) did not beat RNA-only, so the RNA representation looks like the main signal carrier. 1. Evidence: Multiprofile input clearly helps. scVI RNA-only rose from 0.520 single-profile to about 0.650 multiprofile. The best results so far come from RNA-only multiprofile scVI with transformer (0.653) or avgpool (0.650) aggregation, which differ very little. Adding ResNet50 images under avgpool/concat lowered accuracy (0.632), so images have not yet shown a benefit.
