It lets each later gain be attributed to a specific design choice, and it avoids assuming that more complex multimodal or multiprofile models will help.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 established the first baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA encoder (pca_n2000), with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.485 and validation F1 0.464. The similar F1 suggests performance is not driven by a few classes alone, but this is an initial observation. Because no other experiments exist yet, it is unknown whether learned RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image features, or multimodal fusion would improve on this, so later runs should change one factor at a time against this reference. Run-to-run variance and the chance-level baseline for this task are also unknown, so it is unclear how strong this result is or how large a difference would be meaningful.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The only result so far is an RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (acc 0.485, F1 0.464). Nothing is yet known about the image modality, and image encoders appear in 36 of the 50 remaining configurations. 2) What this tests: An image-only, single-profile ResNet50 model with no aggregation or fusion is the simplest image reference. It is directly comparable to the RNA baseline and shows whether images carry signal on their own, and roughly how much compared with RNA. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: This result decides whether the large image and multimodal part of the search space is worth exploring, and it gives the second unimodal reference needed to judge later fusion gains. Finer questions within RNA (scVI or scGPT vs PCA, multiprofile aggregation) affect fewer configurations and can follow next.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested the simplest image reference: an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.208 and F1 0.172, well below the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001: accuracy 0.485, F1 0.464), and the lower F1 suggests performance may be less even across classes. This is an initial observation that this image setup underperforms the RNA baseline, but it does not show that the image modality is inherently weaker, because the two runs differ in both modality and encoder type (a pretrained CNN versus PCA). Chance level, run-to-run variance, and the effect of other image encoders or multiprofile aggregation are unknown, so it remains unclear whether the image signal is meaningfully above chance and whether images could still add complementary information under multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: So far there are only two single-profile runs. RNA-only PCA (config_001) reached accuracy 0.485 and F1 0.464. Image-only ResNet50 (config_010) reached accuracy 0.208 and F1 0.172. So RNA with PCA is the strongest reference so far. We still know nothing about whether multiprofile aggregation helps, and that choice affects most of the remaining search space. 2. What this tests: config_002 changes only one factor from the best baseline. It switches single-profile to multiprofile and uses the simplest aggregation (avgpool), keeping the same RNA-only PCA encoder. This isolates whether aggregating multiple profiles improves accuracy and F1 over single-profile. 3. Why this is the best next use of budget: The profile setting applies across RNA-only, image-only and multimodal configurations, so its answer narrows many future choices at once. Starting from the strongest known baseline gives a clean comparison with a reasonable chance of immediate gains. Avgpool comes before the transformer so that any benefit can be attributed to multiprofile aggregation itself rather than aggregator complexity. Encoder and fusion comparisons can follow once we know which profile setting to build on.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with the same PCA encoder (pca_n2000) as the RNA baseline, using simple average-pooling aggregation and no image encoder or fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.591 and F1 0.573, up from the single-profile RNA PCA baseline (llm_summary_001: accuracy 0.485, F1 0.464). Because profile setting is the only design factor that differs from that baseline, this is the first controlled evidence that multiprofile aggregation improves RNA-only PCA performance, and the similar gains in accuracy and F1 suggest the benefit is broad across classes. This is still a single run with unknown run-to-run variance, so the size of the gain is uncertain. It is also unknown whether more complex aggregators (e.g., a transformer) would add more, and whether the benefit carries over to image-only, other RNA encoders, or multimodal fusion settings.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The clearest result so far is that multiprofile aggregation improves RNA-only PCA. Accuracy rose from 0.485 to 0.591 and F1 from 0.464 to 0.573 when only the profile setting changed. Each result is a single run with unknown variance. It is also unknown whether the aggregation method itself matters, or whether simple average pooling already captures most of the multiprofile benefit. 2. What this tests: config_003 matches the current best run (config_002: RNA-only, multiprofile, pca_n2000) except that it swaps avgpool for transformer aggregation. Aggregation is therefore the only factor that changes. This isolates whether a learned set-level aggregator adds value over mean pooling. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: It builds on the strongest evidence so far while answering a design question that affects every remaining multiprofile configuration, including the multimodal ones. Knowing whether to prefer transformer or avgpool lets later encoder and fusion comparisons use the right aggregator, which saves budget. It is also a low-risk extension that could raise the best accuracy. Encoder (scVI or scGPT) and image-fusion comparisons can follow against whichever aggregator wins.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with the PCA encoder (pca_n2000) and transformer aggregation, with no image encoder or fusion. It differs from the current best run (llm_summary_003, avgpool) only in the aggregation method. It reached validation accuracy 0.519 and F1 0.480, below llm_summary_003 (accuracy 0.591, F1 0.573) and only modestly above the single-profile RNA PCA baseline (llm_summary_001: accuracy 0.485, F1 0.464). Because aggregation is the only changed factor, this is controlled initial evidence that, in this setup, the transformer aggregator did not outperform simple average pooling and may underperform it, so avgpool is the stronger default for now. Each result is a single run with unknown variance, and the transformer's training settings and capacity are unknown, so it is unclear whether the gap is robust or reflects optimization difficulty. Whether this aggregator ranking holds for other RNA encoders, image-only, or multimodal fusion settings is also unknown.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA with avgpool (acc 0.591, F1 0.573). Multiprofile beat single-profile, and avgpool beat the transformer aggregator in controlled comparisons. The RNA encoder choice is untested: every run so far used PCA. That choice also sets up most of the remaining multimodal configurations, and RNA is clearly the stronger modality so far (image-only ResNet50 reached acc 0.208). 2. What this tests: config_005 keeps the best setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps only the encoder from PCA to scVI. This isolates whether a learned, lower-dimensional RNA representation helps or hurts compared with PCA. 3. Why this is the best next run: It is a controlled, one-factor change on the strongest pipeline, so it is informative whichever way it turns out. If scVI wins, it becomes the default RNA encoder for later fusion runs. If it loses, PCA is reinforced and the next runs can test scGPT or adding images on a solid RNA baseline. That is more efficient than jumping to multimodal fusion before the stronger modality's representation is settled.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with avgpool aggregation and no image encoder or fusion, changing only the RNA encoder from PCA (pca_n2000) to scVI (scvi_n200) relative to the previous best run (llm_summary_003). It reached validation accuracy 0.650 and F1 0.628, the best so far and above llm_summary_003 (accuracy 0.591, F1 0.573). Because only the encoder setting differs, this is controlled initial evidence that scvi_n200 outperforms pca_n2000 in this pipeline, with similar gains in accuracy and F1 suggesting a broad benefit across classes; scvi_n200 is a reasonable provisional default RNA encoder for later runs, including fusion. However, the encoder swap changes both the method (learned vs. linear) and the dimensionality (200 vs. 2000), so it cannot say which drove the gain, and with single runs of unknown variance the size and robustness of the ~0.06 accuracy gap are uncertain; whether scVI's advantage holds against other encoders such as scGPT, with other aggregators, or under multimodal fusion remains untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile avgpool clearly beat single-profile in a controlled comparison (0.591 vs 0.485). scvi_n200 beat pca_n2000 under that setting (0.650 vs 0.591), so config_005 is the current best. Image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.208). Fusion has never been tested, so it is unknown whether images add complementary signal to RNA or only add noise. 2) What this tests: config_030 keeps the best RNA pipeline (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds the ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion. Comparing it with config_005 isolates whether adding images through basic fusion helps, hurts or does nothing. 3) Why now: Fusion is the central untested design axis, and this run probes it in the strongest context found so far. Concat is the simplest fusion method, so the result is easy to interpret, and a weighted-fusion follow-up can come next if the result looks promising. The scGPT encoder comparison (config_008) is also informative but only refines a choice we already have evidence on, whereas fusion is completely unexplored.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 tested the first multimodal fusion run. It kept the best RNA pipeline (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) and added a ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion, so adding images via concat is the only change relative to the current best, llm_summary_005 (RNA-only: accuracy 0.650, F1 0.628). It reached validation accuracy 0.632 and F1 0.607, slightly below llm_summary_005 on both metrics, so this is controlled initial evidence that adding ResNet50 image features through naive concatenation did not improve on RNA-only in this setup and may slightly hurt; llm_summary_005 remains the best configuration. The ~0.02 accuracy gap comes from single runs with unknown variance and may not be meaningful, and it is unclear whether the lack of benefit reflects weak image features (image-only ResNet50 scored only 0.208), the fusion method (e.g., an unweighted concat letting a noisy branch dilute the RNA signal), or optimization effects, so weighted or gated fusion, other image encoders, and multiprofile image-only references remain untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: the best result so far is RNA-only scvi_n200 with multiprofile avgpool (acc 0.650, F1 0.628). Adding ResNet50 images through concat fusion (config_030) scored slightly lower (acc 0.632, F1 0.607). We cannot yet tell whether this reflects weak image features (image-only ResNet50 scored 0.208) or unweighted concat letting a noisy image branch dilute the RNA signal. 2) What this tests: config_031 is identical to config_030 except that it uses weighted fusion instead of concat. This isolates the fusion method. If weighted fusion matches or beats RNA-only, fusion design was the bottleneck and multimodal is still promising. If it also falls short, the problem more likely lies with the ResNet50 image features, which would point next to the ViT encoder or to more RNA-encoder work such as scGPT. 3) Why now: it is a single-factor change on the strongest pipeline. It answers a central question for this study, whether images can add value with a better fusion method, before budget is spent on the many other multimodal configurations.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the llm_summary_006 multimodal pipeline (scvi_n200 RNA, ResNet50 images, multiprofile, avgpool) and changed only the fusion method from concat to weighted, which isolates fusion design. It reached validation accuracy 0.678 and F1 0.646. That is the best result so far, above both the concat run (llm_summary_006: accuracy 0.632, F1 0.607) and the RNA-only best (llm_summary_005: accuracy 0.650, F1 0.628), with consistent gains on both metrics. This is controlled initial evidence that weighted fusion outperforms concat in this setup and that ResNet50 image features can add value over RNA-only when fused this way. The concat shortfall therefore looks more like a fusion bottleneck than purely weak image features, and multimodal remains promising. However, these are single runs with unknown variance, so the ~0.03 gain over RNA-only and the ~0.05 gain over concat may not be robust. It is also unknown what weights the fusion learned or how much it relies on the image branch, and whether the benefit holds with other image encoders (e.g., ViT), RNA encoders (e.g., scGPT), aggregators, or gated or attention-based fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The current best is config_031 (scvi_n200, ResNet50, multiprofile avgpool, weighted fusion; accuracy 0.678, F1 0.646). It beat the RNA-only run (0.650) and concat fusion (0.632), so weighted fusion can extract value from images. But ResNet50 alone was weak (image-only accuracy 0.208), and the image encoder choice has never been varied. That makes it the largest untested lever in the most promising pipeline. 2) What this tests: config_037 keeps everything in config_031 fixed and swaps only ResNet50 for imagenet_vit_l. This isolates whether a stronger image representation increases the multimodal gain, and whether the image branch is the bottleneck. 3) Why it is the best use of budget: It exploits the strongest direction (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) while answering a clean, single-factor question about a design choice that affects every multimodal configuration. Its result will guide later choices, such as image-only ViT references or scGPT swaps. If ViT does not help, that suggests image features add only modest complementary signal regardless of encoder.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the best pipeline from llm_summary_007 (multimodal, scvi_n200 RNA, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) and changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to imagenet_vit_l. It reached validation accuracy 0.706 and F1 0.667, the best so far, above llm_summary_007 (accuracy 0.678, F1 0.646) and the RNA-only best (llm_summary_005: accuracy 0.650, F1 0.628). Because the image encoder is the only changed factor, this is controlled initial evidence that imagenet_vit_l gives a larger multimodal gain than ResNet50 in this setup, which suggests the image branch was a bottleneck. It makes imagenet_vit_l a reasonable provisional default image encoder. However, these are single runs with unknown variance, so the ~0.03 accuracy gain may not be robust. The swap also changes both architecture (ViT vs. CNN) and model scale, so it cannot say which drove the gain. No image-only ViT reference exists, and the learned fusion weights are unknown, so it remains unclear how much stronger the ViT features are on their own and how much the fused model relies on them. Whether the benefit holds with other RNA encoders (e.g., scGPT), aggregators, or fusion methods is untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_037 (multimodal, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion), at accuracy 0.706 and F1 0.667. Controlled one-factor comparisons favor multiprofile over single-profile, avgpool over transformer, weighted fusion over concat, and ViT-L over ResNet50. The RNA encoder is the biggest remaining unknown. scGPT has never been tested, yet the PCA-to-scVI swap gave one of the largest single gains (about +0.06), so RNA representation clearly matters. 2. What this tests: config_049 changes only the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to scGPT and keeps every other choice from the best pipeline. This isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation beats scVI in the strongest setting. 3. Why this is the best next run: It explores a completely unsampled level of a high-impact factor while still building on the best configuration, so it could also produce a new best. If scGPT underperforms, scVI is confirmed as the default and later runs can refine aggregation, fusion, or image-only references.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the best pipeline from llm_summary_008 (multimodal, multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l images, avgpool, weighted fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to scGPT, which isolates RNA representation in the strongest setting. It reached validation accuracy 0.542 and F1 0.483, far below llm_summary_008 (accuracy 0.706, F1 0.667) and below even the RNA-only scVI and PCA multiprofile runs (llm_summary_005: 0.650; llm_summary_003: 0.591). This is controlled initial evidence that scGPT embeddings, as used here, underperform scVI in this pipeline, so scvi_n200 remains the provisional default RNA encoder and llm_summary_008 remains the best configuration. The ~0.16 drop is large compared with other single-factor changes, but it comes from single runs with unknown variance. It is also unclear whether the drop reflects scGPT's representation itself or how it was used (e.g., frozen vs. fine-tuned embeddings, preprocessing or gene-vocabulary mismatch, dimensionality, or interaction with weighted fusion). No RNA-only scGPT reference exists to separate encoder quality from fusion effects.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best run is config_037 (multimodal, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; accuracy 0.706, F1 0.667). It improved on the ResNet50 version (0.678) and on the RNA-only scVI run (0.650). However, the only image-only reference is single-profile ResNet50, which scored a weak 0.208. So we do not know how strong ViT image features are on their own, or whether multiprofile avgpool helps the image modality the way it helped RNA (PCA rose from 0.485 to 0.591). 2. What this tests: An image-only, multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool run uses the same image branch, profile setting and aggregation as the best model, with the RNA branch removed. It measures the standalone image signal under the best setup. That shows whether the ViT gain reflects much stronger image features or mainly complementary information picked up by weighted fusion. It also gives a first look at the effect of multiprofile aggregation on images. 3. Why now: Tweaks near the optimum, such as a transformer aggregator, are less promising given the evidence so far, because transformer aggregation underperformed avgpool in the RNA-only PCA run. This run reduces uncertainty about a key modality and representation choice. It will help decide whether further multimodal or image-side exploration is worthwhile under the limited budget.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 tested an image-only, multiprofile model with the imagenet_vit_l encoder and avgpool aggregation. This is the same image branch, profile setting and aggregation as the best run (llm_summary_008: multimodal, accuracy 0.706, F1 0.667), with the RNA branch removed. It reached validation accuracy 0.332 and F1 0.315. That is well above the only other image-only run (llm_summary_002: single-profile ResNet50, 0.208) but far below the RNA-only scVI multiprofile run (llm_summary_005: 0.650) and even the single-profile RNA PCA baseline (0.485). This is initial evidence that ViT image features are weak on their own, so the multimodal gain from ViT over RNA-only (~0.06) more likely reflects complementary information captured by weighted fusion than a strong standalone image signal. However, the run differs from llm_summary_002 in both encoder (ViT vs. ResNet50) and profile setting, so it cannot say whether the ViT architecture or scale, or multiprofile aggregation, drove the image-only improvement. These remain open because single-profile ViT and multiprofile ResNet50 image-only references are missing, and chance level, run-to-run variance and the learned fusion weights are also unknown.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest configuration in the space. It sets a reference baseline for accuracy and F1. Each later design choice can then be judged by changing one factor from it: scVI or scGPT for the encoder, multiprofile with avgpool or transformer for profile setting and aggregation, and adding an image encoder for multimodal fusion. 3) With a limited budget, a clean baseline makes every later comparison easier to interpret. It also guards against assuming that more complex multimodal or multiprofile models are better. Starting from a complex configuration would confound several factors at once.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest configuration in the search space as a reference baseline: RNA-only input, a single profile, a PCA RNA encoder with 2000 components, and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.4849 and a supporting validation F1 of 0.4639. Because this is the first completed experiment, these values are an initial baseline only and say nothing yet about whether other choices would help. The open questions to test by changing one factor at a time are alternative RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile settings with avgpool or transformer aggregation, and adding an image modality with fusion. Run-to-run variance is also unknown, so small future differences from this baseline should be read cautiously.

selection_reason: 1) The only evidence so far is one RNA-only baseline (PCA-2000, single profile) at 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. We do not yet know how informative the image modality is, and that matters before spending budget on the many multimodal and image configurations. 2) config_010 tests image-only input with ResNet50 under the same single-profile setting and no aggregation or fusion. This gives a direct RNA-versus-image comparison under matched conditions, so the result can be attributed to the modality rather than to profile or aggregation choices. 3) This experiment shapes more of the remaining search than any other single test. If images are weak, multimodal gains are less likely and the budget should shift toward RNA encoders and multiprofile settings. If images are comparable or stronger, testing fusion becomes a priority. Encoder swaps such as scVI and scGPT, and the multiprofile comparisons, can follow as one-factor tests once the role of each modality is clearer.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested image-only input with a ResNet50 image encoder under a single-profile setting with no aggregation or fusion. This configuration reached a validation accuracy of 0.2079 (supporting F1 0.1718), far below the RNA-only PCA-2000 baseline from llm_summary_001 (0.4849 accuracy, 0.4639 F1). The comparison holds profile setting, aggregation and fusion fixed, but it changes modality and encoder together, so it shows that this particular image pipeline is much less informative than the PCA RNA baseline rather than proving the image modality itself is weak. Several questions remain open: whether other image encoders or multiprofile aggregation would improve image performance, whether images add complementary signal when fused with RNA despite their weak standalone result, and how large run-to-run variance is, since each configuration has only one run.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile (0.485 acc, 0.464 F1) far outperforms image-only ResNet50 single-profile (0.208 acc). So RNA is the stronger anchor modality. Profile setting, aggregation, RNA encoder and fusion are all still untested, and each result comes from a single run. 2. Test: config_002 changes only the profile setting, from singleprofile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation, while keeping the best-known RNA-only PCA pipeline fixed. This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles helps. 3. Why now: profile setting affects about two-thirds of the remaining search space, across RNA-only, image-only and multimodal configs. Measuring its effect on the strongest baseline, using the simplest aggregator, gives the most information per run. It also sets up a clean follow-up comparison of avgpool against transformer (config_003). If the gain is clear, multiprofile branches become the priority; if not, the search can focus on single-profile encoder and fusion questions.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept the RNA-only PCA-2000 pipeline from llm_summary_001 fixed and changed only the profile setting, from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. Validation accuracy rose from 0.4849 to 0.5907, about +0.106, and supporting F1 rose from 0.4639 to 0.5727, about +0.109. Because only the profile setting changed, this is the cleanest comparison in the study so far and suggests that pooling multiple profiles helps the RNA-only PCA pipeline, though multiprofile and avgpool are tested here only as a combined choice. Several points remain uncertain: each configuration has a single run with unknown variance (although the gain is large); it is unknown whether transformer aggregation would do better than avgpool, whether the benefit carries over to other RNA encoders, image-only or multimodal settings, and whether the gain comes from aggregating profiles in general or from avgpool specifically.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only PCA-2000 multiprofile with avgpool (0.5907 accuracy, 0.5727 F1). It beat the single-profile baseline by about 0.106 accuracy in a clean one-factor comparison. However, multiprofile was only tested together with avgpool, so it is unclear whether the gain comes from aggregating profiles in general or from avgpool specifically. 2) Test: config_003 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, with modality, encoder and profile setting held fixed. This isolates the effect of aggregation on the strongest pipeline. 3) Why now: Aggregation choice appears in nearly every remaining multiprofile configuration, including the multimodal ones. Settling it on a strong, cheap RNA-only base exploits the promising multiprofile direction while reducing uncertainty that affects most of the remaining search space. With single runs, only a clear accuracy difference supported by F1 should be treated as meaningful.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 held the RNA-only PCA-2000 multiprofile pipeline from llm_summary_003 fixed and changed only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer. Validation accuracy fell from 0.5907 to 0.5191 (about -0.072), and supporting F1 fell from 0.5727 to 0.4797 (about -0.093). This clean one-factor comparison suggests that avgpool is the better aggregator for this pipeline. The transformer result still sits modestly above the single-profile baseline from llm_summary_001 (+0.034 accuracy, +0.016 F1), which weakly suggests that multiprofile aggregation helps in general, but that margin is small relative to unknown run-to-run variance. It remains uncertain whether the transformer's deficit reflects an inherent limitation or insufficient tuning/data for a higher-capacity aggregator, whether the avgpool advantage carries over to other RNA encoders, image-only or multimodal settings, and how stable either result is, given single runs.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_002 (RNA-only, PCA-2000, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.591 accuracy and 0.573 F1. In clean one-factor comparisons, multiprofile with avgpool beat both single-profile and transformer aggregation. Image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.208 accuracy), but that result cannot tell us whether images add complementary signal when fused with RNA. Multimodal fusion is the central untested design question in this study. 2) Test: config_018 keeps the best pipeline fixed (PCA-2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes one factor: it adds the ResNet50 image modality with simple concat fusion. Comparing it with config_002 isolates whether adding images helps, hurts or has no effect. 3) Why now: This tests the most consequential open question while building on the strongest configuration, so it has a reasonable chance of beating the current best. Its result will also show whether further multimodal experiments are worth the budget, such as weighted fusion or the ViT-L image encoder. If it does not help, the remaining budget can shift to RNA encoder comparisons such as config_005 or config_008.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 held the best pipeline so far (llm_summary_003: PCA-2000 RNA, multiprofile, avgpool) fixed and added the ResNet50 image modality with concat fusion, the study's first multimodal test. Validation accuracy rose from 0.5907 to 0.6186 (about +0.028), and supporting F1 rose from 0.5727 to 0.6103 (about +0.038), making this the new best configuration. Because adding images and concat fusion form a single combined change, the result is an initial suggestion that ResNet50 images add some complementary signal to RNA despite their weak standalone result (0.2079 accuracy in llm_summary_002). However, the gain is modest compared with the earlier multiprofile effect, and run-to-run variance is unknown from single runs, so it could partly be noise. It also remains untested whether other fusion strategies (e.g., weighted), a stronger image encoder (e.g., ViT-L) or other RNA encoders in the multimodal setting would extend or change this gain.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA carries most of the signal so far. PCA-2000 reached 0.485 accuracy single-profile and 0.591 with multiprofile avgpool, while adding ResNet50 images gave a smaller gain to 0.619. Every experiment has used the PCA RNA encoder, so RNA representation is the largest untested design choice. 2. What this tests: config_008 keeps the strong RNA-only multiprofile avgpool pipeline (config_002) fixed and swaps only PCA-2000 for the scGPT foundation-model encoder. This gives a clean one-factor test of whether a pretrained RNA representation beats PCA. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: a change in the dominant modality's encoder could plausibly move accuracy more than fusion or image-encoder tweaks. Testing it RNA-only avoids confounding with the noisy, smaller image contribution. The result will tell us which RNA encoder to carry into the multimodal configurations (e.g., config_042).
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 held the RNA-only multiprofile avgpool pipeline from llm_summary_003 fixed and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to the pretrained scGPT encoder, to test whether a foundation-model RNA representation beats PCA. Validation accuracy fell from 0.5907 to 0.5305 (about -0.060), and supporting F1 fell from 0.5727 to 0.5152 (about -0.058). In this clean one-factor comparison, PCA-2000 is the better RNA encoder for this pipeline. scGPT still sits above the single-profile PCA baseline (0.4849), so the multiprofile setting may still help it, although that comparison changes two factors. It remains uncertain whether scGPT's deficit is inherent or reflects untuned use of the pretrained embeddings (e.g., frozen vs. fine-tuned, gene-vocabulary overlap), how scVI would compare, whether the encoder ranking holds in the multimodal setting (llm_summary_005, best so far at 0.6186), and how large run-to-run variance is, since each configuration has a single run.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_018 (PCA-2000, multiprofile, avgpool, ResNet50, concat) at 0.6186 accuracy and 0.6103 F1. Adding ResNet50 images gave only a modest gain over RNA-only (+0.028), and ResNet50 alone was weak (0.2079). So it is unclear whether the image modality has limited value or ResNet50 is simply a poor image encoder. The image encoder is the largest untested axis that could change the best result. 2. What this tests: config_024 keeps every config_018 choice fixed and swaps only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This cleanly isolates the effect of image representation in the best multimodal pipeline. If accuracy and F1 rise clearly, image features are the bottleneck and ViT-L multimodal variants are worth exploiting. If not, the multimodal gain is likely capped by the image signal or by fusion, and attention can move to fusion type (config_019) or scVI (config_005). 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: it combines exploitation (a logical extension of the current best) with resolving a key uncertainty about the image modality, using a single-factor change. Fusion type and scVI remain good follow-ups, but the image encoder probably has the larger potential effect given how weak ResNet50 was on its own.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the best multimodal pipeline from llm_summary_005 fixed (PCA-2000 RNA, multiprofile, avgpool, concat fusion) and changed only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, to test whether a weak image representation was limiting the multimodal gain. Validation accuracy rose slightly from 0.6186 to 0.6287 (about +0.010), making it nominally the best configuration so far, but supporting F1 fell from 0.6103 to 0.5993 (about -0.011). The metrics therefore move in opposite directions by small margins, and with single runs and unknown variance this is not clear evidence that ViT-L is a better image encoder or that image features were the main bottleneck. It remains uncertain whether the multimodal gain is capped by the image signal or by concat fusion (weighted fusion is untested), how ViT-L performs on its own compared with ResNet50 (0.2079 image-only), and whether the F1 drop reflects worse performance on some classes or just noise.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best accuracy so far is config_024 (PCA-2000 + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.6287. Its F1 (0.5993) is slightly below the ResNet50 version (config_018: 0.6186 accuracy, 0.6103 F1). The multimodal gain over RNA-only is modest (about +0.03 accuracy) and the two image encoders look roughly equivalent. That suggests the limit may sit in how the modalities are combined rather than in the image features. Fusion strategy is the one major design axis not yet tested: every multimodal run has used concat. 2) What this tests: config_025 keeps everything in config_024 fixed and changes only the fusion, from concat to weighted. This is a clean one-factor test of whether weighted fusion makes better use of the weaker image modality, and whether it lifts both accuracy and F1. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: It extends the strongest pipeline, so it may also give the best immediate result. It answers a question no prior run addresses, and the fusion result will guide whether later multimodal runs (e.g., with scVI or ResNet50) should use concat or weighted fusion. Testing scVI or transformer aggregation in the multimodal setting would be less informative now, given the existing evidence favoring PCA and avgpool.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the best multimodal pipeline from llm_summary_007 fixed (PCA-2000 RNA, ImageNet ViT-L images, multiprofile, avgpool) and changed only the fusion, from concat to weighted, the first test of a non-concat fusion strategy. Validation accuracy rose slightly from 0.6287 to 0.6352 (about +0.007), and supporting F1 rose more clearly from 0.5993 to 0.6183 (about +0.019), so this is the new best configuration on both metrics and its F1 now also exceeds the ResNet50-concat run (llm_summary_005, 0.6103). In this clean one-factor comparison the metrics move in the same direction, which tentatively suggests weighted fusion helps this pipeline, possibly by making better use of the weaker image modality, though the evidence does not show how it helps. However, the accuracy gain is small relative to unknown run-to-run variance from single runs, and it remains untested whether weighted fusion also helps with ResNet50 or other RNA encoders, what modality weights were learned, and whether other fusion strategies could do better.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA carries most of the predictive signal. RNA-only multiprofile avgpool reached 0.591, while the best multimodal pipeline reached 0.635. In that same RNA-only pipeline, PCA-2000 beat scGPT by about 0.06. scVI is the only RNA encoder not yet tested in any setting, so whether PCA is really the best RNA representation is still open. The image-encoder and fusion changes so far gave only small gains of about 0.01 or less in accuracy. 2. What this tests: config_037 keeps the current best pipeline fixed (ImageNet ViT-L images, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swaps only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. This is a clean one-factor comparison against config_025 on the factor that matters most. 3. Why this is the best next use of budget: it explores the largest remaining design gap in the dominant modality and could directly produce a new best configuration. If scVI underperforms, as scGPT did, that strengthens the case for PCA as the RNA encoder and lets later budget go to smaller refinements, such as checking whether weighted fusion also helps with ResNet50 (config_019) or the RNA-only scVI baseline (config_005). Because each configuration has a single run, a small difference either way should be read cautiously.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the best pipeline from llm_summary_008 fixed (ImageNet ViT-L images, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scVI-200, the first test of scVI in any setting. Validation accuracy rose from 0.6352 to 0.7062 (about +0.071) and supporting F1 rose from 0.6183 to 0.6671 (about +0.049), making this clearly the new best configuration. In this clean one-factor comparison, both metrics move the same way by a margin much larger than earlier image-encoder and fusion effects (about 0.01 or less), which suggests scVI-200 is a better RNA representation than PCA-2000 in this multimodal pipeline, unlike scGPT, which underperformed PCA in the RNA-only setting. It remains uncertain whether scVI also beats PCA in RNA-only multiprofile avgpool (the scVI RNA-only baseline is untested), whether its advantage depends on the image modality or weighted fusion (e.g., with ResNet50 or concat), whether the difference reflects scVI itself or its much smaller latent size (200 vs. 2000), and how large run-to-run variance is, since each configuration has a single run.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_037 (scVI-200, ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.7062 accuracy, 0.6671 F1). That run changed only the RNA encoder relative to config_025, and the gain over PCA-2000 (+0.071 accuracy, +0.049 F1) is the largest effect seen apart from the multiprofile switch. However, scVI has only been tested inside the multimodal pipeline. We do not know whether its advantage is a property of the RNA representation itself or depends on interacting with the image branch and weighted fusion. Separately, the images' contribution has looked modest: about +0.03–0.045 accuracy over RNA-only with PCA. 2. What this tests: config_005 runs scVI-200 RNA-only with multiprofile avgpool, which gives two clean one-factor comparisons. Against config_002 (PCA RNA-only, same profile and aggregation; 0.5907), it shows whether scVI beats PCA without images. Against config_037, it shows how much the ViT-L image modality adds when the RNA representation is strong. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: It addresses the most important open question about the strongest design choice found so far, namely the RNA encoder. It also tells us whether the added complexity of multimodal fusion is still justified once scVI is used. That helps decide whether the remaining budget should go to image and fusion refinements or to RNA and aggregation choices. Exploitation options such as concat or transformer variants of config_037 address smaller effects and can follow afterward.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 tested scVI-200 as the RNA encoder in an RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool pipeline. It gives two clean comparisons: one against the PCA-2000 RNA-only run (llm_summary_003), which changes only the RNA encoder, and one against the best multimodal run (llm_summary_009), which removes the ViT-L image branch and weighted fusion together. It reached 0.6501 validation accuracy (supporting F1 0.6275), about +0.060 accuracy and +0.055 F1 over PCA-2000. This suggests scVI's advantage over PCA is largely a property of the RNA representation itself rather than dependent on the image branch, and this RNA-only run also beats every PCA-based multimodal configuration (best 0.6352, llm_summary_008). Adding ViT-L images with weighted fusion on top of scVI (llm_summary_009, 0.7062 accuracy / 0.6671 F1) still adds about +0.056 accuracy and +0.040 F1, so multimodal fusion remains worthwhile with a strong RNA encoder, but the image and fusion contributions cannot be separated here. It remains uncertain whether the gain reflects scVI itself or its smaller latent size (200 vs 2000), whether the image contribution is truly larger with scVI than with PCA (earlier PCA-based image gains of roughly +0.03 to +0.045 came from different encoder/fusion combinations), and how large run-to-run variance is, since every configuration has a single run.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about how modality, representation, profile setting, aggregation or fusion affect performance. 2. What this tests: config_001 is the simplest configuration: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA (n=2000) encoder, with no aggregation or fusion. It sets a clean reference baseline. Later experiments can then each change one factor against it: encoder (scvi_n200 in config_004, scgpt in config_007), profile setting and aggregation (config_002, config_003), modality (config_010 / config_013) and fusion (config_016). 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: Without a simple baseline, gains from more complex multimodal or multiprofile models cannot be attributed to any specific design choice. Starting here is cheap and low-risk, and it makes every later comparison a single-factor change, which keeps the remaining experiments informative.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 set the reference baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder, with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485, with a validation F1 of 0.464. The F1 is close to the accuracy, which gives no clear sign of strong class imbalance effects, but this is only a tentative reading. Because no other experiments have been run, this result is an initial reference point only. It says nothing yet about whether other encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image modality, or fusion would help or hurt, and it gives no information on run-to-run variance. Later single-factor changes against this configuration are needed to attribute any performance differences.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: only one result exists. The RNA-only, single-profile PCA (n=2000) baseline reached 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. We know nothing yet about how encoder, profile setting, aggregation, modality, or fusion affect performance, and we have no estimate of run-to-run variance. 2) Test: config_002 changes a single factor, switching from single-profile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). Encoder and modality stay fixed, so any difference can be attributed to using multiple profiles. 3) Why now: profile setting is a structural choice that applies across the whole search space, including RNA-only, image-only and multimodal settings. Measuring its effect cleanly with the cheapest aggregator tells us whether the multiprofile half of the remaining configurations deserves budget. It also sets up a direct comparison with transformer aggregation (config_003) if pooling looks useful. Single-factor encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT) and an image-only baseline are natural follow-ups, but this experiment informs the largest share of the remaining design space.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 kept the RNA-only PCA (n=2000) setup from the llm_summary_001 baseline and switched from single-profile to multiprofile input combined by average pooling (avgpool), with no image encoder or fusion. Validation accuracy rose from 0.485 to 0.591 (+0.106), and validation F1 rose in step from 0.464 to 0.573, which suggests that multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation is a promising direction for the RNA-only PCA setting. The comparison changes the profile setting and adds an aggregation step together, so it cannot separate the benefit of multiple profiles from the choice of avgpool. Each configuration was run only once with no variance estimate, and it is still unknown whether the gain holds for other aggregators (e.g., transformer), other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image-only or multimodal settings, or repeated runs.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised RNA-only PCA accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591, and F1 rose in step (0.464 to 0.573). That makes multiprofile a promising direction. However, the change confounded using multiple profiles with the specific aggregator (avgpool), and each result comes from a single run. 2) What this tests: config_003 keeps everything from config_002 (RNA-only, PCA n=2000, multiprofile) and changes only the aggregator from avgpool to transformer. This isolates whether learned aggregation adds value over simple pooling. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: Aggregation choice appears in every multiprofile branch of the remaining search space, including RNA-only, image-only and multimodal. Settling avgpool versus transformer in the best-known setting will narrow many later choices. It also exploits the strongest signal so far with a clean single-factor comparison. Encoder and modality questions can follow once the aggregation default is better grounded.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept the RNA-only, multiprofile PCA (n=2000) configuration of llm_summary_002 and changed only the aggregator from avgpool to a transformer, with no image encoder or fusion. Validation accuracy fell from 0.591 to 0.519 (−0.072), and validation F1 fell from 0.573 to 0.480. This single-factor comparison suggests that, in this setting, transformer aggregation did not improve on simple average pooling and may underperform it, though it still scored above the single-profile baseline (0.485 accuracy). Each configuration was run only once with no variance estimate, and transformer hyperparameters and training were not explored, so the gap may reflect tuning, optimization instability, or limited data rather than an inherent weakness of learned aggregation. Whether avgpool's advantage holds for other RNA encoders, image-only or multimodal settings, or repeated runs remains untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: three RNA-only PCA runs suggest that multiprofile input with avgpool works best (0.591 accuracy vs 0.485 for single-profile and 0.519 for transformer). Each result comes from a single run. The image modality is completely untested, so we do not know whether images carry useful signal on their own. That question decides whether the large multimodal part of the search space is worth exploring. 2) Test: config_011 is image-only, multiprofile, ResNet50 with avgpool. It keeps the best-known profile and aggregation setting and changes only the modality, so it measures image signal under the most favorable known conditions. It can be compared directly with config_002 (RNA counterpart) and later with config_018/019 (fusion). 3) Why now: the main open uncertainty is modality, not encoder tuning within RNA. If images are strong, multimodal fusion becomes a priority. If they are weak, the budget can go to RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) with avgpool.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 was the first test of the image modality: an image-only, multiprofile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and avgpool aggregation, no RNA encoder and no fusion. It kept the profile and aggregation settings of the best RNA-only run (llm_summary_002). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.328 and a validation F1 of 0.288, far below its RNA-only counterpart (0.591 / 0.573) and also below the single-profile RNA baseline (0.485 / 0.464). As an initial observation, this suggests that images alone, as encoded here, carry weaker class signal than PCA-encoded RNA. Its F1 trails its accuracy slightly more than in the RNA runs, which may hint at uneven per-class performance. The comparison changes the modality and the encoder together, and it is a single run with no variance estimate, no chance-level reference, and no exploration of other image encoders, pretraining choices, or tuning. It therefore remains uncertain whether the weakness reflects the image modality itself or this particular ResNet50/avgpool setup. It is also untested whether images add complementary information when fused with RNA (e.g., config_018/019).

selection_reason: Evidence: The strongest result so far is RNA-only multiprofile PCA with avgpool (config_002: 0.591 accuracy / 0.573 F1). Avgpool beat the transformer aggregator in that setting. Image-only ResNet50 with the same profile and aggregation settings was much weaker (0.328 / 0.288). The main open question is whether the image modality adds complementary signal when combined with RNA, or whether its weakness means it only adds noise. Test: config_018 keeps everything from config_002 (multiprofile, PCA n2000, avgpool) and adds only the ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion. Any change relative to 0.591 can therefore be attributed to adding images via concatenation. Why now: Whether to fuse modalities is the decision with the largest consequences for the rest of the search, since most remaining configurations are multimodal. Concat is the simplest fusion choice and adds no fusion-weighting factor. If fusion helps despite weak image-only performance, multimodal variants (weighted fusion, ViT-L) become worth exploring. If it hurts or does nothing, the budget can shift to RNA encoder comparisons (scVI, scGPT) under multiprofile avgpool.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_002 (multiprofile, PCA n=2000, avgpool) and changed one thing: it added a ResNet50 image branch joined to the RNA branch by simple concat fusion. Validation accuracy rose from 0.591 to 0.619 (+0.028) and validation F1 rose from 0.573 to 0.610 (+0.038), the best result so far. Because image-only ResNet50 scored only 0.328, this tentatively suggests images add complementary signal rather than just noise, and the slightly larger F1 gain hints at more even per-class performance. However, every configuration was run once with no variance estimate, so a gain of this size may be within run-to-run noise. The added image branch also brings extra model capacity, and it is untested whether the benefit holds for other fusion schemes (e.g., weighted), image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), or repeated runs.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA carries most of the class signal (PCA RNA-only multiprofile 0.591 vs image-only 0.328). Multiprofile avgpool beat both single-profile and transformer aggregation. Adding ResNet50 with concat fusion gave the best result so far (config_018: 0.619 accuracy, 0.610 F1). The RNA encoder, probably the most influential remaining factor, is completely untested: every run so far used PCA n2000. 2) Test: config_042 keeps the best pipeline (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder from PCA to scGPT. Comparing it with config_018 isolates the effect of a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation. 3) Why now: because RNA dominates performance, a better RNA representation is the most likely source of a large gain. Fusion type or image-encoder changes are refinements to a weaker branch and seem likely to give smaller improvements. Running the change inside the current best setup combines exploitation (it could set a new best) with a clean single-factor comparison. If scGPT underperforms, that is also informative, since it would support PCA as a strong default and shift the remaining budget toward fusion and image-encoder choices.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the best pipeline from llm_summary_005 (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA n2000 to scGPT. Validation accuracy fell from 0.619 to 0.512 (−0.107) and validation F1 fell from 0.610 to 0.477 (−0.133). This puts the run below the RNA-only PCA multiprofile run (0.591) and only slightly above the single-profile PCA baseline (0.485). In this single-factor comparison, scGPT embeddings as used here underperformed PCA, which tentatively supports PCA n2000 as a strong default RNA representation and points remaining effort toward fusion and image-encoder choices. Uncertainty remains: each configuration was run once with no variance estimate, scGPT integration choices (fine-tuning vs frozen, embedding dimension, gene vocabulary overlap, preprocessing) and downstream tuning were not explored, and it is untested whether scGPT behaves differently in RNA-only or single-profile settings or how scVI compares.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n2000, ResNet50, avgpool, concat; 0.619 accuracy / 0.610 F1). Its gain over RNA-only (+0.028) is small for a single run, and image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.328). So it is unclear whether the image branch is limited by the image modality itself or by the ResNet50 encoder. The image encoder is a major design choice that no run has varied yet. 2. What this tests: config_024 keeps every setting of config_018 and swaps only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates the effect of image representation inside the strongest pipeline. A clear improvement would mean the image signal was encoder-limited and would make the multimodal benefit more convincing. No change or a drop would suggest the image contribution is modest whatever the encoder, and would point effort toward fusion (config_019) or RNA encoder (scVI) choices. 3. Why now: It is a clean single-factor comparison on the best configuration. It addresses one of the largest remaining uncertainties and has a reasonable chance of beating the current best, so it balances exploitation with uncertainty reduction better than testing weighted fusion or scVI first.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the best pipeline from llm_summary_005 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n2000, avgpool, concat) and changed only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. Validation accuracy rose slightly from 0.619 to 0.629 (+0.010), the highest accuracy so far, while validation F1 fell from 0.610 to 0.599 (−0.011). This mixed result gives no clear evidence that the image branch was encoder-limited. The small accuracy gain paired with lower F1 may hint at less even per-class performance, and both gaps are small enough to fall within run-to-run noise, since every configuration was run once with no variance estimate. Several questions remain open: whether ViT-L would improve image-only performance (not tested), how it interacts with other fusion schemes such as weighted fusion or with other RNA encoders such as scVI, and whether the gain over RNA-only (about +0.038 accuracy) holds up across repeated runs.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: multiprofile PCA n2000 with avgpool and concat fusion is the strongest pipeline so far. ViT-L gave the best accuracy (0.629) and ResNet50 gave a similar result with slightly higher F1, so the image-encoder choice looks minor and may be within noise. Fusion is the one major design choice not yet tested: every multimodal run used concat. 2. What this tests: config_025 changes only concat to weighted fusion on the best-accuracy setup (config_024). This isolates whether learned weighting of the RNA and image branches helps. That seems plausible because image-only performance is much weaker (0.328), and concat may let the weaker image branch add noise. 3. Why this is the best next use of budget: it explores an untested design dimension while staying close to the most promising region. That gives a chance at a new best and a clean single-factor answer about fusion. scVI and scGPT variants would test the RNA encoder, but scGPT already underperformed PCA, so fusion is the higher-value open question.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the best-accuracy pipeline from llm_summary_007 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n2000, ImageNet ViT-L, avgpool) and changed only the fusion from concat to weighted, the first test of a non-concat fusion scheme. Validation accuracy rose slightly from 0.629 to 0.635 (+0.007), a new best, and validation F1 rose from 0.599 to 0.618 (+0.019), now the highest F1 so far (above ResNet50+concat's 0.610). In this single-factor comparison, weighted fusion matched or modestly improved on concat, and the larger F1 gain tentatively hints at more even per-class performance, consistent with but not proving the idea that down-weighting the weaker image branch helps. All gains are small and each configuration was run once with no variance estimate, so the difference may be within noise. The learned branch weights were not reported, and it is untested whether weighted fusion helps with ResNet50 or other RNA encoders such as scVI, or whether the result holds across repeated runs.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_025 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n2000, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted) at 0.635 accuracy and 0.618 F1. Multiprofile input with avgpool clearly beat single-profile and transformer aggregation in the RNA-only runs. RNA representation looks like the largest lever: swapping PCA for scGPT cost about 0.11 accuracy. scVI, the third RNA encoder, is completely untested. That is the biggest open uncertainty in a choice that matters a lot. 2. Test: config_037 keeps the best pipeline fixed and changes only the RNA encoder from PCA n2000 to scVI n200. This shows whether a compact, learned, batch-aware latent can match or beat PCA, or whether PCA's advantage holds for learned embeddings in general and not just scGPT. 3. Why now: It is a clean single-factor comparison against the current best. It could produce a new best, and if it doesn't, it settles the RNA-encoder question so the remaining budget can go to fusion and image choices. Untested fusion and image options, such as weighted fusion with ResNet50 or transformer aggregation in the multimodal setting, would likely yield only small differences within noise.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the best pipeline from llm_summary_008 (multimodal, multiprofile, ImageNet ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA n2000 to scVI n200, the first test of scVI. Validation accuracy rose from 0.635 to 0.706 (+0.071) and validation F1 rose from 0.618 to 0.667 (+0.049), the best results so far by a clear margin. In this single-factor comparison, scVI outperformed PCA, which tentatively reverses the earlier reading from the scGPT run (llm_summary_006) that PCA is the strongest RNA representation and reinforces that RNA encoder choice is a major lever. However, this is a single run with no variance estimate, and the scVI change also alters dimensionality (200 vs 2000), so a compact latent cannot be separated from the learned, batch-aware modeling. The slightly larger gap between F1 and accuracy may hint at less even per-class performance. It is also untested whether scVI's advantage holds in RNA-only or single-profile settings, with concat fusion or ResNet50, at other latent sizes, or across repeated runs.

selection_reason: Evidence: switching the RNA encoder from PCA to scVI in the best multimodal pipeline (config_037) gave the largest single-factor gain so far (0.635 to 0.706 accuracy). However, scVI has only been tested together with the ViT-L image branch and weighted fusion. Earlier, the image branch added only about +0.03 to +0.04 over RNA-only with PCA. So it is unclear whether the gain comes from scVI alone or from scVI pairing better with images. Test: config_005 is RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI, avgpool. It is a clean one-factor comparison against config_002 (PCA RNA-only, 0.591), which isolates the scVI effect without the image modality. It is also a clean comparison against config_037 (same setup with ViT-L and weighted fusion added), which measures how much the image branch contributes on top of scVI. Why now: before spending budget on fusion or aggregation tweaks around config_037, it is more valuable to confirm that the main lever, the RNA encoder, generalizes. This run also tells us whether the multimodal complexity is still justified. If RNA-only scVI comes close to 0.706, later experiments should focus on RNA and aggregation choices rather than image and fusion variants.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with an scVI n200 RNA encoder and avgpool aggregation, with no image encoder or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.650 and a validation F1 of 0.628. Against the PCA RNA-only counterpart (llm_summary_002, 0.591 / 0.573), this single-factor change gained +0.059 accuracy and +0.055 F1, so scVI's advantage over PCA does not depend on the image branch; this RNA-only run even edges out the best PCA multimodal run (llm_summary_008, 0.635 / 0.618). Against llm_summary_009 (0.706 / 0.667), adding the ViT-L image branch with weighted fusion still contributed +0.056 accuracy and +0.040 F1, similar to the roughly +0.045 that image plus weighted fusion added under PCA, which tentatively suggests the RNA-encoder and image-branch gains are roughly additive and that the multimodal pipeline remains justified. Uncertainties remain: every configuration was run once with no variance estimate, so the small apparent scVI-image interaction (+0.071 vs +0.059 scVI gain) may be noise; the scVI change also alters dimensionality (200 vs 2000), so a compact latent cannot be separated from scVI's learned modeling; and other latent sizes, aggregators, and single-profile scVI remain untested.

selection_reason: 1. No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2. config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, lowest-variance baseline. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 that later changes can be measured against one at a time: swapping the RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), adding multiprofile aggregation (configs 002/003), switching to image-only, or adding multimodal fusion. 3. With a limited budget, a simple anchor makes every later comparison easier to interpret. Starting with a complex multimodal or multiprofile model would mix several design choices together and make gains or losses hard to attribute. It would also assume complexity helps, which is not yet established.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) tested the simplest baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.485 (F1 0.464), and the similar F1 suggests performance is not driven only by a few classes, though this is weak evidence. Because no other experiments have been run, this result is a reference point only and says nothing yet about whether other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image features, or multimodal fusion would help. Run-to-run variance and the chance-level accuracy for this task are also unknown, so later differences from this baseline should be read cautiously and, where possible, changed one design choice at a time.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far, the RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (acc 0.485, F1 0.464). We have no information yet on encoder, profile setting, aggregation, image modality, or fusion. 2) Test: config_002 changes one factor, single-profile to multiprofile with simple avgpool, and keeps the same RNA-only PCA encoder. That isolates the effect of using multiple profiles, with the simplest aggregation and few confounds. 3) Why now: profile setting cuts across most of the remaining space, including image-only and multimodal configurations. Learning early whether multiprofile helps tells us whether later budget should go to aggregation and multiprofile variants or stay with single-profile models. Encoder comparisons such as scVI (config_004) and the image-only baselines are natural next steps after this.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_002 kept the RNA-only PCA (2000-component) encoder from the baseline and switched from single-profile to multiprofile input with average pooling (no image encoder or fusion). It reached validation accuracy 0.591 (F1 0.573), compared with 0.485 (F1 0.464) for the single-profile baseline llm_summary_001, a gain of about 0.11 on both metrics. Because only the profile setting and its required aggregation changed, this is initial evidence that multiprofile input with avgpool helps this encoder, but the two changes cannot be separated, and the result rests on one run per configuration with unknown run-to-run variance. Still untested: whether other aggregation methods do better, whether the gain carries over to other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI) or to image and multimodal settings, and whether multiprofile changes the effective sample or evaluation unit in ways that affect comparability.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Both completed runs are RNA-only with PCA. Moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591, and F1 rose by a similar amount. Nothing is known yet about the image modality, even though most remaining configurations (image-only and all multimodal) depend on it. 2. What this tests: config_011 keeps the best profile setting and aggregation (multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps RNA-PCA for image-only ResNet50. This shows how informative image features are on their own under matched conditions, and whether the multiprofile setting looks useful beyond RNA (only partly, since the image single-profile baseline is still untested). 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: if image-only accuracy is near or above 0.59, the large multimodal branch becomes a priority. If it is weak, the search can focus on RNA encoders and aggregation. This resolves more uncertainty about where to spend later experiments than refining aggregation or the RNA encoder, which can be tested next.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_003 tested an image-only model with a ResNet50 image encoder under multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation, with no RNA encoder or fusion, matching the profile and aggregation settings of the best RNA run so far. It reached validation accuracy 0.328 (F1 0.288), well below the matched RNA-only PCA run llm_summary_002 (0.591, F1 0.573) and the single-profile RNA baseline llm_summary_001 (0.485). This is initial evidence that ResNet50 image features alone are much less informative than RNA-PCA features in this setup, though modality and encoder changed together, the result rests on one run with unknown run-to-run variance, and chance-level accuracy is unknown. Still untested: whether multiprofile/avgpool helps images at all (no image single-profile baseline), whether other image encoders do better, and whether image features add complementary signal in multimodal fusion despite weak standalone performance. This suggests prioritizing RNA encoder and aggregation work while still testing at least one multimodal configuration.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile avgpool clearly helped RNA-PCA (0.591 vs 0.485 single-profile). Image-only ResNet50 under the same setting was much weaker (0.328). The central open question is whether images still add complementary signal when combined with RNA. Weak standalone performance does not rule this out. 2. What this tests: config_018 differs from the best run so far (config_002: RNA-PCA, multiprofile, avgpool) only by adding ResNet50 image features with simple concat fusion. Any change in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed to adding the image modality. Concat is the simplest fusion baseline, so it should come before weighted fusion or transformer aggregation. 3. Why now: This single, clean comparison decides whether the limited remaining budget should go to multimodal configurations or to RNA-only refinements such as scVI/scGPT encoders and transformer aggregation. It is both informative and potentially the new best, though a small difference from config_002 should be read cautiously given unknown run-to-run variance.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_004 tested a multimodal, multiprofile model that combines the RNA PCA (2000-component) encoder with ResNet50 image features through simple concat fusion and avgpool aggregation. Its only difference from the best prior run, llm_summary_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool), is the added image modality. It reached validation accuracy 0.619 (F1 0.610), compared with 0.591 (F1 0.573) for llm_summary_002, a gain of about 0.03 accuracy and 0.04 F1. This is initial evidence that ResNet50 image features add complementary signal when combined with RNA, even though image-only performance was weak (0.328 in llm_summary_003). This makes it the best configuration so far. However, the gain is small and rests on one run per configuration with unknown run-to-run variance, so it may not exceed noise. Still untested: whether stronger fusion (e.g., weighted fusion), other aggregation methods (e.g., transformer), or stronger RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) would enlarge or shrink the image contribution, and whether the benefit holds across repeated seeds.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is clearly the dominant modality. RNA-PCA multiprofile reached 0.591 accuracy, against 0.328 for image-only ResNet50. Adding ResNet50 images gave only a small gain (0.619 in config_018), which may be within noise. Multiprofile with avgpool helped PCA by about 0.11. However, only one of three RNA encoders (PCA) has been tested, so the most influential modality has the least explored encoder choice. 2. What this tests: config_005 swaps the PCA encoder for scVI (200 dimensions) and keeps everything else as in config_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool). That isolates the effect of the RNA encoder with a one-variable comparison. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: the RNA encoder is likely to shift performance more than fusion type or image encoder, given how much RNA drives results so far. Its outcome also decides which RNA encoder to carry into later aggregation, fusion and multimodal experiments, so knowing it early saves budget downstream. Testing it in the RNA-only setting avoids confounding it with the uncertain image contribution.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_005 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with avgpool aggregation and swapped the PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder for scVI (200 dimensions), giving a one-variable comparison against llm_summary_002. It reached validation accuracy 0.650 (F1 0.628), compared with 0.591 (F1 0.573) for llm_summary_002, a gain of about 0.06 on both metrics. It also exceeded the multimodal PCA+ResNet50 concat run llm_summary_004 (0.619, F1 0.610), making it the best configuration so far. This is initial evidence that scVI-200 is a stronger RNA encoder than PCA-2000 in this setting, though encoder type and dimensionality changed together and each result rests on one run with unknown run-to-run variance. Still untested: scGPT, whether the scVI advantage holds in single-profile or with other aggregations, and whether adding ResNet50 images on top of scVI still gives the small gain seen with PCA or becomes redundant.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: scVI-200 RNA-only with multiprofile avgpool (config_005, 0.650 accuracy / 0.628 F1) is the best run so far. It beat PCA-2000 RNA-only (0.591) under matched settings. Adding ResNet50 images to PCA with concat fusion gave a small gain (0.591 to 0.619, F1 0.573 to 0.610). The key open uncertainty is whether that image benefit persists with the stronger scVI encoder or was only compensating for weaker PCA features. Each result is a single run, so small gaps may be noise. 2. Test: config_030 changes only the modality relative to config_005, adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion while keeping scVI-200, multiprofile and avgpool fixed. This makes it a clean one-variable test of image complementarity on top of the best RNA encoder. It also mirrors the earlier PCA comparison (config_002 vs config_018), so we can see whether the image contribution grows, shrinks or vanishes as RNA representation quality improves. 3. Why now: it is both a logical exploitation step, likely the highest expected accuracy among untested configurations, and an informative experiment. Its outcome decides whether the remaining budget should go to multimodal variants (fusion type, ViT-L, transformer aggregation) or to RNA-only refinements such as scGPT and aggregation choice.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_006 added ResNet50 image features with concat fusion on top of the best RNA-only run, llm_summary_005 (scVI-200, multiprofile, avgpool), changing only the modality. It reached validation accuracy 0.632 (F1 0.607), slightly below llm_summary_005 (0.650, F1 0.628), so llm_summary_005 remains the best configuration so far. Under PCA, the same image addition gave a small gain (llm_summary_002 to llm_summary_004: 0.591 to 0.619). This is initial evidence that ResNet50+concat images add no benefit with the stronger scVI encoder and may slightly hurt, consistent with images mainly compensating for weaker PCA features. However, both gaps are about 0.02 to 0.03, each configuration has only one run, and run-to-run variance is unknown, so the reversal may be noise. Still untested: whether other fusion methods (e.g., weighted fusion), stronger image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) or transformer aggregation would recover an image contribution with scVI, and whether repeated seeds confirm the result. Together these results weakly favor spending more budget on RNA-only refinements (e.g., scGPT, aggregation choice) than on concat-based multimodal variants.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: multiprofile input clearly helped PCA, raising accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591. scVI-200 beat PCA under multiprofile/avgpool (0.650 vs 0.591, F1 0.628 vs 0.573) and is the best result so far. Adding ResNet50 with concat fusion did not help scVI (0.632). Aggregation is the one design choice never varied: every multiprofile run used avgpool. So it is unknown whether the multiprofile gain depends on simple pooling or could be larger with learned aggregation. 2) What this tests: config_006 keeps the best configuration (RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI-200) and changes only avgpool to transformer. This gives a clean one-variable test of aggregation on the strongest backbone. 3) Why now: it exploits the best direction while resolving uncertainty on a completely untested axis. The answer will guide many remaining configurations that use transformer aggregation, including the multimodal ones. Testing scGPT (config_008) is the natural follow-up, but RNA encoder choice already has two data points, while aggregation has none.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_007 tested transformer aggregation in place of avgpool on the best configuration so far, llm_summary_005 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI-200), changing only the aggregation method. This was the first time aggregation was varied. It reached validation accuracy 0.653 (F1 0.628), essentially the same as llm_summary_005 (0.650, F1 0.628). The difference of about 0.003 accuracy is very likely within noise, so this is initial evidence that learned transformer aggregation gives no meaningful gain over simple avgpool for scVI-200 RNA-only multiprofile input; the multiprofile benefit does not appear to depend on, or grow with, the more complex aggregator. Still uncertain: run-to-run variance (one run per configuration), whether transformer aggregation behaves differently with PCA, scGPT, or multimodal/fusion settings, and whether training choices for the transformer were adequately tuned. Together this weakly suggests aggregation is a low-priority axis compared with RNA encoder choice (e.g., scGPT) or repeated seeds to confirm the small differences seen so far.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA encoder choice has been the strongest lever so far. Swapping PCA-2000 for scVI-200 gave about +0.06 accuracy (0.591 to 0.650) in the RNA-only multiprofile avgpool setting. Aggregation (transformer vs avgpool, 0.653 vs 0.650) and adding ResNet50 images on top of scVI (0.632) showed no meaningful gain. scGPT, the third RNA encoder, is completely untested, which is the biggest open uncertainty on the most influential axis. 2) Test: config_008 runs RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool with scGPT, changing only the RNA encoder relative to config_005 (scVI) and config_002 (PCA). This gives a clean three-way encoder comparison under identical profile and aggregation settings. 3) Why now: it isolates a single, high-impact design choice and could plausibly yield a new best configuration. It also tells us which RNA encoder should anchor any later multimodal, fusion, or aggregation experiments. Avgpool is preferred over transformer here because the two performed about the same, and avgpool is simpler and was the setting used in the earlier encoder comparison.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_008 completed a three-way RNA encoder comparison in the RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool setting by swapping in scGPT, changing only the RNA encoder relative to llm_summary_005 (scVI-200) and llm_summary_002 (PCA-2000). It reached validation accuracy 0.530 (F1 0.515). This is well below scVI-200 (0.650, F1 0.628) and PCA-2000 (0.591, F1 0.573), and only modestly above the single-profile PCA baseline (0.485).
