It is initial evidence that scGPT embeddings, as used here, are the weakest of the three RNA encoders, so scVI-200 remains the best configuration and the preferred anchor for later experiments. The gap of about 0.06 to 0.12 is larger than the small differences seen elsewhere. Still, each configuration has one run with unknown run-to-run variance, and it is unclear whether scGPT underperforms intrinsically or because of how it was applied (e.g., frozen versus fine-tuned, embedding dimensionality, gene vocabulary overlap, preprocessing). It is also untested whether scGPT behaves differently in single-profile, transformer-aggregation, or multimodal settings.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: scVI-200 RNA-only multiprofile is the best so far (0.650 with avgpool, 0.653 with transformer, essentially tied). Adding ResNet50 images by concat helped with PCA (0.591 to 0.619) but slightly hurt with scVI (0.650 to 0.632). All differences rest on single runs, so the reversal may be noise. Fusion method has never been varied; only concat has been tested. 2) This experiment changes only the fusion method from concat to weighted, relative to config_030 (scVI-200, ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool). It tests whether weighted fusion can down-weight the weak image features (image-only 0.328) and recover or exceed RNA-only performance. That would show whether the lack of image benefit with scVI comes from naive concat fusion rather than from the images having no useful signal. 3) Fusion is a completely unexplored design axis, and this is a clean one-variable comparison anchored to the strongest RNA encoder. Aggregation looks low-priority and scGPT looks weak. If weighted fusion helps, it opens a path to the best overall model. If it does not, it strengthens the case for focusing on RNA-only models or on testing a stronger image encoder (ViT-L) next.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_009 tested weighted fusion in place of concat on the multimodal scVI-200 + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool setup, changing only the fusion method relative to llm_summary_006. This was the first time fusion was varied. It reached validation accuracy 0.678 (F1 0.646), up from 0.632 (F1 0.607) with concat in llm_summary_006, and above the best RNA-only runs llm_summary_005 (avgpool, 0.650, F1 0.628) and llm_summary_007 (transformer, 0.653, F1 0.628), making it the best configuration so far. This is initial evidence that the weak image contribution seen with scVI under concat reflected the fusion method rather than a lack of image signal, and that images may add complementary information when fused with weighting. However, each configuration has one run with unknown run-to-run variance, and the roughly 0.025 gain over RNA-only is about the size of differences already suspected to be noise. It also remains untested whether weighted fusion helps with PCA, with stronger image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), or with transformer aggregation, and whether the learned weights actually down-weight the image features, so repeated seeds and those follow-ups are priorities.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best run so far is config_031 (scVI-200 + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; accuracy 0.678, F1 0.646). It suggests images add complementary signal when fused with weighting. Other findings: scVI is the strongest RNA encoder, multiprofile helps, and transformer aggregation added nothing over avgpool. The image encoder has not been varied at all, and ResNet50 alone was weak (0.328). 2) Test: config_037 keeps every setting of config_031 and swaps only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates whether a stronger image representation enlarges the image contribution under weighted fusion, or whether the image gain is already saturated or just noise. 3) Why now: it extends the most promising direction while exploring the largest untested design axis in one controlled comparison. Its result also decides whether later budget should go to the ViT-L multimodal variants or stay with ResNet50 and RNA-focused refinements.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_010 swapped the ResNet50 image encoder for ImageNet ViT-L in the best configuration so far, llm_summary_009 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, avgpool, weighted fusion), changing only the image encoder; this was the first time the image encoder was varied. It reached validation accuracy 0.706 (F1 0.667), up from 0.678 (F1 0.646) for llm_summary_009 and above the best RNA-only scVI run (0.653, F1 0.628), making it the best configuration so far. This is initial evidence that a stronger image representation enlarges the image contribution under weighted fusion, so the gain does not appear saturated with ResNet50, though the roughly 0.03 improvement is close in size to differences already suspected to be noise, and each configuration has only one run with unknown run-to-run variance. Still untested: ViT-L image-only performance, whether ViT-L helps under concat fusion, transformer aggregation, or PCA RNA features, how the learned fusion weights split between modalities, and whether repeated seeds confirm the ranking. Together these results weakly favor spending more budget on ViT-L multimodal variants than on ResNet50-based ones.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet on whether modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, most interpretable reference point. It measures how much signal a classical RNA representation captures without aggregation or fusion. Single-factor comparisons can then branch from it: scVI or scGPT encoders (config_004/007), multiprofile pooling (config_002), image-only (config_010), and multimodal fusion (config_016). 3) With a limited budget, a clean baseline is the best first experiment. Every later result can be read as a controlled change from it, and we avoid assuming that complex multimodal or multiprofile models will win before simpler ones have been measured.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) set a baseline with an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA-2000 RNA encoder, with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485, supported by a validation F1 of 0.464, so a classical RNA representation alone captures some class signal but leaves much room for improvement. Because no other configurations have been run, this is only a reference point, and nothing yet shows whether other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI or scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image features, or multimodal fusion would help. Single-factor comparisons that branch from this baseline are needed to show which design choices matter.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: we have one baseline (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) at 0.485 validation accuracy and 0.464 F1. We have no evidence yet on any other design axis. 2) Test: config_002 changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). RNA encoder and modality stay fixed, so any difference in accuracy or F1 can be attributed to the multiprofile setting. 3) Why now: the profile setting applies to most of the remaining search space across RNA-only, image-only and multimodal configurations. Learning early whether multiprofile helps will sharpen many later choices. Avgpool sets a clean, low-complexity reference before testing transformer aggregation. Encoder and image-modality comparisons can follow as their own single-factor tests.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_002 kept the RNA-only, PCA-2000 baseline fixed and changed only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with simple average-pooling aggregation. Validation accuracy rose from 0.485 to 0.591, about 0.106, and validation F1 rose from 0.464 to 0.573. In this single-factor contrast, multiprofile input with avgpool is therefore associated with a substantial gain for the RNA-only setting. Several things remain uncertain: each configuration was run only once, with no seed or variance estimates; avgpool is the only aggregation tested, so its contribution cannot be separated from the multiprofile setting itself, and it is unknown whether transformer aggregation would do better; and the benefit has not yet been checked with other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), image-only models, or multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: with RNA-only PCA-2000, switching from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised validation accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591 and F1 from 0.464 to 0.573. That gain is large, but it comes from single runs, and avgpool is the only aggregation tested. We cannot yet tell whether the benefit comes from using multiple profiles in general or from this simple pooling choice. 2) Test: config_003 keeps everything from config_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000) and changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer. This isolates the aggregation effect within the setting that currently looks most promising. 3) Why now: aggregation applies to nearly all remaining multiprofile configurations, including the image-only and multimodal ones. Settling it early with a clean single-factor comparison will narrow the search space efficiently. It also builds directly on the strongest result so far. Encoder comparisons (scVI, scGPT) and image or fusion tests can follow once aggregation is better understood.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_003 kept the RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000 setup from llm_summary_002 and changed only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer. Validation accuracy fell from 0.591 to 0.519 (about -0.072), and validation F1 fell from 0.573 to 0.480. In this single-factor contrast, transformer aggregation underperformed simple average pooling, though it still stayed slightly above the single-profile baseline (0.485 accuracy, 0.464 F1). This suggests the multiprofile gain may depend on how profiles are aggregated, but each configuration was run only once with no seed or variance estimates, so the gap may be partly run-to-run noise. It is also unknown whether transformer hyperparameters or training settings were adequate, and whether the avgpool advantage holds with other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image-only models, or multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Multiprofile avgpool gave the largest gain so far, raising accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591 and F1 from 0.464 to 0.573. Transformer aggregation did worse (0.519), so avgpool is the current best aggregation. However, every result so far uses the PCA-2000 RNA encoder, so we do not know whether the representation itself is limiting performance. Each result is also a single run, so small gaps may be noise. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder, from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. That cleanly isolates the effect of RNA representation and also checks whether the avgpool multiprofile benefit holds beyond PCA. 3) The RNA encoder choice feeds into most remaining configurations, including all multimodal ones, so settling it early narrows the search space efficiently. The experiment also builds on the strongest direction found so far, so it balances learning about a key design choice with a reasonable chance of improving accuracy. Image-only and fusion experiments can follow once the RNA side is better understood.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_004 kept the best setup from llm_summary_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool aggregation) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. Validation accuracy rose from 0.591 to 0.650 (about +0.059), and validation F1 rose from 0.573 to 0.628, making this the best configuration so far. In this single-factor contrast, the scVI-200 representation is associated with a further gain, and the multiprofile avgpool setup still performs well with a second encoder. Each configuration was run only once with no seed or variance estimates, so the size of the gap is uncertain. It is also untested whether scVI helps in the single-profile or transformer-aggregation settings, how other encoders (e.g., scGPT) or other scVI dimensionalities compare, and whether these RNA-side findings carry over to image-only or multimodal fusion models.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: All four runs so far are RNA-only. They suggest that multiprofile beats single-profile (+0.106 accuracy), that avgpool beats transformer aggregation (+0.072), and that scVI-200 beats PCA-2000 (+0.059, best so far at 0.650 accuracy and 0.628 F1). Each comparison is a single run, so these gaps are not firm. The image modality is completely untested, yet most remaining configurations depend on it, whether image-only or multimodal. 2. What this tests: config_011 runs an image-only model with a ResNet50 encoder, using the setting that has worked best so far (multiprofile with avgpool). It measures how much class signal images carry by themselves. It also checks whether the multiprofile-avgpool advantage holds outside RNA. 3. Why this is the best next run: This answers a high-impact unknown rather than refining a small RNA-side difference. If images alone are weak, fusion runs are less likely to beat scVI RNA-only. If images are competitive, the case for scVI plus ResNet50 multimodal fusion (e.g., config_030 or config_031) gets much stronger. The result also provides an image-only baseline that later fusion experiments can be compared against.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_005 gave the first image-only result: a ResNet50 image encoder with multiprofile input and avgpool aggregation, the setting that worked best for RNA-only. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.328 and a validation F1 of 0.288, far below the best RNA-only run (scVI-200, 0.650 accuracy) and even below the single-profile PCA-2000 baseline (0.485), which suggests that images alone, as encoded here, carry much weaker class signal than RNA. This is a baseline rather than a controlled contrast, because no single-profile or transformer-aggregation image runs exist, so it is unknown whether the multiprofile-avgpool advantage holds for images, and the result comes from a single run with no seed or variance estimates. It is also uncertain whether other image encoders or training settings would do better, and whether image features could still add complementary signal when fused with scVI RNA features, which later multimodal runs (e.g., config_030 or config_031) would need to test against this image-only reference.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI-200 with avgpool (config_005, 0.650 accuracy / 0.628 F1). Multiprofile avgpool beat single-profile (+0.106) and transformer aggregation (+0.072) under PCA. Image-only ResNet50 in the same multiprofile-avgpool setting was much weaker (0.328 / 0.288). The biggest open question is whether image features add complementary signal on top of the strongest RNA representation, or only add noise. 2) Test: config_030 keeps config_005 fixed (scVI-200, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds ResNet50 image features with simple concat fusion. This gives a clean contrast against config_005 that isolates the effect of adding the image modality, using the image encoder that already has a matching unimodal reference (config_011). 3) Why now: It answers the central modality question in a single run, starting from the best-known setup. If it helps, it is also a strong candidate for the top configuration. If it does not, it tells us that further fusion, ViT-L and weighted-fusion variants are lower priority than finishing the RNA-encoder comparison (e.g., scGPT with avgpool, config_008). Each configuration has been run only once, so a small difference should be read cautiously, using F1 as supporting evidence.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_006 kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_004 (scVI-200, multiprofile, avgpool) and added ResNet50 image features with simple concat fusion, so the contrast isolates the addition of the image modality under this fusion scheme. Validation accuracy fell slightly, from 0.650 to 0.632 (about -0.019), and validation F1 fell from 0.628 to 0.607. Adding ResNet50 image features by concat therefore gave no gain over RNA alone and may have hurt a little, which fits the weak image-only result (0.328 accuracy). Each configuration was run only once with no seed or variance estimates, so the small drop may be run-to-run noise, and it remains untested whether other fusion strategies (e.g., weighted fusion), other image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), or different training settings could extract complementary image signal. These results suggest finishing the RNA-encoder comparison (e.g., scGPT with avgpool) may be a higher priority than further concat-fusion variants.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: multiprofile avgpool beat single-profile and transformer aggregation for RNA. Swapping PCA-2000 for scVI-200 raised accuracy from 0.591 to 0.650, the best result so far. Adding ResNet50 images by concat did not help (0.632), and image-only was weak (0.328). The remaining RNA encoder, scGPT, has not been tested, so we still don't know which RNA representation is best, and RNA carries most of the signal. 2) config_008 changes only the RNA encoder to scGPT and keeps the strongest setup fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool). This gives a clean single-factor, three-way encoder comparison against config_002 and config_005. 3) This is the best use of the next run because it settles an important design choice in the most informative modality. It could also produce a new best configuration. Its result tells us which RNA encoder to carry into later fusion or image experiments, rather than spending budget on weighted-fusion variants with the less certain image modality. These are single runs with no variance estimates, so the result should be read with some caution.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_007 completed the RNA-encoder comparison by keeping the RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool setup fixed and swapping in scGPT as the RNA encoder. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.530 and a validation F1 of 0.515, which is below both PCA-2000 (0.591 accuracy, about -0.060) and scVI-200 (0.650 accuracy, about -0.120) under the same setup, though still above the single-profile PCA baseline (0.485). In this single-factor, three-way contrast the encoders rank scVI-200 > PCA-2000 > scGPT, which supports keeping scVI-200 as the RNA encoder for later fusion or image experiments. All runs are single runs with no seed or variance estimates, and it is unknown whether the scGPT embedding or training settings were well suited to this task or whether the ranking holds under single-profile, transformer-aggregation, or multimodal settings.

selection_reason: Evidence: scVI-200 with multiprofile avgpool is the best setup so far (0.650 acc, 0.628 F1). ResNet50 image-only is weak (0.328), and adding it by concat fusion (config_030) slightly lowered accuracy to 0.632. Concat fusion is the only fusion scheme tested, so it is still unclear whether the image modality is truly unhelpful or whether concat simply lets noisy image features dilute the RNA signal. Test: config_031 changes only the fusion from concat to weighted, keeping scVI-200, ResNet50, multiprofile and avgpool fixed. This isolates the effect of fusion strategy. A weighted scheme can learn to down-weight the weaker image features, so this run shows whether multimodal fusion can match or beat RNA-only. Why now: it is a clean one-factor comparison on the most promising branch, so it serves both exploitation (a possible new best) and uncertainty reduction. Either outcome is useful. If weighted fusion still trails RNA-only, that strengthens the case that ResNet50 images add little, and the next step would be testing a better image encoder (ViT-L). If it helps, fusion design matters and is worth extending.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_008 kept the multimodal scVI-200 + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool setup from llm_summary_006 and changed only the fusion, from concat to weighted. Validation accuracy rose from 0.632 to 0.678 (about +0.046) and validation F1 rose from 0.607 to 0.646. This makes it the best configuration so far, also above the RNA-only scVI-200 run (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1; about +0.028). In this single-factor contrast, weighted fusion is associated with better performance than concat, and the result suggests ResNet50 image features may add complementary signal when fused appropriately, despite their weak image-only performance (0.328). All runs are single runs with no seed or variance estimates, so the modest gain over RNA-only may be partly noise. It is also unknown what the learned modality weights look like, whether stronger image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) or other fusion schemes would extend the gain, and whether the benefit holds under other aggregation or RNA-encoder settings.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_031 (scVI-200 + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. Weighted fusion beat concat (0.632) and RNA-only scVI (0.650). This suggests image features help only when fused with learned weighting, even though ResNet50 alone is weak (0.328). The image encoder is the main design choice not yet tested: ImageNet ViT-L has never been run. 2. Test: config_037 keeps every setting from config_031 and swaps only ResNet50 for ViT-L. This isolates whether a stronger image representation adds more complementary signal in the best-known multimodal setup. 3. Why now: It exploits the strongest direction so far and also answers an open question about image representation with a clean single-factor contrast. It is more likely to improve on the best accuracy than revisiting transformer aggregation or scGPT, both of which underperformed. Either outcome is informative: a gain would point toward stronger image encoders, while no gain would suggest RNA dominates and image encoder choice matters little. All runs are single runs without variance estimates, so small differences should not be overinterpreted.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_009 kept the best multimodal setup from llm_summary_008 (scVI-200, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) and changed only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. Validation accuracy rose from 0.678 to 0.706 (about +0.029) and validation F1 rose from 0.646 to 0.667, making this the best configuration so far and about +0.056 above the RNA-only scVI-200 run (0.650). In this single-factor contrast, ViT-L is associated with better performance than ResNet50, which tentatively suggests that a stronger image representation adds more complementary signal under weighted fusion. All runs are single runs with no seed or variance estimates, so a gain of this size may be partly noise. It also remains untested how ViT-L performs image-only or with concat fusion, what the learned modality weights are, and whether other image encoders or aggregation and fusion schemes would extend the gain.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best run so far is config_037 (scVI-200 + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.706 acc, 0.667 F1). Single-factor contrasts have favored multiprofile, scVI-200, weighted fusion and ViT-L. Aggregation is the least resolved choice. Transformer aggregation was tested only once, in the weaker RNA-only PCA-2000 setting (0.519 vs 0.591 for avgpool). That single run may not generalize to richer multimodal inputs, where attention over profiles and modalities could behave differently. 2. Test: config_039 changes only the aggregation (avgpool to transformer) from the current best. This shows whether the avgpool advantage holds in the strongest multimodal setting, or whether the earlier transformer deficit was specific to the PCA RNA-only setup. 3. Why now: It combines exploitation (a chance to beat 0.706) with exploration of a major design axis supported by only one weak data point. A clear drop would let us confidently fix avgpool for the remaining budget. A gain would open a new direction. Other options mainly refine choices already supported by consistent evidence, such as concat vs weighted fusion or image-only ViT-L.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_010 kept the best multimodal setup from llm_summary_009 (scVI-200 + ImageNet ViT-L, multiprofile, weighted fusion) and changed only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer. Validation accuracy rose from 0.706 to 0.725 (about +0.019) and validation F1 rose from 0.667 to 0.685, making this the best configuration so far. This reverses the earlier RNA-only PCA-2000 contrast, where transformer aggregation trailed avgpool by about 0.072 (0.519 vs 0.591), which suggests the effect of aggregation may depend on input richness or modality rather than favoring avgpool in general. All runs are single runs with no seed or variance estimates, so the modest gain may be partly noise. The PCA result could also reflect transformer training settings rather than an inherent setting dependence, and it remains untested whether transformer aggregation helps in RNA-only scVI-200, ResNet50 multimodal, or concat-fusion settings, so aggregation should not yet be treated as resolved.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion choice matters. 2. What it tests: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, cheapest baseline. It sets a reference accuracy and F1. Each later design choice can then be judged by a one-factor change from it: scVI or scGPT for representation, avgpool or transformer for aggregation, adding an image encoder for modality and fusion. 3. Why now: A simple baseline is the most informative first experiment under a limited budget. Starting with a complex multimodal configuration would change many factors at once and make later gains hard to attribute. It would also wrongly assume that complexity helps.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 established an initial baseline using the simplest configuration: RNA-only, single-profile, with a PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.4849 (primary metric), and its validation F1 of 0.4639 is broadly consistent with that accuracy. This is the first completed experiment, so there is no comparative evidence yet about whether modality, encoder choice, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion affects performance. The result should serve as a reference point for later one-factor changes, such as swapping the PCA encoder for scVI or scGPT, using multi-profile aggregation, or adding an image modality with fusion. Whether these changes help, and whether the baseline is stable across runs, remains untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: The only result so far is the RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_001), with accuracy 0.485 and F1 0.464. There is no evidence yet about how much the image modality alone can achieve. That question determines whether the many multimodal configurations are worth exploring, and it is the largest unexplored axis in the search space. 2. What this tests: config_010 (image-only, single-profile, ResNet50) keeps the simplest setting: single-profile, no aggregation, no fusion. Only the modality changes, so it gives a clean reference point to compare directly with the RNA baseline. 3. Why it is the best next step: It reduces uncertainty about the most consequential design choice, modality, with a single-factor change. If images are weak, the budget can shift toward RNA encoder and profile/aggregation variants. If images are competitive, fusion experiments become well motivated. Encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT) or multiprofile variants are also useful, but they refine within one modality rather than mapping the overall landscape.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile configuration with a ResNet50 image encoder and no aggregation or fusion, as a reference point against the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.2079 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.1718. Both are well below the RNA-only baseline (0.4849 accuracy, 0.4639 F1), which suggests that image-only single-profile modeling is much weaker in this setup. The comparison changes the modality and the encoder together (ResNet50 vs. PCA n=2000), and each result comes from a single run, so it does not show whether the gap reflects the image modality itself, the ResNet50 encoder, or run-to-run variance; it also remains untested whether images add complementary signal when fused with RNA or when used with multi-profile aggregation.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there are only two single runs. RNA-only PCA single-profile (0.485 acc, 0.464 F1) clearly beats image-only ResNet50 single-profile (0.208 acc, 0.172 F1). Nothing is known yet about profile setting, aggregation, alternative encoders or fusion. 2) Test: config_002 changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multi-profile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool), on the RNA-only PCA baseline. This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles helps, without confounding it with encoder or modality changes. 3) Why now: profile setting is a structural choice that splits most of the remaining configuration space, so knowing its effect early guides many later choices (aggregation type, multimodal multi-profile variants). Testing it on the strongest and best-understood modality gives the clearest signal. Because image-only was weak, fusion experiments are lower priority until the RNA-side design factors are better understood.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 changed only the profile setting of the RNA-only PCA (n=2000) baseline, from single-profile to multi-profile with avgpool aggregation, with no image encoder or fusion. Validation accuracy rose from 0.4849 to 0.5907 (primary metric), and validation F1 rose from 0.4639 to 0.5727 in support. Because this was a one-factor change from llm_summary_001, it is initial evidence that multi-profile avgpool aggregation helps the RNA-only PCA setup, though each configuration has only one run, so run-to-run variance has not been ruled out. It is still untested whether other aggregation methods would do better, whether the gain carries over to other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), to image-only models, or to multimodal fusion, and whether the benefit comes from multiple profiles in general or from avgpool specifically.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only PCA multi-profile with avgpool (0.591 accuracy, 0.573 F1). Switching from single-profile to multi-profile was a clean one-factor change and gave a large gain over single-profile (0.485). Image-only ResNet50 was much weaker (0.208). Every result comes from a single run, and avgpool is the only aggregation method tested so far. 2) Test: config_003 keeps everything from config_002 and changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer. This shows whether the multi-profile gain depends on the aggregation method, or whether simple pooling is already enough. 3) Why now: Aggregation is a design choice shared by most remaining configurations, including the multi-profile RNA, image, and multimodal setups. Settling it now builds directly on the strongest result so far and narrows the later search. A clean single-factor comparison is more informative than jumping to a multimodal setup that changes several factors at once.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_003: RNA-only, multi-profile, PCA n=2000, no image encoder or fusion) and changed only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer. Validation accuracy fell from 0.5907 to 0.5191 (primary metric), and validation F1 fell from 0.5727 to 0.4797 in support. Because this was a one-factor change, it is initial evidence that transformer aggregation underperforms simple avgpool in this RNA-only PCA multi-profile setup, though it still beats the single-profile baseline (0.4849). Each configuration has only one run, so run-to-run variance has not been ruled out, and transformer hyperparameters, training stability, or data size may explain the gap. It also remains untested whether this ranking holds for other RNA encoders, image-only models, or multimodal fusion, and whether other aggregation methods (e.g., attention pooling) would do better.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only, multi-profile, PCA n=2000 with avgpool (0.5907 accuracy, 0.5727 F1). It beat both the single-profile baseline (0.4849) and transformer aggregation (0.5191). Image-only ResNet50 single-profile was much weaker (0.2079). No experiment has yet tested whether images add complementary signal when fused with RNA, which is the central question for multimodal profiling. 2) Test: config_018 keeps the best configuration (multi-profile, PCA n=2000, avgpool) and only adds the ResNet50 image modality with simple concat fusion. Any change in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed to adding image features, not to changes in encoder, profile setting or aggregation. 3) Why now: It builds on the strongest direction while answering the most consequential open question. If fusion helps despite weak image-only results, multimodal variants deserve more of the budget. If it does not help, the search can focus on RNA encoder comparisons (scVI, scGPT) instead. Using concat as the simplest fusion avoids adding fusion complexity as a second factor.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_003: multi-profile, PCA n=2000 RNA encoder, avgpool aggregation) and changed only the model setting, adding a ResNet50 image encoder with simple concat fusion. Validation accuracy rose from 0.5907 to 0.6186 (primary metric), and validation F1 rose more clearly, from 0.5727 to 0.6103, in support. This makes it the best result so far, and because it was a one-factor change, it is initial evidence that image features add complementary signal to RNA, even though image-only single-profile performance was weak (0.2079). The accuracy gain is modest and each configuration has only one run, so run-to-run variance has not been ruled out. It also remains untested whether the gain reflects truly complementary image information or simply extra capacity, whether other fusion methods would do better, how image-only multi-profile models perform, and whether the benefit holds with other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT) or aggregation methods.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA carries most of the signal so far (RNA-only multiprofile 0.591 vs image-only singleprofile 0.208). Multiprofile avgpool clearly beat both single-profile and transformer aggregation. Adding ResNet50 with concat fusion gave the best result (0.619 accuracy, 0.610 F1). Every experiment so far used PCA n2000, so the RNA encoder, likely the most influential remaining choice, is completely untested. 2. What this tests: config_042 keeps the best configuration (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder from PCA to scGPT. This isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation improves on PCA. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: because RNA dominates performance, the RNA encoder probably matters more than the fusion method or image encoder. Testing it inside the best configuration gives a clean one-factor comparison and also a real chance of a new best result. Fusion (config_019) and image encoder (config_024) comparisons can follow once the stronger RNA representation is known.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_005: multimodal, multi-profile, ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA n=2000 to scGPT. Validation accuracy fell from 0.6186 to 0.5121 (primary metric), and validation F1 fell from 0.6103 to 0.4771 in support. This puts it below even the RNA-only multi-profile PCA model (0.5907), so it is initial evidence that scGPT embeddings, as used here, underperform PCA in this multimodal setup. Each configuration has only one run, so run-to-run variance has not been ruled out. It remains untested whether the drop reflects scGPT itself or how it was applied (e.g., frozen vs. fine-tuned embeddings, preprocessing or gene-vocabulary mismatch, embedding dimensionality, interaction with concat fusion), how scGPT performs in RNA-only settings, and whether other encoders such as scVI would do better than PCA.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multi-profile, PCA n=2000, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.6186 accuracy and 0.6103 F1. Adding ResNet50 image features gave a modest gain over RNA-only multi-profile (0.5907). Image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.2079), and swapping the RNA encoder to scGPT dropped accuracy sharply. So encoder choice matters a lot, but the image encoder has never been varied. 2) Test: Keep the best configuration fixed and change only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates whether a stronger image representation adds more complementary signal to RNA, or whether the small gain from images is close to the ceiling for this modality. 3) Why now: The image representation is a major untested design axis. Because image-only performance was weak, the image features may be the current bottleneck, so this one-factor change could produce a large gain. If it does not help, we learn that further image-side effort is unlikely to pay off. Fusion type (weighted) and scVI remain good follow-ups once we know which image encoder to carry forward.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_005: multimodal, multi-profile, PCA n=2000 RNA encoder, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) and changed only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. Validation accuracy rose slightly from 0.6186 to 0.6287 (primary metric), making it the best accuracy so far, but validation F1 fell from 0.6103 to 0.5993. Because this was a one-factor change, it is initial evidence that ViT-L features give at most a small accuracy benefit over ResNet50 in this setup, not the large gain expected if image features were the main bottleneck; the opposite movement in F1 suggests the gain may not be spread evenly across classes. With single runs, a roughly 1-point difference may fall within run-to-run variance. It remains untested how ViT-L performs image-only, whether other fusion methods (e.g., weighted) would use the stronger image features better, and whether the result holds with other RNA encoders such as scVI.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: multi-profile avgpool clearly beat single-profile for RNA-only PCA. Adding images with concat fusion gave modest further gains. The current best accuracy is config_024 (PCA + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.6287, though its F1 (0.5993) is slightly below ResNet50 concat (0.6103), so the two image encoders are roughly tied given single runs. Fusion is the one major design axis not yet tested: every multimodal run so far used concat. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only the fusion, from concat to weighted. It directly tests whether a learned modality weighting makes better use of the image features than simple concatenation. That bears on the open question of whether the image gain is genuinely complementary signal or just extra capacity. 3) It is a clean one-factor comparison that fills the largest remaining gap in the design space. It also has a realistic chance of improving on the current best. That makes it a better use of the budget than testing encoders like scVI, which can follow once the better fusion strategy is known.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_007: multimodal, multi-profile, PCA n=2000 RNA encoder, ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, avgpool aggregation) and changed only the fusion, from concat to weighted. Validation accuracy rose slightly from 0.6287 to 0.6352 (primary metric), and validation F1 rose more clearly from 0.5993 to 0.6183, making it the best result so far on both metrics; F1 now also exceeds the ResNet50 concat model (0.6103). Because this was a one-factor change, it is initial evidence that weighted fusion makes somewhat better use of the ViT-L image features than concat, and the larger F1 gain suggests improvement may be spread more evenly across classes. However, the accuracy gain is under 1 point and each configuration has a single run, so run-to-run variance has not been ruled out. Several questions remain untested: whether the learned modality weights actually upweight images (and so whether the image gain reflects complementary signal rather than extra capacity), whether weighted fusion helps ResNet50 similarly, how other fusion methods compare, and whether the result holds with other RNA encoders such as scVI.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is clearly the dominant modality, since image-only single-profile scored 0.208 against 0.485 for RNA-only single-profile. Changing the RNA encoder has produced the largest swings so far: scGPT dropped accuracy from 0.619 to 0.512. scVI is the only RNA encoder that has not been tested at all, so it is the largest remaining uncertainty about an important design choice. The best configuration so far is config_025 (PCA n2000, ViT-L, multi-profile, avgpool, weighted fusion), at 0.635 accuracy and 0.618 F1. 2. What this tests: config_037 keeps everything from config_025 and swaps only PCA for scVI_n200. This isolates whether a compact, learned, count-aware RNA representation beats or matches PCA in the strongest pipeline found so far. It also shows whether scGPT's drop was specific to scGPT or reflects a general weakness of learned or pretrained RNA embeddings in this setup. 3. Why it is the best use of the next run: it explores an entirely untested design axis on a high-performing base, so it has a realistic chance of producing a new best result. Either outcome cleanly tells us which RNA encoder later experiments should build on. Further fine-tuning of fusion or image choices, or image-only checks, can wait, since those changes have so far moved accuracy by only about 1 point.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_008: multimodal, multi-profile, ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA n=2000 to scVI n=200. Validation accuracy rose from 0.6352 to 0.7062 (primary metric) and validation F1 rose from 0.6183 to 0.6671 in support, making it the best result so far by a wide margin. Because this was a one-factor change, it is initial evidence that the compact scVI representation outperforms PCA in this pipeline, and that scGPT's earlier drop (llm_summary_006) was not a general weakness of learned RNA embeddings, though scGPT was tested with ResNet50 and concat fusion, so the two encoders have not been compared directly. Each configuration has a single run, and several questions remain untested: whether the gain holds in RNA-only settings or with other image encoders and fusion methods; whether it comes from scVI's count-aware modeling or from its lower dimensionality (200 vs. 2000); whether other scVI latent sizes would do better; and whether the image contribution under weighted fusion changes with scVI.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_037 (scVI n=200, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion), at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. It beat its PCA counterpart by about 7 points. With PCA, adding images helped only modestly: 0.591 for RNA-only versus 0.619 to 0.635 for multimodal. So we do not know whether config_037's gain comes from scVI alone or from scVI working better together with images. 2. What this tests: config_005 is RNA-only, multi-profile, scVI n=200 with avgpool. Compared with config_002 (PCA RNA-only, 0.591), it isolates the RNA encoder effect without any image interaction. Compared with config_037, it isolates how much the ViT-L image branch and weighted fusion add on top of scVI. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: With a limited budget, the key open question is whether the multimodal setup is worth its complexity once the RNA encoder is stronger. If scVI RNA-only comes close to 0.706, a simpler model may be enough and later experiments should focus on RNA and aggregation. If it falls well short, that supports images adding complementary signal, and further fusion and image-encoder tuning around config_037 is justified.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 tested an RNA-only, multi-profile model with an scVI n=200 RNA encoder and avgpool aggregation (no image encoder or fusion), reaching 0.6501 validation accuracy (primary metric) and 0.6275 F1. Against the PCA RNA-only counterpart (llm_summary_003: 0.5907 / 0.5727), this one-factor encoder swap is initial evidence that scVI improves RNA-only performance by about 6 accuracy points without any image interaction. This scVI RNA-only model also beats every PCA multimodal configuration (0.619–0.635). Against llm_summary_009 (scVI + ViT-L + weighted fusion: 0.7062 / 0.6671), adding the image branch still gives about 5.6 accuracy points and 4 F1 points, similar to or slightly larger than the roughly 4.5-point image gain seen with PCA (0.591 to 0.635). Together, these results suggest the scVI and image contributions are roughly additive rather than strongly dependent on each other, which supports keeping and further tuning the multimodal setup. Uncertainties remain: all results are single runs, so variance has not been ruled out. The comparison with llm_summary_009 changes the image encoder and the fusion method together, so their separate contributions are not isolated. It is also untested whether the scVI gain comes from count-aware modeling or from lower dimensionality, and whether other scVI latent sizes or aggregation methods would change these conclusions.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: no experiments have been run, so every design choice is uncertain: modality, RNA encoder, image encoder, profile setting, aggregation and fusion. 2. Test: config_001 is the simplest setup, RNA-only, single-profile, with a PCA (2000) encoder and no aggregation or fusion. It sets a baseline for validation accuracy and F1 that every more complex choice can be compared against, one factor at a time. Planned follow-ups include changing only the RNA encoder (config_004 or config_007), only the profile setting (config_002), only the modality (config_010), or adding fusion (config_016). 3. Why first: with a limited budget and no prior data, a cheap reference point avoids assuming that complex multimodal or multiprofile models are better. It also makes later comparisons that change a single variable easy to interpret, which is the most efficient way to learn which design decisions matter.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) tested the simplest configuration: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485, with a validation F1 of 0.464. No other experiments have been completed, so this result serves only as a baseline. It cannot show whether the RNA encoder, the profile setting, the modality choice or the lack of fusion helps or limits performance. Single-variable follow-ups are needed to judge whether any design choice improves on this reference: alternative RNA encoders, a multiprofile setting, the image modality, or added fusion. The class count and chance-level accuracy are not given, so how strong this baseline is in absolute terms remains uncertain.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Only one experiment has been run, the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (config_001). It reached 0.485 validation accuracy and 0.464 F1. We therefore have no evidence yet on which design axis matters. 2. Test: config_002 changes just one thing. It switches from single-profile to multiprofile and uses the simplest aggregation (avgpool), keeping the modality and RNA encoder fixed. This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles helps, without adding the extra capacity of a transformer aggregator or a second modality. 3. Why now: The single-profile versus multiprofile choice affects most of the remaining search space across RNA-only, image-only and multimodal settings. Resolving it early tells us whether later experiments should focus on multiprofile variants, which makes it a broadly informative use of the limited budget. The result also sets a reference for a later avgpool versus transformer comparison (config_003).
experiment_summary: llm_summary_002 kept the RNA-only PCA (2000-component) setup from llm_summary_001 but switched from single-profile to multiprofile input, pooled with average pooling. Validation accuracy rose from 0.485 to 0.591, and F1 rose from 0.464 to 0.573 in step. Because the profile setting (with its required aggregation) was the only change, this suggests that multiprofile input may help in the RNA-only setting, although the gain cannot be separated from the specific choice of avgpool. Several points remain uncertain: each configuration has a single run with no variance estimate, it is untested whether a stronger aggregator such as a transformer (planned as config_003) or other modalities would show the same benefit, and the class count and chance level are still unknown.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Moving from single-profile to multiprofile input with avgpool raised RNA-only PCA accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591, and F1 rose with it. This is the strongest signal so far. However, the gain is tied to avgpool, and each result is a single run. 2) Test: config_003 keeps the RNA-only, PCA-2000, multiprofile setup and changes only the aggregator to a transformer. It asks whether the multiprofile benefit depends on how profiles are aggregated, and whether a learned aggregator adds to the gain. 3) Why now: Aggregation affects every later multiprofile configuration, including image-only and multimodal ones, so settling it early narrows the search space. It is a one-variable change from the current best, so it builds on that result while still being an informative comparison. RNA encoder and image modality comparisons are natural next steps once the aggregation choice is clearer.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_003 kept the RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA (2000-component) setup from llm_summary_002 and changed only the aggregator from avgpool to a transformer. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.519 and an F1 of 0.480, well below avgpool's 0.591 and 0.573, though still slightly above the single-profile baseline of 0.485 and 0.464. This single-variable comparison suggests that the multiprofile benefit depends on how profiles are aggregated, and that in this setting the transformer did not add to the gain and appeared to lose most of it. Each configuration is still a single run with no variance estimate, the transformer's hyperparameters and training budget are unknown, it is untested whether the same ordering holds for image-only or multimodal multiprofile models, and the class count and chance level remain unknown.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: So far only RNA-only PCA models have been tested. Multiprofile with avgpool performed best (0.591 acc / 0.573 F1). It beat single-profile (0.485) and the transformer aggregator (0.519). The image modality is completely untested, and it is the largest open question in the design space, since 36 of the remaining configurations involve images. 2. What this tests: config_011 keeps the best-performing profile setting and aggregation (multiprofile + avgpool) and swaps only the modality, from RNA (PCA) to images (ResNet50). This gives a direct comparison of image versus RNA signal under the same aggregation. It also checks whether the avgpool multiprofile benefit carries over to another modality. 3. Why it is the best use of budget: Knowing how strong image-only is, at least with ResNet50, is needed to interpret any later multimodal or fusion result. If images are weak, multimodal gains are unlikely and the budget can shift to RNA encoders such as scVI and scGPT. If images are competitive or strong, multimodal fusion becomes the clear next direction. This makes it more informative than another RNA-encoder tweak or jumping straight to fusion.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_004 kept the multiprofile + avgpool setup from llm_summary_002 and changed the modality from RNA (PCA, 2000 components) to images, encoded with ResNet50 and with no fusion. Validation accuracy was 0.328 and F1 was 0.288. That is well below RNA-only multiprofile avgpool (0.591 / 0.573) and also below the RNA-only single-profile baseline (0.485 / 0.464). Under matched profile and aggregation settings, this initial comparison suggests image-only features from ResNet50 carry weaker class signal than PCA RNA features, so any multimodal gains may be modest. Several points remain uncertain. Each result is a single run with no variance estimate. The image result reflects only one encoder, so other image encoders or a single-profile image model may differ, and it is unknown whether avgpool's multiprofile benefit carries over to images. Images could still add complementary information in fusion despite their weak standalone performance. The class count and chance level are still unknown, so it is unclear how far 0.328 sits above chance.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is clearly the stronger modality so far. RNA-only multiprofile avgpool with PCA reached 0.591 accuracy and 0.573 F1, while ResNet50 image-only under the same settings reached 0.328 and 0.288. Avgpool also beat the transformer aggregator (0.519). However, every RNA result uses the PCA-2000 encoder, so we do not know whether that encoder is a good choice for the dominant modality. 2. What this tests: config_005 keeps the best setup fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the RNA encoder to scVI-200. This isolates the effect of RNA representation. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: any later multimodal fusion experiments will build on the RNA encoder, so settling this choice first is the most useful step. The result will tell us whether to keep PCA or switch encoders, and whether to try scGPT next. It is also a strong candidate for an immediate gain, since a learned latent space may represent expression better than PCA.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_005 kept the best setup so far fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool, as in llm_summary_002) and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA (2000 components) to scVI (200 latent dimensions). Validation accuracy rose from 0.591 to 0.650, and F1 rose with it from 0.573 to 0.628. This is the best result so far, and because only the encoder changed, it suggests scVI-200 is a stronger RNA representation than PCA-2000 in this setting, making it the current default for later fusion experiments. Uncertainties remain: each configuration is a single run with no variance estimate, so the size of the ~0.06 gain is not confirmed. The comparison also mixes encoder type with latent size (200 vs 2000), so which factor drives it is unclear. Other encoders such as scGPT, and whether the gain holds under other aggregators, single-profile input or fusion with images, are untested. The class count and chance level are still unknown.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool. Within that setup, switching the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200 raised validation accuracy from 0.591 to 0.650, and F1 rose with it. This shows the RNA representation strongly affects performance. The third RNA encoder, scGPT, is still untested. Image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.328), so RNA appears to carry most of the class signal. 2. Test: Keep the best setting fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and change only the encoder from scVI-200 to scGPT. This is a single-variable comparison that shows whether a pretrained foundation-model embedding beats scVI. 3. Why now: Every later multimodal experiment depends on choosing the right RNA encoder, and multimodal setups make up most of the remaining search space. Settling the encoder choice under the strongest known setting is the most useful next step before spending budget on fusion. If scGPT wins, fusion should be tested on scGPT. If it loses, scVI is confirmed as the default. These are single runs, so a small difference should not be overinterpreted.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_006 kept the best setup so far fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changed only the RNA encoder from scVI-200 (llm_summary_005) to scGPT. Validation accuracy was 0.530 and F1 was 0.515. That is well below scVI-200 (0.650 / 0.628) and also below PCA-2000 (0.591 / 0.573), though above the single-profile PCA baseline (0.485 / 0.464). Because only the encoder changed, this single-variable comparison suggests scGPT embeddings, as used here, are a weaker RNA representation than scVI-200 in this setting, which supports keeping scVI-200 as the default RNA encoder for later fusion experiments. Uncertainties remain: each result is a single run with no variance estimate, and the scGPT details (pretrained vs fine-tuned, embedding dimension, preprocessing or gene-vocabulary match) are not given, so a differently configured scGPT might perform better. It is also untested whether this encoder ordering holds under other aggregators, single-profile input or fusion with images, and the class count and chance level are still unknown.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_005 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI-200, avgpool), at 0.650 accuracy and 0.628 F1. Multiprofile with avgpool beat single-profile, and it also beat the transformer aggregator. scVI-200 beat both PCA-2000 and scGPT. Image-only ResNet50 was weak on its own (0.328), but whether images add complementary signal in fusion has never been tested. That is the most important design question still open. 2. What this tests: config_030 keeps config_005's best RNA setup fixed and adds only the ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion. It therefore isolates the effect of adding the image modality to the strongest pipeline. ResNet50 is the image encoder already measured in this exact multiprofile avgpool setting (config_011), so the result can be read against known standalone performance for both modalities. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a single-variable extension of the leading configuration, so it serves both exploitation and exploration. A gain would justify further fusion work, such as weighted fusion or ViT-L images. No gain or a drop would suggest RNA-only is sufficient and steer the remaining budget elsewhere. Either way, one run answers whether multimodality matters, which is the axis the search has not yet probed.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_007 kept the best configuration so far fixed (llm_summary_005: multiprofile, scVI-200 RNA encoder, avgpool) and added only a ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion, making this the first multimodal test. It reached 0.632 validation accuracy and 0.607 F1, slightly below RNA-only scVI-200 (0.650 / 0.628) but far above image-only ResNet50 (0.328 / 0.288). In this setting, adding ResNet50 image features through concat fusion did not improve on RNA alone and may have slightly hurt. However, the ~0.02 drop comes from single runs with no variance estimate, so it may fall within run-to-run noise. Several questions remain open: the effect of adding images cannot be separated from the concat fusion choice, so weighted or gated fusion, other image encoders such as ViT-L, or modality-specific normalization might still extract complementary image signal. The class count and chance level are also still unknown.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI-200 with avgpool (0.650 accuracy / 0.628 F1). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion (config_030) gave 0.632 / 0.607, a slight drop that could be noise. Because image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.328), concat may be letting a weak, noisy image branch dilute the strong RNA signal. It is still unknown whether images can add complementary information under a fusion method that can down-weight them. 2. What this tests: config_031 keeps config_030 identical and changes only concat to weighted fusion. This isolates the effect of the fusion strategy. If weighted fusion matches or beats RNA-only, images may contribute when properly balanced. If it stays at or below RNA-only, that strengthens the case that ResNet50 images add little, which would point next toward testing ViT-L image features. 3. Why it is the best next step: It is a clean single-variable comparison that builds on the strongest RNA setup. It addresses the most open design question, whether and how fusion helps. It also has a realistic chance of producing a new best result, so it balances exploitation and uncertainty reduction within the limited budget.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_008 kept llm_summary_007 fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 RNA, ResNet50 images, avgpool) and changed only the fusion method from concat to weighted. It reached 0.678 validation accuracy and 0.646 F1, the best result so far. That is above concat fusion (0.632 / 0.607) and above the RNA-only scVI-200 model (0.650 / 0.628). Because fusion was the only variable changed from llm_summary_007, this suggests weighted fusion makes better use of the weak ResNet50 image branch than concat, and that images may add complementary signal when balanced against RNA. However, each result is a single run with no variance estimate, so the modest gains (~0.046 over concat, ~0.027 over RNA-only) may partly reflect run-to-run noise. It remains untested whether the learned weights actually down-weight images, whether stronger image encoders such as ViT-L or other fusion schemes (e.g., gated or attention-based) would help further, and whether the gain holds under other aggregators. The class count and chance level are still unknown.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_031 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.678 acc / 0.646 F1). It beats RNA-only scVI-200 (0.650) and concat fusion (0.632). This suggests weighted fusion can extract complementary signal from images, even though ResNet50 alone is weak (0.328). The image encoder is the main untested design choice, since ViT-L has not been tried in any setting. 2. Test: config_037 keeps every other choice from config_031 fixed and swaps only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates whether a stronger image representation increases the multimodal gain. 3. Budget rationale: This is a single-variable extension of the current best, so it is both a plausible new best (exploitation) and a direct test of whether the image encoder matters (uncertainty reduction). It is more decision-relevant than retrying transformer aggregation, which hurt in the RNA-only comparison, or scGPT, which underperformed. Because results are single runs, a small difference should be read cautiously, but a clear shift in accuracy and F1 would guide the image-encoder choice for the remaining experiments.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_009 kept the best configuration so far fixed (llm_summary_008: multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 RNA, avgpool, weighted fusion) and changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. It reached 0.706 validation accuracy and 0.667 F1, the new best, above ResNet50 weighted fusion (0.678 / 0.646) and RNA-only scVI-200 (0.650 / 0.628). Because only the image encoder changed, this suggests ViT-L supplies a more useful image representation for weighted multimodal fusion, though the ~0.029 accuracy gain (~0.021 F1) is modest and comes from single runs with no variance estimate, so it may partly reflect run-to-run noise. Several questions remain open. ViT-L has not been tested image-only, so its standalone strength is unknown. It is also untested whether ViT-L would help under concat fusion or other aggregators, and the learned fusion weights, the class count and the chance level are still unknown.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_037 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.706 acc / 0.667 F1). With ResNet50 images, weighted fusion clearly beat concat (0.678 vs 0.632), and concat did not even beat RNA-only (0.650). But that fusion comparison rests on a single image encoder and single runs. It is unknown whether weighted fusion is generally better or only rescues a weak image branch. 2) Test: config_036 keeps config_037 fixed and changes only the fusion method to concat. This gives a second, independent weighted-vs-concat comparison under a stronger image encoder. If concat stays clearly below weighted, the fusion choice is confirmed as a robust design decision. If concat with ViT-L matches weighted, the earlier gap mostly reflected ResNet50's weak features, and the image encoder is the main driver. 3) Why now: fusion is a key decision behind the current best model and later experiments will build on it. A one-variable check that replicates the main fusion finding is cheap and isolates the effect. It is more informative than a transformer-aggregation test, which has already looked unpromising, or a riskier multi-factor change.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_010 kept the previous best configuration fixed (llm_summary_009: multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 RNA, ImageNet ViT-L images, avgpool) and changed only the fusion method from weighted to concat, to check whether weighted fusion's advantage over concat with ResNet50 (0.678 vs 0.632 in llm_summary_008 vs llm_summary_007) holds with a stronger image encoder. Concat reached 0.715 validation accuracy and 0.687 F1, the best result so far. It matched or slightly exceeded weighted fusion with ViT-L (0.706 / 0.667) and clearly beat RNA-only scVI-200 (0.650 / 0.628) and concat with ResNet50 (0.632 / 0.607). So the weighted-over-concat advantage did not replicate under ViT-L, which suggests the earlier gap may have mainly reflected weighted fusion compensating for weak ResNet50 features, with image encoder quality being the larger driver of multimodal gains and fusion choice mattering less when image features are strong. Several uncertainties remain: the ~0.009 accuracy gap (~0.02 F1) between concat and weighted comes from single runs with no variance estimate and may be within run-to-run noise, so neither fusion method can be declared superior with ViT-L; ViT-L image-only performance, the learned fusion weights, other fusion schemes or aggregators, and the class count and chance level are all still unknown.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2. Test: config_001 is the simplest configuration: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA (2000 components), with no aggregation or fusion. It sets a reference point that later experiments can be compared against one factor at a time. For example, scVI or scGPT tests the encoder, avgpool or transformer tests multiprofile aggregation, image-only tests the other modality, and concat or weighted tests fusion. 3. Why now: Under a limited budget, a clean low-complexity baseline makes every later result interpretable as a controlled single-factor comparison. It also guards against assuming that complex multimodal or multiprofile models will win, since any added complexity must beat this baseline.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 established the first reference point for the study: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA encoder (2000 components), with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485 (primary metric), and its validation F1 of 0.464 suggests performance is roughly similar across classes rather than driven by a few. Because no other experiments have been run, this is only a baseline observation, and no conclusions can yet be drawn about whether changing the RNA encoder, adding the image modality, using multiprofile aggregation, or applying fusion would help. Later configurations should change one factor at a time relative to this baseline so differences can be attributed. Run-to-run variance is also unknown, so small differences from 0.485 should be interpreted cautiously.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: There is only one data point so far. The RNA-only, single-profile PCA-2000 baseline (config_001) reached 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. We know nothing yet about the effect of the RNA encoder, the image modality, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion. 2. What this tests: config_002 changes one factor. It keeps the RNA-only PCA-2000 setup and switches from single-profile to multiprofile using the simplest aggregation, avgpool. This isolates whether pooling information across multiple profiles helps on its own. 3. Why now: the profile-setting question affects every later branch, including RNA-only, image-only and multimodal configurations. Answering it cleanly against the existing baseline tells us whether later experiments should favor multiprofile settings. Starting with avgpool rather than a transformer avoids mixing the basic multiprofile effect with the added complexity of learned aggregation. Encoder and modality comparisons (config_004, config_007, config_010) stay as strong follow-up options.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 kept the RNA-only PCA-2000 setup from llm_summary_001 and changed only the profile setting, switching from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. Validation accuracy rose from 0.485 to 0.591 (about +0.106), and validation F1 rose by a similar amount, from 0.464 to 0.573, so the supporting metric agrees with the primary one. Because this was a one-factor change against the baseline, it is initial evidence that multiprofile input with simple average pooling helps in the RNA-only PCA setting. However, profile setting and aggregation change together here, so this run cannot show whether a different aggregator, such as a learned transformer, would do better or worse, whether the gain carries over to other RNA encoders, image-only or multimodal configurations, or how large run-to-run variance is, since each setting has only one run.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool improved the RNA-only PCA-2000 model by about 0.106 accuracy (0.485 to 0.591), and F1 rose by a similar amount. This is the strongest signal so far. However, avgpool is the only aggregator tested, so we do not know whether the gain comes from multiprofile input in general or from this simple pooling choice. Each setting also has only one run. 2. What this tests: config_003 keeps everything from the best configuration (config_002) and changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to a learned transformer. Any difference in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed to the aggregator. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: It exploits the most promising direction while isolating a design choice that recurs across many remaining configurations, including RNA-only, image-only and multimodal multiprofile ones. Settling avgpool versus transformer early helps prune about half of those candidates. Untested encoders and the image modality are left for later controlled comparisons.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept the RNA-only, multiprofile PCA-2000 setup of llm_summary_002 and changed only the aggregator, from avgpool to a learned transformer. Validation accuracy fell from 0.591 to 0.519 (about -0.072), and F1 fell from 0.573 to 0.480, so the supporting metric agrees. Because aggregation was the only change, this is initial evidence that avgpool beats the transformer aggregator in this RNA-only PCA setting, and the transformer still sits slightly above the single-profile baseline (0.485 accuracy). Each setting has only one run, so run-to-run variance is unknown. It is also unclear whether the transformer's weaker result reflects the aggregator itself or untuned training choices. Whether the avgpool advantage carries over to other RNA encoders, image-only or multimodal configurations has not been tested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: all three experiments so far are RNA-only with the PCA-2000 encoder. They give initial single-run evidence that multiprofile with avgpool (0.591 accuracy, 0.573 F1) beats both single-profile (0.485) and transformer aggregation (0.519). The image modality is completely untested, so we do not know whether images carry useful signal for this task. That is the largest open uncertainty and it governs most of the remaining search space. 2. What this tests: config_011 keeps the best-known profile setting and aggregator (multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps only the modality from RNA (PCA-2000) to image (ResNet50). This shows how strong image features are on their own, compared directly against config_002. It also checks whether the multiprofile avgpool setup carries over to a different modality. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: knowing image-only performance tells us whether the many multimodal configurations are worth exploring and gives a reference for judging any fusion gain later. It is more informative now than refining the RNA encoder or aggregator choice within a modality that has already been explored.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the multiprofile avgpool setup of llm_summary_002 and swapped the modality from RNA (PCA-2000) to image-only (ResNet50 encoder, no fusion), giving the first measurement of image features on their own. Validation accuracy was 0.328 (F1 0.288), far below the RNA multiprofile avgpool result (0.591 / 0.573) and also below the RNA single-profile baseline (0.485 / 0.464), so the supporting metric agrees with the primary one. This is initial single-run evidence that ResNet50 image features with multiprofile avgpool are much weaker than PCA-2000 RNA features for this task, though modality and encoder change together, so the run cannot show whether the gap reflects the image modality itself or the ResNet50 encoder and its untuned training choices. It is also unknown whether multiprofile avgpool helps images, since there is no single-profile image run; whether images add complementary signal when fused with RNA; and how large run-to-run variance is.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only PCA-2000 with multiprofile avgpool (0.591 accuracy, 0.573 F1). Multiprofile avgpool beat both single-profile (0.485) and the transformer aggregator (0.519). ResNet50 image-only multiprofile avgpool was much weaker (0.328), but nothing has tested whether images add complementary signal when combined with RNA. 2) This run keeps the best RNA setup (PCA-2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds ResNet50 images with simple concat fusion. Both components have already been measured alone, so this is a near one-factor test of whether adding the image modality helps, does nothing, or hurts. 3) Whether multimodal fusion is worth pursuing is the biggest open design question, and it decides how much of the remaining budget goes to the large multimodal part of the space. Concat is the simplest fusion baseline, and building on the strongest known setup gives this run both high information value and a real chance of a new best.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 kept the best RNA setup so far (PCA-2000, multiprofile, avgpool; llm_summary_002) and added ResNet50 image features with simple concat fusion. This is a near one-factor test of whether the image modality adds signal on top of RNA. Validation accuracy rose from 0.591 to 0.619 (about +0.028), a new best, and F1 rose from 0.573 to 0.610 (about +0.038), so the supporting metric agrees. This is initial evidence that images contribute complementary signal when fused with RNA, even though image-only performance was weak (0.328). However, each setting has only one run and run-to-run variance is unknown, so a gain of this size may be partly noise. The run also cannot show whether other fusion methods, other image or RNA encoders, or other aggregators would do better, or whether the extra model capacity, rather than the image information itself, explains the improvement.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_018 (PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50 image, multiprofile avgpool, concat fusion) at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. It modestly beat RNA-only (0.591), even though ResNet50 image-only was weak (0.328). The image encoder is a major open question: we cannot tell whether the low image signal reflects the image modality itself or the ResNet50 features. 2. Test: config_024 keeps everything in config_018 fixed and swaps only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates the effect of image representation quality on multimodal performance. 3. Rationale: This is a clean one-factor extension of the current best setup, so it combines exploitation with learning about an important design choice. If stronger image features raise the multimodal result, the image path is the bottleneck. If they do not, future budget should go to RNA encoders or fusion instead.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_005: multimodal, PCA-2000 RNA, multiprofile avgpool, concat fusion) and changed only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, to test whether image representation quality limits multimodal performance. Validation accuracy (the primary metric) rose slightly, from 0.619 to 0.629 (about +0.010), a nominal new best. Validation F1, however, fell from 0.610 to 0.599 (about -0.011), so the supporting metric does not agree, and the change may have shifted performance across classes rather than improved it overall. With single runs and unknown run-to-run variance, these differences are small enough to be noise, so this is at most weak evidence that ViT-L improves the image path. It remains open whether the image path is the bottleneck, and an image-only ViT-L run would help show whether ViT-L features are stronger on their own.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is clearly the dominant modality. RNA-only multiprofile avgpool reached 0.591, image-only reached 0.328, and adding images gave only about +0.01 to +0.03. Yet every RNA run so far has used PCA-2000, so the RNA representation is the largest untested design choice. Avgpool beat the transformer aggregator once (0.591 vs 0.519), and fusion and image-encoder differences look small and possibly within noise. 2. What this tests: config_008 matches config_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) except for the encoder, which changes from PCA-2000 to scGPT. This cleanly isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation beats PCA on the modality that drives most of the performance. 3. Why now: the RNA encoder plausibly has a much larger effect than fusion type or image encoder. The result will tell us whether later multimodal runs should switch to scGPT (configs 048/049) or stay with PCA.
