Each configuration was run only once, so run-to-run variance is unknown. The encoders also differ in embedding dimensionality and in how the embeddings are produced (e.g., scGPT pretrained versus fine-tuned, unspecified), so this result may reflect this particular scGPT usage rather than foundation-model representations in general. It is also untested whether the ranking holds with single-profile, transformer aggregation, or multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder so far (0.650 vs 0.591 for PCA and 0.530 for scGPT). Transformer and avgpool aggregation look about equal (+0.003). Images have not clearly helped. ResNet50 image-only scored 0.328. Adding ResNet50 to scVI with concat fusion lowered accuracy slightly (0.632 vs 0.650), although adding it to PCA raised accuracy a little. The largest untested design choice is the image encoder, since ViT-L has never been run. It is therefore unclear whether the weak image results reflect the imaging modality itself or just ResNet50. 2) What this tests: config_036 changes only the image encoder relative to config_030 (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool, concat). Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L isolates whether a stronger image representation lets images add value on top of the best RNA backbone. Comparing it with RNA-only scVI (config_005) also shows directly whether multimodality beats the current best. 3) Why this is the best use of the next run: it tackles the most important open question, whether images are worth including, in the setting that matters most for the final model. It also has a realistic chance of producing a new best result. Weighted fusion and transformer-aggregated multimodal runs can be judged better once the image encoder question is settled.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 swapped the image encoder from ResNet50 to ViT-L in the multimodal, multiprofile scVI (n=200) setup with avgpool aggregation and concat fusion, changing only this one factor relative to llm_summary_006. It also gives a direct comparison against RNA-only scVI (llm_summary_005). It reached validation accuracy 0.7150 (F1 0.6872), well above scVI + ResNet50 (0.6315 / 0.6068; about +0.084 accuracy and +0.080 F1) and above RNA-only scVI with avgpool (0.6501 / 0.6275; about +0.065 / +0.060) or with transformer aggregation (0.6530 / 0.6283), with both metrics agreeing. This makes it the new best configuration and suggests that the earlier weak image contribution was tied to ResNet50 rather than to the imaging modality itself, so ViT-L image features appear to add complementary value beyond the scVI RNA features. Uncertainties remain: each configuration was run only once with unknown run-to-run variance, though this gain is larger than earlier small differences. ViT-L has not been tested image-only or combined with the PCA backbone. It is also untested whether weighted fusion or transformer aggregation would add further gains in this multimodal ViT-L setting.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The current best is config_036 (multimodal scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.7150 accuracy and 0.6872 F1. It clearly beats RNA-only scVI (about 0.650), which suggests ViT-L images add complementary signal. Fusion method has never been varied; every multimodal run used concat. Aggregation was tested once, in RNA-only scVI, where transformer and avgpool were roughly equivalent (+0.003). 2. What this tests: config_037 changes only fusion, from concat to weighted, on the best configuration. This isolates the effect of the fusion strategy, a design dimension that is still completely untested. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: It explores an unknown factor while exploiting the strongest configuration, so it can both improve performance and show whether fusion matters. The transformer-aggregator variant (config_038) is less informative because prior evidence suggests a small aggregation effect. Image-only ViT-L (config_014) is a useful diagnostic, but it is unlikely to improve the best result and can come later.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 changed only the fusion method of the best configuration so far, llm_summary_009 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n=200 + ViT-L, avgpool), from concat to weighted. This is the study's first test of fusion strategy. It reached validation accuracy 0.7062 (F1 0.6671) versus 0.7150 (F1 0.6872) for concat, about -0.009 accuracy and -0.020 F1. The metrics agree in direction, so weighted fusion gave no improvement and may be slightly worse here, while still clearly beating RNA-only scVI (0.6501 / 0.6275); concat with ViT-L remains the best configuration. Each configuration was run only once and run-to-run variance is unknown, so the accuracy gap in particular may be within noise. It also remains untested whether the fusion ranking holds with transformer aggregation, other encoders, or different weighted-fusion settings.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: No experiments have been run yet, so we have no information about any design choice: modality, RNA or image encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion. 2. What this tests: The simplest model (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000 features, no aggregation or fusion) sets a baseline accuracy and F1. Each later experiment can then change one factor from this anchor, such as swapping the encoder to scVI or scGPT, switching to multiprofile with avgpool, or adding image features. That makes the effect of each change easy to attribute. 3. Why it is the best first use of budget: Starting with a complex multimodal configuration would bundle several untested choices together, so any result would be hard to interpret. A cheap, interpretable baseline makes all subsequent comparisons informative. It also checks whether added complexity is needed at all.
experiment_summary: This first experiment set a baseline with the simplest configuration: an RNA-only, single-profile model using PCA features (pca_n2000), with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485 and a supporting validation F1 of 0.464. The similar accuracy and F1 suggest no severe class imbalance in performance, but this is an initial observation only. With no other experiments to compare against, it is unknown whether other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, or adding image features would improve results, so this run should serve as the reference point for later one-factor-at-a-time comparisons.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result so far. The RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_001) reached 0.485 validation accuracy and 0.464 F1. Nothing yet shows whether representation, profile setting, aggregation, or modality matters. 2. What this tests: config_002 keeps the RNA-only PCA encoder and changes one factor, single-profile to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates whether pooling information across multiple profiles helps. The design choice applies to every modality and encoder, and avgpool gives a clean, low-complexity check before trying transformer aggregation. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: a one-factor comparison against the baseline reduces uncertainty about a structural axis that shapes most of the remaining search space (36 of the 50 untested configurations are multiprofile). Comparing RNA encoders (config_004 or config_007) would be similarly informative, but the profile-setting result tells us more about which branch of the space to prioritize.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the RNA-only pca_n2000 baseline (llm_summary_001) fixed and changed only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile, using average pooling across profiles. Validation accuracy rose from 0.485 to 0.591 (+0.106), and validation F1 rose from 0.464 to 0.573, so the gain is consistent across both metrics. Because this is a one-factor comparison, it is initial evidence that multiprofile input helps for this RNA-only PCA setup. Uncertainties remain: each setting has only one run with no variance estimate, multiprofile cannot be separated from the avgpool choice, and it is untested whether the gain holds with other RNA encoders, other aggregators such as transformers, or image and fused modalities.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised validation accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591, and F1 rose from 0.464 to 0.573. This makes multiprofile the most promising direction so far. However, the multiprofile effect is currently tied to one aggregator, so we cannot yet tell whether avgpool is a good choice or merely adequate. 2. Test: config_003 keeps everything from the current best (config_002: rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000) fixed and changes only avgpool to transformer. This isolates the effect of aggregation. If the transformer helps, profile interactions matter and later multiprofile runs should use it. If it does not, the simpler avgpool becomes the default. 3. Why now: it extends the strongest evidence with a clean one-factor comparison. Its answer also shapes many remaining configurations, both RNA-encoder and multimodal ones, that depend on the aggregation choice. That makes it more informative per experiment than changing encoder or modality at this point. Encoder (scVI/scGPT) and image modality comparisons can follow with the aggregator settled.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the current best configuration (llm_summary_002: rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000) fixed and changed only the aggregator, from avgpool to transformer. Validation accuracy fell from 0.591 to 0.519 (-0.072), and validation F1 fell from 0.573 to 0.480. Both metrics moved the same way, so this one-factor comparison is initial evidence that avgpool works better than this transformer aggregator in the RNA-only PCA multiprofile setting, and it supports keeping avgpool as the default for now. The result is still uncertain: each configuration has a single run with no variance estimate, and the transformer may be undertuned or less suited to this data size (its hyperparameters and training details are not reported). It is also unknown whether the ranking holds with other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) or with image and fused modalities.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence so far: all three runs used the RNA-only pca_n2000 encoder. Multiprofile with avgpool is the best result (acc 0.591, F1 0.573). It beat single-profile by about 0.106 and beat transformer aggregation by about 0.072, with F1 moving the same way both times. The RNA encoder choice is still untested, and so is the image modality. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup fixed (rna_only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the RNA encoder, from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200. It is a clean one-factor test of whether the representation matters. It also checks whether the multiprofile/avgpool gain carries over to a different encoder. 3) Why this is the best next step: it builds on the strongest evidence so far while resolving a major open design choice. The answer decides which RNA encoder to carry into the many later multimodal configurations, all of which are paired with a specific RNA encoder. That makes it a high-value use of limited budget. Image-only baselines (for example config_011) remain an important next step after this.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_002: rna_only, multiprofile, avgpool) fixed and changed only the RNA encoder, from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200. Validation accuracy rose from 0.591 to 0.650 (+0.059) and validation F1 rose from 0.573 to 0.628, making this the new best result. Because this is a one-factor comparison with both metrics moving the same way, it is initial evidence that the scVI representation outperforms PCA in this setup, and it suggests the multiprofile/avgpool setup still works with a different encoder, though single-profile and transformer variants were not rerun with scVI. Uncertainties remain: each configuration has a single run with no variance estimate, scVI also differs from PCA in dimensionality (200 vs 2000), so the source of the gain cannot be isolated, other encoders such as scGPT are untested, and it is unknown whether the advantage holds once image or fused modalities are added.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: In the RNA-only multiprofile setting, avgpool beat the transformer with PCA (0.591 vs 0.519). Swapping PCA for scVI under avgpool gave the current best result (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). scGPT, the third RNA encoder, is untested. Every multimodal configuration depends on which RNA encoder is chosen. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup fixed (rna_only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder from scVI to scGPT. That completes the encoder comparison in one clean step and shows whether a foundation-model embedding beats scVI. 3) Under a limited budget, settling the best RNA encoder first is efficient, because it narrows the large multimodal space before image and fusion runs are spent. Either result is useful: scGPT becomes the new best, or scVI is confirmed as the anchor for later image and fusion comparisons. Image-only and multimodal runs remain important next steps once the RNA backbone is settled.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_004: rna_only, multiprofile, avgpool) fixed and changed only the RNA encoder, from scvi_n200 to scGPT. Validation accuracy fell from 0.650 to 0.530 (-0.120) and validation F1 fell from 0.628 to 0.515. That puts scGPT below both scVI and PCA (0.591 under the same setup). Both metrics moved the same way, so this one-factor comparison is initial evidence that scVI is the strongest of the three RNA encoders here and supports keeping scVI as the RNA anchor for later image-only and multimodal runs. Uncertainties remain: each configuration has a single run with no variance estimate, and the scGPT embedding's dimensionality, preprocessing, and whether it was fine-tuned or frozen are not reported, so scGPT may be suboptimally configured rather than inherently weaker. It is also unknown whether the encoder ranking holds with other aggregators, single-profile input, or image and fused modalities.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The RNA side is now fairly well mapped, though each result is a single run. Multiprofile beat single-profile (0.591 vs 0.485), avgpool beat transformer (0.591 vs 0.519), and scVI was the best RNA encoder (0.650), ahead of PCA (0.591) and scGPT (0.530). By contrast, the image modality is completely untested, and that is the largest remaining uncertainty. 2) Test: This runs an image-only baseline with ResNet50, using the multiprofile + avgpool setting that worked best for RNA. It measures how much signal the image features carry on their own, and whether multiprofile avgpool also helps outside RNA. 3) Why now: Knowing standalone image performance is needed before interpreting any multimodal run. Without it, a gain or loss from fusion with scVI (e.g., config_030/031) cannot be attributed to the image features versus the fusion method. Matching the RNA profile and aggregation settings keeps the comparison to the 0.650 scVI anchor as clean as possible. The result will guide whether to compare ViT-L next and whether multimodal fusion is worth pursuing.
experiment_summary: This first image-only experiment used a ResNet50 image encoder with the multiprofile + avgpool setting that worked best for RNA, with no RNA encoder or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.328 and a supporting validation F1 of 0.288, far below every RNA-only run (best: scVI 0.650; weakest: single-profile PCA 0.485). This is an initial baseline suggesting ResNet50 image features carry much less standalone signal than the RNA representations in this setup. Uncertainties remain: it is a single run with no variance estimate; no single-profile or transformer image variants were run, so whether multiprofile/avgpool helps for images is untested; ResNet50 details (pretraining, frozen vs fine-tuned) are not reported; and other encoders such as ViT-L are untested. It is also unknown whether these weak image features would add complementary information or noise when fused with scVI, so this run should serve as the image reference for interpreting later multimodal results.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: scVI with multiprofile avgpool is the best configuration so far (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). The only image-only run, ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool, was much weaker (0.328 accuracy, 0.288 F1). Only one image encoder has been tested, so it is unclear whether images are inherently weak here or ResNet50 is just a poor representation. 2) This run swaps only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, under the same multiprofile avgpool setup. It is a clean one-factor comparison against config_011. 3) Most of the remaining budget lies in multimodal configurations, and each of those needs an image encoder. Knowing which encoder carries more standalone signal makes later fusion tests with scVI more informative. It also avoids rejecting multimodal fusion because the image branch was weak. One cheap image-only run reduces uncertainty about a choice that affects many later experiments.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the image-only multiprofile avgpool setup of llm_summary_006 fixed and changed only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. It isolates the encoder choice to test whether the weak image results came from ResNet50 specifically. Validation accuracy was essentially unchanged (0.332 vs 0.328, +0.004), while validation F1 rose slightly (0.315 vs 0.288). Both image encoders therefore remain far below every RNA-only run (best: scVI 0.650), which is initial evidence that standalone image features carry limited signal here regardless of which of these two encoders is used, with ViT-L at most marginally ahead on F1. Uncertainties remain: each configuration has a single run with no variance estimate, so the small differences may be noise; pretraining and frozen vs fine-tuned details are not reported; image-specific profile or aggregation variants are untested; and it is unknown whether either encoder adds complementary information or noise when fused with scVI, so the choice of image encoder for multimodal runs is not clearly resolved by this comparison.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: In single runs, multiprofile input with avgpool beat single-profile input (0.591 vs 0.485). Avgpool beat the transformer aggregator (0.591 vs 0.519), and scVI was the best RNA encoder (0.650, versus 0.591 for PCA and 0.530 for scGPT). Image-only models are weak, around 0.33 accuracy for both encoders, with ViT-L slightly ahead on F1 (0.315 vs 0.288). The biggest open question is whether image features add complementary signal or just noise when combined with the strong scVI representation. 2. Test: This run keeps the best RNA setup (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool) fixed and adds ViT-L image features through the simplest fusion method, concat. Comparing it with config_005 isolates whether adding the image modality helps. 3. Why now: Multimodal configurations make up most of the remaining search space, so knowing whether image fusion helps at all is the most informative next result. A gain would justify exploring fusion type and image encoder next. A loss would suggest staying RNA-only and refining scVI variants such as single-profile or transformer aggregation.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the best RNA-only setup (llm_summary_004: scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, validation accuracy 0.650) fixed and added ImageNet ViT-L image features via simple concat fusion. Note that the selection rationale cites config_005 as the comparison, but the matching RNA-only baseline is llm_summary_004; llm_summary_005 used scGPT. Validation accuracy rose to 0.715 (+0.065) and validation F1 rose to 0.687 (+0.060 vs 0.628), making this the new best result, even though ViT-L alone reached only about 0.33 accuracy. Because only the image modality was added and both metrics improved together, this is initial evidence that the image features add complementary signal rather than noise when combined with scVI. Uncertainties remain: each configuration is a single run with no variance estimate; the gain could partly reflect added input dimensionality or capacity rather than image content specifically; and other fusion methods, the ResNet50 encoder in fusion, and single-profile or transformer variants of the multimodal model are untested, so fusion type and image encoder are the natural next factors to vary.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_036 (multimodal, scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat fusion) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Adding image features to scVI gave about +0.065 accuracy even though image-only models were weak (about 0.33). Fusion method is the main untested design choice for the multimodal model. Encoder, profile setting, and aggregator already have initial evidence favoring scVI, multiprofile, and avgpool. 2) Test: config_037 keeps everything in config_036 fixed and changes only the fusion, from concat to weighted. This isolates whether fusion type matters. It also helps check whether the multimodal gain depends on how the weak image modality is combined; for example, weighted fusion may down-weight image noise or prevent the image features from dominating. 3) Why now: It is a one-factor change from the current best, so it both exploits the most promising direction and answers a key open design question. Other options are less useful right now. Swapping in ResNet50 changes an encoder that already looked roughly equivalent to ViT-L in image-only runs. Transformer aggregation underperformed in its only RNA test.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_008: multimodal, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool) fixed and changed only the fusion method, from concat to weighted. The selection rationale refers to this baseline as config_036, but the matching completed run is llm_summary_008. Validation accuracy fell slightly, from 0.715 to 0.706 (-0.009), and validation F1 fell from 0.687 to 0.667 (-0.020), so concat remains the best result. Both fusion variants stayed well above the RNA-only scVI baseline (0.650), which is initial evidence that the multimodal gain does not depend on the fusion method and that weighted fusion did not further improve on concat by down-weighting the weak image modality. Uncertainties remain: each configuration is a single run with no variance estimate, so the small accuracy gap may be noise; how the weighted fusion's weights are set (learned vs fixed) and what weights it assigned to each modality are not reported; and other fusion methods (e.g., attention-based), ResNet50 in fusion, and single-profile or transformer multimodal variants are untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_036 (scVI + ImageNet ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat), at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Image features alone are weak, but they add complementary signal when fused with scVI. Weighted fusion did not beat concat. Which image encoder works best in fusion is still unresolved: ResNet50 and ViT-L were nearly tied when used alone (0.328 vs 0.332 accuracy, F1 0.288 vs 0.315). 2) Test: config_030 keeps the best setup fixed (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) and swaps only the image encoder to ResNet50. This shows whether the multimodal gain depends on ViT-L or holds across image encoders. It also helps tell real image content apart from the effect of simply adding input dimensions. 3) Why now: The alternatives are lower value. Profile setting and aggregation already have fairly consistent evidence (multiprofile helped by about 0.1; avgpool beat transformer). The image encoder is the main untested factor in the leading multimodal configuration, and its answer decides which encoder the remaining fusion experiments should use. This makes config_030 a clean one-factor comparison that is both informative and plausibly competitive.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the best configuration (llm_summary_008: multimodal scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, concat; the rationale calls it config_036) fixed and swapped only the image encoder from ImageNet ViT-L to ResNet50. Validation accuracy fell from 0.715 to 0.632 (-0.084) and validation F1 fell from 0.687 to 0.607, which also puts this run below the RNA-only scVI baseline (llm_summary_004: 0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). The two encoders were nearly tied when used alone (about 0.33 accuracy), so this one-factor comparison is initial evidence that the multimodal gain depends on the image encoder: ViT-L features appear complementary to scVI, while concatenated ResNet50 features may add noise. It also weakens, but does not rule out, the idea that the ViT-L gain came only from adding input dimensions. Uncertainties remain: each configuration is a single run with no variance estimate; feature dimensionalities, pretraining, and frozen vs fine-tuned details are not reported; and it is untested whether other fusion methods (e.g., weighted) would let ResNet50 help, so ViT-L remains the preferred image encoder for later fusion experiments.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion matters. 2. Test: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest configuration. It sets a baseline for validation accuracy and F1. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time against it: encoder (scVI or scGPT), profile setting (multiprofile with avgpool), modality (image-only or multimodal), and fusion. 3. Why now: Under a limited budget, a simple anchor comes first. It prevents us from assuming that complexity helps, and it gives an interpretable reference point. That makes every later single-factor comparison more informative than starting with a complex multimodal model whose result could not be attributed to any one design choice.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest configuration as a baseline anchor: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.4849 (primary metric), with a supporting validation F1 of 0.4639. Because no other experiments have been completed, this is only an initial reference point. It does not show whether the RNA modality, the PCA encoder, or the single-profile setting help or hurt performance. Several things remain open: how this compares with alternative RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image-only or multimodal fusion settings, and how much the result might vary across runs. Future experiments should change one factor at a time against this baseline so that any differences can be attributed to a specific design choice.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Only one baseline exists, an RNA-only single-profile PCA model at 0.4849 accuracy and 0.4639 F1. It says nothing about whether the image modality carries useful signal. 2. Test: config_010 is the image-only counterpart of that baseline, a single-profile ResNet50 model with no aggregation or fusion. It keeps the profile setting fixed and swaps only the modality, so it directly compares RNA and image as standalone sources of information. 3. Why now: Most remaining configurations (36 of 50) are multimodal and depend on the image branch adding value. Knowing whether images alone are weaker than, similar to, or stronger than RNA is the most decision-relevant uncertainty. It tells us whether to prioritize RNA encoder variants, image encoders, or fusion next. The simple single-profile, ResNet50 setting gives a clean anchor before testing multiprofile aggregation or ViT-L.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no aggregation or fusion, as the image counterpart to the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.2079 (F1 0.1718), well below the RNA-only baseline's 0.4849 accuracy (F1 0.4639). This is an initial observation that this image-only setup carries less discriminative signal than the RNA-only setup. However, the comparison changes both the modality and the encoder (ResNet50 vs. PCA-2000), so it cannot separate a weaker image modality from a weaker image representation. Several things remain uncertain: whether ViT-L or multiprofile aggregation would improve image-only performance, whether images add complementary value in fusion despite being weak alone, and how much both single-run results vary across seeds.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Only two single-run results exist. RNA-only PCA single-profile reached 0.485 accuracy (F1 0.464). Image-only ResNet50 single-profile reached only 0.208 (F1 0.172). So RNA is the strongest anchor so far. The effect of the profile setting is still completely unknown, even though most of the remaining search space (aggregation choices, and most multimodal configurations) depends on it. 2. What this tests: config_002 changes only one factor from the best baseline, config_001. It moves from single-profile to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool) and keeping the RNA-only PCA-2000 setup fixed. Any difference can therefore be attributed to multiprofile aggregation itself. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: The result is informative either way. A gain would justify exploring multiprofile settings and comparing transformer against avgpool aggregation. No gain would let us deprioritize much of the multiprofile space. Running it on the strong RNA modality gives a cleaner signal than running it on the weak image setup. Encoder comparisons (scVI, scGPT) and fusion tests remain good follow-ups once this broad structural question is clearer.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 changed one structural factor from the best baseline (llm_summary_001, RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile). It switched to the multiprofile setting with avgpool aggregation and kept the RNA-only PCA-2000 setup otherwise fixed. Validation accuracy rose from 0.4849 to 0.5907 (F1 from 0.4639 to 0.5727), the best result so far. This is an initial indication that multiprofile aggregation helps the RNA-only setup and supports further exploration of multiprofile configurations. However, each configuration is a single run with unknown seed variance, and the change bundles the multiprofile input with the specific avgpool aggregator. It also remains untested whether the gain carries over to other aggregators (e.g., transformer), other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), the weaker image modality, or multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is RNA-only PCA-2000 with multiprofile avgpool (config_002, accuracy 0.5907, F1 0.5727). It clearly beat the single-profile baseline (0.4849). However, that gain combines two things: the multiprofile input and the specific avgpool aggregator. It is not yet known whether a learned aggregator captures more from multiple profiles. 2. What this tests: config_003 keeps the modality, encoder and multiprofile setting from config_002 and changes only the aggregator to a transformer. Any difference can therefore be attributed to aggregation. It will show whether the multiprofile gain is robust to the aggregator and whether a learned aggregator adds further value. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: Aggregation is a decision shared by most remaining configurations, including all multiprofile RNA, image and multimodal options. Settling it early, on the strongest and simplest pipeline, narrows the search space efficiently. It is also a low-risk exploitation of the most promising direction. Encoder and fusion questions can then be tested against a firmer multiprofile reference.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 isolated the aggregation choice. It kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_003: RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000) fixed and replaced avgpool aggregation with a transformer aggregator. Validation accuracy fell from 0.5907 to 0.5191 (F1 from 0.5727 to 0.4797), which is still above the single-profile baseline (0.4849 accuracy, 0.4639 F1). This is an initial indication that, in this setup, the learned transformer aggregator does not improve on avgpool and may be worse, and that the multiprofile benefit holds across both aggregators tested, though with a smaller margin under the transformer. All results are single runs with unknown seed variance, and transformer hyperparameters or training adequacy were not explored, so the gap may reflect tuning or optimization rather than a fundamental limit. It also remains untested whether this aggregator ranking carries over to other RNA encoders, the image modality, or multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: the best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000 with avgpool (config_002, accuracy 0.591, F1 0.573). Avgpool beat the transformer aggregator, and multiprofile beat single-profile. Image-only ResNet50 was much weaker (accuracy 0.208). It is still unknown whether images add complementary signal when fused with RNA, which is the central multimodal question of this study. 2. What this tests: config_018 keeps the best configuration fixed (PCA-2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes one thing, adding the ResNet50 image modality with the simplest fusion method (concat). Any difference in accuracy and F1 can therefore be attributed mainly to adding image information. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: a gain would justify exploring fusion variants (weighted fusion, ViT-L) built on the strong RNA multiprofile setup. No gain or a loss would suggest focusing the remaining budget on RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) instead. Either outcome sharply narrows the search space, while staying close to the best-known configuration so the chance of a strong result remains reasonable.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 tested the central multimodal question by keeping the best configuration so far fixed (llm_summary_003: multiprofile, PCA-2000 RNA encoder, avgpool aggregation) and changing one factor: it added the ResNet50 image modality with simple concat fusion. Validation accuracy rose from 0.5907 to 0.6186, and F1 rose from 0.5727 to 0.6103, making this the new best result. This is an initial indication that images may add complementary signal when fused with RNA, even though image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.2079 accuracy, single-profile). However, the gain is modest (about 2.8 accuracy points) and comes from single runs with unknown seed variance, so it may not be robust. It also remains untested whether other fusion methods (e.g., weighted), stronger image encoders (ViT-L), alternative RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), or other aggregators would increase, preserve, or erase this multimodal benefit.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, ResNet50, avgpool, concat), at 0.6186 accuracy and 0.6103 F1. Adding images gave a modest gain of about 2.8 points over RNA-only multiprofile, even though image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.208). Because only ResNet50 has been tried, we cannot tell whether the image modality itself is weak or whether ResNet50 is a poor representation for it. This is a key open question raised in earlier summaries. 2. What this tests: config_024 keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only the image encoder to ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates the effect of image representation within the fusion setting, where it matters for the objective. A clear gain would mean the image representation was a bottleneck and that fusion has more room to improve. No gain would suggest the image contribution is capped and that later experiments should focus on RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) or the fusion method. 3. Why it is the best use of budget: It is a one-factor extension of the strongest configuration, so it can plausibly improve performance while also being informative. It also directly addresses the largest unresolved ambiguity about the image modality, and either outcome guides where the remaining budget should go.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 isolated the image encoder. It kept the best configuration (llm_summary_005: multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 RNA, avgpool, concat fusion) fixed and replaced ResNet50 with ImageNet ViT-L. Validation accuracy rose slightly from 0.6186 to 0.6287, the new best on the primary metric, but F1 fell from 0.6103 to 0.5993. Because the metrics move in opposite directions by roughly 1 point each, this is at best a weak initial indication that ViT-L may modestly help accuracy in fusion; it does not clearly show that the image representation was the main bottleneck, and it may reflect a shift in per-class performance rather than a uniform gain. All results are single runs with unknown seed variance, so a difference this small may not be robust. Several questions remain open: whether ViT-L is stronger than ResNet50 in the image-only setting, and whether larger gains would come from alternative RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) or other fusion methods (e.g., weighted).

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA carries most of the signal so far (RNA-only 0.485–0.591 vs. image-only 0.208). Multiprofile avgpool is the strongest RNA-only setting (0.591). Adding images gave modest gains (0.619–0.629), and the ResNet50 vs. ViT-L difference is ambiguous because accuracy and F1 moved in opposite directions. Every run so far has used PCA-2000, so the RNA encoder is the largest untested design choice on the dominant modality. 2. What this tests: config_008 changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scGPT, relative to config_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool). It leaves out image encoder and fusion effects, so any change in accuracy or F1 can be attributed to the RNA representation. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: the RNA encoder probably has more leverage than further tweaks to the image encoder or fusion method, given that the image-side differences so far are small. A clear scGPT gain would justify swapping it into the best multimodal setup (config_048). A loss would support keeping PCA and redirecting budget to scVI or to fusion. A single run cannot settle the question, but this is a clean one-factor comparison.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 isolated the RNA encoder. It kept the best RNA-only setting (llm_summary_003: RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) fixed and replaced PCA-2000 with scGPT. Validation accuracy fell from 0.5907 to 0.5305, and F1 fell from 0.5727 to 0.5152, though both remain above the single-profile PCA baseline (0.4849 accuracy). This is an initial indication that, in this setup, scGPT embeddings do not improve on PCA-2000 for the dominant RNA modality and may be worse, which weakens the case for swapping scGPT into the best multimodal configuration (llm_summary_006, 0.6287 accuracy). However, these are single runs with unknown seed variance, scGPT usage details (e.g., frozen vs. fine-tuned, preprocessing compatibility) were not explored, and it is untested whether scVI would do better or whether scGPT would behave differently under multimodal fusion or other aggregators.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_024 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.6287 accuracy. Multiprofile avgpool has looked better than single-profile and transformer aggregation. PCA has beaten scGPT for RNA. Adding images gave a modest gain. Fusion method, however, has never been varied: every multimodal run used concat. Because image-only performance is weak, simple concat may let RNA dominate or let noisy image features dilute it. 2. What this tests: config_025 changes only concat to weighted fusion, keeping every other choice of the current best fixed. This isolates whether the fusion mechanism matters. It also checks whether weighted fusion can recover the F1 drop seen with ViT-L (0.5993 vs 0.6103 with ResNet50). 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: it is a clean one-factor comparison on a completely unexplored design axis, and it extends the strongest configuration. So it combines exploration with plausible immediate improvement. Testing the remaining scVI encoder is also worthwhile but can follow once the fusion choice is better understood.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 isolated the fusion method for the first time. It kept the best configuration (llm_summary_006: multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 RNA, ImageNet ViT-L, avgpool) fixed and replaced concat with weighted fusion. Validation accuracy rose slightly from 0.6287 to 0.6352, the new best, and F1 rose more clearly from 0.5993 to 0.6183, recovering the F1 drop seen when switching from ResNet50 to ViT-L (ResNet50 concat F1 was 0.6103). Because only the fusion method changed, this is an initial indication that weighted fusion helps in this setup, with both metrics improving together rather than diverging. However, the accuracy gain is under 1 point and all results are single runs with unknown seed variance, so the effect may not be robust. It also remains untested how the fusion weights behave (e.g., whether they down-weight the weak image branch), whether the benefit holds with ResNet50 or with other RNA encoders such as the still-untested scVI, and whether other fusion variants would do better.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best configuration so far is config_025 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.6352 accuracy, 0.6183 F1). Multiprofile, avgpool and fusion all show consistent, if modest, gains. RNA is clearly the dominant modality, yet scVI, one of only three RNA encoders, has never been tested. scGPT underperformed PCA (0.5305 vs 0.5907), but that single run says little about scVI, which is a different kind of embedding. 2) What this tests: config_037 keeps every other choice in the best configuration fixed and swaps only PCA-2000 for scVI-200. Any difference can then be attributed to the RNA representation, measured in the setting that matters for final performance. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: the RNA encoder is the largest remaining unexplored axis and acts on the strongest modality, so it has the most potential to shift performance. Further fusion or aggregator variants have so far moved accuracy by less than one point. This experiment exploits the best known setup while resolving a major open uncertainty. If scVI clearly beats or trails PCA here, an RNA-only follow-up (config_005) can confirm whether the effect is intrinsic to the encoder or depends on fusion.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 isolated the RNA encoder within the best configuration so far (llm_summary_008: multimodal, multiprofile, ImageNet ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) by replacing PCA-2000 with scVI-200. Validation accuracy rose from 0.6352 to 0.7062 and F1 rose from 0.6183 to 0.6671. This is the new best result and the largest single-change gain seen in fusion settings, where earlier fusion and image-encoder swaps moved accuracy by about 1 point or less. It is an initial indication that the scVI RNA representation substantially helps in this multimodal setup, which contrasts with scGPT underperforming PCA in the RNA-only setting. However, this is a single run with unknown seed variance, and scVI has not been tested RNA-only (e.g., config_005), so it remains unclear whether the gain is intrinsic to the encoder or depends on weighted fusion or interaction with ViT-L. It also remains untested whether the gain holds with concat fusion, ResNet50, other aggregators, or other scVI dimensionalities.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Swapping PCA-2000 for scVI-200 inside the best fusion setup (config_037) produced the largest single-change gain so far, from 0.635 to 0.706 accuracy. However, scVI has never been tested RNA-only. So it is unclear whether the gain comes from a better RNA representation itself or from an interaction with weighted fusion and ViT-L. It is also unclear whether images still add value once RNA is strong. 2. What this tests: config_005 is RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool with scVI-200, so it differs from config_002 (PCA, 0.591) only in the RNA encoder. That comparison isolates the encoder effect. Comparing it with config_037 (0.706) also measures how much the image branch and weighted fusion contribute on top of a strong RNA encoder. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: One run answers two central attribution questions, the encoder effect and the multimodal benefit. Its result also guides later choices, either exploiting scVI further in fusion variants or concluding that RNA-only scVI is nearly as good and simpler. Fusion-variant tweaks such as concat or a transformer aggregator could not answer these questions.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 isolated the RNA encoder in the RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool setting by replacing PCA-2000 (llm_summary_003) with scVI-200. Validation accuracy rose from 0.5907 to 0.6501 and F1 from 0.5727 to 0.6275. This is an initial indication that scVI is a stronger RNA representation on its own, not only within fusion, and RNA-only scVI even edges out the best PCA-based fusion model (llm_summary_008, 0.6352 accuracy). It still falls about 5.6 accuracy points short of the scVI fusion model (llm_summary_009, 0.7062 accuracy, 0.6671 F1), which suggests that the ViT-L image branch with weighted fusion may add complementary value on top of a strong RNA encoder. However, that multimodal gap bundles the image encoder and the fusion method, so their separate contributions are not isolated. All results are single runs with unknown seed variance. Also untested: whether the scVI multimodal gain holds with concat fusion or ResNet50, other scVI dimensionalities, and other aggregators.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we have no evidence on the value of any modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice. 2. What this tests: config_001 is the simplest configuration, RNA-only, single-profile, with a PCA (2000) encoder and no aggregation or fusion. It sets a reference baseline, and each later comparison can change one factor against it: encoder (scVI or scGPT), profile setting (multiprofile with avgpool or transformer), modality (image-only), or adding fusion. 3. Why it is the best use of budget: Starting with a cheap, low-variance baseline makes every later experiment interpretable as a single-factor change. It also guards against assuming that complex multimodal or multiprofile models are needed before we know how well a simple model performs.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest configuration as a reference baseline: RNA-only, single-profile, with a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485, with a supporting validation F1 of 0.464. Because no other experiments have been run, this is only an initial baseline and says nothing yet about the value of other encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, the image modality, or fusion. It is also unknown how this level compares to chance or class-balance baselines, and run-to-run variance has not been measured, so later single-factor comparisons against this configuration are needed to judge which design choices matter.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: Only one result exists, the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (acc 0.485, F1 0.464). Nothing is known yet about the image modality, other RNA encoders, multiprofile aggregation, or fusion. The most basic open question is how informative images are on their own compared with RNA. 2) What this tests: config_010 is the simplest image-only setup (single-profile, ResNet50, no aggregation or fusion). It mirrors the baseline's minimal structure and changes only the modality, so it gives a clean RNA-vs-image reference point. 3) Why now: knowing the standalone strength of each modality is a prerequisite for judging later multimodal fusion experiments, which make up most of the search space. A weak image result would argue for focusing on RNA encoders and aggregation. A comparable or stronger result would justify investing in image encoders and fusion. Either way, the outcome reshapes the most of the remaining budget, which makes it more valuable than an incremental RNA-encoder or aggregation tweak at this stage.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested the simplest image-only setup: single-profile, a ResNet50 image encoder, and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.208 (F1 0.172), well below the RNA-only PCA baseline from llm_summary_001 (accuracy 0.485, F1 0.464). This is an initial observation that this image configuration is much weaker than this RNA configuration on its own. However, the comparison changes both the modality and the encoder at once (ResNet50 vs. PCA-2000), so it does not show whether images are inherently less informative or whether this particular image encoder or setup is the limitation. Several things remain unknown: the chance or class-balance level, run-to-run variance, whether other image encoders or multiprofile aggregation would help, and whether image features add complementary value when fused with RNA despite their weak standalone performance.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Only two single-profile baselines exist. RNA-only PCA-2000 reached 0.485 accuracy (F1 0.464), and image-only ResNet50 reached 0.208 (F1 0.172). RNA is clearly the stronger starting point. The effect of the profile setting is completely untested, and it is a design choice that applies across every modality and encoder in the search space. 2. What this tests: config_002 changes one factor from the best configuration so far. It moves from single-profile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool), keeping the RNA-only setting and the PCA-2000 encoder fixed. This isolates whether pooling information across profiles improves accuracy and F1. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: It builds on the stronger modality and answers a broadly relevant structural question with a clean single-variable comparison. If multiprofile helps, later tests of transformer aggregation, other RNA encoders and multimodal fusion can focus on the multiprofile space. If it does not help, roughly half of the remaining space can be deprioritized. Testing fusion or new encoders first would leave this cross-cutting factor unresolved.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000 RNA encoder, avgpool aggregation, no image encoder or fusion. It changed only the profile setting (single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool) relative to the llm_summary_001 baseline. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.591 (F1 0.573), up from 0.485 (F1 0.464), about +0.106 accuracy and +0.109 F1, making it the best configuration so far. Within RNA-only PCA-2000, this single-variable comparison suggests that multiprofile avgpool improves performance, so the multiprofile space looks like a promising focus for later aggregation, encoder, and fusion tests. Several things remain uncertain. Run-to-run variance is unmeasured, so the size of the gain is not confirmed. It is unknown whether the benefit carries over to other RNA encoders, the image modality, or fused models. It is also unknown whether a richer aggregator such as a transformer would add further gains over avgpool.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Within RNA-only PCA-2000, moving from single-profile to multiprofile avgpool improved accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591 (F1 0.464 to 0.573), the largest and cleanest gain so far. However, we have only one aggregator, so we cannot tell whether avgpool is near the ceiling or whether the multiprofile benefit depends on how profiles are combined. 2. Test: config_003 changes only the aggregation (avgpool to transformer) and keeps the modality, encoder and profile setting fixed. This isolates whether a learned, attention-based aggregator gains more from multiple profiles than simple averaging. 3. Why now: Multiprofile is the strongest lead, and aggregation is a design choice that affects every later multiprofile configuration, including other RNA encoders, image-only and fused models. Settling avgpool vs. transformer on the strongest base will narrow many downstream options. This exploits the promising direction while still answering one specific question. Encoder (scVI/scGPT) and fusion tests remain good follow-ups once the aggregator choice is better grounded.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 tested RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000 RNA encoder with transformer aggregation (no image encoder or fusion), changing only the aggregator relative to llm_summary_003 (avgpool). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.519 (F1 0.480), well below avgpool's 0.591 (F1 0.573) but still above the single-profile baseline's 0.485 (F1 0.464). This single-variable comparison suggests that, in this setup, the transformer aggregator did not beat simple averaging, and avgpool remains the best configuration so far. It is uncertain whether this reflects the aggregator itself or untuned transformer training (e.g., capacity, regularization, number of profiles per sample), since run-to-run variance is unmeasured and it is unknown whether the ranking holds for other RNA encoders, image-only, or fused multiprofile models.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is clearly the stronger modality so far (PCA RNA 0.485 vs. ResNet50 image 0.208, single-profile). Within RNA PCA-2000, multiprofile avgpool gave the best result (0.591 accuracy, 0.573 F1). It beat both the single-profile baseline and transformer aggregation (0.519). However, every RNA result so far uses PCA-2000, so it is unknown whether the RNA encoder is a major lever. 2) What this tests: config_008 keeps the best setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder, from PCA-2000 to the pretrained scGPT. This cleanly isolates the effect of RNA representation. It also checks whether the multiprofile avgpool gain carries over to a different encoder. 3) Why now: RNA carries most of the signal, so the RNA encoder choice will shape all later multimodal fusion experiments. It is better to settle the strongest RNA representation before spending budget on fusion with a weak image branch. A one-factor change from the current best also gives a reasonable chance of improving on it.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 tested RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool aggregation with a pretrained scGPT RNA encoder (no image encoder or fusion). It changed only the RNA encoder relative to the current best, llm_summary_003, which used PCA-2000. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.530 (F1 0.515). That is below PCA-2000's 0.591 (F1 0.573) by about 0.060 accuracy and 0.057 F1, though still above the single-profile PCA baseline (0.485) and slightly above multiprofile transformer aggregation with PCA (0.519). This single-variable comparison suggests that, in this setup, scGPT embeddings did not beat PCA-2000, so PCA-2000 with multiprofile avgpool remains the best configuration so far. The multiprofile setting also appears to remain competitive with this encoder, although no single-profile scGPT run exists to confirm this directly. Several things remain uncertain. Run-to-run variance is unmeasured. It is unknown whether the gap reflects scGPT itself or how its embeddings were used (e.g., frozen vs. fine-tuned, embedding dimensionality, or preprocessing compatibility). Other encoders such as scVI are untested, as is how the encoder ranking would carry over to fused multimodal models.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Within RNA-only, multiprofile avgpool with PCA-2000 (config_002, 0.591 acc / 0.573 F1) is the best so far. It beats single-profile (0.485), transformer aggregation (0.519) and scGPT (0.530). Image-only ResNet50 single-profile is weak (0.208), but that result says nothing about whether image features add complementary signal when fused with RNA. Fusion is a core design axis and has not been tested at all. 2) Test: This run adds ResNet50 image features with simple concat fusion to the current best setup (multiprofile, PCA-2000, avgpool). Modality is the only change relative to config_002, so the result directly measures the marginal value of adding images. 3) Why now: It resolves the largest open uncertainty, whether multimodality helps, using a clean single-variable comparison against the strongest baseline. If it helps, it opens a promising direction for testing fusion type, image encoder and RNA encoder. If it does not, it argues for focusing the remaining budget on RNA-only refinements such as scVI. Either outcome is more decision-relevant than another encoder swap within RNA-only.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 added ResNet50 image features with concat fusion to the best RNA-only setup (multiprofile, PCA-2000, avgpool), changing only the modality relative to llm_summary_003. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.619 (F1 0.610), up from 0.591 (F1 0.573), about +0.028 accuracy and +0.038 F1, making it the best configuration so far. This single-variable comparison is an initial indication that image features add complementary signal when fused with RNA, despite the weak image-only single-profile result (0.208). The gain is modest and run-to-run variance is unmeasured, so it may not be robust. It also remains unknown whether other fusion methods, other image encoders, other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI), or image-only multiprofile runs would change this picture.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. That is a modest gain over RNA-only multiprofile avgpool (0.591). It suggests images add complementary signal, even though ResNet50 alone was weak (0.208 single-profile). ResNet50 is the only image encoder tested, so the large uncertainty is whether that weak image signal reflects the modality or the encoder. Fusion type and scVI are also untested, but PCA already beat scGPT and avgpool beat the transformer, so the image encoder looks like the biggest unresolved factor. 2) What this tests: config_024 changes only the image encoder (ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L) within the current best setup. This isolates whether a stronger image representation increases the multimodal gain. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: it exploits the most promising direction while resolving a key design choice. A clear gain would point the search toward ViT-L multimodal variants. No gain would suggest the image contribution is limited by the modality rather than the encoder, and would shift focus to fusion type or the RNA encoder (scVI).
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 changed only the image encoder (ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L) within the previous best setup (llm_summary_006: multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, avgpool, concat fusion). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.629, slightly above llm_summary_006's 0.619 (about +0.010), which makes it nominally the best configuration so far. However, validation F1 fell from 0.610 to 0.599 (about -0.011), so this single-variable comparison gives mixed and inconclusive evidence on whether a stronger image representation increases the multimodal gain. Both differences are small, and run-to-run variance is unmeasured, so neither encoder can yet be ranked with confidence. The opposite shifts in accuracy and F1 may reflect changes in per-class behavior rather than a real overall improvement. Fusion methods other than concat, scVI, image-only ViT-L performance, and possible replicate runs remain untested and are likely more informative next steps than further image-encoder swaps alone.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile avgpool clearly helps RNA-only PCA (0.485 to 0.591). Adding image features with concat fusion gave a modest further gain (0.619 with ResNet50, 0.629 with ViT-L). The ResNet50 vs ViT-L difference is small and mixed, since accuracy rose but F1 fell. Fusion is a core design choice that has never been varied; every multimodal run so far used concat. 2. What this tests: config_025 changes only fusion (concat to weighted) relative to the nominal best, config_024 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, ViT-L, avgpool). This isolates whether the fusion mechanism affects how much the weak but complementary image signal helps. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: It explores an entirely untested factor while staying in the most promising region of the space, so it has both exploitation value (it may beat 0.629) and diagnostic value (it shows whether fusion matters). This is more informative than another encoder swap, and more informative than revisiting the transformer aggregator, which already underperformed avgpool.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 changed only the fusion method, from concat to weighted, relative to the nominal best llm_summary_007 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, ImageNet ViT-L, avgpool), making it the first test of fusion as a design factor. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.635 (F1 0.618), up from 0.629 (F1 0.599), about +0.007 accuracy and +0.019 F1. It also slightly exceeds the ResNet50 concat run (0.619, F1 0.610) on both metrics, so it is now the best configuration so far on both accuracy and F1. This single-variable comparison is an initial indication that weighted fusion may help slightly, with the F1 gain larger than the accuracy gain. However, the accuracy difference is small and run-to-run variance is unmeasured, so whether fusion meaningfully matters is not established. It also remains unknown whether weighted fusion would help with ResNet50 or other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI), and how other fusion schemes (e.g., attention or gated fusion) would compare.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best configuration so far is config_025 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion), with 0.635 accuracy and 0.618 F1. Earlier single-factor comparisons favor multiprofile avgpool over transformer aggregation, and PCA over scGPT. Adding images and switching to weighted fusion each gave small gains. The scVI RNA encoder is the one major design choice not yet tested at all. 2. What this tests: Config_037 changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scVI-200, inside the current best setup. It shows whether a compact probabilistic RNA representation helps or hurts compared with PCA when fused with image features. 3. Why it is the best next step: It removes the largest remaining uncertainty, about the RNA encoder, which has had the biggest effect on performance among the RNA-side choices tested so far. Because it builds on the strongest known setup, it also has a realistic chance of improving on the current best. Further fusion or image-encoder swaps have only shown small, variance-sized differences, so they are less informative right now.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scVI-200, within the previous best setup (llm_summary_008: multimodal, multiprofile, ImageNet ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion). It was the first test of scVI. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.706 (F1 0.667), up from 0.635 (F1 0.618), about +0.071 accuracy and +0.049 F1, making it clearly the best configuration so far on both metrics and the largest gain since the switch to multiprofile avgpool. This single-variable comparison suggests that the RNA representation is a high-impact factor and that, in this fused setup, scVI-200 outperforms PCA-2000. Several things remain uncertain. Run-to-run variance is unmeasured. No RNA-only scVI run exists, so it is unknown whether scVI is better on its own or interacts favorably with the image features and weighted fusion. It is also unclear which scVI properties drive the gain (e.g., probabilistic modeling vs. compact 200-dimensional latent size), and the fusion, aggregation and image-encoder choices tuned under PCA may need re-checking with scVI.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Swapping PCA-2000 for scVI-200 gave the largest gain so far (0.635 to 0.706 accuracy, F1 0.618 to 0.667). However, that comparison was made only inside the fused ViT-L/weighted setup. We cannot yet tell whether scVI is a better RNA representation on its own or whether it interacts favorably with the image features and fusion. The image contribution under PCA was modest (about +0.03 accuracy). 2) What this tests: config_005 is RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI-200 with avgpool. It is a clean single-variable comparison against config_002 (PCA-2000, same setting: 0.591 accuracy, 0.573 F1), which isolates the RNA encoder effect without images. It is also a modality comparison against config_037, which measures how much ViT-L plus weighted fusion adds once RNA is represented by scVI. 3) Why this is the best next use of budget: One run answers two key questions, the source of the scVI gain and whether the image branch is still worth its complexity. That tells us whether later experiments should focus on RNA representation or on fusion, image-encoder and aggregation tuning around the scVI multimodal setup.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 tested RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI-200 with avgpool (no image encoder or fusion). Relative to llm_summary_003, it changed only the RNA encoder (PCA-2000 to scVI-200), and it is also a modality comparison against the fused scVI run llm_summary_009 (ImageNet ViT-L, weighted fusion). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.650 (F1 0.628), up from PCA's 0.591 (F1 0.573), about +0.059 accuracy and +0.055 F1. This single-variable comparison suggests that scVI-200 is a stronger RNA representation on its own, not only when fused with images, and this RNA-only run even exceeds every PCA-based multimodal configuration (best 0.635). Adding ViT-L with weighted fusion on top of scVI still gave about +0.056 accuracy and +0.040 F1 (0.706 vs 0.650), at least as large as the corresponding image gain under PCA (+0.044 accuracy), so the image branch appears to remain worthwhile. The scVI gain was slightly larger in the fused setting (+0.071) than RNA-only (+0.059), but that difference is small and does not establish an interaction. Several things remain uncertain. Run-to-run variance is unmeasured. It is unknown which scVI properties drive the gain (e.g., probabilistic modeling vs. the 200-dimensional latent). The fusion, image-encoder and aggregation choices, which were tuned under PCA, have not been re-checked with scVI.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion choice matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA) is the simplest configuration in the space. It sets a baseline that later changes can each be compared against one at a time: encoder (scVI, scGPT), profile setting and aggregation (avgpool, transformer), modality (image-only, multimodal) and fusion. 3) Starting with a cheap, low-variance baseline is the best first use of the limited budget. It gives a reference point for judging whether added complexity actually helps, rather than assuming multimodal or multiprofile models are better.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) tested the simplest configuration in the search space as a baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA encoder (pca_n2000), with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485 (validation F1 0.464), which serves as an initial reference point rather than evidence that any design choice helps or hurts. No comparisons exist yet, so it is still unknown whether other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile settings with aggregation (avgpool, transformer), image-only models, or multimodal fusion would improve on this baseline. The variance of this result across seeds or splits has not been measured either.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there is one result so far. The RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_001) reached 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. We do not yet know how much signal the image modality carries, and that is the most important open question for the whole multimodal search space. 2) Test: config_010 (image-only, single-profile, resnet50) matches the baseline in every respect except modality and encoder. Comparing the two shows whether images alone can match or beat RNA, which tells us whether multimodal fusion is worth pursuing. Because the image side has no baseline yet, the simpler resnet50 encoder is the natural starting point. 3) Why now: knowing whether the image signal is weak or strong determines how much budget to give the 36 multimodal configurations versus RNA-encoder and aggregation choices. This makes it more useful than refining RNA encoders or profile settings first. One limitation is that config_001 has no variance estimate, so a small gap between the two runs should not be overinterpreted.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a resnet50 image encoder (no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion) to give a first estimate of how much signal the image modality carries, using the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001) as the point of comparison. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.208 (validation F1 0.172), well below the RNA-only baseline's 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. This initial observation suggests that images processed this way carry less standalone predictive signal than RNA under PCA. However, the two runs differ in both modality and encoder, so the gap cannot be attributed to modality alone, and both are single runs with no variance estimate. It remains unknown whether other image encoders, multiprofile aggregation, or fusion with RNA could make the image signal useful, including as a complementary contribution in multimodal models.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The RNA-only PCA baseline (config_001) reached 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. Image-only resnet50 (config_010) reached only 0.208 accuracy and 0.172 F1. So images carry much less standalone signal, but we do not know whether they add complementary information when combined with RNA. Most of the remaining search space (36 of 49 untested configurations) is multimodal, so this is the most consequential open question. 2. What this tests: config_016 keeps the baseline's RNA encoder (pca_n2000) and single-profile setting, and adds the already-tested resnet50 image encoder with the simplest fusion (concat). Compared against config_001, the only change is adding the image modality, so any gain or loss can be attributed to multimodal fusion itself. Compared against config_010, it shows how much RNA adds to the image-only model. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: A weak modality could add complementary signal or could add noise that hurts performance. The result will tell us whether multimodal configurations deserve more of the limited budget, or whether we should focus on RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) and multiprofile aggregation. It reuses known components, so we avoid changing several design choices at once.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested a multimodal, single-profile model that concatenates the pca_n2000 RNA encoder with the resnet50 image encoder (no aggregation). Relative to the RNA-only baseline (llm_summary_001), adding the image modality is the only configuration difference. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.527 (F1 0.510), compared with 0.485 (F1 0.464) for RNA-only and 0.208 (F1 0.172) for image-only. This is an initial observation that the weak image signal may be complementary rather than noise when fused with RNA, and that multimodal configurations may merit further budget. However, the roughly 4-point accuracy gain comes from single runs with no seed or split variance estimate, so it may not be robust. It also remains unknown whether the gain persists with other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), other fusion methods, or multiprofile aggregation.

selection_reason: Evidence: RNA carries most of the signal (PCA RNA-only 0.485 vs. image-only resnet50 0.208). Adding resnet50 images with concat fusion raised accuracy to 0.527 (F1 0.510), which tentatively suggests the image signal is complementary. All three runs are single-profile, so the profile setting is a major design axis with no evidence yet. Test: config_018 keeps the current best configuration (pca_n2000 + resnet50, concat) and changes only the profile setting to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This shows whether pooling multiple profiles per sample improves on single-profile, with a clean one-factor comparison against config_016. Why now: it builds on the strongest result so far while opening a whole untested dimension. If multiprofile helps, a later run can compare transformer against avgpool aggregation. If it does not, the budget can shift to RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT) or fusion comparisons.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the best configuration so far, multimodal pca_n2000 RNA + resnet50 image with concat fusion (llm_summary_003), and switched from single-profile to multiprofile input pooled with avgpool aggregation. Profile setting and aggregation change together here, because aggregation is only defined for multiprofile, so the comparison tests the multiprofile+avgpool package rather than either factor alone. It reached validation accuracy 0.619 (F1 0.610), versus 0.527 (F1 0.510) for the single-profile multimodal run, a roughly 9-point gain and the best result so far. Accuracy and F1 rose together, which tentatively suggests that pooling multiple profiles per sample is a productive direction. However, these are single runs with no seed or split variance estimate. It remains unknown whether transformer aggregation would beat avgpool, whether multiprofile gives similar gains for RNA-only or image-only models, and whether other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) or fusion methods would interact differently with the multiprofile setting.

selection_reason: Evidence: the best result so far is multimodal multiprofile avgpool concat (config_018, 0.619 accuracy, 0.610 F1). It improved about 9 points over single-profile multimodal (0.527). Single-profile, adding images to RNA gave about +4 points. Image-only was weak (0.208). The open question is whether the multiprofile gain still depends on the image modality, or whether multiprofile pooling of RNA alone explains most of it. What this tests: config_002 (RNA-only pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) differs by one factor from two completed runs. Compared with config_001, it isolates the effect of multiprofile+avgpool for RNA alone. Compared with config_018, it isolates the image contribution under multiprofile. Why now: this decides whether later budget should go to multimodal refinements (fusion type, ViT encoder, transformer aggregation) or to RNA-focused multiprofile variants (scVI, scGPT). Running it before more multimodal tuning avoids building on a possibly confounded conclusion. These are single runs, so small differences should be read cautiously.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 tested RNA-only pca_n2000 with multiprofile input and avgpool aggregation (no image encoder or fusion). It differs by one package of factors from two earlier runs: against llm_summary_001 it tests multiprofile+avgpool for RNA alone (these two factors change together because aggregation applies only to multiprofile), and against llm_summary_004 it tests the image contribution under multiprofile. It reached validation accuracy 0.591 (F1 0.573), about 10.6 points above single-profile RNA-only (0.485, F1 0.464) and about 2.8 points below multimodal multiprofile (0.619, F1 0.610). This is initial evidence that multiprofile pooling of RNA accounts for most of the multiprofile gain, while adding images still coincides with a small improvement (a slightly larger gap in F1, about 3.8 points) similar in size to the single-profile image gain (about 4 points). All are single runs with no seed or split variance estimate, so it is uncertain whether the roughly 3-point image benefit is robust. This makes RNA-focused multiprofile variants (scVI, scGPT, transformer aggregation) at least as promising as further multimodal refinement, and it remains untested whether those variants change the size of the image contribution.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA carries most of the signal. RNA-only accuracy rose from 0.485 to 0.591 with multiprofile plus avgpool, while adding resnet50 images gave a smaller gain of about 3 points (0.619). Every result so far uses the pca_n2000 RNA encoder, so the effect of the RNA representation, likely the most influential design choice, is completely unknown. 2. What this tests: config_005 changes only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200, keeping the strong RNA-only multiprofile avgpool setup of config_002 fixed. This isolates how much the RNA representation matters, without image or fusion effects confounding the comparison. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: the encoder result will decide whether later multimodal and transformer-aggregation experiments should be built on PCA or scVI. That makes it more informative than refining aggregation or fusion on an encoder that has not been compared against anything. Running it RNA-only keeps the comparison clean and cheaper to interpret, and scGPT can be tested next in the same way.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 tested an RNA-only multiprofile model with avgpool aggregation, changing only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 relative to llm_summary_005, so the comparison isolates the RNA representation. It reached validation accuracy 0.650 (F1 0.628), about 6 points above the PCA counterpart (0.591, F1 0.573) and also above the best multimodal PCA run (llm_summary_004: 0.619, F1 0.610), making it the best result so far. Accuracy and F1 rose together, which is initial evidence that the RNA representation is a highly influential choice and that scVI may be a stronger base than PCA for later experiments. However, all results are single runs with no seed or split variance estimate. It also remains untested whether scVI's advantage holds in single-profile or multimodal settings, whether adding resnet50 images still gives a roughly 3-point gain on top of scVI, and how scGPT or transformer aggregation would compare.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_005 (RNA-only scVI, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.650 accuracy and 0.628 F1. Two design choices have shown large effects: multiprofile pooling added about 10 points, and swapping PCA for scVI added about 6 points. Adding images gave a small but repeated gain of about 3-4 points. Aggregation is the one important factor never tested: every multiprofile run used avgpool, and transformer aggregation is completely unexplored. 2) Test: config_006 changes only the aggregation (avgpool to transformer) on the current best base, keeping RNA-only scVI and multiprofile fixed.
