The comparison therefore isolates the effect of aggregation. 3) Why now: Adding images (config_030) would likely give a modest, already-signalled gain and little new information. Testing aggregation resolves a fully open design question that applies to every multiprofile setting, including the multimodal and scGPT variants. It also has real upside for the best score. Whether transformer beats avgpool tells us which aggregation to use for all later experiments, which is high value under a limited budget. These are single runs, so a small difference should be treated as tentative.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 changed only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer on the best configuration so far (RNA-only scvi_n200, multiprofile; llm_summary_006), so the comparison isolates the aggregation choice. It reached validation accuracy 0.653 (F1 0.628), essentially the same as avgpool (0.650, F1 0.628). This is a nominal new best, but the roughly 0.3-point accuracy difference and near-identical F1 are too small to show that transformer aggregation beats avgpool. In this setting the two aggregators look roughly interchangeable. These are single runs with no seed or split variance estimate, and it remains untested whether transformer aggregation behaves differently with PCA or scGPT encoders, with image or multimodal inputs, or when profile counts per sample vary. Since avgpool is simpler and performs about as well here, aggregation appears to be a lower-priority lever than the RNA encoder or adding images on top of scVI.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The RNA encoder is the strongest lever found so far. Switching to scvi_n200 under multiprofile avgpool gave 0.650 accuracy versus 0.591 for PCA. Aggregation barely mattered (transformer 0.653 vs avgpool 0.650). Adding resnet50 images to PCA RNA coincided with a gain of about 3 to 4 points twice, in both single-profile and multiprofile settings. It is still unknown whether that image gain survives once RNA uses the stronger scVI representation, or whether scVI already captures the information images added. 2. Test: config_030 (scVI + resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) differs from config_005 only by adding the image modality with concat fusion. It keeps the simpler avgpool aggregator, which performed as well as transformer. This isolates the image contribution on top of scVI. 3. Why now: This is both a plausible new best and a clean single-factor test of whether multimodal fusion is worth more budget. A null or negative result would point remaining experiments toward RNA-only encoder choices (e.g., scGPT, config_008) rather than image or fusion variants.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 added resnet50 images with concat fusion to the scvi_n200 RNA-only multiprofile avgpool model (llm_summary_006), so adding the image modality is the only configuration difference. It reached validation accuracy 0.632 (F1 0.607), about 1.9 points below the scVI RNA-only run (0.650, F1 0.628) and below the nominal best, transformer RNA-only scVI (llm_summary_007: 0.653). This is initial evidence that the roughly 3-to-4-point image gain seen with PCA RNA (llm_summary_003 vs 001, and 004 vs 005) does not carry over to scVI under concat fusion, and that images may be redundant with, or even slightly harmful to, the stronger RNA representation in this setup. All results are single runs with no seed or split variance estimate, so a gap of about 2 points may fall within noise, and it remains untested whether other fusion methods, transformer aggregation, or other encoders (e.g., scGPT) would recover an image benefit. RNA-only encoder choices therefore currently look like a higher-priority direction than further concat-based multimodal variants.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The RNA encoder is the largest lever seen so far. Swapping PCA for scVI in RNA-only multiprofile avgpool raised accuracy from 0.591 to 0.650, with F1 rising alongside. Aggregation made almost no difference (avgpool 0.650 vs transformer 0.653). Adding resnet50 images with concat fusion on top of scVI slightly hurt (0.632). scGPT is the main RNA representation not yet tested. 2) Test: config_008 changes only the RNA encoder (scVI to scGPT) relative to the best simple configuration, config_005. It also forms a three-way encoder comparison with config_002 (PCA) under the same multiprofile avgpool setup. This shows whether a foundation-model embedding beats scVI or whether scVI stays the best base. 3) Why now: It directly probes the most influential design choice in a clean single-factor comparison. It also has a realistic chance of a new best result. Its outcome would guide which RNA encoder to carry into later fusion experiments (e.g., weighted fusion) rather than spending budget on multimodal variants built on a possibly suboptimal encoder. Avgpool is used because it is simpler and matched the transformer aggregator.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 changed only the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to scGPT in the RNA-only multiprofile avgpool setup (llm_summary_006), completing a single-factor three-way encoder comparison with PCA (llm_summary_005) under otherwise identical settings. It reached validation accuracy 0.530 (F1 0.515), about 12 points below scVI (0.650, F1 0.628) and about 6 points below PCA (0.591, F1 0.573), making it the weakest RNA-only multiprofile result so far. Accuracy and F1 fell together, which adds evidence that the RNA encoder is the most influential lever and suggests that scVI should remain the base for later experiments such as alternative fusion methods. These are single runs with no seed or split variance estimate, and it remains untested whether scGPT's underperformance reflects the embedding itself or how it was extracted and used here (no fine-tuning or dimensionality details are given), or whether it would behave differently in single-profile, transformer-aggregation, or multimodal settings.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The RNA encoder is the strongest lever so far; scVI clearly beats PCA and scGPT. Aggregation looks roughly interchangeable (transformer 0.653 vs avgpool 0.650). Adding resnet50 images with concat fusion gave about 3–4 points with PCA RNA, but scVI multimodal concat (0.632) fell about 2 points below scVI RNA-only (0.650). It is therefore unclear whether images are redundant with scVI or whether concat fusion fails to use them well. Fusion method is a whole design dimension that has never been tested. 2. Test: config_031 changes only the fusion, from concat to weighted, relative to config_030 (scVI + resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool). This isolates the fusion effect on the strongest RNA base. A weighted fusion could down-weight the noisier image branch. If it matches or beats 0.650, images may still be complementary under a better fusion. If it stays below, that strengthens the case that images add little on top of scVI. 3. Why now: It is a clean single-factor comparison on the best-performing base. It resolves the most consequential open question, whether multimodal fusion is worth further budget. Its answer guides later choices, such as testing imagenet_vit_l or transformer aggregation in multimodal settings, while still having a plausible chance of a new best.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 changed only the fusion method from concat to weighted in the multimodal scvi_n200 + resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool setup (llm_summary_008), so the comparison isolates the fusion choice on the strongest RNA base. It reached validation accuracy 0.678 (F1 0.646), about 4.6 points above concat fusion (0.632, F1 0.607) and about 2.5 to 2.8 points above the best RNA-only scVI runs (avgpool 0.650, transformer 0.653; F1 about 0.628), making it the best result so far. Accuracy and F1 rose together, which is initial evidence that fusion method matters and that resnet50 images can be complementary to scVI when fused with weighting rather than concatenation. This revises the earlier reading that images were redundant with scVI. However, all results are single runs with no seed or split variance estimate, so the margin over RNA-only, a comparison that also differs by adding images, may partly reflect noise. It also remains untested why weighted fusion helps (for example, whether it actually down-weights the image branch) and whether the benefit holds with PCA RNA, transformer aggregation, other image encoders such as imagenet_vit_l, or other fusion methods.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest baseline in the space, with no aggregation or fusion components. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 that every more complex choice must beat to justify itself. Later one-factor changes can then be compared directly against it: encoder (scVI, scGPT), profile setting (multiprofile with avgpool or transformer), and modality (image-only, multimodal). 3) Under a limited budget, starting with a cheap, interpretable anchor avoids assuming that complex multimodal models are better. It also makes each later experiment informative as an isolated comparison.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 established the first baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.4849, with a supporting validation F1 of 0.4639. Because no other experiments have been run, this is an initial reference point only and says nothing yet about the relative value of other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation (avgpool, transformer), image-only models, or multimodal fusion. Those effects remain uncertain until one-factor comparisons against this anchor are completed, and the variance of this single-run estimate is also unknown.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: We have only one result, an RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (acc 0.4849, F1 0.4639). We know nothing yet about the image modality, even though most of the remaining search space (image-only and all multimodal configurations) depends on how informative images are. 2. What this tests: config_010 is the simplest image-only anchor (single profile, resnet50, no aggregation or fusion), matched to the baseline's single-profile, no-aggregation setup. It measures how much signal the image modality carries on its own compared with RNA. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: Knowing whether images are weak, comparable or stronger than RNA tells us whether multimodal fusion is worth exploring and which unimodal branch to prioritize. That makes it the highest-information use of the budget at this stage. Encoder and multiprofile one-factor comparisons, such as config_004 and config_002, can follow once both modality anchors exist.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 established the first image-only anchor: a single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder, no RNA encoder, and no aggregation or fusion, matched in profile and aggregation setup to the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.2079, with a supporting validation F1 of 0.1718. The RNA-only PCA baseline reached 0.4849 accuracy and 0.4639 F1, so this initial observation suggests that, in this single-profile setup, ResNet50 image features carry less label-relevant signal than PCA RNA features. That bears on whether to prioritize the RNA branch and how much to expect from multimodal fusion. Several things remain uncertain: both results are single runs with unknown variance, only one encoder per modality has been tested, and the comparison changes the modality and the encoder together, so it does not isolate the modality itself. It is also unknown whether other image encoders, multiprofile aggregation, or fusion with RNA would let image information contribute complementary signal.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: We have two single-run anchors. The RNA-only PCA single-profile model reached 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. The image-only ResNet50 model reached 0.208 accuracy and 0.172 F1. This suggests RNA is the stronger branch in the single-profile setting. We still know nothing about the effect of profile setting/aggregation, the RNA encoder choice, or fusion. 2) Test: config_002 changes one factor from the strongest anchor (config_001). It moves from single-profile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation, keeping the PCA RNA encoder and the RNA-only setting fixed. This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles adds label-relevant signal. 3) Why now: Profile setting appears in most remaining configurations, including the multimodal ones, so learning its effect early tells us how to read much of the search space. Avgpool is the simplest aggregation, so it gives a clean baseline before testing the transformer variant (config_003). Building on the strongest branch also keeps the expected performance reasonable, balancing exploitation with reducing a key uncertainty.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested an RNA-only model with the PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder in the multiprofile setting with avgpool aggregation. It differs from the RNA-only single-profile anchor (llm_summary_001) only in profile setting, with avgpool as the necessary aggregation choice. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5907, up about 0.106 from 0.4849, and a supporting validation F1 of 0.5727, up from 0.4639. This suggests that pooling multiple profiles adds label-relevant signal for the PCA RNA branch, which makes multiprofile settings a promising direction. Uncertainties remain: all results are single runs with unknown variance, the multiprofile and avgpool effects cannot be separated until another aggregator such as the transformer is tested, and it is unknown whether the gain carries over to other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), to image-only models, or to multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: moving the PCA RNA-only model from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591, and F1 rose with it. This is the strongest signal so far. However, avgpool is the only aggregator tested, so the multiprofile benefit cannot yet be separated from the choice of aggregator. Image-only ResNet50 performed poorly (0.208), so the RNA branch is the most promising place to build. 2) This experiment keeps the RNA-only setting, the PCA encoder and the multiprofile setting, and swaps only avgpool for transformer aggregation. It shows whether a learned aggregator adds signal beyond simple pooling, or whether avgpool is enough. 3) Aggregation is a decision that will carry into every later multiprofile run, including scVI, scGPT and multimodal ones. Settling it with a one-factor comparison against the current best anchor is the most informative use of the budget. It also has a good chance of matching or beating the current best result.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 ran a one-factor comparison against the current best anchor (llm_summary_003, RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA n2000, avgpool). It kept the same configuration and replaced avgpool with transformer aggregation. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5191, about 0.072 below avgpool's 0.5907, with a supporting F1 of 0.4797 versus 0.5727. That accuracy is still above the single-profile PCA baseline of 0.4849, and its F1 is only slightly higher (0.4797 vs 0.4639). This suggests that for the PCA RNA branch, simple average pooling is at least as effective as the learned transformer aggregator, and avgpool remains the stronger default for later multiprofile runs. Because the transformer also beat the single-profile baseline, the multiprofile benefit appears not to be unique to avgpool, though its size depends on the aggregator. All results are single runs with unknown variance, and the transformer's hyperparameters, capacity and training stability were not explored, so it may be undertrained or overfitting rather than inherently worse. It is also unknown whether this ranking holds for other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image-only models, or multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The RNA branch clearly dominates so far. PCA RNA single-profile reached 0.485 accuracy, while ResNet50 image-only reached 0.208. Multiprofile avgpool raised PCA to 0.591 accuracy and 0.573 F1. The transformer aggregator underperformed avgpool (0.519). The largest untested factor in the strongest branch is the RNA encoder, since only PCA n2000 has been tried. 2. Test: Run scVI (n200) in the best known setting (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool). This changes only the RNA encoder relative to the current best anchor (config_002). It shows whether a learned probabilistic latent representation beats or matches PCA, and whether the multiprofile avgpool gain carries over to another encoder. 3. Why now: The RNA encoder choice carries into every later multimodal configuration, so settling it early narrows the large fusion search space. Given how weak the image features are, the RNA representation is the most likely lever for further gains. This is a clean one-factor comparison that also has a realistic chance of beating the current best.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 ran a one-factor comparison against the best prior anchor (llm_summary_003: RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool, PCA n2000), replacing the PCA RNA encoder with scVI (n200). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6501, about 0.059 above PCA's 0.5907, with a supporting F1 of 0.6275 versus 0.5727, making it the new best configuration. In this setting, scVI latents appear to carry more label-relevant signal than PCA features, and because both encoders improved over the single-profile PCA baseline (0.4849), multiprofile avgpool seems to work with more than one encoder. Uncertainties remain: all results are single runs with unknown variance, and the encoder change also changes dimensionality (200 vs 2000 components), so the gain cannot be attributed specifically to scVI's probabilistic modeling. scVI has not been tested single-profile, with transformer aggregation, or in multimodal fusion, and scGPT is still untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile avgpool is the strongest setup so far. It beat single-profile (0.591 vs 0.485 with PCA) and transformer aggregation (0.519). Within that setup, scVI beat PCA (0.650 vs 0.591, with F1 agreeing). scGPT, the third RNA encoder, is completely untested, so it is unknown whether scVI is the best RNA branch. 2. What this tests: config_008 is a clean one-factor comparison against the current best anchor (config_005). It keeps RNA-only, multiprofile and avgpool fixed and swaps scVI for scGPT. This shows whether a foundation-model embedding adds label-relevant signal beyond scVI and completes the RNA encoder comparison in the best-performing setting. 3. Why now: RNA is clearly the dominant modality, since image-only ResNet50 reached only 0.208. The RNA encoder choice will therefore carry into every later multimodal run. Settling it first means the limited fusion experiments can be built on the strongest RNA branch. It also has a realistic chance of producing a new best configuration, so it balances exploration and exploitation.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 ran a one-factor comparison against the current best anchor (llm_summary_005: RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool, scVI n200). It kept that configuration and swapped the RNA encoder to scGPT, reaching a validation accuracy of 0.5305 with a supporting F1 of 0.5152. That is about 0.120 below scVI (0.6501 / 0.6275) and also below PCA in the same setting (0.5907 / 0.5727), though still above the single-profile PCA baseline (0.4849). In this multiprofile avgpool setting, the scGPT embeddings as used here appear to carry less label-relevant signal than scVI or PCA, so scVI remains the strongest RNA branch tested and the natural default for later fusion runs. Uncertainties remain: all results are single runs with unknown variance, and scGPT's embedding dimensionality, extraction procedure, and any fine-tuning were not explored, so the deficit may reflect how scGPT was applied rather than its inherent value. Its behavior with other aggregators, single-profile, or in multimodal fusion is also unknown.

selection_reason: Evidence: multiprofile avgpool has beaten single-profile in every run so far. scVI is the strongest RNA encoder (0.650 accuracy / 0.628 F1, versus 0.591 for PCA and 0.530 for scGPT). Avgpool beat the transformer aggregator. The only image result is weak (ResNet50 single-profile, 0.208), so it is still unknown whether image features add complementary signal or just noise. Test: this run keeps the best anchor fixed (RNA scVI n200, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds only a ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion. This isolates the effect of adding the image modality to the strongest RNA setup. Why now: whether multimodal fusion helps is the largest remaining design question, and it decides how much budget should go to image encoders and fusion variants. Concat is the simplest fusion baseline. If accuracy and F1 rise above 0.650 / 0.628, fusion and image-encoder upgrades (ViT-L, weighted fusion) are worth pursuing. If not, the budget can shift to strengthening the RNA branch.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 ran a one-factor comparison against the best anchor (llm_summary_005: RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool, scVI n200, 0.6501 accuracy / 0.6275 F1). It kept that RNA setup and added a ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion, reaching a validation accuracy of 0.6315 and a supporting F1 of 0.6068, about 0.019 and 0.021 below the anchor. This initial observation suggests that adding ResNet50 image features through concat fusion gives no gain over the strongest RNA-only configuration and may add slight noise. That is consistent with the weak single-profile image-only result (0.2079), and it tilts the budget toward strengthening the RNA branch unless better image encoders or fusion methods change the picture. Uncertainties remain: all results are single runs with unknown variance, so a gap this small may be within noise. The run changes the image branch and the fusion method together, so it cannot tell whether the image modality itself lacks complementary signal or concat is simply a poor way to combine it. Stronger image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), weighted or learned fusion, and an image-only multiprofile run remain untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: scVI with multiprofile avgpool is the best configuration so far (0.6501 acc / 0.6275 F1). Adding a ResNet50 image branch with concat fusion (config_030) slightly lowered performance (0.6315 / 0.6068). That run did not show whether the image modality lacks complementary signal or whether concat simply lets a weak, noisy image representation dilute the strong RNA features. 2) What this tests: config_031 keeps config_030 identical and changes only the fusion method from concat to weighted. This is a clean one-factor test of fusion. If weighted fusion recovers or exceeds the RNA-only anchor, the multimodal deficit came from how the modalities were combined. If it still underperforms, that points to the ResNet50 image features themselves, which would justify testing a stronger image encoder such as ViT-L next. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: fusion method is a core design axis that has not been tested yet. This comparison is fully isolated against an existing run and builds on the strongest RNA setup. Its outcome directly determines whether the remaining multimodal budget should go toward fusion strategies or image encoders.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 was a one-factor test against llm_summary_007 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200 + ResNet50, avgpool), changing only the fusion method from concat to weighted. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6776 with a supporting F1 of 0.6464, about 0.046 and 0.040 above concat (0.6315 / 0.6068) and about 0.027 and 0.019 above the best RNA-only anchor llm_summary_005 (0.6501 / 0.6275), making it the new best configuration. Because the comparison with llm_summary_007 isolates fusion, the earlier multimodal deficit appears tied to concat fusion rather than to the ResNet50 image features lacking any usable signal; the gain over RNA-only also suggests the image branch can add complementary information when weighted, although that comparison changes the image branch and the fusion method together. Uncertainties remain: all results are single runs with unknown variance, so the margins may be partly noise; the learned modality weights were not reported, so how much the model relies on images is unknown; and other fusion strategies, stronger image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), and whether weighted fusion helps with other RNA encoders or aggregators are untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_031 (scVI n200 + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.6776 accuracy and 0.6464 F1. It beats the best RNA-only run (0.6501) and concat fusion (0.6315). This suggests that weighted fusion lets image features add some complementary signal. However, the only image encoder tested so far is ResNet50, which was weak on its own (0.2079 single-profile), so the image encoder is the largest remaining uncertainty in the leading configuration. 2) Test: config_037 keeps everything in config_031 the same and swaps only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates the image encoder's effect inside the best-performing setup. A gain would suggest the image branch is limited by its features rather than by the modality. No gain or a loss would suggest that ResNet50 is enough, or that the image contribution is small regardless of encoder. 3) Why now: this is a one-factor extension of the current best configuration. It has a reasonable chance of improving accuracy while directly answering an untested design question (which image encoder to use) that affects every remaining multimodal run. That makes it a better use of the limited budget than revisiting aggregators or RNA encoders, where avgpool and scVI have already shown clear advantages. Since all results are single runs with unknown variance, a small difference in either direction should be read cautiously.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 was a one-factor test against the best prior configuration (llm_summary_008: multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200, avgpool, weighted fusion with ResNet50, 0.6776 accuracy / 0.6464 F1), swapping only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.7062 with a supporting F1 of 0.6671, about 0.029 and 0.021 above the ResNet50 version, making it the new best configuration. Because image encoder choice is the only change, this suggests that within weighted fusion the image branch's contribution was partly limited by ResNet50 features, and ViT-L is a reasonable default for later multimodal runs. All results are single runs with unknown variance, so a gap of this size may be partly noise. The learned modality weights and an image-only ViT-L baseline (single- or multiprofile) are unavailable, so how much signal ViT-L carries on its own, or how heavily the model relies on it, is unknown. Whether the gain holds under concat fusion, with other aggregators or RNA encoders, or with other image encoders is also untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_037 (scVI n200 + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion), at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Fusion and the image encoder have each been isolated in one-factor tests. Aggregation has been compared only once, in the RNA-only PCA setting, where the transformer trailed avgpool by about 0.07. It is unclear whether that ranking holds with a stronger RNA encoder, richer ViT-L image features and weighted fusion, where a learned aggregator might have more to work with. 2) Test: config_039 keeps config_037 fixed and swaps only avgpool for transformer aggregation. This shows whether avgpool's advantage generalizes or was specific to PCA RNA-only. 3) Value: Aggregation is the main design choice not yet checked in the leading configuration family. The run is a clean single-factor comparison against the current best, so it is informative whichever way it turns out. A gain would give a new best; a loss would confirm avgpool as the default and let the remaining budget go to other questions, such as image-only ViT-L or single-profile multimodal baselines.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 was a one-factor test against the best prior configuration (llm_summary_009: multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200 + ImageNet ViT-L, weighted fusion, avgpool, 0.7062 accuracy / 0.6671 F1). It changed only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer and reached a validation accuracy of 0.7250 with a supporting F1 of 0.6847. That is about 0.019 and 0.018 above avgpool, making it the new best configuration. This reverses the earlier PCA RNA-only result (llm_summary_004), where the transformer trailed avgpool by about 0.072, so the aggregator ranking appears to depend on context: the learned aggregator may benefit from stronger scVI and ViT-L features or from weighted multimodal fusion, though these runs do not isolate which factor matters. Uncertainties remain: all results are single runs with unknown variance, so a gain this small may be partly noise. Transformer hyperparameters were not explored, transformer aggregation has not been tested with scVI RNA-only or with ResNet50 multimodal to locate where the reversal arises, and image-only ViT-L and single-profile multimodal baselines are still missing.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: No experiments have been run yet, so there is no information about how modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion affect performance. 2. Test: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest configuration in the space. It establishes a reference accuracy and F1 against which later experiments can be compared one factor at a time: encoder (scVI, scGPT), profile setting and aggregation (avgpool, transformer), and adding image features or fusion. 3. Why now: Under a limited budget, a simple anchor makes every later result interpretable. Starting with a complex multimodal multiprofile model would leave it unclear which design choice caused any gain or loss. We should not assume complexity helps, and this experiment is cheap and informative regardless of its absolute score.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) tested the simplest configuration in the search space: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It was chosen as a reference point for later one-factor-at-a-time comparisons. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.4849, with a supporting validation F1 of 0.4639. Because no other experiments have been run, this is only an initial baseline. It gives no evidence yet about whether alternative RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile settings with aggregation, or adding image features and fusion would improve or hurt performance, and the run-to-run variability of this score is unknown.

selection_reason: 1) The only evidence so far is one RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (acc 0.485, F1 0.464). We know nothing yet about any design factor, and run-to-run noise is unknown. 2) config_002 keeps the modality and encoder fixed (RNA-only, pca_n2000) and changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles per sample helps. 3) Profile setting is a structural choice that affects more than half of the search space (all aggregation variants and most multimodal configurations). Settling it early with a clean one-factor comparison, using simple averaging rather than a transformer, gives the most reusable information for later decisions. Encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT) and image or multimodal tests can follow as further one-factor contrasts against this baseline.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an RNA-only model with the same PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder as the llm_summary_001 baseline, but switched from single-profile to multiprofile input with average pooling (no image encoder or fusion). Validation accuracy rose from 0.4849 to 0.5907 (about +0.106), and validation F1 rose from 0.4639 to 0.5727 (about +0.109). This is an initial indication that the multiprofile-with-avgpool setting may help RNA-only PCA models. However, the contrast rests on one run per configuration with unknown run-to-run variability. It also changes profile setting and aggregation together (avgpool versus none), so the gain cannot be attributed to pooling multiple profiles alone. It remains untested whether the gain holds for other aggregators (e.g., transformer), other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), or image and multimodal configurations.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: with the PCA RNA-only setup, moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised validation accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591, and F1 rose by a similar amount. This is the strongest signal so far, but it rests on one run per configuration. It also leaves open whether the aggregator matters, since profile setting and aggregation changed together. 2. Test: config_003 keeps the RNA-only, PCA, multiprofile setup and changes only the aggregator from avgpool to transformer. This isolates the aggregation effect within the setting that looked promising. If the transformer does better, that strengthens the case for learned aggregation. If it ties or does worse, avgpool can serve as a simpler default for later multiprofile runs, including image and multimodal ones. 3. Why now: it is a one-factor extension of the strongest observed direction, so it serves both exploitation and uncertainty reduction. Aggregation recurs across most remaining configurations, so settling it early makes later comparisons of encoders, modalities and fusion more efficient.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept the RNA-only, PCA (2000-component), multiprofile setup from llm_summary_002 and changed only the aggregator from avgpool to transformer, isolating the aggregation choice in this setting. Validation accuracy fell from 0.5907 to 0.5191 (about −0.072) and F1 fell from 0.5727 to 0.4797 (about −0.093). The transformer result remained only modestly above the single-profile baseline (0.4849 accuracy, 0.4639 F1). Within this configuration, the evidence tentatively favors avgpool over transformer aggregation and supports avgpool as a simpler default for later multiprofile runs. However, each configuration has only one run with unknown run-to-run variability, transformer hyperparameters or training settings were not explored, and it is untested whether this ordering holds for other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image-only, or multimodal configurations.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: all three runs so far are RNA-only PCA models. Multiprofile with avgpool (config_002, 0.591 acc / 0.573 F1) clearly beat both single-profile (0.485) and transformer aggregation (0.519), so it is the current best. Each result is a single run, though. The largest open question is whether image features add value at all, and most of the remaining search space is multimodal. 2) Test: config_018 keeps config_002 unchanged (PCA RNA, multiprofile, avgpool) and only adds a ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion. Adding the image branch necessarily brings an image encoder and a fusion method together, and concat is the simplest fusion. The comparison therefore shows whether images help, hurt or do nothing on top of the strongest RNA setup, without assuming that multimodal will win. 3) Why now: the answer decides whether to spend later budget on the large multimodal region (fusion type, image encoder, RNA encoder combinations) or to focus on RNA-only encoder choices (scVI, scGPT). That makes it the most decision-relevant single experiment, and it also has a reasonable chance of beating the current best.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_002 (PCA 2000-component RNA encoder, multiprofile, avgpool) and added a ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion. This made it the first multimodal run, and it changed the image encoder and fusion together as a single addition. Validation accuracy rose from 0.5907 to 0.6186 (about +0.028) and F1 from 0.5727 to 0.6103 (about +0.038), making it the current best and giving an initial indication that image features may add modest value on top of the strongest RNA configuration. However, the gain is small relative to the unknown run-to-run variability of single runs, the effect of ResNet50 cannot be separated from concat fusion, and it remains untested whether other fusion methods, image encoders, RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), aggregators, or image-only settings would do better or worse.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is multimodal PCA + ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool and concat fusion (0.619 accuracy, 0.610 F1). It beat the matched RNA-only model (0.591 accuracy, 0.573 F1) by only about 0.03, which is small given unknown run-to-run variability. We have no image-only result, so we cannot tell whether ResNet50 features are informative on their own or are adding little. 2. What this tests: config_011 runs ResNet50 image-only with the same multiprofile avgpool setting as the RNA-only and multimodal runs. It changes only the modality, giving a matched three-way comparison: RNA-only vs image-only vs multimodal. This shows how much signal the image branch carries and whether the multimodal gain is plausibly a real complementary effect. It also checks whether the benefit of multiprofile avgpool extends beyond RNA. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: Most remaining configurations are multimodal variants built on image encoders and fusion choices. Knowing whether image features are useful decides whether to spend later runs on fusion and image encoders (weighted fusion, ViT-L) or to focus on RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT). This one experiment reduces uncertainty about a major branch of the search space before committing budget to it.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 tested a ResNet50 image-only model using the same multiprofile avgpool setting as the RNA-only (llm_summary_002) and multimodal (llm_summary_004) runs, changing only the modality to complete a matched three-way comparison. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.3275 and F1 of 0.2884, far below RNA-only PCA (0.5907 accuracy, 0.5727 F1), the single-profile RNA baseline (0.4849), and the multimodal concat model (0.6186, 0.6103). This is an initial indication that, in this setup, ResNet50 image features carry much weaker standalone signal than PCA RNA features, and that RNA likely drives most of the multimodal performance. It remains uncertain whether the small multimodal gain over RNA-only (about +0.028) reflects real complementary image information or run-to-run noise, because each configuration has only one run with unknown variability. It is also untested whether other image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), other aggregators, or other fusion methods would extract more useful image signal, and whether multiprofile avgpool helps image-only models, since no single-profile image-only run exists for comparison.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA appears to drive most of the performance. RNA-only PCA multiprofile avgpool reached 0.591 accuracy, image-only ResNet50 reached 0.328, and adding images gave only a small gain to 0.619. Multiprofile with avgpool has so far beaten both single-profile and transformer aggregation. The RNA encoder is still completely untested, with only PCA 2000 tried. Given RNA's dominance, it is probably the most important open design choice. 2) What this tests: config_005 keeps the best RNA-only setup (multiprofile, avgpool, no image) and changes only the RNA encoder from PCA 2000 to scVI 200. This directly isolates the effect of the RNA representation against config_002. 3) Why it is the best use of the budget: if scVI beats PCA, it marks a better RNA backbone for the multimodal runs (config_030/031). If it does worse, PCA remains a justified default. Either result narrows a large part of the search space more than adjusting fusion or the image encoder, which have so far contributed only modest signal.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_002 (multiprofile, avgpool, no image or fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA (2000 components) to scVI (200 latent dimensions), isolating the RNA representation within this configuration. Validation accuracy rose from 0.5907 to 0.6501 (about +0.059) and F1 from 0.5727 to 0.6275 (about +0.055). This makes it the current best run, above even the multimodal PCA+ResNet50 concat model (0.6186 accuracy, 0.6103 F1), and is an initial indication that scVI may be a stronger RNA backbone than PCA here. However, each configuration has only one run with unknown run-to-run variability, and encoder type is confounded with representation dimensionality (200 vs 2000). It also remains untested whether the scVI advantage holds with images and fusion, with other aggregators such as transformer, or against other RNA encoders such as scGPT.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: the RNA encoder is the strongest lever seen so far. Swapping PCA for scVI under multiprofile avgpool raised validation accuracy from 0.591 to 0.650 (F1 0.573 to 0.628), making scVI the current best. Adding ResNet50 images gave a smaller gain (+0.028 with PCA), and image-only scored only 0.328, so RNA appears to drive most performance. The third RNA encoder, scGPT, is still completely untested. 2. What this tests: config_008 keeps the best setup fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder from scVI to scGPT. This directly shows whether scGPT beats, matches or trails scVI. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: most remaining configurations are multimodal runs that depend on which RNA backbone is chosen. Settling the RNA encoder comparison first, with a clean single-factor experiment, tells us which encoder to carry into the more expensive image and fusion runs. It also tests whether the scVI gain reflects a general advantage of learned representations over PCA. Testing scVI plus images (config_030) is a natural follow-up once the best RNA encoder is identified.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool setup from llm_summary_002 and llm_summary_006 fixed and changed only the RNA encoder to scGPT, completing a single-factor comparison of the three RNA encoders. scGPT reached a validation accuracy of 0.5305 and F1 of 0.5152, trailing both scVI (0.6501 accuracy, 0.6275 F1; about −0.120) and PCA (0.5907, 0.5727; about −0.060), though it stayed above the single-profile PCA baseline (0.4849). This is an initial indication that scVI is the strongest RNA backbone in this setting and should be carried into the multimodal runs. It also suggests that the scVI gain does not reflect a general advantage of learned or pretrained representations over PCA. Uncertainties remain: each configuration has a single run with unknown run-to-run variability, and encoder type is confounded with representation dimensionality and any scGPT-specific preprocessing or embedding choices. It is also untested whether this encoder ordering holds with image features and fusion, or with other aggregators such as transformer.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: scVI is the strongest RNA encoder in the matched RNA-only multiprofile avgpool setting (0.650 accuracy vs 0.591 for PCA and 0.530 for scGPT). Adding ResNet50 with concat fusion to the PCA backbone gave a small gain (+0.028 accuracy, +0.038 F1). That gain is within plausible single-run noise, and image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.328). 2) This run adds the same ResNet50 concat branch to the best scVI RNA-only setup and changes nothing else. It is a single-factor comparison against config_005, and it parallels the config_002 to config_018 comparison. It tests whether the image benefit holds with a stronger RNA representation, or whether scVI already captures what the images added to PCA. 3) This is the best use of the next run because it serves two purposes. It exploits the strongest backbone with a likely candidate for best overall, and it replicates the image-contribution question across a second RNA encoder. That replication directly reduces uncertainty about whether multimodality is worth pursuing before spending budget on fusion types or ViT-L variants.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 added the ResNet50 image branch with concat fusion to the best RNA-only setup (scVI 200-dim, multiprofile, avgpool; llm_summary_006) and changed nothing else. This makes it a single-factor test of image contribution that parallels the PCA comparison (llm_summary_002 to llm_summary_004). Validation accuracy fell from 0.6501 to 0.6315 (about −0.019) and F1 from 0.6275 to 0.6068 (about −0.021), so scVI RNA-only remains the best run. In contrast, adding images to PCA gave a gain of about +0.028 accuracy and +0.038 F1. Across the two RNA encoders, the image effect therefore does not replicate consistently, and both shifts are small enough that they may reflect run-to-run noise (single runs, unknown variability) rather than a real benefit or harm. Together with the weak image-only result (0.3275), this tentatively suggests that ResNet50 with concat adds little reliable value, and possibly that scVI already captures what images added to PCA. It remains untested whether other fusion methods, image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), aggregators, or repeated runs would change this picture.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: scVI with multiprofile avgpool is the best run so far (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). Adding ResNet50 with concat fusion helped PCA slightly (+0.028) but hurt scVI slightly (-0.019). The ResNet50 image-only model is weak (0.328). So whether images add any reliable value is unresolved, and fusion method is the only major design factor not yet tested. 2) What this tests: holding scVI, ResNet50, multiprofile and avgpool fixed, this changes only concat to weighted fusion (single factor vs config_030). It asks whether concat diluted the strong scVI signal with weak image features, and whether a learned weighting can downweight images and match or beat the scVI RNA-only result. 3) Why now: it builds on the strongest backbone, so it is a plausible new best, and it cleanly isolates fusion. If weighted fusion still fails to beat scVI RNA-only, that strengthens the case for RNA-only or for trying a different image encoder (ViT-L) next. If it succeeds, it points to fusion as the bottleneck for using images.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the scVI (200-dim) + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool multimodal setup from llm_summary_008 and changed only the fusion method from concat to weighted, isolating fusion in this configuration. Validation accuracy rose from 0.6315 to 0.6776 (about +0.046) and F1 from 0.6068 to 0.6464 (about +0.040). This makes it the new best run, above scVI RNA-only (0.6501 accuracy, 0.6275 F1; about +0.027 accuracy), and is an initial indication that weighted fusion may use ResNet50 image features better than concat and that images may add some value on top of scVI. However, every configuration has a single run with unknown run-to-run variability, and the margin over RNA-only is small and similar in size to earlier shifts that did not replicate (+0.028 and −0.019 for concat with PCA and scVI). It is also unclear whether the learned weights actually downweight images, and it remains untested whether weighted fusion helps with PCA, with other image encoders such as ViT-L, or with other aggregators.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The current best run is config_031 (scVI 200-dim + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.6776 accuracy, 0.6464 F1). It edges out scVI RNA-only by about 0.027 accuracy, a margin that may be within noise. ResNet50 carries weak standalone signal (0.3275 image-only), and the image encoder is the one major design factor not yet tested: ViT-L has never been run. 2) What this tests: config_037 keeps the best setup and changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates whether a stronger image representation gives weighted fusion more complementary signal. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: It exploits the best configuration while exploring the largest untested factor in a single change. If ViT-L improves the result, it may give a new best and strengthen the case that images add real value. If it does not, that is further evidence that image features contribute little, and that the remaining budget should go to RNA, aggregation, or replicating the weighted-fusion gain (e.g., with PCA).
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 kept the best setup from llm_summary_009 (scVI 200-dim RNA, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) and changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, isolating the image representation in this configuration. Validation accuracy rose from 0.6776 to 0.7062 (about +0.029) and F1 from 0.6464 to 0.6671 (about +0.021). This makes it the new best run, about +0.056 accuracy above scVI RNA-only (0.6501). It is an initial indication that a stronger image encoder may give weighted fusion more complementary signal and that images may add real value on top of scVI. However, every configuration has a single run with unknown run-to-run variability, and the ViT-L gain is similar in size to earlier shifts that did not replicate. No ViT-L image-only run exists to confirm stronger standalone image signal, and it remains untested whether ViT-L helps with concat fusion, PCA, or other aggregators, or how the learned fusion weights treat the image branch.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing about how much signal each modality carries, which encoders work, or whether multiprofile aggregation and fusion help. 2. What this tests: config_001 is the simplest RNA-only baseline (single profile, PCA with 2000 components, no aggregation or fusion). It sets a reference level of performance. Later runs can then each change one factor against it: scVI or scGPT encoders, multiprofile with avgpool or transformer, image-only runs, and multimodal fusion. 3. Why now: Under a limited budget, a cheap, low-variance anchor makes every later comparison easier to read. Starting with a complex multimodal configuration would confound many design choices at once and could not show whether added complexity is actually needed.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 established the first baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA encoder with 2000 components (pca_n2000), with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485, with a validation F1 of 0.464, which suggests RNA expression alone carries some predictive signal. No other experiments exist yet, so this result is a reference point and supports no comparative conclusion. It is still unknown how alternative RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), image-only inputs, multiprofile aggregation, or multimodal fusion would perform relative to this anchor, and run-to-run variance has not been measured.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: We have only one result, an RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline at 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. We know nothing yet about the image modality. Most of the remaining search space is image-only or multimodal, so whether images carry useful signal is the biggest open question. 2. What this tests: config_010 is an image-only single-profile ResNet50 model with no aggregation or fusion. It changes only the input modality relative to the baseline, so it directly compares image signal with RNA signal under the same profile setting. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: this result determines how much of the remaining budget should go to multimodal and image configurations. If images are weak, we can focus on RNA encoders and multiprofile aggregation. If they are comparable or stronger, fusion experiments become well-motivated. Testing ResNet50 before ViT-L gives a simpler reference point, and it also serves as the reference for later single-change comparisons of image encoder and aggregation.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.208 and a validation F1 of 0.172, well below the RNA-only PCA (pca_n2000) single-profile baseline (0.485 accuracy, 0.464 F1). This is an initial indication that this image configuration carries weaker predictive signal than the RNA baseline. Because the comparison changes both the modality and the encoder type (ResNet50 vs. PCA), it cannot separate weak image signal from a poor fit of ResNet50 features. Several things remain unknown: whether other image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) or multiprofile aggregation would recover performance, whether image features add complementary value in fusion despite weak standalone performance, and how much run-to-run variance there is.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence so far: the RNA-only PCA single-profile baseline (0.485 acc / 0.464 F1) clearly beats image-only ResNet50 single-profile (0.208 / 0.172). This suggests RNA is the stronger modality, though only one run each exists. We know nothing yet about whether multiprofile aggregation helps. That choice affects about two-thirds of the remaining configuration space. 2) This experiment changes only the profile setting (single to multiprofile), using the simplest aggregation (avgpool), on the strongest known baseline (RNA-only, pca_n2000). The comparison with config_001 therefore isolates the effect of multiprofile input. 3) The answer guides many later choices: whether to prioritize multiprofile variants, whether the transformer aggregation is worth testing, and how to set up multimodal runs. Testing it on the stronger RNA modality gives a clearer signal than testing on weak image features. It also has a reasonable chance of improving the best accuracy, which balances exploration and exploitation.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with the PCA encoder (pca_n2000) and avgpool aggregation, with no image encoder or fusion. Relative to llm_summary_001, it changes only the profile setting (single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.591 and F1 of 0.573, compared with 0.485 and 0.464 for llm_summary_001, the current best result. This is an initial indication that multiprofile input with avgpool helps the RNA PCA model by about 0.11 in both metrics, although the gain applies to multiprofile and avgpool together and rests on single runs with unmeasured run-to-run variance. Still unknown: whether other aggregations (e.g., transformer) do better than avgpool, whether the multiprofile gain carries over to image-only or multimodal fusion settings, and whether it holds with other RNA encoders.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA PCA single-profile reached 0.485 accuracy. Switching to multiprofile with avgpool raised this to 0.591, the current best, with F1 rising by a similar amount. ResNet50 image-only single-profile was much weaker at 0.208. The multiprofile gain is promising, but avgpool is the only aggregation tested, so we cannot tell how much of the gain comes from multiprofile input itself and how much from the choice of aggregator. 2) Test: config_003 keeps everything from config_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, pca_n2000) and changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer. This isolates the effect of the aggregation method. 3) Why now: aggregation will apply to every later multiprofile configuration, including image-only and multimodal ones, so settling avgpool versus transformer early narrows much of the remaining search. It builds directly on the strongest result so far and is a clean one-variable comparison. Testing alternative RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) or fusion is a natural next step once the better aggregator is known.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with the PCA encoder (pca_n2000) and transformer aggregation, with no image encoder or fusion. It differs from the current best, llm_summary_003, only in using transformer instead of avgpool aggregation. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.519 and F1 of 0.480, about 0.07 and 0.09 below avgpool (0.591, 0.573), though still slightly above the single-profile baseline (0.485, 0.464). In this one-variable comparison avgpool outperformed transformer, but each result is a single run with unmeasured run-to-run variance, and the transformer's configuration and tuning were not varied, so a better-tuned transformer could perform differently. It also remains unknown whether this aggregator ranking holds for image-only, multimodal, or other RNA-encoder (e.g., scVI, scGPT) settings.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA carries most of the signal so far. RNA-only PCA reached 0.485 accuracy, while image-only ResNet50 reached only 0.208. Multiprofile avgpool is the current best (0.591 accuracy, 0.573 F1) and beat transformer aggregation (0.519 accuracy) in a one-variable comparison. However, every RNA result uses pca_n2000, so we do not know whether the RNA encoder is a major lever. 2. What this tests: config_005 keeps the best setting (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder from PCA to scVI (scvi_n200). This isolates the effect of RNA representation, and it also checks whether the multiprofile avgpool gain holds for another encoder. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: since RNA dominates the signal, the encoder choice will shape every later multimodal comparison. It also has a realistic chance of beating the current best. It is cleaner and more broadly informative than testing fusion with a weak image encoder before the RNA backbone is settled.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with avgpool aggregation and no image encoder or fusion. It differs from the previous best, llm_summary_003, only in the RNA encoder, using scVI with 200 dimensions (scvi_n200) instead of PCA (pca_n2000). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.650 and F1 of 0.628, about 0.06 and 0.05 above the PCA version (0.591, 0.573), making it the new best result. In this one-variable comparison scvi_n200 outperformed pca_n2000, and multiprofile avgpool again gave the strongest result, but scVI was never tested in a single-profile setting, so the multiprofile gain has not been measured for this encoder. Still unknown: whether the encoder advantage holds given unmeasured run-to-run variance across single runs, whether it comes from the scVI method itself or from its latent dimensionality (200 vs. 2000, neither varied independently), how other encoders (e.g., scGPT) or scVI with transformer aggregation compare, and whether this stronger RNA backbone changes the value of adding image features through fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Within RNA-only runs, scvi_n200 with multiprofile avgpool is the best result so far (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). It beat pca_n2000 under the same setup, and avgpool beat the transformer aggregator in the PCA comparison. Image-only ResNet50 single-profile was weak (0.208 accuracy). Multimodal fusion, which makes up most of the remaining search space, has not been tested at all, so we do not know whether image features add complementary signal despite their weak standalone performance. 2) Test: This run keeps the best RNA backbone (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds ResNet50 image features with simple concat fusion. Because only the image modality is added, any change relative to config_005 is attributable to fusion with image features. 3) Why now: The result decides how to spend the remaining budget. A gain would justify exploring image encoders and fusion types. No gain or a loss would let us deprioritize many multimodal configurations and focus on RNA choices, such as the scGPT encoder (config_008). This is more valuable than refining the RNA encoder comparison first, though a single run cannot rule out a small effect and run-to-run variance is still unmeasured.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 tested the first multimodal configuration. It kept the best RNA-only setup (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool; llm_summary_005) and added ResNet50 image features with concat fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.632 and F1 of 0.607, about 0.02 below the RNA-only scvi_n200 run (0.650, 0.628), so llm_summary_005 remains the best result. This is an initial indication that adding ResNet50 image features through simple concatenation does not help, and may slightly hurt, the strong RNA backbone, which fits the weak image-only result (0.208 accuracy). However, the gap is small and rests on single runs with unmeasured run-to-run variance, so it may not be a real decline. Only one image encoder and one fusion type were tested, so it remains unknown whether other image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), other fusion methods, or multiprofile image aggregation would add complementary signal, and this run alone does not justify ruling out multimodal configurations as a whole.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The RNA encoder is the strongest lever seen so far. Swapping pca_n2000 for scvi_n200 in the multiprofile avgpool setting raised accuracy from 0.591 to 0.650. Multiprofile avgpool has beaten both single-profile and transformer aggregation. Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion slightly hurt (0.632). The third RNA encoder, scGPT, has never been tested, so it is unknown whether scVI is the best RNA backbone. 2) Test: config_008 changes only the encoder relative to the current best (scvi_n200 to scgpt, same rna_only, multiprofile, avgpool). This is a clean one-variable comparison of a foundation-model embedding against scVI and PCA. 3) Why now: The encoder has shown the largest effect, and every later multimodal comparison depends on which RNA backbone is used. Settling this choice first is likely to give both a performance gain and a decision about the most important design axis. Fusion and image-encoder questions can be explored afterward on the strongest RNA backbone.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile avgpool model with a scGPT RNA encoder and no image encoder or fusion. It differs from the current best, llm_summary_005 (scvi_n200), only in the RNA encoder. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.530 and F1 of 0.515, about 0.12 below scVI (0.650, 0.628) and about 0.06 below PCA (pca_n2000; 0.591, 0.573), so llm_summary_005 remains the best result. In this one-variable comparison scGPT embeddings underperformed both scVI and PCA, which is an initial indication that the foundation-model embedding as used here is the weakest RNA backbone tested. Still unknown: whether this ranking holds given single runs with unmeasured run-to-run variance; whether scGPT's weaker result comes from the embedding itself or from how it was extracted, its dimensionality, or a poor fit with avgpool aggregation (none were varied); and whether scGPT would compare differently in single-profile, transformer-aggregation, or multimodal settings.

selection_reason: Evidence: The best result is RNA-only scvi_n200, multiprofile with avgpool (0.650 acc, 0.628 F1). Adding ResNet50 image features through concat fusion (config_030) gave a slightly lower 0.632 acc and 0.607 F1. Image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.208 acc). It is unclear whether images truly add no complementary signal, or whether naive concatenation lets the weak image features dilute the strong RNA representation. Test: config_031 changes only the fusion method from concat to weighted, keeping scvi_n200, ResNet50, multiprofile and avgpool fixed. Weighted fusion can down-weight a weaker modality. If it matches or beats the RNA-only best, the concat result reflects a fusion limitation rather than a lack of image value. If it still falls short, that strengthens the case that ResNet50 features do not help. Why now: This is a clean one-variable comparison that resolves the fusion question for the strongest RNA backbone. It also tells us whether the many remaining multimodal configurations should favor weighted fusion, before we spend budget on image-encoder (ViT-L) or aggregation variants.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 tested a multimodal, multiprofile avgpool model with scvi_n200 RNA and ResNet50 image features, changing only the fusion method from concat (llm_summary_006: 0.632 acc, 0.607 F1) to weighted. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.678 and F1 of 0.646, about 0.05 above concat fusion and about 0.03 (accuracy) and 0.02 (F1) above the RNA-only scvi_n200 run (llm_summary_005: 0.650, 0.628), making it the new best result. In this one-variable comparison weighted fusion outperformed concat. Exceeding the RNA-only run is an initial indication that ResNet50 features can add complementary signal despite their weak standalone performance (0.208 acc), and that the earlier concat shortfall may reflect a fusion limitation. However, all results are single runs with unmeasured run-to-run variance, so the small margin over RNA-only may not be robust. It also remains unknown what weights the fusion learned, whether the weighted-fusion advantage holds with other image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), other aggregations, or other RNA backbones, and whether other fusion methods would do better.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The current best is config_031 (scvi_n200 RNA, ResNet50 image, multiprofile avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.678 accuracy, 0.646 F1). Weighted fusion beat concat by about 0.05, and it slightly beat RNA-only scVI (0.650). This suggests image features can add signal when fused well. However, ResNet50 is the only image encoder tested so far, and it was weak on its own (0.208 accuracy). The biggest remaining uncertainty is whether a stronger image representation (ViT-L) would add more complementary signal. 2) Test: config_037 keeps everything from the best configuration and changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to imagenet_vit_l. This gives a clean one-variable comparison of image representation inside the strongest pipeline found so far. 3) Why now: It answers an important open design question while also having a good chance of improving the best result. A gain would favor ViT-L for later multimodal runs. No gain would suggest the image contribution is limited by the modality or the fusion method rather than the encoder. Either outcome is informative under the limited budget.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 tested a multimodal, multiprofile avgpool model with scvi_n200 RNA and weighted fusion, changing only the image encoder from ResNet50 (llm_summary_008: 0.678 acc, 0.646 F1) to ImageNet ViT-L (imagenet_vit_l). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.706 and F1 of 0.667, about 0.03 and 0.02 above the ResNet50 version and about 0.06 and 0.04 above the RNA-only scvi_n200 run (0.650, 0.628), making it the new best result. In this one-variable comparison ViT-L outperformed ResNet50 within the strongest pipeline, an initial indication that a stronger image representation can add more complementary signal through weighted fusion. However, the margin is small and rests on single runs with unmeasured run-to-run variance; ViT-L was never tested image-only, with concat fusion, or with other aggregations, so it remains unknown whether its standalone signal is stronger, what fusion weights were learned, and whether the gain holds in other settings or with other image encoders.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The current best is config_037 (scvi_n200 + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.706 accuracy, 0.667 F1). It was reached through one-variable steps: encoder, then fusion, then image encoder. Aggregation has been compared only once, in the weakest relevant setting (RNA-only PCA), where transformer trailed avgpool by about 0.07. That single result may not carry over to multimodal inputs, where attention over profiles could weight informative cells or image features differently. 2) Test: This run changes only the aggregation (avgpool to transformer) within the best pipeline. It shows whether the avgpool advantage is general or specific to that RNA-only PCA setting. 3) Why now: Aggregation is the least-tested major design choice in the strongest configuration. This one-variable comparison either confirms avgpool as the default or reveals a gain in the most promising part of the search space. That makes it both informative and a plausible candidate for a new best.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 tested a multimodal, multiprofile model with scvi_n200 RNA, ImageNet ViT-L image features and weighted fusion, changing only the aggregation from avgpool (llm_summary_009: 0.706 acc, 0.667 F1) to transformer. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.725 and F1 of 0.685, about 0.02 above the avgpool version in both metrics, making it the new best result. This reverses the earlier RNA-only PCA comparison (llm_summary_004), where transformer trailed avgpool by about 0.07, an initial indication that the aggregator ranking depends on setting and that transformer aggregation may benefit from multimodal or stronger inputs. However, the margin is small and rests on single runs with unmeasured run-to-run variance, transformer settings were not tuned, and it remains unknown whether transformer would also beat avgpool in RNA-only scVI, with ResNet50, or with concat fusion, and which of these differences drives the reversal.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: no experiments have been run, so we know nothing about how much the modalities, encoders, profile settings, aggregation or fusion contribute. 2. What this tests: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components) is the simplest model in the space. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 that later experiments can be compared against one change at a time: scVI or scGPT encoders, multiprofile avgpool or transformer aggregation, image modality, and multimodal fusion. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: without a simple reference point, gains from more complex configurations cannot be attributed to any specific design choice. Starting with a cheap, low-variance baseline also avoids assuming that multimodal or multiprofile models are better, and it makes the following single-factor comparisons informative under the limited budget.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest configuration in the search space: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA encoder with 2000 components, with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.4849 and a validation F1 of 0.4639. Because no other experiments have been completed, this is only an initial baseline, not evidence for or against any design choice. It is still unknown how alternative RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation (avgpool, transformer), the image modality, or multimodal fusion would compare, and the run-to-run variance of this baseline has not been measured.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The only result so far is the RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (accuracy 0.485, F1 0.464). Nothing is known yet about the image modality, even though it appears in most of the remaining search space (all image-only and multimodal configurations). 2. What this tests: The image-only, single-profile ResNet50 model mirrors the baseline's simplest setup: single profile, no aggregation, no fusion. Its result can be compared directly with the RNA baseline to show how informative images are on their own. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: Knowing whether images carry useful signal decides whether the large multimodal portion of the space is worth exploring. A strong image result would justify fusion experiments. A weak one would shift the budget toward RNA encoders and multiprofile aggregation. This experiment reduces the most uncertainty per run while changing only the modality and keeping every other design choice at its simplest setting.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no aggregation or fusion, mirroring the simplicity of the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.2079 and a validation F1 of 0.1718, well below the RNA-only baseline (0.4849 / 0.4639). This is an initial observation that this image-only setup was much weaker than this RNA-only setup, but the comparison changes both modality and encoder (ResNet50 vs PCA), so it cannot be attributed to the image modality alone. It remains uncertain whether other image encoders, multiprofile aggregation, or fusion with RNA could make image features useful, since weak standalone performance does not rule out complementary signal. The chance-level accuracy and run-to-run variance for either configuration are also unknown.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The RNA-only PCA single-profile baseline (0.485 acc / 0.464 F1) clearly beat image-only ResNet50 (0.208 / 0.172). That is one run each, so the gap is suggestive, not conclusive. It does not show whether image features add complementary signal when combined with RNA. 2) Test: config_016 adds the ResNet50 image branch to the existing RNA PCA single-profile baseline with simple concat fusion. Everything else stays the same as config_001, so any change in accuracy or F1 can be attributed to adding the image modality. 3) Why now: Most of the remaining search space (36 of 49 configurations) is multimodal. Learning early whether image features help, hurt or do nothing alongside RNA tells us whether to spend the budget on fusion variants or focus on RNA encoders and profile aggregation. A gain would justify exploring multimodal options. No gain or a drop would let us deprioritize that large branch. Either outcome is informative.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 added a ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion to the RNA-only PCA (n=2000) single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001); all other settings were unchanged. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5266 and F1 of 0.5104, about +0.042 accuracy and +0.047 F1 over the RNA-only baseline (0.4849 / 0.4639) and far above image-only ResNet50 (0.2079 / 0.1718). Because this comparison changes only the addition of the image branch, it is initial evidence that ResNet50 image features carry signal that complements RNA, which supports exploring the multimodal branch further. However, each configuration has only one run and run-to-run variance is unmeasured, so the modest gain may partly reflect noise or extra model capacity rather than image information. Whether other fusion methods, RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) or multiprofile aggregation would increase or erase this benefit is still unknown.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: the best run so far is multimodal PCA+ResNet50 single-profile with concat fusion (config_016, 0.527 acc / 0.510 F1). It beat RNA-only (0.485), which gives initial single-run evidence that the image features complement RNA. The profile setting has not been tested at all, and it is a major design axis that affects every modality. 2) What this tests: config_018 keeps everything from config_016 the same except switching to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation, avgpool. That isolates whether aggregating multiple profiles helps the current best model, without also changing the encoder or fusion method. 3) Why it is the best use of the budget: it exploits the most promising direction while answering a high-value question about a whole design dimension. Using avgpool before transformer gives a clean, low-complexity first test of multiprofile. Whatever the result, it will guide whether later runs, including RNA-only and image-only variants, should prioritize multiprofile settings or move on to encoder and fusion comparisons.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the best prior configuration (llm_summary_003: multimodal PCA n=2000 RNA + ResNet50 image, concat fusion) unchanged except for switching from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, the first test of the profile-setting axis. It reached validation accuracy 0.6186 and F1 0.6103, about +0.092 accuracy and +0.100 F1 over the single-profile version (0.5266 / 0.5104), making it the best run so far. Because only the profile setting changed, this is initial evidence that multiprofile aggregation substantially helps this multimodal model, and the gain is larger than the earlier gain from adding the image branch. Uncertainties remain: each configuration has a single run and run-to-run variance is unmeasured. It is also unknown whether the benefit transfers to RNA-only or image-only models, whether transformer aggregation would do better than avgpool, and how it interacts with other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) or fusion methods.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best run so far is config_018 (multimodal PCA + ResNet50, multiprofile avgpool, concat; 0.619 acc / 0.610 F1). Going from single-profile to multiprofile gave about +0.09, which is larger than the roughly +0.04 gain from adding the image branch in the single-profile setting. All results are single runs. We do not yet know whether the multiprofile gain comes mostly from RNA, or whether the image branch still adds anything once profiles are aggregated. Image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.208). 2. Test: config_002 is RNA-only PCA multiprofile avgpool. It is config_018 with the image branch removed, and config_001 with only the profile setting changed. It therefore answers two questions at once. First, does multiprofile aggregation also help RNA-only models? Second, does the image branch still help under multiprofile? If config_002 comes close to 0.619, the image branch and its fusion choices matter little, and the budget should shift toward RNA encoders and aggregation. If it falls well short, the case for exploring image encoders and fusion methods gets stronger. 3. Why now: Most remaining configurations are multimodal, so it is the most decision-relevant uncertainty. It changes only one factor relative to the two existing anchors. It is also cheap and simple, so it tests the multimodal assumption before committing more of the budget to it.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model (PCA n=2000, avgpool aggregation, no image branch or fusion). It differs from the RNA-only single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001) only in profile setting, and from the best run (llm_summary_004, multimodal + ResNet50 concat) only in removing the image branch. It reached validation accuracy 0.5907 and F1 0.5727. That is about +0.106 accuracy and +0.109 F1 over llm_summary_001 (0.4849 / 0.4639), which is initial evidence that multiprofile avgpool aggregation also substantially helps RNA-only models.
