Validation accuracy rose from 0.485 to 0.591, and validation F1 rose in step from 0.464 to 0.573. Because only the profile setting differs, this is initial evidence that multiprofile aggregation helps in the RNA-only PCA setting. However, each configuration has a single run with uncharacterized seed and split variance, so the size and reliability of the roughly 0.11 gain are uncertain. It is also unknown whether the benefit carries over to other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), to image-only or multimodal settings, or whether a richer aggregator such as a transformer would add further gains.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool (config_001 to config_002) raised accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591, and F1 rose with it. This is initial but fairly strong evidence that profile aggregation matters. It is still unknown whether the aggregation method itself matters, since simple averaging may discard profile-level structure that a learned aggregator could use. 2. What this tests: config_003 keeps everything from the current best config_002 (RNA-only, pca_n2000, multiprofile) and changes only avgpool to transformer. Any difference can therefore be attributed to the aggregator. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: It builds directly on the strongest signal so far while staying a clean one-factor comparison. Aggregation choice also recurs across many remaining configurations, including image-only and multimodal ones, so knowing whether a transformer is worth it will help prune or prioritize much of the search space. Encoder and modality comparisons are better run once the aggregation question is partly settled. Because each configuration has only one run, a small difference here should not be overinterpreted.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 changed only the aggregator relative to the best prior configuration (llm_summary_002): it replaced avgpool with a transformer while keeping RNA-only input, the pca_n2000 encoder, multiprofile input, and no image encoder or fusion. Validation accuracy fell from 0.591 to 0.519 and validation F1 fell from 0.573 to 0.480, leaving it only slightly above the single-profile baseline (0.485 / 0.464). This is a clean one-factor comparison, so it is initial evidence that in this RNA-only PCA setting the transformer aggregator, as configured, did not beat simple averaging and may have hurt. The evidence is not conclusive: each configuration has a single run with uncharacterized seed and split variance, and transformer training choices (capacity, regularization, optimization, number of profiles) were not explored. It is also unknown whether the result carries over to other RNA encoders, image-only settings, or multimodal settings.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: All three runs so far are RNA-only PCA models. Multiprofile with avgpool is the best so far (0.591 accuracy / 0.573 F1). Single-profile (0.485) and the transformer aggregator (0.519) were both clearly worse, though each result is a single run. The image modality is completely untested, yet most of the remaining configurations (36 of 48) depend on image features. 2. What this tests: config_011 keeps the best-performing profile and aggregation setting (multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps the RNA PCA input for ResNet50 image features. This gives a direct image-only comparison against config_002. It shows how much signal images carry alone, and it is an early check on whether the avgpool advantage holds in a second modality. 3. Why now: Knowing the strength of the image modality is the largest open question under the limited budget. It determines whether multimodal fusion experiments are worth pursuing and how to interpret their gains. An RNA-encoder swap (e.g., config_005) would be useful, but it would only refine a modality we already have a reference for.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 was the first image-only run. It used ResNet50 image features with multiprofile avgpool aggregation, matching the best prior configuration (llm_summary_002) except that image features replaced RNA pca_n2000 input. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.328 and F1 of 0.288, well below RNA-only multiprofile avgpool (0.591 / 0.573) and the RNA single-profile baseline (0.485 / 0.464), with a slightly wider accuracy–F1 gap than the RNA runs. This is initial evidence that ResNet50 image features, as used here, carry less class signal than RNA PCA features. However, modality and encoder change together, so the comparison cannot separate weak image signal from a poorly suited image encoder or feature pipeline, and no image-only single-profile or transformer run exists yet to test whether the avgpool advantage holds in this modality. With single runs and uncharacterized seed and split variance, it is also unknown whether image features add complementary value when fused with RNA, which is the key question for the many remaining image-dependent configurations.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only PCA multiprofile with avgpool (config_002: 0.591 accuracy / 0.573 F1). Multiprofile avgpool beat both single-profile and the transformer aggregator. Image-only ResNet50 with avgpool was much weaker (0.328 / 0.288). It is still unknown whether image features add complementary signal when combined with RNA, and most remaining configurations (36 of 47) are multimodal. 2) Test: config_018 keeps everything from config_002 (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds ResNet50 image features through simple concat fusion. Because only one factor changes, the comparison isolates the effect of adding the image modality. 3) Why now: weak image-only performance does not rule out complementary value, and this result will decide whether the large multimodal branch deserves budget. If it beats config_002, the next steps are fusion type and image encoder. If it does not, the budget can shift toward RNA encoders such as scVI and scGPT.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 kept the best prior configuration (llm_summary_002: RNA pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) fixed and changed one factor, adding ResNet50 image features through simple concat fusion. Validation accuracy rose from 0.591 to 0.619 and F1 from 0.573 to 0.610, making this the best result so far, with a narrower accuracy–F1 gap than any prior run. Because only the image modality was added, this is initial evidence that image features carry signal complementary to RNA PCA, even though image-only performance was weak (0.328 / 0.288), and it supports giving budget to the multimodal branch (fusion type, image encoder). However, the roughly 0.03 accuracy gain is small, each configuration has a single run with uncharacterized seed and split variance, and it is unknown whether the gain holds with other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), other fusion methods, or other image encoders, or whether it partly reflects added input dimensionality rather than image-specific information.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is clearly the dominant signal. RNA-only multiprofile avgpool reached 0.591 accuracy, image-only only 0.328, and adding ResNet50 features via concat gave a further 0.619 (F1 0.610). Within RNA, multiprofile avgpool beat both single-profile and the transformer aggregator. The RNA encoder is still the biggest untested axis, since every RNA and multimodal result so far uses pca_n2000, and about two-thirds of the remaining configurations depend on the scVI or scGPT choice. 2. What this tests: config_005 changes only the RNA encoder (pca_n2000 to scvi_n200) relative to config_002, keeping RNA-only, multiprofile and avgpool fixed. That gives a clean one-factor comparison of RNA representation quality, without image features or fusion as confounds. 3. Why this is the best next use of budget: whether a learned 200-dimensional scVI latent beats 2000-component PCA directly decides which RNA encoder to carry into the multimodal branch. That makes it more informative than smaller multimodal tweaks such as weighted fusion or ViT-L image features, which act on a weaker modality. If scVI wins, configs 030 and 031 become logical exploitation steps. If it loses, budget can go to scGPT or to fusion and image-encoder refinements of config_018.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 changed only the RNA encoder relative to llm_summary_002, replacing pca_n2000 with a 200-dimensional scVI latent (scvi_n200) while keeping RNA-only input, multiprofile input, and avgpool aggregation, with no image encoder or fusion. Validation accuracy rose from 0.591 to 0.650 and F1 from 0.573 to 0.628. This makes it the best result so far, ahead of the multimodal PCA+ResNet50 concat run (0.619 / 0.610), even without image features. Because this is a clean one-factor comparison, it is initial evidence that scVI is a stronger RNA representation than PCA in this setting and supports carrying scVI into the multimodal branch. Several points remain uncertain: each configuration has a single run with uncharacterized seed and split variance; the accuracy–F1 gap (about 0.023) is slightly wider than in the multimodal PCA run; scGPT is untested; and it is unknown whether image features still add complementary value on top of scVI, or whether the avgpool-over-transformer advantage holds with this encoder.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: scVI with RNA-only multiprofile avgpool (config_005: 0.650 / 0.628) is the best run so far. It beat PCA in a clean one-factor comparison. Adding ResNet50 through concat fusion helped the PCA model (0.591 to 0.619 accuracy, with a larger F1 gain from 0.573 to 0.610). It is unknown whether the image signal is still complementary once the stronger scVI RNA representation is used, or whether it was only making up for weak PCA features. 2) Test: config_030 keeps config_005 fixed (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes one factor, adding ResNet50 with concat fusion. This mirrors the config_002 to config_018 comparison. The result shows whether the multimodal gain holds on top of scVI. That decides whether the many image-dependent configurations are worth budget, or whether effort should go to RNA encoders such as scGPT. 3) Why now: this is a single-factor exploitation of the two strongest findings so far, and it is a likely candidate for a new best. Either outcome is informative. If it fails to beat 0.650, that is evidence that image features add little beyond a good RNA encoder. Fusion type and the ViT image encoder can then be tested from whichever baseline proves stronger.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the best prior configuration (llm_summary_006: RNA-only scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, 0.650 / 0.628) fixed and changed one factor, adding ResNet50 image features through concat fusion, which mirrors the PCA comparison from llm_summary_002 to llm_summary_005 where adding images raised accuracy from 0.591 to 0.619. Here validation accuracy fell slightly from 0.650 to 0.632 and F1 from 0.628 to 0.607, so this did not produce a new best, and llm_summary_006 remains the strongest configuration. Because only the image modality changed, this is initial evidence that ResNet50 concat features add no measurable value on top of scVI, and that the earlier multimodal gain may have partly compensated for weaker PCA features; this favors directing budget toward RNA-side improvements such as scGPT over image-dependent configurations built on this fusion setup. The roughly 0.02 drop is small, each configuration has a single run with uncharacterized seed and split variance, and other fusion methods, the ViT image encoder, and possible concat-specific issues (for example, mismatch between the 200-dimensional scVI latent and the image feature scale or dimensionality, or training choices) are untested, so it remains open whether images could still be complementary to scVI under a different integration.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The RNA representation has been the strongest single lever so far. Replacing PCA with scVI in the RNA-only multiprofile avgpool setting raised accuracy from 0.591 to 0.650 and F1 from 0.573 to 0.628, giving the current best. Adding ResNet50 through concat fusion did not help on top of scVI (0.632 / 0.607). scGPT, the third RNA encoder, is completely untested. 2. What this tests: config_008 changes only the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to scGPT relative to the best configuration (config_005), keeping RNA-only input, multiprofile input and avgpool aggregation fixed. This cleanly asks whether a foundation-model RNA embedding beats scVI. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: It directly exploits the most influential design axis found so far and has a realistic chance of a new best. It also tells us which RNA encoder should anchor the many remaining multimodal configurations, including tests of weighted fusion and ViT image features. Weighted fusion is the main alternative, but image-dependent experiments are better chosen once the strongest RNA backbone is known, so the reduction in uncertainty per run is highest here.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 changed only the RNA encoder relative to the best configuration (llm_summary_006: RNA-only scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, 0.650 / 0.628), replacing scVI with scGPT embeddings and adding no image encoder or fusion. Validation accuracy fell sharply to 0.530 and F1 to 0.515, well below both scVI (0.650) and PCA (0.591) in the same setting and only modestly above the single-profile PCA baseline (0.485 / 0.464). Because this is a clean one-factor comparison, it is initial evidence that scGPT embeddings, as used here, are a weaker RNA representation than scVI or PCA, and it supports keeping scVI as the RNA backbone for the remaining multimodal configurations. However, each configuration has a single run with uncharacterized seed and split variance, and scGPT-specific choices were not explored (for example, pretrained versus fine-tuned embeddings, embedding extraction or gene-vocabulary overlap, and embedding dimensionality or scaling relative to avgpool), so it remains open whether scGPT is inherently less informative or poorly integrated in this pipeline.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: the best result so far is RNA-only scVI with multiprofile avgpool (0.650 accuracy / 0.628 F1). Adding ResNet50 through concat fusion helped the weaker PCA backbone (0.591 to 0.619) but slightly hurt scVI (0.650 to 0.632). The earlier summary raised a possible cause: concat may handle the mismatch between the 200-dimensional scVI latent and the image features poorly in scale or dimensionality. Weighted fusion is completely untested. 2. What this tests: config_031 changes only the fusion method relative to config_030 (scVI + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat to weighted). This isolates whether the image drop comes from concat itself or from images adding no value on top of scVI. If weighted fusion lets the model down-weight the weaker image modality, it could match or beat 0.650. If it does not, that strengthens the case for RNA-only scVI or for trying a better image encoder such as ViT. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: fusion type affects every remaining multimodal configuration, so this clean one-factor test answers a high-leverage design question. It also has a reasonable chance of producing a new best, which balances exploration and exploitation under the limited budget. The roughly 0.02 differences involved are small and come from single runs, so the result should be read as initial evidence rather than a conclusive answer.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 changed only the fusion method relative to llm_summary_007 (multimodal scvi_n200 + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool), replacing concat with weighted fusion. Validation accuracy rose from 0.632 to 0.678 and F1 from 0.607 to 0.646, making this the best result so far, ahead of RNA-only scVI (llm_summary_006: 0.650 / 0.628). Because fusion was the only factor changed, this is initial evidence that the earlier scVI+image drop was tied to concat fusion rather than images lacking value on top of scVI, and that ResNet50 features may be complementary to scVI when integrated through weighted fusion. Uncertainties remain: each configuration is a single run with uncharacterized seed and split variance, so the gains of about 0.03 over RNA-only and 0.05 over concat are small. The mechanism is also unverified, since learned modality weights were not inspected. Weighted fusion is untested with PCA, with other fusion methods, and with the ViT image encoder. The accuracy–F1 gap (about 0.031) is slightly wider than in prior scVI runs, which may hint at uneven per-class gains.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_031 (scVI + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.678 accuracy / 0.646 F1). It suggests images add value on top of scVI when fused with learned weights rather than concatenated. Several choices have initial single-run support: scVI over PCA and scGPT, avgpool over transformer, and weighted over concat. The image encoder is the major design choice that remains completely untested, since the ImageNet ViT-L has never been run. ResNet50 alone was weak (0.328), so whether a stronger image representation adds more complementary signal is a key open question. 2. What this tests: config_037 changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ViT-L, and keeps every other part of config_031 fixed. This cleanly isolates the effect of image representation inside the current best pipeline. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: If ViT-L helps, it is a direct path to a new best. If it does not, we learn that the image branch is limited by modality signal rather than encoder choice, which would rule out about half of the remaining configurations. Both outcomes are informative, which makes this better than lower-value checks such as transformer aggregation (already weak with PCA) or scGPT variants (weak RNA encoder).
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 changed only the image encoder relative to the best prior configuration (llm_summary_009: multimodal scvi_n200 + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.678 / 0.646), replacing ResNet50 with ImageNet ViT-L. Validation accuracy rose from 0.678 to 0.706 and F1 from 0.646 to 0.667, making this the best result so far, with an accuracy–F1 gap (about 0.039) slightly wider than in prior scVI runs, which may hint at uneven per-class gains. Because this is a clean one-factor comparison, it is initial evidence that the image encoder matters in this pipeline and that ViT-L features provide more complementary signal than ResNet50 under weighted fusion, which argues against the image branch being limited purely by modality signal. Uncertainties remain: each configuration is a single run with uncharacterized seed and split variance, so the roughly 0.03 gain is small; ViT-L has not been tested image-only, with concat fusion, or with PCA, so it is unknown whether the gain reflects a stronger standalone image representation or an interaction with weighted fusion; and learned modality weights were not inspected.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so we have no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components, no aggregation or fusion) sets the simplest reference point. Later experiments can each change one factor against it: scVI or scGPT encoders, multiprofile avgpool or transformer aggregation, image-only models, or multimodal fusion. That way any gain can be attributed to a specific design decision. 3) With a limited budget, a cheap, interpretable anchor gives more information than starting with a complex multimodal configuration, whose result could not be explained without simpler references. It also avoids assuming that complexity helps.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 ran the simplest reference configuration: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA encoder (2000 components) and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.4849 and validation F1 0.4639. The close F1 suggests performance is fairly even across classes, though this is not confirmed. This is the first completed experiment, so the result is a baseline and does not show whether any design choice helps or hurts. It remains unknown whether other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image-only models, or multimodal fusion would improve on it, and run-to-run variance is uncharacterized.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far, the RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (acc 0.485, F1 0.464). The biggest open question is whether the image modality carries comparable, weaker, or stronger signal, since that determines whether the large image and multimodal part of the search space is worth exploring. 2) Test: config_010 is image-only, single-profile, with ResNet50, the simplest image counterpart to the baseline. Comparing it with config_001 isolates the effect of modality while keeping the profile setting fixed (no aggregation or fusion). 3) Why now: most remaining configurations depend on image features, so knowing their standalone strength is the most informative next step. It tells us whether multimodal fusion is promising and gives a reference for later choices between image encoders and between single-profile and multiprofile settings. Testing RNA encoders or aggregation first would leave this major uncertainty unresolved.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.2079 and F1 0.1718, well below the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001: acc 0.4849, F1 0.4639). Under these settings, ResNet50 image features carry weaker standalone signal than PCA RNA features. Because the comparison changes both the modality and the encoder type, and each is a single run with uncharacterized variance, it remains unknown whether the gap reflects the image modality itself or this encoder, whether other image encoders or multiprofile aggregation would narrow it, and whether image features add complementary value in multimodal fusion despite their weak standalone performance.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The RNA-only PCA single-profile baseline (config_001: acc 0.485, F1 0.464) is far ahead of image-only ResNet50 (config_010: acc 0.208, F1 0.172). RNA is the strongest signal so far. Profile setting, aggregation, RNA encoder and fusion are all untested, and each result is a single run. 2. Test: config_002 changes only one factor from the best configuration, switching single-profile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool) while keeping the PCA encoder. This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles adds signal. 3. Why now: Profile setting affects most of the remaining search space, including the RNA-only, image-only and multimodal multiprofile configurations. Answering it on the strongest modality gives a clean, low-confound result that can prune or prioritize many later configurations. Image fusion (e.g., config_016) and alternative RNA encoders remain good follow-ups.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested an RNA-only multiprofile model with a PCA encoder (2000 components) and avgpool aggregation, changing only the profile setting from the single-profile RNA-only baseline (llm_summary_001: acc 0.4849, F1 0.4639). It reached validation accuracy 0.5907 and F1 0.5727, about 10.6 points higher in accuracy, with F1 rising by a similar amount. Because profile setting is the only factor that differs between the two, this is the cleanest comparison so far and suggests that pooling multiple profiles adds useful signal for RNA PCA features. However, each result is a single run with uncharacterized variance, and it remains unknown whether the gain carries over to other RNA encoders, to image-only or multimodal multiprofile configurations, or whether aggregation methods other than avgpool would perform better.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only PCA multiprofile avgpool (config_002: acc 0.5907, F1 0.5727). It beat the single-profile version by about 10.6 points, and that comparison changed only the profile setting. Image-only ResNet50 was weak on its own (acc 0.2079). Whether image features add complementary value when fused with RNA is still unknown, and this is a central design question for a multimodal study. 2) Test: config_018 keeps the best setup unchanged (PCA, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds ResNet50 image features with simple concat fusion. Any difference from config_002 can therefore be attributed to adding the image modality. 3) Why now: This builds on the strongest direction found so far and answers the highest-stakes open question in one clean, single-factor comparison. If fusion helps, the multimodal branch is worth exploring further. If it hurts or does nothing, the remaining budget can go toward RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) and aggregation choices instead. Encoder and aggregation comparisons are also valuable, but they refine choices within a branch whose relevance does not depend on this result.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 added ResNet50 image features with simple concat fusion to the previously best setup (RNA-only PCA n2000, multiprofile, avgpool; llm_summary_003: acc 0.5907, F1 0.5727), keeping all other settings unchanged. It reached validation accuracy 0.6186 and F1 0.6103, the best so far. Accuracy rose by about 2.8 points and F1 by about 3.8 points. Because the only difference is adding the image modality via concat, this is an initial single-factor observation that image features may add complementary value to RNA features, even though image-only ResNet50 was weak on its own (llm_summary_002: acc 0.2079). However, each result is a single run with uncharacterized variance, so a gain of a few points may fall within run-to-run noise. It also remains unknown whether other fusion methods, image encoders, RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), or aggregation choices would enlarge, shrink, or reverse this benefit.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence so far: RNA is the dominant signal source. PCA RNA reached 0.485 single-profile and 0.591 multiprofile, while ResNet50 image-only reached only 0.208. Adding images via concat gave a modest gain to 0.619, which could be within run-to-run noise. All RNA results so far use one encoder (PCA n2000), so the RNA representation is the largest untested design choice that could plausibly move performance. 2) This experiment changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA n2000 to scVI n200, and keeps the best RNA-only setting (multiprofile, avgpool). This gives a clean single-factor comparison with config_002. Running it RNA-only avoids a confound that a multimodal test would add: in concat fusion, a 200-dimensional scVI embedding would sit against image features in a different dimensional balance than the 2000-dimensional PCA embedding. 3) It is the best use of the next experiment because it explores a high-impact, still-unknown factor in an isolated way. A gain would point the search toward scVI-based multimodal configurations, and a loss would make PCA the RNA backbone. The result informs which part of the remaining grid to pursue, rather than only fine-tuning the current best.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 swapped the RNA encoder from PCA n2000 to scVI n200 while keeping the RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool setup unchanged, giving a clean single-factor comparison with llm_summary_003 (acc 0.5907, F1 0.5727). It reached validation accuracy 0.6501 and F1 0.6275, about 5.9 and 5.5 points higher. This is the best result so far and also exceeds the multimodal PCA+ResNet50 concat run (llm_summary_004: acc 0.6186), though that second comparison changes more than one factor. The result suggests scVI n200 is a stronger RNA representation than PCA n2000 in this setting, but each result is a single run with uncharacterized variance. It also remains unknown whether the gain comes from the scVI model itself or from the lower dimensionality, whether it carries over to multimodal fusion with image features (where the dimensional balance would differ), and how other RNA encoders (e.g., scGPT) or aggregation methods would compare.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only scVI n200 with multiprofile avgpool (config_005: acc 0.650, F1 0.628). It beat PCA n2000 by about 6 points in a clean single-factor comparison. Separately, adding ResNet50 image features via concat to the PCA multiprofile model gave a modest gain (+2.8 acc, +3.8 F1). That gain is a single run and may be noise. It is also unknown whether it holds with a stronger, lower-dimensional RNA encoder, which changes the balance between the two modalities. 2. Test: config_030 adds ResNet50 concat fusion to the best scVI multiprofile avgpool setup, changing only the modality. This checks whether the image benefit replicates with a second RNA encoder, and whether it shrinks or reverses once the RNA representation is stronger. 3. Why now: it is a logical exploitation step with the highest expected immediate performance, and it remains a single-factor comparison. Whichever way it comes out, it tells us whether to pursue the multimodal branch (fusion method, image encoder) with scVI or to focus on RNA-only refinements such as scGPT or transformer aggregation.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 added ResNet50 image features with concat fusion to the best RNA-only setup (scVI n200, multiprofile, avgpool; llm_summary_005: acc 0.6501, F1 0.6275), changing only the modality, and reached validation accuracy 0.6315 and F1 0.6068, about 1.9 and 2.1 points lower. In the PCA setting, adding the image modality the same way gave a gain of about 2.8 points (llm_summary_003 to llm_summary_004), so this initial observation suggests the image benefit did not replicate with scVI and may have slightly reversed. That would be consistent with concat-fused ResNet50 features adding little beyond a stronger RNA representation, though the cause is not isolated: possibilities include redundancy with scVI, the dimensional imbalance between 200-d scVI and the image features, or the simple concat fusion. Both the earlier gain and this drop are single runs of a few points with uncharacterized variance and may fall within noise, so RNA-only scVI remains the best result, and it is still unknown whether other fusion methods, image encoders, or modality balancing would recover a multimodal benefit.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile avgpool clearly beat single-profile for PCA, by about 10.6 points. scVI n200 then beat PCA by about 5.9 points, making RNA-only scVI multiprofile avgpool the best result (acc 0.650, F1 0.628). Adding ResNet50 with concat fusion helped PCA but slightly hurt scVI, so the image benefit is uncertain and may be noise. Aggregation has never been varied; every multiprofile run used avgpool. 2. What this tests: config_006 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer on the current best configuration. This gives a clean single-factor test of whether learned attention over profiles improves on simple mean pooling. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: Aggregation is a fully unexplored design axis that applies to every multiprofile configuration, including all multimodal ones. Resolving it on the strongest, simplest RNA-only setup is informative whatever the outcome, and it has a realistic chance of a new best result. It also avoids the confounded multimodal question until the RNA-side choices are better pinned down.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 changed only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer on the best configuration so far (RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI n200; llm_summary_005: acc 0.6501, F1 0.6275). This is the first time aggregation has been varied. It reached validation accuracy 0.6530 and F1 0.6283, nominally the best result so far. The differences are only about 0.3 points in accuracy and 0.1 points in F1, so this clean single-factor comparison suggests learned attention over profiles performs about the same as mean pooling in this setting, with no clear benefit. Each result is a single run with uncharacterized variance, so the tiny gap is likely within noise. It also remains unknown whether transformer aggregation would matter more with PCA features, image-only or multimodal multiprofile setups, or different numbers of profiles, and whether its extra complexity is justified over avgpool.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: the RNA encoder has been one of the strongest levers so far. Switching from PCA n2000 to scVI n200 under RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool raised accuracy from 0.591 to 0.650. By contrast, changing aggregation from avgpool to transformer gave a negligible 0.3-point difference, and adding ResNet50 concat fusion gave inconsistent results: +2.8 points with PCA and -1.9 points with scVI. The third RNA encoder, scGPT, has never been tested, so this is the largest remaining gap in our understanding of representation. 2. What this tests: config_008 keeps the best-understood setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder to scGPT. This gives clean single-factor comparisons with config_005 (scVI) and config_002 (PCA). It shows whether a foundation-model embedding beats scVI, falls between scVI and PCA, or underperforms. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: it resolves the most impactful open design axis with a single clean comparison, and it could plausibly produce a new best result. Its outcome also guides later experiments. If scGPT wins, the next step is to revisit fusion (for example, weighted fusion or ViT-L image features) on top of scGPT. If it loses, budget can be concentrated on scVI-based fusion and image-encoder tests.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 tested scGPT as the RNA encoder for the first time. It changed only the encoder in the RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool setup, which gives clean single-factor comparisons with scVI n200 (llm_summary_005: acc 0.6501, F1 0.6275) and PCA n2000 (llm_summary_003: acc 0.5907, F1 0.5727). It reached validation accuracy 0.5305 and F1 0.5152, about 12 points below scVI and about 6 points below PCA in accuracy, with F1 following the same ordering. This suggests that scGPT embeddings, as used here, are the weakest of the three RNA representations in this setting, so scVI-based configurations (RNA-only scVI with avgpool or transformer, about 0.65) remain the best. Each result is a single run with uncharacterized variance, although the gaps are larger than the few-point differences seen elsewhere. It remains unknown whether the shortfall reflects scGPT itself or how it was applied (for example, embedding dimensionality, frozen versus fine-tuned use, gene-vocabulary overlap, or preprocessing), and whether scGPT would behave differently with transformer aggregation or multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only scVI multiprofile is the best result so far (avgpool 0.650, transformer 0.653). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion helped PCA (+2.8 points) but slightly hurt scVI (-1.9 points). That pattern suggests concat may let weak or high-dimensional image features dilute a compact 200-d scVI representation. However, the weighted fusion option has never been tested, so fusion method remains a wholly unexplored design choice. 2) What this tests: config_031 changes only the fusion method from concat to weighted, relative to config_030 (scVI, ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool). This gives a clean single-factor test of whether learned modality weighting can recover a multimodal benefit over the scVI RNA-only baseline, or at least avoid the drop. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: it addresses the most direct hypothesis raised by the last multimodal result, it isolates fusion without confounding it with encoder or aggregation changes, and it has a realistic chance of producing a new best. If it fails, that is useful evidence that images add little beyond scVI with ResNet50 features, which would point the search toward testing the ViT-L image encoder next.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 changed only the fusion method from concat to weighted in the multimodal scVI n200 + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool setup (llm_summary_006: acc 0.6315, F1 0.6068), the first test of weighted fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.6776 and F1 0.6464, about 4.6 and 4.0 points higher than concat. It also beat the RNA-only scVI avgpool baseline (llm_summary_005: acc 0.6501, F1 0.6275) by about 2.7 and 1.9 points, making it the best result so far. This clean single-factor comparison suggests weighted fusion can recover, and possibly exceed, a multimodal benefit that concat did not deliver with scVI. That fits the hypothesis that concat let image features dilute the compact scVI representation, though the mechanism, such as learned down-weighting of images versus better scale balancing, is not directly shown. All results are single runs with uncharacterized variance, and the roughly 2.7-point gain over RNA-only may fall within noise. It also remains unknown whether weighted fusion helps PCA or other image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), whether it combines with transformer aggregation, and what modality weights were actually learned.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best result so far is multimodal scVI n200 + ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool and weighted fusion (config_031: acc 0.6776, F1 0.6464). Weighted fusion appears to recover an image benefit that concat did not deliver with scVI. The image encoder has never been varied. ResNet50 is the only image representation tested, and it was weak on its own (acc 0.2079). Aggregation has been varied once (avgpool vs transformer for RNA-only scVI) and made almost no difference. 2. Test: Swapping only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, with all other settings matching config_031, isolates whether a stronger image representation adds more complementary signal under weighted fusion. A gain would show that image representation quality is a key lever. No change or a drop would suggest the image contribution is capped or redundant with scVI. 3. Why this is the best next run: It explores a completely untested design dimension through a single-factor change from the current best setup, so it also has a realistic chance of improving on it. Transformer aggregation (config_033) is less informative given its null effect so far. Re-testing weighted fusion with PCA (config_019) would mostly confirm a fusion effect that has already been observed once.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L in the previous best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200, avgpool, weighted fusion; llm_summary_009: acc 0.6776, F1 0.6464). This was the first time the image encoder was varied. It reached validation accuracy 0.7062 and F1 0.6671, about 3.0 and 2.1 points higher, making it the best result so far and about 5.6 points above RNA-only scVI avgpool (llm_summary_005: acc 0.6501). This clean single-factor comparison is an initial observation that image representation quality may be a useful lever under weighted fusion, which argues against the image contribution being capped by ResNet50-level features. However, all results are single runs with uncharacterized variance, so a 3-point gain may fall partly within noise. ViT-L has not been tested image-only, so its standalone strength is unknown. The learned modality weights are also unknown, and it remains untested whether the gain holds with concat fusion, PCA RNA features, transformer aggregation, or other image encoders.
